## 2026-09-20 — French/mBART verification (next_step.md Phases 1-3) analyzed; recipe fails to replicate

- Confirmed from existing run artifacts (`Code_Experiments/phase*_results_v2.json`,
  `phase*_run_v2.log`, re-run `phase2_failure_analysis.py` /
  `phase3_failure_analysis.py`) that Phases 1-3 of `next_step.md` were
  already executed in a prior session; Phases 4-6 were not. No write-up
  existed for any of this until now.
- Phase 1 (lemma-disjoint centroid selectivity): decodability is actually
  *better* than previously measured — selectivity +0.42 to +0.49 (pooled
  0.9075 real / 0.4177 control), vs. the lemma-disjoint discriminative
  probe's 0.1152.
- Phase 3 (scaled steering, 33-44 lemmas, fit/val/test split): **fails the
  pre-registered 0.90 whole-word-flip-rate criterion by ~4.7x** — 0.1905
  on held-out sentences of a known lemma (0.2143 on the metric-valid
  "clean" subset after excluding 7/21 lemmas where masc/fem share mBART's
  first subword id, a real metric-degeneracy bug independently diagnosed
  by `phase3_failure_analysis.py`). Held-out-lemma and held-out-class
  generalization are indistinguishable from the zero-effect controls
  (0.0000 vs. controls' 0.0000). Wilcoxon signed-rank on the continuous
  p(flip) metric IS significant (p=0.0006 vs. random, p=0.0026 vs.
  orthogonal-null) but McNemar on the binary whole-word outcome is not
  (p=0.25, n=14, underpowered) — a real but weak effect, not yet reliable
  enough to call "working."
- Found two confounds not previously documented anywhere in this repo: (1)
  all mined test/fit sentences are built by space-joining raw UD FORM
  tokens with no re-contraction step, so 221/503 (44%) of mined chains
  contain ungrammatical uncontracted sequences ("de le", "à le", "de les")
  that never occur in real French — a systematic distributional-shift
  confound feeding mBART out-of-distribution input on nearly half of all
  material; (2) the whole-word success metric doesn't penalize
  repetition-collapse generation — found hand-checked examples (e.g. "une
  critique sérieux sérieux sérieux de l'économie politique") counted as
  successes at high alpha despite being degenerate, unquantified fraction.
- Also found Phase 2 (n=20 pilot) showed `target_only` (whole-word
  rate 0.400) numerically beating `multi_position` (0.333), yet
  `multi_position` was the condition scaled up in Phase 3 with no recorded
  justification — likely carried over from the toy model's winning
  condition rather than re-derived from French's own Phase 2 data.
- Wrote up as `french_phase123_critique_prompt.md` (evidence-grounded,
  for an external LLM critique, mirroring `critique_prompt.md`'s
  convention) plus a direct critical review in-conversation. No code
  changes made this session — analysis and write-up only.
- Next: get external critique on the two confound hypotheses above before
  spending more mBART compute; Phase 4 (controller-only factorial on real
  mBART) and Phase 5 (fluency/coherence check) are the two cheapest
  un-run experiments that would most directly test whether the 0.19-0.21
  number is architecture-limited, confound-limited, or a genuine
  technique-transfer failure.

## 2026-09-20 (cont.) — Take 2: isolated two of the four candidate causes; recipe partially recovers

- Got external critique response (`frenchmbartsteeringcritique.md`):
  agreed the negative result is real but said we hadn't isolated *why* --
  four live candidate causes (bad input, wrong location, architecture
  mismatch, metric contamination), plus objected to Phase 3's alpha
  selection being effectively tie-broken zeros for held-out conditions,
  and to over-precise "indistinguishable from zero" language. Published a
  phased disambiguation plan as `French_steering_take_2.md` and executed
  Phases A and B (see that file for full tables).
- **Phase A (free re-analysis, no new inference):** built
  `strict_metric.py` (flags repeated flip word / repetition-collapse) and
  re-scored every existing saved generation -- metric contamination is
  real at Phase 2 scale (whole_word_rate 0.289->0.178) but does **not**
  explain Phase 3's specific 0.19 headline (unchanged under strict
  scoring, 0 downgrades). Characterized Phase 3's 11 fitting-failure
  lemmas (`colonial, dur, grec, iranien, local, normal, occidental,
  régional, sportif, suivant, tout`) -- no obvious frequency/class bias.
  Built and validated `repair_contractions.py` (232/503 chains needed a
  `de le->du`/`à le->au`/etc. fix, 0 index-remapping failures).
- **Phase B (paired malformed-vs-repaired x 3 locations, n=20 chains,
  encoder-side, strict metric):** **`target_only` is now confirmed, not
  just suggested, as the better condition** -- strict whole-word rate
  0.333 (malformed) / 0.667 (repaired) vs. `multi_position`'s 0.133 /
  0.333 -- `multi_position`'s apparent successes are disproportionately
  repetition-collapse artifacts. Contraction repair helped in a paired
  comparison (6 pairs: 2 flipped fail->success, 0 the other way, for both
  `target_only` and `multi_position`) though n=6 is still small.
  `controller_only` stayed flat/zero regardless of repair (0.067->0.000),
  suggesting its weakness is not a data problem. **`repaired x
  target_only` (0.667 strict) clears the plan's 2-3x-the-baseline gate**
  against the original Phase 3 number (0.19) with controls still near
  zero (0.02-0.05) -- licenses moving toward a Phase E rescale.
- **Phase C (decoder-side localization pilot, n=8 sentences):** new
  infrastructure `decoder_patch_lib.py` + `phase_c_localization_pilot.py`
  (patches `model.model.decoder.layers` with `use_cache=False`, reusing
  `mbart_agreement_lib`'s hook classes unmodified). **Decisive result**:
  on the 5 sentences evaluable on both sides, decoder-side target-adjacent
  patching hit 5/5 strict successes with p(flip)=1.0000 in every single
  case, vs. encoder-side target-only's 2/5 with wildly variable
  probabilities (0.001-0.998) on the *identical* sentences -- the
  strongest evidence yet for the architecture-mismatch hypothesis.
  `decoder_controller_adj` was unusable in 8/8 cases: partly fit failures,
  partly a genuine structural finding -- 4/8 are pre-nominal-adjective
  chains (`premier tour`, `grande partie` x2, `petit espace`) where the
  target's decoder position comes *before* the controller's, which a
  causal decoder cannot use for that direction of influence.
- **Phase E2 (decoder-side scaled rescale, same fit/val/test design as
  Phase 3, 34/44 lemmas fitted):** held-out SENTENCE/known-lemma strict
  rate **0.3182** (n=22, controls flat 0.0000) -- roughly *doubles*
  Phase 3's original 0.19, with zero repetition-collapse contamination
  this time (strict rate == raw rate). held-out LEMMA and held-out CLASS
  both remain exactly 0.0000 -- decoder-side patching does not unlock any
  cross-lemma/class generalization either. Encoder-side companion rerun
  (target_only + repaired prompts, `phase_e_rescale.py`) launched for a
  same-scale comparison; result pending.
- **Net picture so far**: two of the four candidate causes (wrong
  location, architecture mismatch) each produce real, control-clean,
  additive improvements on the known-lemma condition, but neither closes
  more than a fraction of the gap to 0.90, and neither touches
  cross-lemma/class transfer, which stays a hard zero under every
  configuration tested.

- The Phase E background run was killed mid-eval (10/34 lemmas done, no

  process-level OOM kill). Re-ran `phase_e_rescale.py` to completion from

  the earlier partial progress was safely discarded, not resumed).
- **Phase E result (encoder-side, `agreement_chains_repaired.json`,
  `target_only`, 34/44 main-pool lemmas, 8/8 validation lemmas,
  alpha_same=40, alpha_lemma=20, alpha_class=20):** held-out
  SENTENCE/known-lemma whole-word rate **0.2273** (n=22, strict rate
  identical, mean p(flip)=0.2063); held-out LEMMA and held-out CLASS both
  **0.0000** (n=21/22); random and orthogonal-null controls both
  **0.0000**.
- **Encoder- vs. decoder-side comparison, same fit/val/test design, same
  repaired data, same condition:** encoder 0.2273 vs. decoder (Phase E2)
  0.3182. Architecture/location (decoder-side) accounts for most of the
  improvement over Phase 3's original 0.19 baseline; contraction repair
  alone on the encoder side buys comparatively little (0.19 → 0.23).
  Both effects are individually real and control-clean, just unequal in
  size.
- **Cross-lemma/class generalization is now 0.0000 under four independent
  configurations** (Phase 3 original encoder/malformed, this Phase E
  encoder/repaired, Phase E2 decoder/target-adjacent) — the single most
  reproducible number in the investigation. No combination of location,
  architecture, or input-cleanliness fix unlocks any transfer beyond the
  exact lemma a direction was fit on.
- **Interpretation communicated to the user**: decodability of gender is
  real and reasonably robust; causal steerability of a *known* target is
  real but still ~3x short of the pre-registered 0.90 criterion even
  under the best (decoder-side) configuration; steerability that
  *transfers* to an unseen lemma or morphological class — the property
  the Kitaita subspace-transplant bet actually needs — has never been
  observed, in the toy model (plateaus at 0.42-0.49, short of 0.90) or in
  French (exact 0.0000, every configuration). Per `French_steering_take_2.md`'s

  as the critique's formulation — *decodable grammatical information does

  project has not earned (no Swahili/Kitaita work has been attempted; all
  evidence so far is within-French). Next move per the plan's own
  decision rule: test the subspace/lookup-style mechanisms that already
  outperformed a single direction in the toy model
  (`subspace_steering.py`, `train_adapter.py`) on real French, before

- No other code changes this session; `phase_e_results.json` now exists

## 2026-09-21 — Found and fixed a real sign-convention bug in cross-lemma/class direction averaging; the "hard 0.0000" finding was partly a bug, not a clean null

- User asked to work on a richer (subspace/adapter) mechanism, per the open
  question above. Before building one, checked a candidate confound first:
  `flip_form_of()` defines each chain's fit target as "whichever gender it
  currently ISN'T" (Masc-attested chains fit a push toward Fem,
  Fem-attested chains fit a push toward Masc). The pool's fit sentences
  are close to a 50/50 split (33 Masc-origin / 31 Fem-origin, confirmed by
  direct count). **`mean_dir()`** — used identically by every prior
  held-out-lemma/held-out-class evaluation (Phase 3, Phase B, Phase C,
  Phase E, Phase E2) — averages per-lemma directions with **no sign
  correction** for this, and the resulting mean is then applied with a
  fixed positive alpha regardless of which direction the CURRENT test
  chain actually needs. For roughly half of all held-out test chains,
  this pushes in the wrong physical direction by construction.
- **Fix** (`held_out_sign_fix.py`): canonicalize each pool lemma's
  direction to a universal "points toward Fem" convention (negate it when
  its own attested gender is Fem), average canonicalized directions as
  before, then de-canonicalize the result per TEST chain (negate again if
  THAT test chain's own attested gender is Fem, since it then needs a
  push toward Masc). Same chains file/condition/layer/split as
  `phase_e_rescale.py` throughout, for a direct comparison.
- **Result, with random/orthogonal-null controls added afterward**
  (`held_out_sign_fix_controls.py`, same pool, alpha_lemma=40,
  alpha_class=80 from a validation sweep):

  | condition | whole-word rate | strict rate | mean p(flip) |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | SIGN-FIXED held-out LEMMA (n=21) | 0.0952 | 0.0952 | 0.1959 |
  | — random control, same alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0002 |
  | — orthogonal-null control, same alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0002 |
  | SIGN-FIXED held-out CLASS (n=22) | 0.2273 | 0.0909 | 0.0865 |
  | — random control, same alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0014 |
  | — orthogonal-null control, same alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0019 |

  Both controls are a clean, flat zero while the sign-fixed direction
  produces a real effect (mean p(flip) ~1000x the control floor for
  held-out lemma, ~50x for held-out class) — this clears the project's
  standard control bar, unlike several early false positives in this
  investigation that didn't. Held-out CLASS shows a real raw/strict gap
  (0.2273 vs 0.0909) from repetition-collapse contamination at alpha=80;
  held-out LEMMA has none (0.0952 both ways) and is the cleaner number of
  the two. A secondary sanity check (mean pairwise cosine similarity
  across pool directions, raw=+0.1930 vs. canonicalized=+0.0989) did NOT
  show the expected increase from canonicalizing — the behavioral fix
  comes specifically from the PER-TEST-CHAIN re-signing step, not from
  the pool becoming more mutually aligned, and this distinction is not
  yet fully understood.
- **This retracts a claim made earlier in this same session**: cross-
  lemma/class generalization is NOT a clean 0.0000 confirmed under every
  configuration — three of the four configurations tested so far (Phase
  3 encoder/malformed, Phase E encoder/repaired, Phase E2
  decoder/target-adjacent) share this exact same unsigned-averaging bug
  and have not yet been re-run with the fix. Their true corrected numbers
  are currently unknown, not zero.
- **Not yet done**: (1) re-running the decoder-side setup (Phase E2's
  site, which had the best known-lemma number, 0.32) with the same sign
  fix — likely to show an even larger effect than encoder-side's 0.095/
  0.091, and needed before any real cross-configuration comparison; (2)
  checking whether the fix changes `same_lemma`'s own number at all (it
  shouldn't much, since 38/44 pool lemmas are internally gender-
  homogeneous, but the 6/44 mixed-gender lemmas were previously averaging
  their own OWN fit sentences unsigned too); (3) the originally-planned
  richer (subspace/adapter) mechanism test, which should now be built on
  this corrected baseline rather than the old buggy one.
- Next: decoder-side sign fix first (cheap, direct comparison), then the
  k-dim subspace mechanism on whichever site's corrected baseline is
  stronger.

## 2026-09-21 (cont.) — Decoder-side sign fix: best held-out-generalization result in the project so far

- Applied the identical canonicalize/decanonicalize fix to Phase E2's
  decoder-side target-adjacent site (`held_out_sign_fix_decoder.py`, same
  chains/split as `phase_e2_decoder_rescale.py`), controls included from
  the start this time:

  | condition | whole-word rate | strict rate | mean p(flip) |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | SIGN-FIXED held-out LEMMA, decoder (n=21) | 0.3333 | 0.3333 | 0.2865 |
  | — random control, same alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0025 |
  | — orthogonal-null control, same alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0002 |
  | SIGN-FIXED held-out CLASS, decoder (n=22) | 0.0909 | 0.0909 | 0.1286 |
  | — random control, same alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0024 |
  | — orthogonal-null control, same alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0001 |

  Both controls flat zero; no raw/strict gap this time (unlike the
  encoder-side held-out-class number, this one has zero repetition-
  collapse contamination). Held-out LEMMA (0.3333) is **>3x the encoder-
  side sign-fixed number (0.0952)** — consistent with decoder-side
  already being the stronger site for the known-lemma case (0.32 vs.
  0.23). Held-out CLASS lands at essentially the same rate either site
  (0.0909 strict both ways).
- **This is now the best held-out-generalization result anywhere in this
  investigation**: a real, control-validated 33% success rate on a
  genuinely unseen lemma, decoder-side, sign-corrected — up from a hard
  0.0000 in every configuration reported before today. Still well short
  of the 0.90 known-lemma criterion and even of known-lemma's own 0.32,
  but no longer a flat null.
- Fit-sentence orig_gender tally for this pool: Masc=25, Fem=18 (still a
  meaningful mix, confirming the sign bug was live here too).
- Next: build the k-dim PCA subspace mechanism on this corrected
  decoder-side baseline (canonicalize -> build basis -> joint-fit a
  subspace-constrained coefficient -> decanonicalize per test chain),
  per the open question of whether a richer-than-single-direction
  mechanism improves further on 0.3333/0.0909, mirroring
  `subspace_steering.py`'s toy-model recipe.

## 2026-09-21 (cont.) — k-dim subspace test (held-out CLASS, decoder-side): does not beat the sign-fixed single-direction baseline

- Built `subspace_steering_mbart_decoder.py`: Bolukbasi-style k-dim PCA
  basis (SVD on canonicalized per-lemma directions) + joint Adam
  optimization of a k-dim, subspace-constrained coefficient, using the
  SAME canonicalize/decanonicalize convention as the sign fix, on the
  decoder-side target-adjacent site (the stronger of the two sites).
  Scoped to held-out-CLASS only (4 folds: cons+e=21 lemmas, other=9,
  en_enne=3, eux_euse=1 among the 34-lemma pool) -- a true per-LEMMA
  leave-one-out version was estimated at several hours on CPU and
  deferred (see below).
- **Result, fixed alpha=80 (already-validated from the single-direction
  sign fix, not re-tuned here), opt_steps=12, n=22:**

  | condition | whole-word rate | mean p(flip) |
  |---|---|---|
  | baseline: single mean direction, sign-fixed | 0.0909 | 0.1286 |
  | k=1 (subspace, jointly optimized) | 0.0455 | 0.0597 |
  | k=2 | 0.0909 | 0.0882 |
  | k=4 | 0.0455 | 0.0944 |

  **None of k=1/2/4 beats the baseline.** k=2 ties it on the binary
  metric but scores lower on mean p(flip); k=1 and k=4 are worse on
  both. The per-fold TRAINING objective did improve monotonically with
  k (expected, more free parameters), but this did not transfer to
  held-out performance -- the same overfitting signature
  `subspace_steering.py` already documented for its own under-resourced
  k=8 toy-model run.
- **This is very likely data-starved, not a clean disproof of low-
  dimensional shared structure.** This run used 16-41 pooled fit
  examples per fold and 12 optimization steps; the toy-model version
  that actually worked (k=4: 0.467 vs. single-direction's 0.057) used
  150 fit sentences and 150 steps -- roughly an order of magnitude more
  on both axes. At n=22, a single flipped example is a ~4.5-point swing
  in the reported rate, so 0.0909 vs. 0.0455 is one example either way,
  not a large-sample-confirmed gap. No random/orthogonal controls were
  run for k=1/2/4 (deliberately deferred, since no k cleared the
  baseline enough to justify the extra compute -- would be needed
  before trusting k=2's tie as anything more than noise).
- **Deferred, not done**: true held-out-LEMMA subspace test (proper
  per-lemma leave-one-out would need ~34 separate basis+joint-fit
  reconstructions, estimated several hours on CPU); increasing
  opt-steps (cheap, could be tried first); pooling held-out-lemma AND
  held-out-class folds together for a larger joint-fit basis per fold.
- Asked the user how to prioritize next: push further on the subspace
  approach (more steps; combined lemma+class pooling), pivot to
  `train_adapter.py`'s per-target lookup mechanism, or pause the French
  track and move to the Swahili pilot (open thread #7, still untouched).

## 2026-09-21 (cont.) — k-dim subspace, 5x optimization budget: confirms the negative result, doesn't overturn it

- User chose to push further on the subspace approach. Re-ran
  `subspace_steering_mbart_decoder.py` with `--opt-steps 60` (5x the
  first pass's 12) and added random/orthogonal-null controls (deferred
  in the first pass). Two machine interruptions during this work: a
  reboot at 17:14:43 (user: power outage) killed the run after 1/4
  folds; added incremental checkpointing (save + resume per completed
  fold) to `subspace_steering_mbart_decoder.py` before relaunching, so a
  third interruption would only cost the in-progress fold, not the
  whole ~3.3-hour run. Total wall time for the completed run: 11796s.
- **Final result, all 4 folds, n=22 (matches the single-direction
  baseline's sample exactly):**

  | method | whole-word rate | mean p(flip) |
  |---|---|---|
  | baseline: single mean direction, sign-fixed | 0.0909 | 0.1286 |
  | subspace k=1 | 0.0455 | 0.0597 |
  | subspace k=2 | 0.0909 | 0.0877 |
  | subspace k=4 | 0.0909 | 0.1106 |

  Random and orthogonal-null controls are flat at ~0.0000-0.0006 for
  every k -- clean, not a validity problem. **No k beats the baseline.**
  k=4 comes closest (ties the binary rate, nearest on p(flip)) but still
  doesn't exceed it; k=2 ties the binary rate with a lower p(flip); k=1
  is worse on both.
- **This is now a three-way-replicated negative result**: the 12-step
  first pass, the 3-fold interim checkpoint (mid-run, before the
  largest-basis fold `other` was included), and this final 4-fold
  60-step run all land on the same qualitative conclusion --
  extra optimization steps did not change fold 1's outcome at all
  (numerically identical to the 12-step run), and extra basis lemmas
  (25-33 per fold vs. the toy model's 12-24 pairs) did not unlock the
  k=4 gains the toy model saw (0.467 vs. single-direction's 0.057
  there). The data-starvation hypothesis raised after the first pass is
  now substantially weakened, though not fully closed -- this pool's
  ceiling (34 lemmas across only 4 classes, one of which has just 1
  member) is a hard data limit that can't be pushed further without
  mining more French text, which is out of scope for "more compute."
- **Conclusion for this open question**: at the data scale available in
  this project's mined French corpus, a richer (multi-dimensional,
  jointly-optimized) subspace mechanism provides no measurable
  improvement over the much simpler sign-corrected single mean
  direction for held-out-class generalization. The sign-fix itself
  remains the real, load-bearing finding of this investigation
  (0.0000 -> 0.33 held-out-lemma / 0.09 held-out-class); the subspace
  extension on top of it did not add further gains at this scale.
- Not done: the true held-out-LEMMA subspace test (still deferred, same
  compute-cost reason as before); a version of this test on a larger
  mined French corpus (more classes, more lemmas per class) if that
  becomes available; the adapter/lookup mechanism
  (`train_adapter.py`) on real French; the Swahili pilot (open thread
  #7, still untouched -- this is now the most clearly under-explored
  open thread in the project).

## 2026-09-21 (cont.) — External critique round 2 (ChatGPT + Gemini) converges on a real second-order sign bug; roadmap built and Phase 0-1 underway

- Sent `sign_fix_subspace_critique_prompt.md` to two external LLMs
  (ChatGPT, Gemini) -- responses saved as `french_steering_critique2_chat.md`
  / `french_steering_critique2_gemini.md`. Both independently confirmed the
  core sign-fix diagnosis but converged, unprompted, on the SAME weak
  point: the 6/44 mixed-gender-lemma majority-vote canonicalization step,
  plus the same three confounds in the subspace test (lemma-averaged
  basis erasing variance, `cons+e`'s 62%-of-pool dominance in an
  unweighted joint objective, borrowed alpha=80 never re-swept for the
  subspace method). Both also flagged that the 0.3182-vs-0.3333
  known-lemma/held-out-lemma "parity" is literally the same numerator (7
  successes) over different denominators, not yet real evidence of
  equivalence, since same-lemma was never re-run through the sign-fixed
  pipeline. Full roadmap: `sign_fix_roadmap.md`.
- **Phase 0a** (`test_sign_fix.py`, 11 synthetic unit tests, zero model
  compute): 10/11 pass; the one designed failure **confirms a real
  second-order bug** exactly where both critiques predicted. Feeding the
  current production majority-vote-after-averaging logic a synthetic
  1-Masc/1-Fem lemma with a known true axis recovers cos=+0.0003 with
  that axis (total destructive interference, indistinguishable from
  random); canonicalizing each sentence individually before averaging
  recovers cos=+0.981.
- **Phase 0b** (manual code audit for a duplicated/hidden sign flip,
  ChatGPT's "(-1)(-1)=+1" concern): clean. Exactly two gender-conditioned

- **Phase 0c** (`sign_consistency_audit.py`, Gemini's S = ||sum(v)|| /
  sum(||v||) metric on real decoder-side data): launched, in progress.
- **Phase 1**: fixed the actual bug. `fit_lemma_direction_tagged` /

- Not yet done at the time this entry was written: re-running

## 2026-09-21 (cont.) — Phase 1+2 results: known-lemma ceiling revised up to 0.50; the "parity" was an artifact, but a more precise (and more useful) finding replaces it

- `phase2_matched_same_vs_heldout.py` completed. Fully fixed pipeline
  (per-sentence canonicalization), each condition's alpha independently
  validated (never reused across conditions, unlike every prior run):

  | condition | alpha | whole-word rate | mean p(flip) | median p(flip) |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | SAME LEMMA (known-lemma) | 20 | **0.5000** (n=22) | 0.4703 | 0.3608 |
  | HELD-OUT LEMMA | 80 | 0.2857 (n=21) | 0.2907 | 0.0022 |
  | HELD-OUT CLASS | 80 | 0.1364 (n=22) | 0.1353 | 0.0002 |
  | random / orthogonal controls | -- | 0.0000 | ~0.0001 | 0.0000 |

- **Known-lemma ceiling revised upward from 0.3182 to 0.5000.** Not
  mainly the sign fix itself (only 2/34 lemmas affected) -- `same_lemma`
  had NEVER been independently re-tuned for alpha in this project before
  this run; every prior number reused alpha=40 from the very first,
  pre-fix sweep. Alpha=20 (found via a proper validation sweep under the
  current pipeline) is meaningfully better. A real, if mundane,
  methodological gap, now closed.
- Held-out-lemma/class barely moved (0.3333->0.2857, 0.0909->0.1364),
  both within one-example noise -- consistent with only 2/34 lemmas
  being affected by the mixed-gender bug, and confirms the earlier
  held-out numbers were not meaningfully wrong in aggregate even though
  2 specific lemmas' own directions were badly wrong.
- **This resolves the "parity" question both critiques flagged as
  uninterpretable**: known-lemma (0.50) now clearly exceeds held-out-lemma
  (0.29) under a fair, matched, independently-tuned comparison -- the
  earlier 0.3182-vs-0.3333 apparent equality was an artifact of an
  under-tuned same-lemma alpha, exactly as both critiques suspected.
- **But the matched, paired comparison reveals something more precise
  than "fitting matters"**: across 21 lemmas evaluable both ways, the
  MEDIAN paired difference (same_lemma - held_out_lemma p(flip)) is
  +0.0000, while the MEAN paired difference is +0.1543. A long-tail
  structure: for the TYPICAL lemma, a transferred (held-out) direction
  works exactly as well as one fitted directly on it -- zero marginal
  benefit from per-lemma fitting -- but a MINORITY of lemmas get a
  large, idiosyncratic boost from direct fitting that pulls the mean up.
  This is a materially more useful characterization than either "fitting
  doesn't matter" or "fitting matters": most of the vocabulary shares
  structure fine; a subset needs item-specific handling. Consistent with
  (not contradicting) this project's existing "suppletive items may need
  a lookup mechanism, not a direction" hypothesis from the toy-model
  track.
- **Concrete individual-level confirmation the fix has real behavioral
  effect**: `national` (one of the two mixed-gender lemmas identified in
  Phase 0c) now succeeds at known-lemma steering under the fix
  (p_flip=0.8035, clean whole-word success, no repetition-collapse) --
  direct behavioral proof, not just a synthetic-test or S-metric
  argument, that this specific bug fix matters in practice. (`seul`, the
  other mixed lemma, failed eval for an unrelated reason -- target word
  not found in the model's own baseline reconstruction -- not evidence
  against the fix.)
- Next: Phase 3 (the three subspace-test confounds: per-sentence PCA
  basis, lemma/class-balanced joint objective, per-k alpha sweep) --
  now more clearly motivated, since we know there IS a long-tail subset
  of lemmas where shared structure alone isn't enough, which is exactly
  the case a richer (multi-dimensional) mechanism would need to help
  with if it's going to help at all.

## 2026-09-22 — Phase 3 completed: fixing all three confounds makes the subspace result WORSE, not better

- `subspace_steering_phase3.py` finished (total_elapsed=42333s ~= 11.75h,
  most of it during an intentional machine sleep the user requested
  mid-run; the process survived the sleep cleanly -- no reboot this
  time, `systemctl suspend` preserves process state unlike the two
  earlier interruptions -- and resumed correctly from its own
  checkpoint/resume logic on wake).
- **Final result, all 4 leave-one-class-out folds, per-sentence PCA
  basis + lemma/class-balanced joint objective + independently-swept
  per-k alpha (k=1->80, k=2->80, k=4->40), n=22:**

  | condition | whole_word_rate | mean_p_flip |
  |---|---|---|
  | baseline (single mean direction, sign-fixed) | 0.0909 | 0.1286 |
  | Phase-3-PREDECESSOR (lemma-avg basis, unweighted, alpha=80 fixed) | k=1:0.0455 k=2:0.0909 k=4:0.0909 | -- |
  | **Phase 3 (all three fixes applied)** | **k=1:0.0000 k=2:0.0909 k=4:0.0000** | k=1:0.0230 k=2:0.0034 k=4:0.0003 |
  | random / orthogonal-null controls (all k) | 0.0000 | <=0.0002 |

  **This is a MORE decisively negative result than before, not less.**
  k=2 ties the baseline exactly (same as its predecessor); k=1 and k=4
  are now WORSE than in the flawed predecessor test, and mean_p_flip
  collapsed to near-zero for every k (0.023, 0.0034, 0.0003 vs. the
  baseline's 0.1286) -- the subspace-constrained directions are
  producing almost no causal push at all under the properly-swept
  alphas, not just failing to beat the baseline on the binary metric.
  Controls stay flat and clean throughout, so this isn't a validity
  problem -- it's a genuine, now more rigorously-established null.
- **This directly bears on the "is the subspace bigger than we think"
  question raised in conversation the same day.** Measured mean pairwise
  cosine similarity between the pool's 34 per-lemma directions is only
  +0.0347 (derived from the already-computed S=0.2512 metric) -- barely
  above the +/-0.0312 standard deviation expected from RANDOM unrelated
  vectors in mBART's 1024-dim embedding space (vs. the toy model's
  per-stem directions at cosine 0.94-0.96, a completely different
  regime). Two candidate explanations were laid out as not yet
  distinguished by prior evidence: (A) one shared low-dim axis heavily
  masked by per-sentence noise (averaging recovers it), vs (B)
  genuinely heterogeneous per-lemma/class structure. Phase 3's result
  -- that EVEN AFTER fixing the basis construction, the objective
  weighting, and the alpha search, a richer multi-dimensional mechanism
  still cannot beat (and mostly underperforms) a simple mean direction
  -- is more consistent with (A) than (B): if there were real,
  exploitable higher-dimensional structure, giving the fitting procedure
  every advantage identified by two independent external critiques
  should have surfaced at least some of it. It didn't. (This is
  evidence, not proof -- the joint-optimization MECHANISM itself could
  still be the wrong tool for extracting real higher-dim structure even
  if it exists; see open thread below.)
- **Proposed next step (not yet run, awaiting user direction)**: a
  cheap, already-mostly-available diagnostic to further distinguish (A)
  from (B) directly, rather than more subspace-fitting compute --
  compare WITHIN-lemma cosine similarity (two different attested
  sentences of the SAME word, available for most of the 34-lemma pool
  since max_fit_sentences=2) against ACROSS-lemma cosine similarity
  (+0.0347, already measured). If within ~= across, that's strong
  further evidence for (A) -- a single gradient sample is just generically
  noisy, not specifically informative about lemma identity. If within >>
  across, that's evidence each lemma has estimable individual structure
  beyond generic noise, motivating a fresh look at why the joint-fit
  subspace mechanism specifically failed to exploit it (mechanism
  problem, not absence-of-structure problem).

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Within-vs-across-lemma cosine test: decisively overturns the Story-A reading, replaces it with a more precise "lemma-identity-dominated" picture

- `within_vs_across_lemma_cosine.py`: per-sentence canonicalized decoder
  directions, same fitting convention as Phase 3, no optimization loop
  (fast, ~245s total).
- **Result:**

  | | n | mean | median |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | WITHIN-lemma (same word, 2 different sentences) | 9 pairs | +0.7893 | **+0.9946** |
  | ACROSS-lemma (different words) | 894 pairs | +0.0440 | +0.0271 |

  Permutation test (20000 shuffles): p=0.0000. 8/9 lemmas show
  near-perfect within-lemma reproducibility (`second`=0.9996,
  `petit`=0.9989, `sérieux`=0.9985, `grand`=0.9957, `premier`=0.9946,
  `seul`=0.9597, `supérieur`=0.8606, `national`=0.6517); one outlier,
  `royal`=-0.3557 (n=1, not over-interpreted).
- **This overturns the tentative "Story A" reading from Phase 3's
  result.** If a single gradient sample were just generically noisy, two
  sentences of the SAME word would look no more similar than two
  different words. They don't -- within-lemma is ~0.99, across-lemma is
  ~0.03-0.04 (matching the random-vector baseline). The correct picture
  is a THIRD story, more precise than either A or B as originally
  framed: **each lemma's fitted direction is dominated by a highly
  reliable, lemma-SPECIFIC "identity" component (not noise -- real and
  reproducible), with only a small transferable "gender" component
  riding underneath it.**
- **This single picture now explains every finding from this session at
  once**: within-lemma reproducibility (the identity component is real
  and stable); near-random across-lemma cosine (identity components are
  unrelated between different words); real control-validated transfer
  after averaging over MANY lemmas (uncorrelated identity components
  cancel under averaging the same way noise would, while the small
  shared component reinforces -- same math as Story A's averaging
  argument, just applied to structured-but-uncorrelated signal instead
  of true noise); the "long-tail" lemmas from Phase 2 (`final`, `grand`,
  `petit`, etc. -- near-perfect known-lemma steering, poor transfer,
  because their fitted direction is mostly their own identity); and
  **Phase 3's richer subspace making things WORSE**: PCA on
  identity-dominated directions surfaces MORE lemma-identity axes in its
  higher components (PC2-4), not more shared gender structure, so
  handing the joint-fit optimizer those extra dimensions gives it more
  ways to overfit to whichever few lemmas are in a given fold's basis --
  matching Phase 3's collapsing mean p(flip) as k increased.
- **Concrete implication for next steps**: Phase 3's PCA basis was built
  on raw canonicalized directions, which this result shows are
  identity-dominated -- the WRONG input for finding shared structure.
  The toy model's ORIGINAL subspace method (`subspace_steering.py`,
  never adapted to French with this specific construction) builds its
  basis from DEVIATIONS from each defining pair's own midpoint --
  designed specifically to cancel per-item identity before PCA ever
  sees the data. This is a different, more targeted next experiment
  than "more k, more steps," and hasn't been tried on French yet.
- Not yet done / awaiting user direction: building the deviation-based
  (Bolukbasi-style, per the toy model's actual original construction)
  basis for French and re-testing whether IT recovers a k>1 gain that
  the identity-dominated PCA basis could not.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Sent both findings to external critique (round 2); user requested strict self-review before building anything; both critiques converged on "don't build yet, re-analyze first"

- Wrote `lemma_identity_critique_prompt.md` and sent it out. Before that,
  did my own strict step-by-step review and found a real problem with my
  own prior report: manually reading the fit sentences showed 3 of the 9
  within-lemma pairs share literal collocations (`second tour`, `grande
  partie`, "École ... supérieure"), which the original p≈0.0000
  permutation test did not control for. Also flagged: the `premier`
  lemma has near-perfect within-lemma reproducibility (0.9946) yet
  held-out slightly BEAT same-lemma for it in Phase 2 (-0.0608 diff) --
  an unresolved inconsistency with the identity-dominance story as
  originally stated.
- **Both ChatGPT and Gemini's responses converged independently**: do
  NOT build the deviation-based subspace mechanism yet. Both flagged
  `royal`'s negative within-lemma cosine (-0.3557) as a real
  counterexample against any strong identity-dominance claim. Both
  proposed the same core re-analysis (exclude/weight by lexical overlap,
  re-run the permutation test restricted to low-overlap pairs). Gemini
  additionally proposed a cross-frequency steering test (does a
  high-frequency-lemma pooled direction steer low-frequency lemmas' test
  chains and vice versa) to directly address the frequency-selection-
  bias concern, and gave a precise mechanistic account of the `premier`
  inconsistency: high cosine between raw gradients means near-parallel
  orientation, but if that direction carries high-magnitude non-causal
  (positional/syntactic) components, applying it can trigger side
  effects that make it perform WORSE than a "cleaner" pooled cross-lemma
  average for that specific lemma's own test case.
- **Ran ChatGPT's "does reproducibility predict transfer failure" test**
  (join within-lemma cosine with Phase 2's same-vs-held gaps, n=5):
  naive Pearson r=-0.81 (opposite sign from the original story's
  prediction), but this is driven by two non-comparable points
  (`national`=mixed-gender, different question entirely; `second`=
  collocation-confounded AND a complete same-lemma failure, i.e.
  reproducibly NON-FUNCTIONAL, not reproducibly identity-encoding).
  Excluding both leaves 3 clean points (`grand`, `petit`, `premier`)
  whose cosines (0.9946-0.9989) are nearly identical despite very
  different transfer gaps (-0.06 to +0.19) -- **no variance left to test
  anything.** Reproducibility does not detectably predict transfer
  failure, not because the effect is weak, but because there isn't
  enough clean, comparable data to ask the question at this corpus's
  scale.
- **Ran the Jaccard-filtered re-analysis both critiques asked for --
  first attempt was itself flawed, caught and corrected in the same
  session.** My first implementation computed Jaccard over ALL content
  UNIGRAMS, which dilutes a short shared phrase across a whole
  sentence's vocabulary: it scored `second` and `supérieur` at
  jaccard=0.0556 (below my 0.1 threshold) despite both being confirmed,
  literal collocation repeats by direct manual inspection -- only
  `grand` (0.1000, right at the boundary) got caught. **Redid it with
  the 3 manually-confirmed confounded lemmas explicitly excluded
  instead**: result SURVIVES this correct filtering --
  n=6 (or n=5 excluding `national` too): mean=+0.708 (or +0.719),
  p=0.0000, vs. the across-lemma floor of +0.044. Four of five remaining
  clean lemmas (`petit`, `premier`, `seul`, `sérieux`) show near-perfect
  reproducibility (>0.95) with `sérieux` specifically having ZERO shared
  vocabulary between its two sentences. **Correction to what was
  reported earlier in this same conversation: within-lemma
  reproducibility is NOT fully explained by phrase repetition -- it
  survives proper exclusion of the confirmed confounds.** `royal`
  remains a genuine, unexplained negative outlier (still n=1).
- **Net position now**: within-lemma reproducibility is real (survives
  correct confound removal) but its causal relevance to transfer failure
  remains unestablished (the reproducibility-predicts-transfer test came
  back null/uninformative due to lack of clean comparable data, not
  because the relationship was tested and found absent). Still do NOT
  build the deviation-based subspace mechanism -- that recommendation's
  justification (identity dominates AND is responsible for transfer
  failure) is only half-supported.
- Cross-frequency steering test (`cross_frequency_steering.py`, Gemini's
  proposal: does v_high steer low-freq lemmas' test chains and
  vice-versa) launched, in progress -- addresses the remaining
  unaddressed critique point (is the 9-lemma high-frequency subsample
  representative of the pool).

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Cross-frequency steering test completed: confirms the frequency-selection-bias concern, adds a new, largely-orthogonal explanation

- Pool split: 20 HIGH-freq lemmas (>=3 corpus occurrences), 24 LOW-freq
  (exactly 2 occurrences, i.e. the MAJORITY of the pool). 2x2 design,
  decoder-side, alpha=80 fixed, controls included:

  | cell | direction -> test target | whole_word_rate | mean_p_flip | n |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | (high,high) | v_high [LOO] -> high-freq own test | 0.5000 | 0.5316 | 10 |
  | (low,low) | v_low [LOO] -> low-freq own test | 0.0833 | 0.1026 | 12 |
  | (high,low) | v_high -> low-freq test | 0.2500 | 0.1492 | 12 |
  | (low,high) | v_low -> high-freq test | 0.4000 | 0.3244 | 10 |

  All controls flat at 0.0000 -- every cell is a real, control-validated
  effect.
- **Test-TARGET frequency matters far more than source-direction
  frequency.** High-freq targets are easy to steer regardless of source
  (0.50 same-frequency-sourced, 0.40 cross-sourced); low-freq targets
  are hard regardless of source (0.25 cross-sourced, only 0.083
  same-frequency-sourced). Strikingly, the HIGH-freq-sourced direction
  steers LOW-freq targets better (0.25) than low-freq lemmas steer each
  other (0.083) -- pooling among noisy, single-occurrence words produces
  a WORSE direction than pooling among well-represented ones, even when
  applied to a harder target population.
- **Confirms the frequency-selection-bias concern from Gemini's
  critique**: the 9 lemmas used in the within/across-lemma cosine test
  are not representative of the pool. **Adds a new, largely-orthogonal
  explanation to the session's findings**: roughly half the pool
  (24/44 lemmas, single-occurrence) appears to have less reliable
  underlying mBART representations, independent of the identity-vs-
  shared-structure question -- a data-quality/frequency effect that no
  amount of subspace sophistication would be expected to fix, since it's
  upstream of which mechanism is used to combine directions.
- **Practical implication**: a meaningful share of why held-out
  generalization caps around 0.29-0.33 overall is likely not "is there
  enough shared linear structure to extract" but "roughly half the
  pool's words are intrinsically harder to steer for reasons upstream of
  any mechanism choice" -- this reframes part of the project's own
  ceiling as a data/frequency problem, not purely a representation-
  geometry problem.
- **Net state after this full round of external critique + re-analysis**:
  do not build the deviation-based subspace mechanism (still not
  justified -- identity-dominance is real for a small clean sample but
  its causal role in transfer failure remains unestablished, and now a
  separate, real frequency confound has also been identified). Two live,
  well-evidenced threads for whoever picks this up next: (1) whether
  restricting evaluation/steering to higher-frequency vocabulary
  substantially changes the ceiling; (2) whether the small residual
  shared-gender signal (still real, still control-validated, ~0.03-0.05
  mean pairwise cosine) is best exploited by a fundamentally different
  mechanism (adapter/lookup) rather than more linear-subspace variants,
  per the toy model's own precedent for its structurally similar
  irregular-item case.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Controller-side (noun) steering pilot: does not outperform target-side, but for identifiable, informative reasons

- Motivated directly by the user's observation that noun/controller-
  driven agreement is the structure shared by both French (noun gender
  -> adjective agreement) and Swahili (noun class -> agreement across
  the whole sentence) -- every French experiment run all session (and
  in this project generally) had patched at the TARGET (the adjective),
  never the CONTROLLER (the noun). Built `controller_side_steering.py`,
  reusing `decoder_patch_lib.py`'s existing general
  `fit_direction_decoder`/`test_direction_decoder` (already accept an
  arbitrary decoder patch position -- built for an earlier "Phase C"
  pilot that found controller patching "unusable in 8/8 cases", which
  turned out to be because that n=8 pilot was mostly PRE-nominal
  adjectives (`grand tour`), where a causal decoder generates the target
  BEFORE it has even produced the controller -- no causal pathway can
  exist). **Fix applied this round**: restricted to POST-nominal chains
  only (noun before adjective -- the majority pattern, 245/380
  non-invariable chains, 124 distinct lemmas, 39 with >=2 occurrences),
  where the causal pathway can genuinely exist.
- Built with every applicable lesson from this session's critique rounds
  baked in from the start (not retrofitted): per-sentence
  canonicalization, independently-tuned alpha per condition, full
  random/orthogonal controls.
- **Baseline (single-gradient-snapshot fitting, matching every prior
  French direction in this project) result:**

  | condition | whole_word_rate | n |
  |---|---|---|
  | SAME LEMMA (controller patch) | 0.2857 | 7 |
  | HELD-OUT LEMMA | 0.0000 | 5 |
  | HELD-OUT CLASS | 0.0000 | 7 |
  | controls | 0.0000 | 7 |

  Attrition was much higher than any target-side run: only 12/31 pool
  lemmas and 4/8 validation lemmas usable, and only 1 of those 4 had an
  evaluable test chain -- every alpha selection in this baseline was
  effectively chosen from n=1, undermining confidence in the held-out
  zeros specifically.
- **Optimized (multi-step Adam, full-rank/unconstrained per-lemma
  fitting -- k=d_model special case of the subspace joint-fit machinery,
  mirroring `gradient_transfer_matrix.py`'s already-validated toy-model
  recipe, applied to French for the first time) result, with
  n_validation_lemmas raised to 15 (17 available at >=3 occurrences) to
  fix the n=1 alpha-selection problem:**

  | condition | whole_word_rate | n |
  |---|---|---|
  | SAME LEMMA (optimized) | 0.4000 | 5 |
  | HELD-OUT LEMMA | 0.0000 | 3 |
  | HELD-OUT CLASS | 0.0000 | 5 |
  | controls | 0.0000 | 5 |

  Multi-step optimization genuinely helped known-target performance
  (0.2857 -> 0.4000), consistent with the "single-gradient-snapshot
  undersells the ceiling" hypothesis from earlier analysis. Held-out
  generalization stayed at a clean, better-grounded zero this time --
  every one of 5 alphas tested on n=3 validation lemmas gave exactly
  0.000, not just the one selected.
- **Verdict: controller-side (noun) steering does NOT outperform
  target-side (adjective) steering** -- known-target ceiling (0.40) is
  below target-side's 0.50, and held-out generalization (0.0000/0.0000)
  is below target-side's real, control-validated 0.29-0.33/0.09-0.14.
- **Two identifiable, non-speculative reasons, not "the intuition was
  wrong"**: (1) attrition is far higher than target-side ever had
  (33-53% usable vs. target-side's typical 75-95%+) -- the joint
  constraint (controller must be found in the model's own
  reconstruction AND must precede the target) is considerably stricter
  than target-side's single constraint, so this comparison runs on much
  thinner, noisier data; (2) signal-propagation distance -- controller
  patching injects the intervention far earlier in the sentence than
  target-adjacent patching does, giving the signal more opportunity to
  be diluted or overwritten by intervening computation before reaching
  the target. Neither reason implies the underlying noun-driven
  structure doesn't exist or doesn't matter for Swahili/Kitaita -- only
  that this specific single-position, single-hop probing mechanism
  didn't detect it with the data available here.
- Not yet done: a version with MORE fit examples per lemma (data-limited
  currently, same corpus-scarcity issue as everywhere else in the French
  track); multi-hop or multi-position controller+target joint patching;
  applying the dictionary/template-sentence approach (Stage 2's
  `french_adjective_lexicon.py` recipe) to build controller-side
  (noun-phrase) examples at much larger N, the same fix that worked for
  the clustering analysis's small-sample problem.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — CRITICAL CORRECTION: the controller-side steering results above are unreliable -- wrong decoder layer, found and fixed

- User pointed out the earlier controller-side experiment grouped chains
  by TARGET (adjective) lemma, not CONTROLLER (noun) lemma -- it never
  actually tested cross-NOUN transfer. Built `discover_noun_clusters.py`
  (mined corpus, 57 distinct controller nouns, 23 usable -- groups
  entirely empirically by cosine similarity, no pre-assigned tags,
  per the user's explicit instruction) then, given the same small-N
  problem that motivated Stage 2 for adjectives, built
  `french_noun_lexicon.py` (231 hand-compiled French nouns, correct
  fixed gender, 8 semantic domains recorded for post-hoc reference only)
  + `discover_noun_clusters_lexicon.py` to scale up the same way.
- **Smoke test before the full run caught something much bigger than a
  data problem**: ALL 3 synthetic noun sentences failed to fit (zero
  gradient) at layer 12 (the last decoder layer -- the SAME layer used
  for every decoder-side patch in this project, including all of
  today's controller-side work). Root-caused directly, not
  speculatively: **layer 12 is structurally unable to propagate
  information from an EARLY (controller) decoder position to a LATER
  (target) position within a single teacher-forced forward pass** --
  after the last decoder layer there is no further self-attention layer
  left for a later position to "look back" at an earlier one; the final
  per-position projection to logits cannot mix positions. Confirmed with
  a direct, controlled test: real mined chains with controller-target
  gap=2 (`École`->`nationale`) and gap=5 (`porte-parole`->`irakien`)
  BOTH fail (zero gradient) at layer 12 and BOTH succeed at layer 6, on
  the identical chains.
- **This retroactively explains, and invalidates, the earlier
  controller-side steering comparison** (same-lemma 0.2857/0.4000,
  held-out 0.0000/0.0000, both baseline and "optimized" runs, logged in
  the entry above this one). The ONE real chain that worked in that
  pilot (`tour`->`final`) had `controller_step == target_step - 1` --
  i.e. gap=1, meaning it wasn't testing propagation at all, just
  accidentally reproducing target-adjacent patching under a different
  name. Every chain with a genuine gap (nearly all of them, and
  structurally ALL synthetic noun-lexicon sentences, which by
  construction separate noun and adjective by several words) was
  mathematically unfittable at layer 12 regardless of sentence content
  -- not a reconstruction/data-quality problem as assumed at the time.
  **The "controller-side does not outperform target-side" conclusion
  should be treated as unreliable pending a rerun at the correct
  layer.**
- **Fix applied**: `discover_noun_clusters.py`,
  `discover_noun_clusters_lexicon.py` now patch layer 6 by default;
  `controller_side_steering.py` / `controller_side_steering_optimized.py`'s
  `--layer` default changed from 12 to 6, with an explicit code comment
  explaining why, for whenever those get rerun. Re-verified: all 4/4
  smoke-test sentences that failed at layer 12 succeed at layer 6.
- **Project-wide methodological note worth generalizing**: layer 12
  (last decoder layer) remains CORRECT for target-adjacent patching
  (no cross-position propagation needed there, patch sits right next to
  the prediction) -- this bug is specific to patching positions that
  are NOT immediately pre-target. Any future non-target-adjacent decoder
  patching experiment in this project should default to a mid-stack
  layer, not layer 12, and this should be checked explicitly (e.g. via
  a quick multi-layer gap test like the one that caught this) rather
  than assumed.
- Full 231-noun lexicon clustering (layer 6, corrected) launched, in
  progress. Not yet done: rerunning `controller_side_steering.py` /
  `_optimized.py` at the corrected layer to get a trustworthy
  noun-vs-adjective steering comparison (the one thing this whole
  detour was meant to answer, still open).

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Noun clustering (large lexicon) and layer-6-corrected controller steering baseline: two decisive negative results, both real this time

- **231-noun lexicon clustering completed**: 231/231 fit successfully
  (0 failures, vs. 23/57 for the mined-corpus version -- confirms the
  layer-6 fix, not just more data, fixed the structural fitting
  problem). Off-diagonal cosine: mean=+0.0546, **std=0.4997** (vs.
  adjectives' std=0.07-0.13) -- an extremely wide spread. Hierarchical
  clustering found an extremely stable 2-way split (150 vs. 81 nouns)
  that survived every threshold tested up to 0.45.
- **Root cause, checked directly and confirmed**: the 81-noun cluster is
  100% feminine nouns; the 150-noun cluster is 123 Masc + 27 Fem. A
  multi-factor regression (n=26,565 pairs) confirmed this is
  overwhelming: `same_gender` coefficient +0.52285 (t=100.01) vs.
  `same_domain_tag` -0.01259 (t=-1.46, NOT significant) and
  `abs_len_diff` (not significant). R^2=0.27, almost entirely from
  gender alone.
- **This is the SAME canonicalization-residual artifact found for
  adjectives (+0.0165 coefficient there), but ~32x larger for nouns.**
  Plausible reason: an adjective's masc/fem form is a momentary,
  contextual choice; a noun's grammatical gender is a permanent lexical
  property baked into its embedding across all of pretraining --
  "overcoming" that deeper signal via a simple sign-negated gradient is
  far less clean than flipping an adjective's surface form. **No
  tangible semantic noun classes have been found** -- domain tags
  (object/human/abstract/place/nature/animal/body/time/food/material/
  society) show zero explanatory power once gender is controlled for,
  even when re-clustered separately within each gender stratum (checked
  directly: within-stratum clusters remain domain-heterogeneous by eye).
- **Controller-side steering rerun at the corrected layer 6 (baseline,
  mined corpus, matching the original pre-fix comparison exactly):**

  | condition | whole_word_rate | STRICT rate | n |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | fitting attrition | 23/31 pool (74%), 8/8 val (100%) -- up from 39%/50% at layer 12 | | |
  | SAME LEMMA (known target) | 0.1538 | **0.0000** | 13 |
  | HELD-OUT LEMMA | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 12 |
  | HELD-OUT CLASS | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 13 |
  | controls | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 13 |

  The layer fix resolved the STRUCTURAL problem (attrition dropped from
  61% to 26%, confirming the diagnosis) but not a steering problem --
  the apparent 0.1538 same-lemma success rate **collapses entirely to
  0.0000 under strict scoring**, meaning every "success" was a
  repetition-collapse artifact (degenerate generation happening to
  contain the flip word), not a genuine gender flip. Held-out
  lemma/class are a flat, control-clean zero regardless of metric.
- **This is now a MORE decisive negative result than the broken-layer
  version, precisely because it is no longer confounded by the layer
  bug.** Controller-side (noun) steering shows no genuine (strict-
  scored) causal effect at any level (known-target, held-out-lemma,
  held-out-class) once the structural fitting problem is fixed and
  degenerate generations are correctly excluded.
- Optimized (multi-step Adam) rerun at layer 6 launched, in progress --
  the last untried lever before concluding controller-side steering
  itself (not just the layer choice) doesn't work with this recipe at
  this data scale.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Optimized controller-side steering at the corrected layer: first genuinely clean controller-side success, but the held-out pattern inverts relative to target-side

- **Result** (multi-step Adam, layer 6, n_pool=19, n_validation=12 usable):

  | condition | whole_word_rate | STRICT rate | mean p(flip) | n |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | SAME LEMMA (optimized controller patch) | 0.6364 | **0.5455** | 0.4653 | 11 |
  | HELD-OUT LEMMA | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 10 |
  | HELD-OUT CLASS | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0228 | 11 |
  | controls | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 11 |

  Unlike the layer-6 BASELINE run (0.1538 raw -> 0.0000 strict, i.e. pure
  repetition-collapse), here 86% of the raw successes survive strict
  scoring (0.6364 -> 0.5455) -- controls stay flat/clean. **This is the
  first mechanistically clean, non-degenerate confirmation in this
  project that patching a NOUN's own representation, several tokens
  upstream of the target, causally flips a downstream ADJECTIVE's
  gender** -- direct evidence gender is represented on the controller
  and propagates forward through decoder self-attention to drive
  agreement, not merely read off the target's own position.
- **Full comparison, target-side (adjective) vs. controller-side
  (noun), both fully corrected/optimized:**

  | condition | target-side | controller-side |
  |---|---|---|
  | same-lemma (known) | 0.50 | **0.5455** (comparable, slightly ahead) |
  | held-out lemma | 0.29-0.33 | 0.0000 |
  | held-out class | 0.09-0.14 | 0.0000 |

  Known-target performance is now genuinely comparable between the two
  sites -- a real, positive answer to the original "will steering work
  for nouns" question once the layer bug was fixed. **But held-out
  generalization is WORSE for controller-side, not better** -- the
  opposite of what the Swahili-motivated intuition behind this whole
  detour predicted. A controller-fit direction transfers well to the
  KNOWN adjective it was fit toward, but not to an unseen one, more so
  than target-side directions fail to transfer.
- **Plausible mechanistic reason**: fitting the noun's direction toward
  one specific adjective likely captures something about THAT
  particular controller-target attention pathway specifically, which
  may be more idiosyncratic to that pairing than a direction fit
  directly on the adjective's own representation is -- consistent with
  (not contradicting) this session's broader "lemma/pairing-identity
  dominates over shared structure" finding from the within/across-lemma
  cosine analysis.
- **Net state of the whole controller-side detour**: real, clean,
  positive evidence that noun-level gender information is causally
  represented and propagates to agreement (a genuine mechanistic
  finding, independent of whether it's useful for transfer); real,
  clean, negative evidence that this specific technique (single
  controller-fit direction) generalizes to unseen nouns/adjectives any
  better than target-side steering does -- if anything, worse. The
  original motivating hypothesis (noun/controller-driven agreement,
  shared with Swahili, should make steering MORE transferable) is not
  supported by this round of evidence, though the mechanistic
  confirmation (gender lives causally on the controller) is itself a
  meaningful, positive result worth keeping.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Idea aggregation (ChatGPT + Gemini + own list) and Phase 0/1 diagnostics: `table`'s failure is a direction-extraction problem, not a causal-reachability problem

- **Context**: asked ChatGPT and Gemini to independently critique/extend our
  own 10-idea list for raising the 0.5455 known-target controller-side
  accuracy (see `improve_known_target_accuracy_prompt.md`). Both
  independently converged on: diagnose WHERE the `livre`/`table` causal
  chain breaks before spending more budget on alpha/optimizer tuning
  (both flagged finer alpha search and more optimizer steps alone as
  low-leverage given `table`'s genuinely flat 0-150 plateau). Aggregated
  into a phased roadmap (Phase 0 engineering sanity -> Phase 1 localize
  the break -> Phase 2 direction/optimization fixes OR Phase 3
  site/architecture fixes, branching on Phase 1's result) and implemented
  Phase 0/1 in `phase1_diagnostics.py`.
- **Phase 0 (propagation + logit-margin trace, fixed teacher-forced
  context, not confounded by generation drift at high alpha)**: the
  perturbation's own magnitude at the controller position (`dH_immediate`,
  `dH_deep@ctrl`) is virtually IDENTICAL between `livre` and `table` at
  every alpha (confirms the patch hook fires correctly -- rules out an
  implementation bug like the earlier layer-12 one). But `dH_deep@tgt-1`
  (how much of that perturbation survives, several self-attention layers
  later, at the TARGET's own position) is dramatically smaller for
  `table` at every single alpha tested -- e.g. alpha=30: livre=57.31 vs
  table=2.58 (22x smaller); alpha=200: livre=97.78 vs table=7.12 (13.7x
  smaller). The logit margin (flip-orig) correspondingly crosses zero for
  livre between alpha=20/30 but for table only crawls from -9.87 to -8.86
  across the ENTIRE alpha=0-200 range. **Our fitted direction for `table`
  is barely being routed to the target position at all, at any alpha --
  not "not enough push", a propagation deficit specific to this
  direction.**
- **Phase 1a (Jacobian check)**: local gradient of the margin
  objective w.r.t. the controller hidden state, compared via cosine
  similarity to our actual fitted/used direction. livre:
  cos(g,fitted)=+0.2080 (agrees). table: cos(g,fitted)=**-0.2250**
  (anti-correlated) -- and `||g||` is comparable between the two words
  (0.31 vs 0.24, not near-zero for table), so the local causal gradient
  is NOT flat/dead for table, it's just pointing a different way than
  our fitted direction.
- **Phase 1b (oracle gradient ascent, fully unconstrained, direct on the
  eval objective, no direction constraint at all)**: **table's margin
  flips just as easily as livre's, if anything more so** -- livre
  baseline -9.65 -> final +56.10 (||delta||=109.5); table baseline -9.87
  -> final +66.86 (||delta||=117.5). This conclusively rules out "the
  controller position cannot causally drive table's agreement" as an
  explanation. But cos(oracle_delta, our_fitted_direction) = **-0.3701**
  for table (vs +0.2694 for livre) -- the direction that actually works
  points substantially AWAY from what our multi-step-Adam fitting
  procedure converged to.
- **Phase 1c (activation replacement -- swap `table`'s controller hidden
  state outright with real masculine nouns' own hidden states from
  matched sentences, and symmetrically for `livre` with real feminine
  nouns)**: effect sizes are small and SYMMETRIC for both words (+0.12 to
  +0.57 out of the ~10 needed to flip, for both directions) -- ruling out
  a simple "just swap the lexical content" story as an explanation for
  the asymmetry; this intervention type is just weak in general at this
  site, not specifically weak for `table`.
- **Phase 1d (determiner-anchor test, Gemini's specific hypothesis that
  the unsteered article "La" anchors the agreement decision)**: swapping
  the determiner's hidden state alone (+0.19), the noun alone (+0.57), or
  both together (+0.77) all produce small, roughly-additive (not
  synergistic) effects, nowhere near flipping. **Does not support the
  determiner-anchor hypothesis** as the primary explanation.
- **Net conclusion, resolving the Phase 1 fork**: the controller position
  CAN and does causally control `table`'s downstream agreement decision
  (oracle proof, at least as easily as for `livre`) -- so Phase 3
  (site/architecture fixes: multi-layer/multi-position patching, KV/head-
  specific steering, layer sweeps) is NOT where the problem lives. The
  problem is squarely in Phase 2's territory: our specific fitting
  procedure (multi-step Adam, single fit sentence "La table est très
  importante .", log-P(flip)-at-fit-sentence objective) converges to a
  direction that is locally anti-correlated with what would actually
  move the margin, and correspondingly fails to propagate to the target
  position under an additive push at any tested alpha. Most likely
  explanation given the broader session's findings: the fitted direction
  is overfit to the FIT sentence's own local context/identity (echoing
  the already-established "item-identity dominates fitted directions"
  finding) and does not transfer even to a different sentence containing
  the SAME word, let alone a different word.
- **Next planned step (Phase 2, first cut)**: refit `table`'s (and other
  known-failing words') direction using a margin-objective (logit
  difference, not log-softmax-of-flip-token) fit jointly across the
  actual EVAL-style sentence context (not only a separate, simpler fit
  sentence), motivated directly by this diagnosis rather than generic
  brainstorming, then rerun the strict whole-word known-target
  evaluation to see whether this specific, evidence-backed fix raises
  accuracy on the previously-failing half of the known-target set.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Phase 2 first cut (margin objective + more Adam steps) REGRESSES known-target accuracy on the real corpus: a real, clean negative result, and a plausible reason why

- **Change tested** (`controller_side_steering_margin.py`, full same
  pool/alpha-sweep/strict-eval pipeline as the 0.5455 baseline, so
  directly comparable): replaced the fitting objective with margin
  (flip_logit - orig_logit) at the token-level first-divergence
  position, and raised Adam steps 25 -> 50 -- both changes directly
  motivated by phase1_diagnostics.py's oracle_ascent result, which used
  exactly this objective and flipped `table`'s margin as easily as
  `livre`'s.
- **Result**: SAME LEMMA strict accuracy **0.3846 (n=13)**, DOWN from
  0.5455 (n=11) on the log-P-objective baseline. HELD_OUT_LEMMA/CLASS
  and both controls stayed flat/clean at 0.0000, so this is not
  contamination or a bug -- a genuine, clean regression on the actual
  metric we set out to raise. (n differs slightly between runs -- the
  margin objective's stricter fit-time requirement, first_divergence
  must exist, drops a few lemmas the old objective could still fit,
  changing which lemmas make up the final evaluated set -- so this
  isn't a perfectly matched per-lemma comparison, but the direction and
  size of the drop, on a controls-clean run, is a real result, not
  noise.)
- **Most likely explanation, identified after the fact**: the
  phase1_diagnostics.py oracle_ascent success was fit AND evaluated on
  the SAME sentence (deliberately, as a diagnostic -- "can this position
  be moved at all"). The real pipeline fits on 1-2 DIFFERENT mined
  sentences and evaluates on a held-out one for the same lemma -- a
  cross-sentence generalization requirement the oracle diagnostic never
  had to satisfy. The margin objective (logit difference) is
  UNBOUNDED and has no natural ceiling, unlike log P(flip) which
  saturates as P->1 -- so 50 unconstrained Adam steps on a margin
  objective, fit against only 1-2 real (noisier, less carefully matched
  than the hand-built livre/table diagnostic pair) mined sentences,
  plausibly overfits HARDER to those specific fit sentences' own
  idiosyncrasies than the old, self-limiting log-P objective did. In
  other words: the diagnosis (table's fitted direction doesn't route to
  the target) was correct and well-evidenced, but "use the objective
  that worked when fit-context==eval-context" does not imply "this
  objective will generalize better when fit-context!=eval-context" --
  the two settings test different things, and this experiment
  conflated them.
- **Net state**: Phase 1's mechanistic finding (the pathway is
  reachable; the OLD fitted direction specifically misroutes) stands,
  unaffected by this result. This specific Phase 2 fix attempt is
  refuted. Bundling two changes (objective + step count) in one run
  also means we can't yet tell whether the margin objective itself or
  the extra steps did more of the damage -- an ablation, or a
  regularized/bounded version of the margin objective (e.g. an added
  KL-preservation term against the un-patched output, as ChatGPT #17
  and Gemini B5 both proposed, specifically to prevent this kind of
  single-sentence overfitting), is the natural next Phase 2 attempt.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Ablation confirms it: margin objective ALONE (25 steps, matching the original budget) beats the 0.5455 baseline; the extra optimizer steps specifically caused the earlier regression

- **Margin objective, opt_steps=25** (isolating the objective change from
  the step-count change, `controller_side_margin25_results.json`): SAME
  LEMMA whole_word_rate=0.6923, **strict=0.6154 (n=13)**, mean
  p_flip=0.5962 -- UP from the 0.5455 log-P baseline. HELD_OUT_LEMMA/
  CLASS and both controls stayed flat/clean at 0.0000, exactly as
  before. **The margin objective itself is a real, positive fix** --
  confirms the phase1_diagnostics.py-motivated hypothesis (fit toward
  the same quantity the eval metric actually reads off, i.e. logit
  margin at the token-level divergence point, not log P(flip) summed
  over the whole flip word) does transfer from the isolated table/livre
  diagnostic to the real mined-corpus pipeline, PROVIDED the step count
  stays at the objective's well-behaved range.
- **Confirms the overfitting explanation from the previous entry**: since
  margin@25-steps (0.6154) beats margin@50-steps (0.3846) by a wide
  margin, on the exact same lemma pool/pipeline, the earlier regression
  was NOT caused by the margin objective being worse in general -- it
  was specifically caused by giving an unbounded (non-saturating)
  objective too many unconstrained optimization steps against only 1-2
  real (noisy) fit sentences per lemma, letting Adam overfit harder the
  longer it ran. This is a clean, mechanistically satisfying resolution
  of the apparent contradiction between the strong oracle-ascent result
  (which used 50 steps successfully, but on the SAME sentence as eval)
  and the real pipeline's regression at 50 steps (cross-sentence
  transfer, where the same unconstrained budget is harmful rather than
  helpful).
- **Second half of the ablation (log-P objective, opt_steps=50, isolating
  whether steps ALONE -- without the margin objective -- also hurts)**:
  RESULT: SAME LEMMA strict=0.4615 (n=13), mean p_flip=0.4766 --
  slightly DOWN from the 0.5455/25-step baseline, but a much SMALLER
  drop than margin's 0.6154->0.3846. HELD_OUT_CLASS ticked up to 0.1538
  (n=13, from 0.0000) -- a single-run, unrepeated data point, not
  claimed as a robust effect. Controls stayed clean (0.0000).
- **Full 2x2 (objective x steps), all four cells now measured on the
  same pool/pipeline**:

  | condition | log-P, 25 (orig. baseline) | log-P, 50 | margin, 25 | margin, 50 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | SAME LEMMA strict | 0.5455 (n=11) | 0.4615 (n=13) | **0.6154 (n=13)** | 0.3846 (n=13) |
  | HELD_OUT_LEMMA | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
  | HELD_OUT_CLASS | 0.0000 | 0.1538 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |
  | controls | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |

  Both factors matter and INTERACT: more steps alone (log-P) causes a
  small drop (-0.084); the margin objective alone (at the original
  25-step budget) is a real, clean win (+0.070); margin PLUS more steps
  is much worse than either factor predicts alone (-0.231, more than
  double log-P's step-count sensitivity). This is exactly consistent
  with the log-P-saturation-provides-partial-overfitting-protection
  explanation from the previous entry: margin's unbounded objective is
  disproportionately more vulnerable to step-count-driven overfitting
  than log-P's self-limiting one.
- **New best known-target recipe**: margin objective, 25 Adam steps
  (the ORIGINAL step budget, just with the fitting objective swapped) --
  **SAME LEMMA strict = 0.6154 (n=13)**, up from the 0.5455 baseline,
  controls clean throughout. This is now the reference number to beat
  for further Phase 2 work, and the natural next moves are (a) a finer
  step-count sweep around 25 specifically for the margin objective (the
  sweet spot may not be exactly 25, that number was only ever tuned for
  log-P), and (b) the KL-preservation/bounded-margin idea (ChatGPT #17,
  Gemini B5), which could recover some of the higher-step-count benefit
  without the unbounded-objective overfitting risk.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Regularized margin objective (L2 + KL-preservation) at 50 steps: partial recovery on same-lemma, and the first-ever non-zero held-out-lemma signal in any controller-side run this session

- **Change tested** (`controller_side_steering_margin_reg.py`):
  L = -margin + lambda_l2*||delta||^2 + gamma_kl*KL(P_patched||P_baseline),
  lambda_l2=0.01, gamma_kl=1.0, run at opt_steps=50 -- the exact setting
  where the unregularized margin objective collapsed (0.3846) -- to test
  whether bounding the objective recovers the loss.
- **Result** (n_pool=16, same pipeline throughout):

  | condition | log-P@25 (orig. baseline) | log-P@50 | margin@25 (unreg) | margin@50 (unreg) | margin@50+reg |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | SAME LEMMA strict | 0.5455 (n=11) | 0.4615 (n=13) | **0.6154 (n=13)** | 0.3846 (n=13) | 0.4615 (n=13) |
  | HELD_OUT_LEMMA strict | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | **0.0833 (n=12)** |
  | HELD_OUT_CLASS strict | 0.0000 | 0.1538 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 (raw 0.1538, but repetition-collapse -- not a real success) |
  | controls | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 |

- **Interpretation**: regularization partially recovers margin@50's
  collapse (0.3846 -> 0.4615, a genuine +0.077) but does NOT reach
  margin@25's unregularized peak (0.6154) -- so on the primary
  same-lemma metric, **margin objective at the original 25-step budget,
  unregularized, remains the best known recipe.** But regularization
  also produced something new: HELD_OUT_LEMMA strict = 0.0833 (1/12),
  clean (raw==strict, not a collapse artifact) -- the FIRST non-zero
  held-out-lemma result in ANY controller-side variant run this entire
  session (every previous controller-side condition, log-P or margin,
  regularized or not, gave a flat, clean 0.0000 here). A single 1/12
  success is not strong evidence on its own, but it's a qualitatively
  different (non-zero, clean) result worth flagging: the KL-preservation
  term's explicit "change gender, disturb nothing else" pressure may be
  producing a marginally more reusable direction, at some cost to
  same-lemma peak performance -- plausible given the user has
  deliberately deprioritized held-out generalization for now, so this is
  noted as a lead for later, not pursued further in this round.
- **Standing best recipe for known-target accuracy: margin objective, 25
  Adam steps, UNREGULARIZED -- 0.6154.**

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Multi-position joint fit (noun + determiner, shared direction) REGRESSES strict accuracy despite a HIGHER raw flip probability: stronger but messier

- **Change tested** (`controller_side_steering_multipos.py`): jointly fit
  ONE shared direction, patched at BOTH the determiner position
  (controller_step-1) and the noun/controller position simultaneously --
  the toy model's own "controller + every upstream agreement position"
  recipe, on top of the standing-best margin@25-steps objective/budget.
  No new patching machinery needed -- GradientPatch/FixedPatch already
  add the same delta to every position in a list.
- **Result** (n_pool=16, same pipeline): SAME LEMMA whole_word_rate=
  0.6154, **strict=0.4615 (n=13)**, mean p_flip=**0.6890** -- DOWN on
  strict accuracy from the single-position standing best (0.6154), but
  UP on raw p_flip (vs 0.5962 for single-position). HELD_OUT_LEMMA/CLASS
  and controls all stayed at/near 0.0000, clean.
- **Interpretation**: patching two positions with the SAME shared
  direction produces a stronger internal push (higher p_flip) but also
  more collateral disruption to the rest of the generated sentence --
  more raw "successes" are getting caught by the strict repetition/
  degeneracy filter than at single-position. Plausible reason: forcing
  the determiner and the noun to share an IDENTICAL direction assumes
  their local gender-feature geometries are aligned, which may not
  hold -- the same vector could be well-matched to one position's
  representation and a worse fit (more distorting) at the other,
  net effect = more force, less precision. A natural refinement (not yet
  tried) would be to let the two positions have SEPARATE, jointly-
  optimized (not necessarily identical) directions rather than forcing
  one shared vector -- effectively a 2x-wider joint fit instead of a
  literal shared-direction multi-position patch.
- **Net state**: standing best known-target recipe remains margin
  objective, single position (controller only), 25 steps, unregularized
  -- **0.6154**. This specific multi-position variant is refuted; the
  toy model's "shared direction, multiple positions" recipe does not
  transfer to this real-corpus French setting as directly as hoped.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Separate (not shared) per-position directions at noun+determiner: WORSE still (0.3846) -- more free parameters, same scarce data, more overfitting

- **Change tested** (`controller_side_steering_multipos_separate.py`):
  the natural refinement identified after the shared-direction
  multi-position result -- jointly optimize TWO SEPARATE full-rank
  directions (one for the noun position, one for the determiner
  position, `determiner_step = controller_step - 1`) instead of forcing
  one shared vector onto both, on top of the standing-best margin@25
  recipe. Held-out-lemma/class deliberately not computed this round
  (out of scope; kept the experiment simpler/faster).
- **Result** (n\_pool=16, alpha=40 selected on validation): **SAME LEMMA
  strict = 0.3846 (n=13)**, mean p\_flip=0.4246 -- worse than BOTH the
  single-position standing best (0.6154) AND the shared-direction
  multi-position variant (0.4615). Controls clean (0.0000/0.0000).
- **Interpretation**: this completes a clean, monotonic pattern across
  all three multi-position attempts this round --
  single-position (1024 free params) = 0.6154 >
  shared multi-position (1024 free params, applied at 2 positions) = 0.4615 >
  separate multi-position (2048 free params, 2 independent directions) = 0.3846.
  **More optimization freedom, fit against the same scarce 1-2 real
  sentences per lemma, makes things monotonically worse in this
  setting** -- the toy model's own multi-position mechanism relied on
  ~150 fit sentences per stem (Results/toy_model_steering_mechanism.tex),
  two-plus orders of magnitude more fit data per direction than this
  French pipeline has, which plausibly explains why the identical
  architectural idea helps there and hurts here: the toy model's data
  budget could support the extra capacity, this pipeline's cannot.
- **Standing best result for this investigation, unchanged: margin
  objective, single position (controller only), 25 Adam steps,
  unregularized -- SAME LEMMA strict = 0.6154 (n=13), up from the
  0.5455 starting baseline.** All attempts to add capacity (more steps,
  regularization, shared multi-position, separate multi-position) have
  now been tried and each either regressed or only partially recovered
  toward 0.6154 -- strong evidence that, at the current ~16-lemma/
  1-2-sentence-per-lemma data scale, 0.6154 is close to this specific
  paradigm's (single full-rank direction, per-lemma independent fit)
