  ceiling, and further gains toward something like 0.90 most plausibly
  require attacking data scarcity directly (more fit sentences per
  lemma, synthetic augmentation, or sharing statistical strength jointly
  across lemmas) rather than further per-lemma optimization-procedure
  engineering. This is now documented in
  `Results/controller_side_steering_optimization.tex` (compiled PDF via
  tectonic, installed this session).

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — Attacking data scarcity directly: uncapped real fit data per lemma (first attempt confounded, self-caught and corrected)

- **Motivation**: per the standing-best analysis above, every attempt to
  add optimizer capacity (more steps, regularization, multi-position)
  either regressed or only partially recovered toward 0.6154 -- pointing
  at data scarcity (1-2 real fit sentences per lemma, capped by
  `--max-fit-sentences 2`) as the more promising remaining lever. A
  direct check of `agreement_chains_repaired.json` found real,
  already-mined data was being discarded: one lemma (*français*) has 26
  real occurrences and only 2 were ever used for fitting; 10 lemmas total
  have >=4 real occurrences. Raising `--max-fit-sentences` to a large
  number (100) uses ALL available real sentences per lemma (reserving
  one as held-out test) at zero new data-collection cost.
- **First attempt: confounded, self-caught.** Ran uncapped data WITHOUT
  explicitly passing `--opt-steps 25` -- `controller_side_steering_margin.py`'s
  own CLI default is `opt_steps=50` (a leftover from before the
  steps-ablation finding), not the standing-best 25. Result (opt_steps=50,
  uncapped data): SAME LEMMA strict=0.2857 (n=14), mean p_flip=0.7128 --
  worse than even the capped-data 50-step run (0.3846), consistent with
  MORE data at 50 steps still being dominated by the already-established
  overfitting-at-50-steps effect, but this run cannot isolate the data
  effect on its own since two variables changed at once. Caught before
  drawing any conclusion from it; relaunched immediately with
  `--opt-steps 25` explicitly specified to isolate the data effect
  cleanly.
- **Corrected, clean result** (margin objective, `opt_steps=25`,
  uncapped real fit data, `controller_side_margin_alldata25_results.json`):
  SAME LEMMA whole_word_rate=0.6429, **strict=0.5714 (n=14)**, mean
  p_flip=0.6268. HELD_OUT_LEMMA/CLASS and both controls stayed at/near
  0.0000 (held_out_lemma mean p_flip ticked to a small, non-repeated
  0.0314, no raw successes). **This is essentially flat relative to the
  capped-data standing best (0.6154, n=13) -- slightly lower, not
  higher** (n differs by one lemma, within noise for this sample size).
- **Interpretation: raw quantity of already-mined real data is NOT the
  binding constraint, contrary to the motivating hypothesis.** Most
  lemmas in the pool still have only 1-2 real occurrences (only ~10 of
  124 distinct lemmas have >=4), so uncapping mainly enriched a handful
  of high-frequency lemmas (*français*=26, *américain*=15, *national*=13,
  *supérieur*=10, ...) while leaving the majority of the pool unchanged
  -- and even for those enriched lemmas, the additional real sentences
  are heterogeneous, naturally-occurring contexts, not controlled/
  matched ones. More (heterogeneous) real constraints on the same shared
  direction plausibly pull it toward a compromise across genuinely
  different local contexts rather than a cleaner, more general one --
  echoing this project's much earlier finding (within/across-lemma
  cosine analysis) that even within-lemma directions vary more than
  expected, not just across-lemma. This refines, rather than closes, the
  data-scarcity hypothesis: it suggests **data quality/consistency**
  (controlled, matched synthetic template sentences reusing the same
  word, as built earlier this project for the noun/adjective lexicon
  clustering work) is the more promising next test of "does more data
  help," not simply pooling more raw heterogeneous mined sentences.
- **Standing best result, unchanged: margin objective, single position,
  25 Adam steps, capped at 2 real fit sentences/lemma -- SAME LEMMA
  strict = 0.6154 (n=13).** Every lever tried this round (more steps,
  regularization, shared multi-position, separate multi-position, more
  raw real data) has now either regressed or landed statistically flat
  relative to this number.

## 2026-09-22 (cont.) — CRITICAL BUG FOUND: every controller-side "SAME LEMMA" number this session has actually been measuring cross-noun generalization, not known-target performance

- **Root cause**: `controller_side_steering.py` (and every script built
  on it this session: `_optimized`, `_margin`, `_margin_reg`,
  `_multipos`, `_multipos_separate`) groups fit/held-out-test sentences
  via `by_lemma[c["target_lemma"]]` -- the ADJECTIVE's lemma. This
  convention is correct for TARGET-side (adjective-patching) steering
  (the original code this was copied from), where "same lemma" genuinely
  means "same word being patched". It is WRONG for CONTROLLER-side
  (noun-patching) steering, where the position actually being patched is
  the NOUN's, and grouping by the adjective's lemma pools together
  sentences containing COMPLETELY DIFFERENT NOUNS that merely happen to
  be modified by the same adjective somewhere in the corpus.
- **Direct confirmation**: `target_lemma="français"` (26 "occurrences")
  spans 15 distinct `controller_lemma` values: artiste, auteur, chef,
  critique, diplomate, dirigeant, employé, journaliste, ligue, marine,
  ministre, pilote, politique, école, écrivain. Every chain already
  carries a correct `controller_lemma` field -- it was simply never used
  by any controller-side script.
- **Consequence**: every "SAME LEMMA" strict number reported this
  session for controller-side steering (the original 0.5455 baseline,
  every Phase 2 variant, the final 0.6154 standing best) has actually
  been measuring a disguised, weaker form of CROSS-NOUN generalization
  (fit a shared direction from OTHER nouns that happen to share an
  adjective with the test sentence, evaluate on yet another different
  noun) -- not genuine "same known noun, different sentence" performance
  as intended and as reported. This also retroactively and fully
  explains the "uncapped data" result that prompted this investigation:
  raising `--max-fit-sentences` for a `target_lemma` group added MORE
  DIFFERENT NOUNS to the pooled fit (e.g. up to 15 for "français"),
  making the already-known-to-fail cross-noun generalization problem
  harder, not giving one noun's direction more supporting real-sentence
  evidence -- "more data doesn't help" made complete sense once the
  actual unit of pooling was understood.
- **Fix**: `controller_side_steering_margin_by_noun.py`, identical to
  `controller_side_steering_margin.py` in every respect (margin
  objective, single position, layer 6) except grouping by
  `controller_lemma` instead of `target_lemma`, and with `--opt-steps`
  defaulted correctly to 25 (fixing the same leftover-50-default trap
  that caused the earlier confounded uncapped-data run). Data landscape
  under the corrected grouping is if anything richer than before: 39
  distinct nouns with >=2 real occurrences (was the same count under the
  old, wrong grouping, but now genuinely repeated nouns), 26 with >=3
  (vs 8 before), richest noun has 19 genuine repeated occurrences.
  Rerunning the standing-best recipe under the corrected grouping now --
  this is the number that should have been reported as "known-target
  controller-side accuracy" throughout this whole session.
- **Corrected results** (`controller_side_margin_by_noun_results.json`,
  n_pool=21 real distinct nouns, margin objective, single position, 25
  steps, layer 6 -- identical recipe to the mislabeled 0.6154 run, only
  the grouping key fixed):

  | condition | whole_word_rate | strict | mean p_flip | n |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | SAME LEMMA (genuine same noun) | 0.4545 | **0.3636** | 0.3671 | 11 |
  | HELD-OUT LEMMA (genuine cross-noun, same adj.\ pattern class) | 0.2000 | **0.2000** | 0.2037 | 10 |
  | HELD-OUT CLASS (cross-noun, different pattern class) | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 11 |
  | controls (random / orthogonal) | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 11 |

- **Two genuinely new findings, not just a corrected number**:
  1. **True same-noun accuracy (0.3636) is LOWER than the mislabeled
     0.6154.** Makes sense once understood: a real noun typically has
     only 1-2 total sentences in the whole mined corpus, so fitting AND
     testing on that one noun alone is maximally data-starved, with no
     cross-item diversity to regularize the fit -- exactly the
     overfitting mechanism this whole Phase 2 investigation kept
     re-discovering (unbounded objectives, more steps, more capacity all
     made things worse under scarce single-item data). The old,
     mislabeled "same lemma" number was inadvertently benefiting from
     pooling several DIFFERENT nouns' sentences together, which acted as
     an accidental regularizer despite testing the wrong thing.
  2. **HELD-OUT-LEMMA is, for the first time all session, cleanly
     non-zero at reasonable n** (0.2000, n=10, controls clean at
     0.0000) -- every previous held-out-noun number in this entire
     controller-side investigation (dating back through this whole
     session) was a flat, control-clean 0.0000, except one single-run,
     n=12, 1/12 flicker from the regularized-margin experiment. This is
     qualitatively different: real, repeatable-looking, moderate-sample
     evidence that a DIRECTION POOLED ACROSS OTHER NOUNS sharing the
     held-out noun's adjective's morphological suffix pattern DOES
     transfer to a noun never included in that pool -- and the contrast
     with HELD_OUT_CLASS (different pattern class, flat 0.0000) shows
     this isn't just "any pooling helps": it's specifically tied to
     shared morphological structure, echoing this project's much
     earlier finding (this session, adjective-side) that real
     morphological micro-clusters (al/ale, if/ive, el/elle) carry
     genuine shared structure.
- **This inverts the working assumption held throughout the whole
  session** (same-item/same-lemma always beats held-out generalization)
  --  under a properly data-honest single-noun fit, a POOLED cross-noun
  direction (0.2000) is closer to same-noun performance (0.3636) than
  the old numbers suggested, and both are far above the previously
  assumed held-out ceiling of 0.0000. **Practical implication for
  future known-target work**: given how data-starved individual nouns
  are, pooling structurally-similar nouns' directions (matched by
  adjective morphological pattern) may be a BETTER known-target recipe
  than fitting a noun's direction from its own 1-2 sentences alone --
  worth testing directly as a next step (fit toward a noun using ITS
  OWN sentence(s) PLUS other same-pattern-class nouns' sentences pooled
  in, rather than choosing between purely-own-noun or purely-other-noun
  data).
- **Correction needed**: `Results/controller_side_steering_optimization.tex`
  (and its compiled PDF) reports the pre-bugfix, mislabeled numbers
  (0.5455 baseline, 0.6154 standing best) under the "known-target"/
  "same lemma" framing throughout -- needs a correction section or
  revision once the post-fix picture is fully worked out, not yet done.

## 2026-09-23 — Idea-generation round (ChatGPT/Gemini ideas requested + own brainstorm); five pooling-combination variants tried, all fail to beat 0.3636

- **Context**: user confirmed 0.3636 (SAME LEMMA strict, controller-side,
  margin objective, 25 steps, layer 6, n=11 -- the bug-fixed number above)
  as the number to improve. No tool in this environment can call ChatGPT
  or Gemini directly, so per this project's established convention
  (`sign_fix_subspace_critique_prompt.md` -> `french_steering_critique2_chat.md`/
  `_gemini.md`), wrote `improve_known_target_accuracy_v2_prompt.md` for
  the user to paste externally and get raw responses back as
  `known_target_v2_chat.md`/`known_target_v2_gemini.md` (not yet done).
  Built `experiment_chart_known_target_v2.md`, a 15-item prioritized
  chart combining still-untested ideas from the *original* ChatGPT/Gemini
  rounds (layer sweep, multi-layer patching, nonlinear adapter, Bolukbasi
  midpoint-deviation basis, activation-patching diagnostic, synthetic
  templates, seed-ensembling) with new ideas from this session.
- **Item 1 (free, no compute)**: Masc-origin vs Fem-origin split of the
  existing n=11 same-lemma result: 0.3333 (n=6) vs 0.4000 (n=5) strict --
  inconclusive, does not replicate the earlier adjective-direction-level
  asymmetry, n far too small to mean anything. Not pursued further.
- **Item 2, hybrid pooling** (`controller_side_steering_hybrid_pool.py`):
  convex combination of a noun's own fitted direction with its
  morphological-pattern-class mean, weight `w` swept on validation. FIRST
  RUN HAD A REAL BUG: the (w, alpha) grid search validation set was only
  n=4 usable lemmas, so most cells tied (several at whole_word_rate=0.25,
  most at 0.0) and `max(dict, key=dict.get)` silently picked the first
  tied cell by loop-insertion order (w=0.0) rather than anything
  meaningfully better -- caught, NOT reported as a finding. Fixed
  (tie-break by mean_p_flip, evaluate every w on the pool instead of only
  the single argmax-selected one) and rerun. **Corrected result**: w=1.0
  (pure own-noun) strict=0.3636 remains best; every blend (w=0.25-0.75)
  is WORSE (0.09-0.27 strict) despite HIGHER mean_p_flip (0.42-0.50 vs
  0.37) -- same signature as the earlier multi-position-patching
  regression (stronger push, more collateral damage, more strict-filter
  rejections despite more raw movement).
- **Item 8, sign-consistency audit WITH a proper random-vector control**
  (not done in earlier project rounds -- Gemini's original S-metric
  proposal was never checked against a null): loaded the fitted
  directions saved by the hybrid-pool run and computed S = ||sum(v_i)|| /
  n for each pattern class, then generated a matched random-vector null
  (200 trials, same n and d_model=1024) for comparison. cons+e (n=11):
  observed S=0.3709 vs random-null 0.3012+/-0.0063 (~11 sigma above null).
  "other" (n=6): observed S=0.4374 vs null 0.4083+/-0.0086 (~3.4 sigma).
  **Conclusion: the small (~0.03-0.05) mean pairwise cosine within a
  pattern class is real, not an artifact of high-dimensional random-vector
  noise** -- confirms and properly controls the earlier same-session
  finding (adjective-direction identity-component analysis) at the noun
  level too. The signal is genuine but weak, and evidently gets
  diluted/misapplied by naive uniform pooling (item 2's result).
- **Item 4 variant, similarity-weighted pooling**
  (`controller_side_similarity_weighted_pool.py`), reusing the SAME saved
  directions (no refit -- near-free, ~6 min, forward passes only).
  Replaces the hand-defined "same morphological class" grouping with a
  data-driven one: pool only OTHER pool nouns (any class) with positive
  cosine similarity to the target's own direction, weighted by that
  cosine. **First attempt used cos>0 as the filter -- too loose**: checked
  the whole-pool pairwise cosine distribution directly (mean=0.0318,
  std=0.177, n=210 pairs) and found 52% of ALL pairs already have
  cos>0 -- the filter was admitting roughly half the pool regardless of
  class, diluting with cross-class noise. Result: strict=0.0909 (n=11),
  WORSE than even the coarse same-class mean (0.2000) -- consistent with
  behaving like a diluted version of the HELD_OUT_CLASS control (0.0000)
  rather than HELD_OUT_LEMMA (0.2000). Caught the flaw before treating
  this as a real finding about similarity-weighting per se.
  **Corrected (strict top-3 nearest-neighbor pooling, not cos>0)**:
  similarity-pool-only strict=0.0909 (still weak alone), but **50/50
  blend of own + top-3-similarity-pool: strict=0.3636 (n=11), an exact
  TIE with pure own-noun**, not a win -- and checking which specific
  nouns succeed shows a different set (own-only: heure/ministre/voile/
  politique; blend: gens/heure/politique/secrétaire) -- a lateral shuffle
  in outcomes, not a real improvement, at this sample size.
- **Net conclusion, closing this line of investigation**: five distinct
  own+pooled combination strategies were tried this session (uniform
  same-class mean, three intermediate convex-blend weights, loose
  cos>0-weighted pooling, strict top-3-weighted 50/50 blend) -- none beat
  pure own-noun fitting (0.3636), and the best any of them achieved was
  an exact tie with a different success set. **Standing best known-target
  recipe remains unchanged: margin objective, single position, 25 Adam
  steps, own-noun-only fit -- strict = 0.3636 (n=11).** Combining a
  data-starved item's own signal with a same-class pooled signal, in
  every form tried so far, either hurts (via collateral push/degeneracy)
  or at best does nothing -- the genuine, statistically-confirmed shared
  structure across nouns (item 8) does not translate into a usable
  combination recipe via simple weighting/blending of already-fit
  full-rank directions.
- **Also found and corrected in passing**: the original alpha selection
  behind 0.3636 itself (not a bug, but a real fragility worth flagging)
  rests on an n=4 validation set where alpha=40.0 "won" with exactly 1
  success out of 4 against 0 elsewhere -- the thinnest possible margin a
  discrete metric can express, not a tie-breaking bug like item 2's, but
  worth remembering when interpreting how robust 0.3636's own alpha choice
  is.
- **Recommended next steps** (not yet started, queued in
  `experiment_chart_known_target_v2.md`): since pooling-based combination
  is now a fairly well-exhausted dead end at this data scale, the next
  levers should attack the OWN-NOUN fit directly instead of trying to
  borrow cross-noun signal: (a) a layer sweep for the pure own-noun
  recipe (layer 6 was chosen only because it's the earliest layer where
  the controller position causally precedes the target, never because
  it's optimal for signal quality -- 7-10 untested), or (b) synthetic,
  matched template sentences for the actual corpus nouns (the existing
  `french_noun_lexicon.py` template lexicon only overlaps 3/19 pool nouns
  as-is, but its `SENTENCE_FRAMES`/`determiner()` machinery is generic
  and could be reused with corpus-derived noun+gender+exemplar-adjective
  info instead of the fixed lexicon) -- directly attacks the 1-2-real-
  sentence data floor that both the own-noun baseline and its overfitting
  failure mode are built on.

## 2026-09-23 (cont.) — Synthetic data-scale pilot (10 nouns): SCARCE(2) vs MANY(12) fit sentences, then alpha sweep; motivated by the recommended next step above. Laptop shut down mid-session; two non-comparable runs resulted, no clean "more data helps" verdict yet

- **Setup** (`synthetic_data_scale_pilot.py`, new): single-variable comparison
  (rule 9) -- SAME noun, SAME held-out test sentence, SAME recipe (margin
  objective, controller/noun side, layer 6, single position, 25 Adam
  steps) -- only fit-set size differs: 2 sentences (SCARCE, matches the
  standing real-corpus recipe's `--max-fit-sentences 2`) vs. 12 template
  sentences (MANY) drawn from a 16-sentence-per-noun synthetic pool via
  new `synthetic_noun_templates.py` (wraps `french_noun_lexicon.py`'s
  `SENTENCE_FRAMES`). Pool: entreprise, problème, compagnie, peintre,
  frère, rocher, peur, famille, or, place (5 masc, 5 fem). Alpha fixed at
  40.0 (carried over from the real-corpus recipe, not freshly swept --
  flagged explicitly in the script docstring as untested-for-this-regime).
- **Run 1 ("v1"), completed before the shutdown**
  (`synthetic_data_scale_pilot_v1_alpha40_results.{json,log}`): SCARCE
  strict=0.0000, MANY strict=0.0000 (both n=7; 3/10 nouns errored as
  "unscoreable" -- orig/flip token sequences never diverge on that test
  sentence). Strict is a flat floor for both conditions, so this run
  alone cannot support or refute "more data helps." But mean_p_flip
  clearly separates from control noise: SCARCE 0.0077, MANY 0.0147 (~2x),
  vs. random-control 0.0001 and orthogonal-null 0.0002 (40-150x below
  either real condition) -- the fitted directions are doing something
  real, just not enough to cross the strict threshold at alpha=40.
- **Laptop shut down mid-session** after v1 completed. Before the
  shutdown, `synthetic_noun_templates.py` and `synthetic_data_scale_pilot.py`
  were BOTH edited (timestamps ~12:42, between v1's completion at 12:37
  and the eventual restart) -- the exact diff was not captured (no git
  history, old versions not saved) beyond confirming `pilot.py` gained
  directions-saving (`torch.save(..., "*_directions.pt")`) needed for a
  planned follow-up alpha sweep. A rerun launched to regenerate those
  directions was killed by the shutdown before finishing (no output).
- **Rerun ("v2"), completed after restart**
  (`synthetic_data_scale_pilot_results.{json,log}`, same script/CLI as
  v1 but the edited templates/script noted above): SCARCE
  strict=0.2500 (n=4), MANY strict=0.1429 (n=7). **These numbers are NOT
  comparable to v1 or to each other at face value**: (a) the underlying
  templates/script differ from v1 in an untracked way, so this is a
  second, independent data point, not a replication; (b) SCARCE and MANY
  scored different, only partially-overlapping noun subsets (SCARCE:
  compagnie/peintre/frère/rocher; MANY: entreprise/problème/compagnie/
  peintre/frère/rocher/or) -- checked directly, and SCARCE's 0.25 is a
  SINGLE success (compagnie) out of its 4 scored nouns, MANY's 0.14 is a
  single success (problème) that SCARCE never even scored. Logged as a
  second pilot data point, explicitly flagged as not poolable with v1.
- **Alpha sweep** (`synthetic_data_scale_alpha_sweep.py`, new; reuses the
  v2 rerun's saved per-noun directions, forward passes only, no refit;
  grid {40,80,150,300,600,1000}; explicitly flagged per rule 5 as a
  selection made on n=4-7, below the n=8 threshold -- exploratory
  calibration only, not a final claim):
  - Strict rates stay noisy/near-floor at every alpha for both
    conditions (single-success artifacts as above) -- **no usable strict
    signal from this sweep at this n.**
  - mean_p_flip response curves diverge in a mechanistically legible
    way: MANY rises monotonically with alpha (0.1022 -> 0.1409 -> 0.1794
    -> 0.2155 at alpha=300, then eases to 0.1907 / 0.1750) -- the shape
    of a real, well-conditioned direction that benefits from stronger
    push. SCARCE does the OPPOSITE -- it falls monotonically as alpha
    increases (0.0050 -> 0.0014 -> 0.0009 -> 0.0005 -> 0.0004 -> 0.0006)
    -- consistent with this project's standing finding that data-starved
    (n=2) single-item fits are noise-dominated and degrade under
    stronger push rather than sharpen (same signature as the earlier
    multi-position-patching and hybrid-pool-blend regressions).
- **Net read**: no clean "more fit data improves known-target steering"
  verdict yet -- strict accuracy is too noisy (n=4-7, non-overlapping
  noun sets between conditions, single successes driving every nonzero
  cell) to trust in either direction. But the mean_p_flip alpha-response
  shapes are a real, qualitatively different, mechanistically sensible
  signal in MANY's favor (well-behaved vs. degenerate-under-push) that is
  independent of the strict-metric noise. **Not a finding, a lead**:
  worth pursuing with (a) a larger noun pool (>=8 per condition, matched
  N) to get a trustworthy strict comparison, and (b) pinning down what
  actually changed in `synthetic_noun_templates.py`/`pilot.py` between v1
  and v2 before treating either as characterizing "the" synthetic-data
  pilot result.
- **Housekeeping**: this session is a concrete instance of why rule 4
  ("log the full resolved config") and checkpoint/resume matter --
  losing the machine mid-run cost one wasted ~19min fit run (no data
  loss, just time) and, more importantly, silently introduced an
  untracked confound (the templates/script edit) between what was meant
  to be a single experiment's before/after. No process-level fix applied
  yet; worth adding a lightweight config/file-hash stamp to result JSONs
  so a future interruption doesn't require reconstructing this by
  timestamp archaeology.

## 2026-09-23 (cont.) — N-matched, n=30-pool synthetic data-scale run: clean negative result, "more fit data" does NOT beat the 2-sentence baseline on strict accuracy

- **Motivation** (per this session's own recommendation above): the v1/v2
  n=10 pilots were too small and, in v2's case, asymmetrically excluded
  ("unscoreable") nouns between SCARCE and MANY (only 4/10 overlapping),
  so no trustworthy same-noun-set comparison existed yet.
- **Fix, in `synthetic_data_scale_pilot.py`** (same script, extended, not
  forked -- rule 10): added an N-MATCHED summary block that restricts
  SCARCE vs. MANY vs. both controls to the intersection of nouns scored
  (non-None) in ALL FOUR conditions, prints that matched noun list
  explicitly, and warns if matched n < 8 (rule 5). The old unmatched,
  per-condition-denominator summary is kept alongside it for transparency,
  not replaced. Also scaled the pool: `--n-nouns 30` (up from 10; lexicon
  has 231 nouns total, 123 Masc/108 Fem, plenty of headroom), seed=0,
  same recipe otherwise (alpha=40, layer 6, margin objective, 25 Adam
  steps, single position) -- output to a new file
  (`synthetic_data_scale_pilot_n30_results.json`), v1/v2 files untouched.
- **Result -- N-MATCHED, n=19** (comfortably above the rule-5 n=8 floor;
  19/30 nouns scored in every condition):

  | condition | strict | whole_word_rate | mean_p_flip |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | SCARCE (2 sentences) | 0.3684 (7/19) | 0.3684 | 0.1036 |
  | MANY (12 sentences) | 0.3684 (7/19) | 0.4211 | 0.2529 |
  | random control | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0003 |
  | orthogonal-null control | 0.0000 | 0.0000 | 0.0003 |

  **Strict accuracy is an EXACT TIE, 7/19 either way.** Both conditions
  are far above the control floor (mean_p_flip ~350x higher), so the
  steering effect itself is real -- it is specifically "more data" that
  shows no strict-accuracy benefit here, on a properly matched,
  adequately-powered sample. This is a genuine finding, not an
  underpowered non-result: n=19 > the rule-5 threshold, controls are
  clean, and it replaces the earlier "lead, not yet a finding" language
  from the n=10 rerun+sweep entry above.
- **But the two conditions succeed on almost entirely DIFFERENT nouns**
  (checked directly): SCARCE-only successes = actrice, compagnie, gare,
  or, pied, place (6); MANY-only successes = famille, ouvrier, peur, sel,
  table, tapis (6); overlap = sac (1 of 7). This is the SAME "lateral
  shuffle in outcomes, not a real improvement" signature already found
  this session with the pooling-blend experiments (item 4,
  `controller_side_similarity_weighted_pool.py`) -- more data/more
  pooled signal changes WHICH nouns steer, not HOW MANY, at this
  alpha/recipe.
- **mean_p_flip genuinely differs** (MANY 0.2529 vs SCARCE 0.1036, ~2.4x)
  even though strict counts tie -- consistent with the earlier alpha-sweep
  finding (n=10 rerun) that MANY's fitted direction is a stronger,
  better-conditioned push. The stronger push is real; it just reallocates
  which nouns cross the strict threshold rather than adding net
  successes, matching the standing pattern (stronger push = more
  collateral, not more wins) seen repeatedly this session (multipos
  patching, hybrid-pool blends).
- **Standing answer to "does more data help known-target steering,"
  properly tested now**: NO, not at alpha=40 / this recipe, on strict
  accuracy -- confirmed at n=19 matched, not just suggested. The null
  hypothesis (relatedness/more-data helps) is NOT beaten here; record
  it as a negative result per CLAUDE.md's own rule ("relatedness helps"
  must be beaten, not assumed -- symmetric point: "more data helps"
  must also be beaten, not assumed, and here it wasn't). Open question
  this does NOT resolve: whether a per-condition alpha re-optimization
  (MANY's own best alpha, not SCARCE's borrowed 40) would change this --
  the n=10 sweep found MANY's mean_p_flip peaks near alpha=300, untested
  yet on strict accuracy at matched n. That is the natural next step if
  this line is pursued further, and must be run as its own single-variable
  experiment (rule 9), not folded into a rerun of this one.

## 2026-09-23 (cont.) — RETRACTION: "more data doesn't help" (n=19 matched result, above) does not hold up. External critique (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) plus a directly-verified leakage confound

- **What happened**: wrote `synthetic_data_scale_critique_prompt.md`
  (self-contained, per convention) asking for a harsh critique of the
  n=19 N-matched tie and its "more data doesn't help" reading. Got
  independent responses from Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini (saved as
  `synthetic_data_scale_response_claude.txt`, `_chatgpt.txt`,
  `syntetic_data_scale_response_gemini.txt` [sic, typo in filename,
  left as-is]). All three converge on the same core objection, and one
  of Claude's specific claims was checked and found to be factually
  wrong, and one further problem (not raised by any of the three) was
  found by directly interrogating the fit data.
- **RETRACTED**: "more fit data does not improve strict known-target
  accuracy," stated as an unqualified finding in the previous entry.
  That claim does not survive this critique round. Correct statement:
  **inconclusive** -- the n=19 tie (7/19 both) does not distinguish "more
  data doesn't help" from "more data helps, but alpha=40 (borrowed from
  the SCARCE regime, never tuned for MANY) prevents it from showing up
  in strict accuracy," and separately, from a real data-construction
  leak described below.
- **Convergent critique points (all three)**:
  1. Alpha=40 was never actually validated as SCARCE's optimum -- it
     "won" an n=4 validation cell 1-success-to-0, the thinnest possible
     margin (already flagged in the 2026-09-23 idea-generation entry
     above, under-weighted when writing the n=30 result). Calling it
     "SCARCE's optimum" in the critique prompt was itself an overclaim.
  2. The unqualified "more data doesn't help" claim should be "at
     alpha=40," not stated as a general result. Precise recommended fix
     (ChatGPT and Gemini, independently, near-identical designs; Claude
     compatible): select alpha SEPARATELY for SCARCE and MANY on a
     validation split disjoint from the test sentence, using a
     pre-declared grid and selection metric (mean_p_flip preferred over
     strict, since strict is too sparse to select on), freeze both
     alphas, THEN evaluate once on the untouched test sentence. Re-running
     MANY at alpha=300 against SCARCE at alpha=40 (the "natural next
     step" proposed in the previous entry) was explicitly rejected by
     ChatGPT and Gemini as answering the wrong question (post-hoc,
     biased toward MANY).
  3. **"Lateral shuffle" retracted as an interpretation.** Both Claude
     (hypergeometric, P(overlap<=1) ~ 0.14) and Gemini (Poisson-style,
     E[overlap]=19*(7/19)^2 ~ 2.6, observed=1, ~within normal variance)
     independently computed that an overlap of 1/7 is NOT statistically
     distinguishable from two independent 7/19 processes. The specific
     claim in the previous entry ("more data changes WHICH nouns steer")
     is retracted as unsupported by this sample size -- a single test
     sentence per noun is too noisy to characterize per-noun identity
     effects at all, per Claude's point that test-retest reliability
     (SCARCE vs SCARCE on a different 2-sentence draw) was never
     measured.
  4. **N-matching is post-treatment selection** (all three,
     independently flagged as the same issue): requiring a noun to be
     scoreable under BOTH real conditions AND both control conditions
     means the matched set is filtered by properties of the model's
     behavior UNDER INTERVENTION, not just properties of the test
     sentence -- a form of collider/selection bias. Gemini's specific
     framing: this could select for nouns "prone to flipping under
     minimal noise," flattening the true delta. Recommended fix
     (ChatGPT, Claude): intention-to-treat -- score all 30 nouns, treat
     non-divergence under a real intervention as a scored FAILURE (not
     an exclusion), and only exclude a noun for a genuine test-sentence
     property (e.g. gold original and flipped forms already tokenize
     identically, independent of any direction).
  5. mean_p_flip is not a validated proxy for strict success in this
     project -- Claude points out that BOTH the earlier hybrid-pool
     blends and multi-position patching (this session, controller-side
     track) showed higher mean_p_flip going WITH worse strict accuracy,
     not better. Treating MANY's 2.4x higher mean_p_flip as "the real
     effect, just under threshold" (previous entry) is not automatically
     safe given that history; better diagnostic (Claude): split strict
     failures into under-push (target never flipped) vs. over-push
     (target flipped but something else broke) to see which regime each
     condition is actually in.
  6. Claude flagged a **factual error, now corrected**: the critique
     prompt (and this file, in the stage-3 section above) described
     layer 6 as "the earliest layer where the controller position
     causally precedes the target" -- wrong. Layer 12 is invalid because
     no attention layer follows it; every layer 0-11 is structurally
     valid for propagation, so layer 6 is a MIDDLE choice never
     re-swept, not a constrained minimum. This does not change any
     reported number, but it reopens the layer-sweep question as a freer
     lever than previously stated (echoes the still-open item in CLAUDE.md
     section 8: "best layer for controller-side patching, only L6 and L12
     tested").
  7. Claude flagged, unresolved: the exploratory alpha-sweep's SCARCE
     mean_p_flip at alpha=40 (0.0050, from the n=10 rerun's 4-noun
     overlap set) doesn't match this n=30 run's SCARCE mean_p_flip at
     alpha=40 (0.1036, 19 nouns) -- a ~20x gap. Checked: these are
     DIFFERENT noun populations (4-noun v2-rerun overlap vs. this
     independently-reseeded 19-noun matched set) with DIFFERENT
     synthetic data (templates.py/pilot.py were edited between v2 and
     this n=30 run's underlying pool generation is otherwise the current
     version, but the noun SAMPLE differs), so this is not necessarily a
     bug -- but it was not verified before publishing the sweep result
     and should not be treated as directly comparable across those two
     runs. Not re-checked further this round; flag for whoever next
     touches the alpha-sweep numbers.
  8. **One specific Claude claim checked and found FALSE**: "all 19 test
     items share a frame and an adjective" (implying the whole matched
     result characterizes one template cell). Directly verified against
     `synthetic_noun_templates.build_noun_pool(30, seed=0)`: the 19
     matched nouns' test sentences span 3 of the 4 adjective-pair
     classes (petit/petite, important/importante, grand/grande) and
     multiple distinct sentence frames -- each noun's chain order is
     independently shuffled (per-noun seed = `seed*1000+i`), so test
     items are NOT the same cell across nouns. Recorded so this specific
     claim isn't propagated into a future entry.
  9. **Norm-artifact concern (Claude) checked and RESOLVED, not an
     issue**: read `optimize_full_rank_direction_margin` directly
     (`controller_side_steering_margin.py`) -- it returns
     `final / final.norm()`, i.e. BOTH SCARCE's and MANY's fitted
     directions are always unit-normalized before decanonicalization and
     alpha-scaling, regardless of how many sentences went into the joint
     fit. Alpha=40 multiplies a unit vector in both conditions; the
     2.4x mean_p_flip gap is not a direction-magnitude artifact.
- **NEW finding, not raised by any of the three critics -- a genuine
  fit/test leakage confound in SCARCE's construction**, found by
  directly cross-tabulating each matched noun's fit-set pattern_classes
  against its test sentence's pattern_class (4 adjective-pair classes
  total, 4 frames x 4 classes = 16 chains/noun, `fit_scarce` = first 2
  of a per-noun-shuffled 16, `fit_many` = first 12, `test` = 16th):
  - `fit_many` contains a sentence of the SAME adjective-pair class as
    the test sentence for all 19/19 matched nouns (expected: 12 of 16
    draws against 4 classes of 4 each makes this near-certain by
    construction, not a bug, but worth stating plainly).
  - `fit_scarce` (only 2 draws) contains the test's class for just 7/19
    nouns -- pure luck of the per-noun shuffle seed.
  - **Cross-tabulated directly against strict success**: when
    `fit_scarce` DOES include the test's adjective class, SCARCE succeeds
    5/7 (71%); when it does NOT, SCARCE succeeds only 2/12 (17%). This is
    a large, directly-observed gap suggesting a meaningful share of
    SCARCE's apparent successes are close to near-memorization of the
    exact target adjective FORM (not generalization across frames), not
    a fair test of "steering quality" comparable to MANY's genuinely
    frame/class-diverse fit set.
  - This is a real design flaw in `synthetic_data_scale_pilot.py`'s
    "first k of a shuffled pool" fit-set construction, independent of
    the alpha confound -- it means the n=19 tie is not even a clean
    comparison of "2 sentences vs 12 sentences," but partly "2 sentences
    that sometimes already contain the answer vs. 12 sentences that
    (almost) always do."
- **Standing status, replacing the previous entry's conclusion**: the
  question "does more fit data improve known-target steering accuracy"
  remains OPEN. The n=19 tie is retracted as evidence either way. Three
  design problems must be fixed before the next run is trustworthy, not
  one: (a) alpha must be selected independently per condition on a
  validation split, never the test sentence; (b) scoring must be
  intention-to-treat over a fixed noun cohort selected independently of
  intervention outcome, not post-treatment N-matching; (c) fit-set
  construction must guarantee NEITHER condition's fit set contains the
  test sentence's exact adjective-pair class (hold out one full class,
  or better, one class x frame combination, from every fit set,
  matching ChatGPT's and Claude's independent suggestions) -- otherwise
  SCARCE keeps a lucky-leak escape hatch MANY doesn't need. Not yet
  implemented; next session's actual next step, not a further rerun of
  the current script.

## 2026-09-23 (cont.) — v3 redesign implemented and run (n=30 requested, cohort=23): class-holdout + intention-to-treat + independently-selected alpha per condition. Strict accuracy floors at 0/23 for BOTH conditions; two well-controlled continuous signals now favor MANY

- **Implemented all three fixes from the retraction entry**, rewriting
  `synthetic_data_scale_pilot.py` in place (not forked, rule 10):
  1. Class-holdout fit sets: one of 4 adjective-pair classes randomly
     held out per noun; BOTH conditions' fit sentences drawn only from
     the other 3 classes (12-sentence pool); SCARCE is now a random
     2-sentence draw from that pool, not positionally the first 2. Test
     sentence and up to 3 validation sentences come only from the held-
     out class, disjoint from every fit set by construction.
  2. Intention-to-treat scoring: cohort membership decided once per
     noun from the TEST sentence's properties alone (baseline generation
     contains the target word, controller precedes it, gold orig/flip
     forms diverge in token space) -- same cohort for every condition.
     A condition whose fit produces no usable direction is scored as a
     failure (`fit_failed=True`), not excluded.
  3. Per-condition alpha selection: grid {10,20,40,80,160,300} swept on
     validation sentences only (never the test sentence), argmax
     mean_p_flip aggregated across the WHOLE cohort, one alpha per
     condition, frozen before Phase 3.
- **Process note**: this run died TWICE before completing -- once when
  the underlying shell session was torn down mid-run (all background
  tasks, including the actual python process, were killed; the earlier
  laptop-shutdown incident this session had at least left completed
  work behind, this one lost ~40 min of Phase-1 fitting with nothing
  written to disk, since the script has no checkpointing). Restarted
  with `nohup ... & disown` the second time specifically so a future
  session/shell teardown can't kill it; that run completed. Per-noun
  checkpointing (skip already-fit nouns on restart) is the agreed next
  addition to this script, not yet done as of this entry.
- **Verified, not assumed, why nouns get excluded**: `orig_flip_never_
  diverge` (~23%, 7/30) is NOT about any noun being hard to steer -- it's
  a single adjective-pair class, `différent`/`différente`, tokenizing in
  mBART as `[147800]` vs `[147800, 13]` (masc is a strict token-prefix of
  fem, so there is no position where the two forms' token sequences
  disagree). Checked directly against the tokenizer: the other 3 classes
  (`grand/grande`, `important/importante`, `petit/petite`) all diverge
  cleanly at index 0. Since each noun's held-out class is drawn uniformly
  from the 4, ~1/4 of nouns draw the bad class and get excluded --
  matches the observed ~23-27% rate across both attempts exactly. Pure
  tokenizer artifact of one specific French adjective pair, unrelated to
  steering.
- **Result, N=23 (cohort), intention-to-treat, alpha selected
  independently per condition**:

  | condition | strict | mean_p_flip | fit_fail_rate |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | SCARCE (2 fit, alpha=20.0) | 0.0000 (0/23) | 0.0115 | 8.7% (2/23) |
  | MANY (12 fit, alpha=20.0) | 0.0000 (0/23) | 0.0519 | 0.0% (0/23) |
  | random control @ scarce alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0003 | 0.0% |
  | orthogonal control @ scarce alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0002 | 0.0% |
  | random control @ many alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0003 | 0.0% |
  | orthogonal control @ many alpha | 0.0000 | 0.0002 | 0.0% |

  Both conditions INDEPENDENTLY selected the SAME alpha (20.0) on
  validation data -- direct evidence the old fixed alpha=40 was over-
  pushing both conditions, not specifically mismatched to one side (the
  critique round's central worry). With that confound closed, strict
  accuracy is now a flat floor of 0/23 for BOTH conditions -- a harder
  floor than the old 7/19 tie, and STILL uninformative on its own about
  "does more data help": there is no room for either condition to show
  an advantage on this metric at this alpha/layer/recipe/template
  population.
- **Two well-controlled continuous signals now favor MANY, with the
  leakage and alpha confounds closed**:
  1. mean_p_flip is 4.5x higher for MANY (0.0519 vs 0.0115), both far
     above the clean control floor (~0.0002-0.0003, i.e. 40-170x below
     either real condition) -- a larger gap than the pre-critique
     result's 2.4x, now measured at each condition's own honestly-
     selected alpha rather than one alpha borrowed from the other
     condition's regime.
  2. NEW signal, not visible in any earlier run: SCARCE's direction-
     FITTING itself fails outright for 2/23 nouns (8.7%) -- no usable
     direction could be produced from only 2 sentences for those nouns
     -- versus 0/23 for MANY. This is evidence for "more data helps"
     that is independent of steering strength entirely: it's about
     whether the recipe can even produce a candidate direction, not
     about how well that direction works once produced.
- **Standing read, replacing the previous (retracted) entry**: "more
  data does not help" remains NOT supported -- if anything, the
  properly-controlled continuous evidence now points the other way,
  more strongly than before. But "more data helps" is ALSO not
  demonstrated on the metric that actually matters for deployment
  (strict, whole-word generation success) -- that metric simply doesn't
  discriminate at all here, for either condition, at any alpha up to
  300. This reframes the open question: it may no longer be primarily
  "does fit-set size matter" so much as "why does this controller-side/
  layer-6/margin-objective recipe never cross the strict threshold on
  synthetic template sentences regardless of fit-set size" -- a
  different, more basic question than the one this pilot was designed
  to answer. Worth a fresh critique round or a targeted diagnostic
  (e.g. per-token trace of where generation diverges from the flip form
  under the best available direction) before investing in another
  data-scale variant.
- **Agreed next step (not yet done)**: add per-noun checkpointing to
  `synthetic_data_scale_pilot.py` (save each noun's fit/eval result as
  it completes; skip already-completed nouns on restart) so a third
  mid-run interruption doesn't cost another ~80 minutes of recompute --
  directly motivated by this run dying twice in one session.

## 2026-09-23 (cont.) — Checkpointing added; under-push/over-push diagnostic (Claude's critique-round suggestion) run on the v3 result: 100% under-push, zero over-push, for BOTH conditions

- **Checkpointing implemented** in `synthetic_data_scale_pilot.py`
  (agreed next step from the entry above): a `<output-json>_checkpoint.pt`
  file is written after every noun in Phase 1 and again once Phase 2's
  alpha_star is selected; rerunning the same command auto-resumes,
  skipping already-fit/excluded nouns and an already-selected alpha_star.
  `--fresh` ignores an existing checkpoint. Verified working (killed a
  3-noun smoke run mid-Phase-1, rerun resumed from the checkpoint rather
  than refitting the completed noun).
- **Diagnostic** (`synthetic_data_scale_pilot_failure_diagnostic.py`,
  new, pure post-hoc analysis of the already-saved v3 results, no new
  compute): classifies every non-success Phase-3 record as `under_push`
  (flip form never appears anywhere in the generated text at all) or
  `over_push` (flip form appears as a whole word, but strict still fails
  -- repetition or other collateral damage), per Claude's critique-round
  suggestion (synthetic_data_scale_response_claude.txt, "mean_p_flip
  isn't a validated proxy" section) that this split would show whether
  the fix is "push harder" or "push more precisely."
- **Result**: SCARCE 21/23 under_push, 0 over_push (2/23 fit_failed,
  already known). MANY 23/23 under_push, 0 over_push. **Every single
  strict failure, in both conditions, is the steering never moving the
  model's actual word choice at all -- there is no collateral-damage
  failure mode present here whatsoever.** At the point of failure, mean
  p_orig (the model's confidence in the UNSTEERED original form) is
  0.8123 for SCARCE and 0.5796 for MANY -- the model still strongly
  prefers the original word even after steering; p_flip (0.0126 / 0.0519
  respectively, matching the earlier aggregate numbers) never gets
  competitive with p_orig in the actual argmax decision during
  generation.
- **This rules out one explanation and constrains what's left**: "the
  direction is fine but overshoots and breaks other tokens" is not
  happening at all, at this alpha, for either condition -- so a tighter/
  more targeted patch is not the fix. It also means "just raise alpha
  further" is not a free win on its own: the Phase-2 sweep already
  tested up to alpha=300 on this exact validation metric and found it
  COLLAPSES past ~20-40 rather than climbing (see the alpha-selection
  entry above) -- so blindly pushing harder makes things worse on the
  very metric that would need to improve, not better.
- **Reframes the open question again**: given more data helps the
  continuous signal (mean_p_flip, fit reliability) but neither condition
  can convert that into an actual word-choice flip at a sensible alpha,
  the bottleneck looks less like "data scale" and more like one of: (a)
  layer 6 (chosen only for structural validity -- earliest layer where
  the causal pathway CAN exist -- never swept for signal strength, per
  the corrected note in the earlier retraction entry), (b) the margin
  objective / 25-step budget being miscalibrated for this steering site,
  or (c) short synthetic template sentences genuinely being harder to
  move than the real mined corpus sentences the original 0.3636 known-
  target baseline was built on (those sentences are longer/more varied;
  p_orig here is unusually high, 0.58-0.81, versus whatever it is on the
  real corpus -- not yet checked). Not yet investigated further this
  session; a layer sweep is the most direct next lever and is already
  an explicitly open item (CLAUDE.md section 8).

## 2026-09-23 (cont.) — Layer sweep, mechanism dig, and a 4x generalization jump from swapping the fitted direction for a raw embedding difference. Session closes here for today; one control check is outstanding.

- **Layer sweep run** (`layer_sweep_controller_side.py`, new; same
  class-holdout/ITT/independent-alpha methodology as the retracted-then-
  fixed data-scale pilot, only the patched layer varies: 4, 6, 9; MANY-
  only, n=11 cohort after exclusions, same cohort reused across layers
  since the class-holdout split is layer-independent): layer 6 --
  already known 0/11 -- REPLICATES exactly on this smaller cohort
  (strict=0.0000, mean_p_flip=0.0522, matching the n=23 run's 0.0519).
  **Layer 4: strict=0.1818 (2/11)**, the first nonzero strict result on
  synthetic template sentences all session. Layer 9: strict=0.0909
  (1/11) but highest mean_p_flip of the three (0.1205). Controls clean
  at every layer (~0.0002-0.0005). Script died mid-run twice more this
  session (shell/session teardowns) before completing on a `nohup ...
  & disown`'d restart -- per-noun checkpointing (see below) now prevents
  this from costing full reruns.
- **Checkpointing added** to both `synthetic_data_scale_pilot.py` and
  `layer_sweep_controller_side.py`: a `<output>_checkpoint.pt` written
  after every noun (and, for the layer sweep, after every layer);
  rerunning the same command auto-resumes. Verified working directly
  (killed a 3-noun test mid-run, confirmed the rerun skipped the
  completed noun).
- **Under-push/over-push diagnostic** on the v3 n=23 floor: 100% of
  failures under_push (flip word never appears), 0% over_push, for both
  fit-set sizes -- ruled out "over-steering breaks things" as an
  explanation and showed raising alpha further (already tested to 300)
