## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — Ported the mBART combined-mechanism French->Italian pilot (fleur/table) to NLLB-200-3.3B before touching Swahili. First attempt: clean null, root-caused to an alpha-scale mismatch, not a mechanism failure. Corrected attempt: REPLICATES mBART's exact headline sentence, control-validated, with the dictionary-substitution step also reproducing cleanly.

- **Why this test, not Swahili noun classes directly**: the fleur/table
  French->Italian pilot (2026-09-24 entry above) is this project's
  strongest end-to-end validation of the full deployment pipeline
  (generate in a related/available language -> steer known nouns via a
  dictionary-supplied target gender/class -> substitute vocabulary) on a
  real, independently-judgeable language pair. Before spending compute on
  Swahili's ~15-way noun-class system (a much harder, harder-to-judge
  target), re-ran this exact known-working recipe on the new model to
  isolate "does the MECHANISM survive an architecture port" from "does
  Swahili noun-class steering work" -- two different questions, and
  CLAUDE.md's own hard rule #9 (one change per experiment) argues for not
  conflating them.
- **New scripts** (not reusing mBART's `mmt_*` files, which are hardcoded
  to `MBart50TokenizerFast`/`MBartForConditionalGeneration` and
  `tokenizer.lang_code_to_id`, an attribute NLLB's tokenizer doesn't
  have): `nllb_fr_it_steering_pilot.py` (v1, direction fitting + first
  grid), `nllb_fr_it_steering_pilot_v2.py` (v2, corrected-scale grid,
  reuses v1's saved fitted directions). Confirmed reusable as-is:
  `mbart_agreement_lib.py`'s `GradientPatch`/`FixedPatch`/
  `full_word_subword_ids`/`first_divergence`/`random_direction_like`/
  `orthogonal_null_direction_like` are all pure-tensor/tokenizer-generic,
  no mBART-specific code in any of them despite the module's name.
- **Architecture confirmed by direct inspection, not assumed**: NLLB-200-
  3.3B loads as `M2M100ForConditionalGeneration`, d_model=2048 (vs
  mBART-50's 1024), 24+24 encoder/decoder layers (vs 12+12),
  `tie_word_embeddings=True` with `model.model.shared.weight` tied across
  encoder/decoder embed_tokens and lm_head -- same tied-embedding
  structure the mechanism depends on, just a bigger model.
- **Encoder-direction fitting ported cleanly**: same 25-step Adam margin
  recipe as `mmt_encoder_prenominal_steering.py` (target: Cette/Ce
  determiner margin), same `"This X is big/small."` template sentences,
  substituting flower/table for book. Both fit successfully; NLLB's own
  baseline translations of the fit sentences confirmed the Cette/Ce
  determiner paradigm holds for these nouns too ("This flower is big." ->
  "Cette fleur est grande.", etc.) before any steering was applied.
- **First grid (v1) result: a clean, byte-identical NULL across all 9
  cells** (EMBED_ALPHA_GRID=[0.15,0.30,0.60] x
  ENCODER_ALPHA_GRID=[20,40,80], copied directly from the mBART recipe's
  effective range) -- every single combination produced the exact
  unsteered baseline `"La fleur est sur la table."`, byte-for-byte.
- **Root-caused, not assumed, before concluding the mechanism failed**:
  a quick diagnostic (embedding row norms, `model.config.scale_embedding`,
  actual encoder.embed_tokens forward-output norms, and an isolated
  encoder-only push at absurdly large alphas) found `scale_embedding=True`
  with `embed_scale=sqrt(2048)=45.25` (vs mBART's `sqrt(1024)=32`), and
  that the hook fires on `encoder.embed_tokens`'s OUTPUT -- which NLLB's
  `M2M100ScaledWordEmbedding` already multiplies by `embed_scale`
  internally -- giving per-position residual-stream norms of ~200-390,
  not the raw weight rows' norm of ~8. mBART's grid values (alpha
  15-80) were tuned to mBART's own residual-stream scale, never
  NLLB's -- an isolated encoder push at alpha=500 (no embed edit) DID
  flip the determiner (`"Le fleuriste est sur le tableau."`) but
  substituted both nouns rather than preserving them, the same pattern
  mBART showed when embed_alpha was too weak relative to encoder_alpha.
  This is a genuine architecture-scale calibration finding, not a
  refutation of the mechanism.
- **Second grid (v2), rescaled by ~10x based on the diagnostic
  (EMBED_ALPHA_GRID=[2,5,10] x ENCODER_ALPHA_GRID=[200,400,600], reusing
  v1's saved fitted directions, no refitting)**: real, non-null,
  alpha-dependent structure appears -- word substitution at low
  embed_alpha (`"Le fleuriste est sur le tableau."`,
  `"La rose est sur le table."`), degenerate repetition-collapse at the
  highest embed_alpha (`"Le fle fle fle est sur le fle fle fle."`), and
  at **embed_alpha=5.0, encoder_alpha=600.0**:
  **`"Le fleur est sur le table."`** -- both nouns spelled EXACTLY as in
  the baseline, both determiners flipped Fem->Masc, reproducing
  mBART's original flagship sentence (2026-09-24 entry) VERBATIM,
  word-for-word, on a completely different architecture.
- **Caught and corrected a real bug in the script's own auto-selection
  logic, not silently**: `check_flip()`'s "is the noun preserved" check
  used a bare substring test (`"fleur" in text.lower()`), which is a
  false positive for `"fleuriste"` (florist) and `"table"` inside
  `"tableau"` (board/painting) -- both real but WRONG French words that
  happen to contain the target noun as a substring. This caused the v2
  script to auto-select `embed_alpha=2.0, encoder_alpha=600.0`
  (`"Le fleuriste est sur le tableau."`) as its "best cell" and run
  controls/dictionary substitution on it instead of the genuinely clean
  `embed_alpha=5.0, encoder_alpha=600.0` cell -- caught by manually
  reading the grid output rather than trusting the script's own verdict,
  consistent with this project's practice of not taking a script's
  self-reported success at face value. Re-ran controls and substitution
  by hand on the correct cell (ad hoc, not saved as a new script --
  logged here in full instead).
- **Controls at the correct cell (embed_alpha=5.0, encoder_alpha=600.0),
  same alpha, directions swapped**: random-direction control reproduces
  the exact unsteered baseline (`"La fleur est sur la table."`) -- a
  clean null, same as every prior control in this project.
  Orthogonal-null control is NOT a clean null this time
  (`"Le tour est sur la table."` -- flower substituted to an unrelated
  real word "tour" [turn/tower] with an accidentally-flipped article,
  table stays completely at baseline) -- a partial, honestly-reported
  effect, not a perfectly flat 0/2, but still clearly weaker/qualitatively
  different from the REAL direction's full clean double-flip-plus-
  preservation. Noted rather than smoothed over, matching this project's
  norm from the original mBART pilot's own imperfect control (1/20
  random-direction hit, honestly reported rather than hidden).
- **FR->IT dictionary substitution on the correct cell's output**
  (`"Le fleur est sur le table."`), nouns-only via `fr_it_gender_dict.py`
  (function words and the su+il->sul-style contraction NOT handled, same
  scope limitation as the original mBART pilot): **`"Le fiore est sur le
  tavolo"`** -- both nouns correctly rendered in real Italian, correct
  Masc gender, matching mBART's original `"Il fiore è su il tavolo."`
  result in substance (only the untouched French function words/articles
  differ, a known, deliberately out-of-scope gap both times).
- **Verdict**: the combined embedding-edit + encoder-push mechanism
  PORTS to NLLB-200-3.3B. It required no change in kind -- same fit
  recipe, same two-part design, same qualitative alpha-magnitude pattern
  (too low = no effect, too high = word substitution or repetition
  collapse, a narrow middle band = clean flip+preserve) -- only a
  ~10x rescaling of both alpha ranges to match NLLB's larger
  `embed_scale`. This is encouraging for Stage 3 (Swahili noun classes):
  the mechanism itself is not mBART-specific, though this remains a
  single sentence/single noun-pair replication (n=1, same caveat the
  original mBART pilot carried) and the alpha range for Swahili's
  different noun-class geometry (~15-way, not binary) will need its own
  calibration, likely following the same "diagnose the model's actual
  activation scale first" approach rather than reusing either model's
  raw alpha numbers.
- **Not yet done**: a wider control sweep (more than 1 random + 1
  orthogonal draw, per this project's usual practice of noting when n is
  small); testing generalization to a second FR/IT noun pair on NLLB
  (only fleur/table tested, matching the original pilot's own n=1 scope);
  the function-word/contraction cleanup step for the IT substitution;
  and the actual next step this was all in service of -- Stage 3 Swahili
  noun-class steering itself, now with both a working baseline model
  (this session's earlier entry) and a confirmed-portable mechanism.

## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — Stage 3 begins: Swahili noun-CLASS centroid/selectivity analysis, embedding space only (no layer, no forward pass). Mixed result -- real within-class signal, but NO between-class separation advantage over a random-relabeling control, and the one large pairwise similarity looks like a tokenization artifact, not grammar.

- **Why this step, in this order**: direct multi-class generalization of
  `mmt_noun_centroid_direction.py`/`mmt_noun_gender_probe.py`'s French
  recipe (check the STATIC embedding geometry before spending any
  forward-pass/gradient compute on steering) -- per the user's explicit
  instruction this round, deliberately embedding-space-only, no layer.
- **New lexicon, `swahili_noun_lexicon.py`** (159 nouns, 11 usable
  classes): built from the author's own knowledge of Swahili grammar,
  NOT corpus-verified -- flagged explicitly, same convention as
  `french_noun_lexicon.py`/`fr_it_gender_dict.py`. Two deliberate,
  documented scope decisions, not gaps: (1) classes 9 and 10 are
  collapsed into one "9/10" label -- the large majority of class 9/10
  nouns are IDENTICAL in singular and plural surface form (`nyumba` =
  "house" or "houses", the distinction lives only in verbal/adjectival
  agreement, never the noun's own token), so tagging them as two
  separate classes would fabricate a distinction the token stream
  cannot support -- a structural fact worth carrying into the steering
  design later (this pair can never be a controller-side embedding-edit
  target the way class 1 vs 2 can, since there's only one embedding row
  to edit for both). (2) class 14 (abstract/mass, shares class 11's
  exact u-/w- prefix) and the locative classes 16/17/18 (near-closed-
  class grammatical markers, not an open lexical category) are omitted.
  Classes and counts: 1(18), 2(18), 3(14), 4(13), 5(14), 6(15), 7(14),
  8(14), 9/10(16), 11(9), 15(14).
- **New script, `swahili_noun_centroid_analysis.py`**: pure embedding
  lookups on `model.model.shared.weight`, no `model()`/`model.generate()`
  call anywhere -- honors "embedding space only, not any layer" exactly.
  87/159 words fragment into >1 subword under NLLB's tokenizer (first
  subword used as the word's representative token throughout, same
  convention the French analysis used); logged, not silently absorbed.
- **WITHIN-class cohesion (mean cosine of each noun to its own
  mean-centered class centroid): real=0.3878 vs. a 50-shuffle
  random-relabeling control (same class sizes, labels shuffled) at
  0.2518.** Real is meaningfully, consistently above the control --
  a genuine, non-trivial positive signal that grouping-by-class captures
  SOME real structure, not nothing.
- **BETWEEN-class separation (mean pairwise cosine similarity among the
  11 class centroids): real=-0.0951 vs. control=-0.0989 -- essentially
  TIED, no separation advantage over random relabeling at all.** This is
  a materially different, weaker picture than the French gender axis,
  where masc/fem centroids were maximally, cleanly separated by
  construction (that separation WAS the whole basis of the mechanism).
  Here, the 11 classes' centroids are about as mutually similar to each
  other as randomly-grouped same-sized word sets would be.
- **Caught a likely confound, not just reported the number**: the single
  largest pairwise similarity anywhere in the matrix is classes 1-3,
  cos=0.6120 -- more than 5x the next-highest pair (4-6, cos=0.1066),
  and wildly out of line with the near-zero/negative similarities
  everywhere else. Classes 1 (human singular) and 3 (natural-object
  singular) share the EXACT SAME surface prefix in Swahili (m-/mw-).
  This 0.61 is far more likely a tokenization/orthographic artifact --
  shared subword prefixes pulling first-subword embeddings together --
  than evidence of genuine grammatical or semantic proximity between
  those two classes, and should NOT be read as "classes 1 and 3 are
  related" without first controlling for shared-prefix tokenization
  overlap. Not yet disentangled; flagged rather than either ignored or
  over-interpreted.
- **A second, related, un-ruled-out confound**: this lexicon was built
  with each class drawn from a roughly similar but not controlled
  semantic domain (class 1/2 = people, class 15 = actions, etc.). The
  positive within-class cohesion signal could be driven by SEMANTIC
  similarity within each hand-picked class (e.g. class 1's people-nouns
  sharing embedding space because they're all human-referring words) as
  much as by any grammatical class-marking signal per se -- the same
  semantic-vs-grammatical confound this project already had to rule out
  for French gender (`mmt_noun_gender_probe.py`'s lemma-disjoint
  control). Consistent with this: class 9/10, the class with the most
  semantically HETEROGENEOUS membership in this lexicon (animals,
  objects, abstractions mixed together), has the LOWEST within-class
  cohesion of all 11 classes (0.2964) -- exactly what a semantic-domain
  explanation would predict, and not yet distinguished from a
  grammatical-class explanation.
- **Verdict**: NOT yet evidence that Swahili noun-class information is
  cleanly, separably linear in NLLB's raw embedding space the way French
  gender was. The within-class signal is real but modest; the
  between-class separation -- the property the French mechanism actually
  depended on -- shows no advantage over chance at all in this first
  pass. Two concrete, un-ruled-out confounds (shared-prefix
  tokenization, semantic-domain clustering) could each independently
  explain the modest positive signal without any grammatical-class
  content being involved. Per this project's null-hypothesis rule
  ("relatedness helps must be beaten, not assumed"), this result does
  NOT yet license moving to a steering attempt on the strength of "class
  1 vs class 7" or similar single-class-pair directions the way
  French's masc-fem axis did.
- Results saved: `swahili_class_centroids.pt` (per-class mean-centered
  centroids + global mean, for reuse), `swahili_noun_centroid_analysis_results.json`
  (full numbers).
- **Not yet done, concrete next steps**: (1) a semantic-domain-controlled
  lexicon (same semantic categories represented in EVERY class, so
  within-class cohesion can't be explained by domain alone) -- the
  single highest-value next check; (2) a shared-prefix control (compare
  1-3's similarity against OTHER same-prefix class pairs, e.g. any
  m-/mw- vs ki-/vi- pairing, to see if prefix-sharing predicts
  similarity generally, not just for this one pair); (3) whole-word
  (not first-subword) embedding pooling, since 87/159 words fragment and
  first-subword-only may be diluting or distorting the signal; (4) only
  after those are checked, decide whether ANY layer/gradient-based
  steering work on Swahili classes is justified, or whether the project
  needs a different starting representation (e.g. a probe trained with
  regularization, mirroring how the French probe direction was
  ultimately preferred over the naive centroid).

## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — User correction: group by AGREEMENT, not morphological shape. Empirically re-derived Swahili noun groupings via NLLB's own concord behavior; confirms a real animacy-override class; centroid rerun replicates the earlier mixed result AND independently confirms the shape-prefix-artifact hypothesis.

- **User's correction, stated directly**: "let's not identify classes
  based off of morphological similarity. Let's identify them based of
  agreement. so mtu and kipepeo are in one class." This reframes the
  whole premise of the centroid work above: Swahili/Bantu agreement can
  be driven by ANIMACY, overriding a noun's own shape-prefix class --
  kipepeo (butterfly) is ki-/vi- BY SHAPE but, per the user, patterns
  with mtu (person) for AGREEMENT. Exactly the "steer by what the model
  knows agrees with what, not by class label" capability CLAUDE.md
  section 1 identifies as the actual target.
- **Chosen method (user's explicit pick from 3 options)**: hybrid --
  draft agreement groupings from model-generated test sentences,
  user spot-checks.
- **Validated the test frame first, on a 10-word pilot, before scaling**
  (`swahili_agreement_probe_validation.log`, ad hoc, no saved script):
  Swahili's "-ko" locative-existential copula ("X is here") inflects
  with a class-specific marker. Result: EVERY animate noun tested (mtu,
  mwalimu, kipepeo, paka, mbwa) got "yuko"/"yuko" (the class-1/animate
  marker) REGARDLESS of shape (kipepeo is ki-/vi-, paka/mbwa are N-class
  by shape); every inanimate noun (kitabu, mti, nyumba, gari, kiti) kept
  its shape-predicted marker. Clean 5/5 vs 5/5 split, directly confirming
  the user's kipepeo example AND validating the test frame itself.
- **Scaled to all 159 lexicon words** (`swahili_agreement_class_probe.py`):
  71/159 flagged (word not found in output, or no/ambiguous marker
  detected) on the first pass. Root-caused, not just reported: (a) 8
  entries (exactly the class-9/10 ANIMALS most needed for this
  question: paka, mbwa, simba, ng'ombe, nyoka, ndizi, nyumba, safari)
  were broken by MY OWN bug -- glosses like "cat(s)" were fed verbatim
  into the English prompt ("The cat(s) is here."), producing garbage
  output; (b) the remaining ~63 (body parts, abstract nouns, and EVERY
  class-15 infinitive) failed because "The X is here." is semantically
  awkward for them, so NLLB reasonably used the invariant "ni" copula
  instead of a class-marked form -- a frame-design gap, not bad data.
- **User chose the fix for (b)**: retry with a possessive "my X" frame
  (grammatical for nearly any noun, including abstractions/infinitives).
  `swahili_agreement_class_probe_retry.py`: fixed the "(s)" bug for the
  8 animals with the original frame, retried the other ~63 with "my X"
  using the author's recollection of Swahili possessive concord
  (wangu=classes 1/2/3/11, yangu=4/6/9, langu=5, changu=7, vyangu=8,
  zangu=10, kwangu=15 -- flagged as unverified, same as every other
  linguistic claim here). Result: 71 -> 14 still flagged. The possessive
  frame held up with ZERO contradictions across ~50 words, and
  INDEPENDENTLY reconfirmed the animacy finding: simba, paka, mbwa,
  ng'ombe, nyoka all confirmed "yuko" via the fixed -ko frame; a BONUS
  finding emerged unplanned -- possessive concord distinguishes class 9
  (yangu) from class 10 (zangu) even though subject concord ("iko" for
  both) could not.
- **One anomaly surfaced and the user resolved it directly**: "wajomba"
  (uncles, plural) gave "wajomba zangu" where "wangu" was expected
  (matching every other class-1/2 human). User: "for familial nouns this
  is expected" -- a known kinship-term possessive irregularity, not a
  problem with the method. Dropped from the consolidated lexicon rather
  than forced into either bucket.
- **Consolidated into `swahili_noun_lexicon_agreement.py`**
  (`build_swahili_agreement_lexicon.py`, auto-generated, not hand-edited):
  144 of 159 words labeled by OBSERVED agreement (yuko/wako -> ANIMATE-SG/
  PL regardless of shape; inanimate words labeled by their marker's
  shape-class, with the two genuine STRUCTURAL homophonies in Swahili
  itself -- classes 3/11 sharing "uko"/"wangu", classes 4/6/9 sharing
  "yangu" -- broken by the word's own shape prefix only where concord
  itself cannot distinguish them, a legitimate tie-break since it's not
  assuming shape determines agreement, just resolving what concord
  can't). 15 words dropped: 14 with no clean translation match in either
  pass (mismatched lexeme, e.g. kifaru->"Panyabuku"), plus wajomba.
  Final counts: ANIMATE-SG=25, ANIMATE-PL=17, class 3=14, 4=12, 5=11,
  6=15, 7=11, 8=13, 9/10=10, 11=7, 15=9.
- **Centroid analysis rerun** (`swahili_noun_centroid_analysis_agreement.py`,
  identical method to the shape-based run above, just the corrected
  lexicon) -- **replicates the earlier mixed picture almost exactly**:
  within-class cohesion real=0.3807 vs. 50-shuffle random-relabeling
  control=0.2727 (real above control, same magnitude as the shape-based
  run's 0.3878 vs 0.2518); between-class separation real=-0.0927 vs.
  control=-0.0971 -- again essentially TIED, no separation advantage
  over chance, same as before. **Fixing the grammatical mislabeling did
  NOT fix the separation problem.**
- **The shape-prefix-artifact hypothesis from the earlier run is now
  INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED, not just suspected**: the single highest
  pairwise similarity in this run is class-3 vs. ANIMATE-SG, cos=0.5382
  -- essentially the same pairing (and similar magnitude) as the
  earlier run's suspicious class-1-vs-3 cos=0.6120. This persists even
  though ANIMATE-SG is now the CORRECTLY-labeled agreement class (no
  longer "class 1" as a shape bucket) -- strong evidence the similarity
  really is driven by ANIMATE-SG and class 3 sharing the same m-/mw-
  surface prefix (most ANIMATE-SG members are shape-class-1 humans),
  not by any grammatical or semantic relationship between the classes.
- **A second, genuinely new finding from this rerun**: ANIMATE-SG's own
  within-class cohesion (0.2578) is LOWER than shape-based "class 1"
  alone was before (0.3671) -- mixing in the non-human animals (samaki,
  simba, paka, mbwa, ng'ombe, nyoka) that the corrected, agreement-true
  labeling requires REDUCED cohesion relative to the human-only,
  semantically-homogeneous shape bucket. This is independent evidence
  for the semantic-domain-confound hypothesis raised in the prior
  entry: at least part of the earlier "class 1" cohesion was humans
  clustering because they're semantically about people, not because of
  shared grammatical marking -- true grammatical animates (humans +
  animals together) cohere less tightly in raw embedding space than a
  semantically-narrower human-only group did.
- **ANIMATE-SG vs ANIMATE-PL centroid similarity: cos=-0.2520** -- notably
  NEGATIVE, despite both sharing the same downstream "personal" agreement
  behavior (yuko/wako). Consistent with this project's French finding
  (`within_vs_across_lemma_cosine.py`, lemma-identity-dominated
  directions): each word's raw embedding is dominated by its own
  morphological/lexical identity (m-/mw- singular vs wa- plural surface
  prefix, in this case), with any shared grammatical-class signal a much
  smaller, harder-to-detect residual underneath it -- the same picture
  as French gender, now replicated in a structurally different language.
- **Overall verdict, updated**: the user's agreement-based correction was
  linguistically necessary and is now robustly confirmed (animacy
  override is real, replicated across many nouns and two independent
  concord types) -- but it does NOT by itself resolve the open question
  from the previous entry. Raw embedding-space class separation remains
  no better than chance even under the corrected labeling; the
  shape-prefix confound is now confirmed rather than merely suspected;
  and a new semantic-vs-grammatical dissociation (ANIMATE-SG's cohesion
  drop when animals are correctly included) adds further evidence that
  whatever within-class signal exists is at least partly non-grammatical.
  Per the null-hypothesis rule, this still does not license moving to a
  steering attempt on the strength of raw embedding centroids alone.
- Saved: `swahili_noun_lexicon_agreement.py` (consolidated lexicon),
  `swahili_class_centroids_agreement.pt`, `swahili_noun_centroid_analysis_agreement_results.json`,
  plus the full probe trail (`swahili_agreement_class_probe.py` +
  `_retry.py` + their `_results.json` files) for anyone re-deriving or
  auditing the labels.
- **Not yet done**: the three follow-ups from the prior entry (semantic-
  domain control, systematic shared-prefix control beyond this one
  confirmed pair, whole-word pooling) are now MORE clearly motivated,
  not less -- this session added evidence for two of the three
  candidate confounds (prefix, semantic domain) without ruling out
  either. Still open whether ANY layer/gradient steering work is
  justified before those are resolved.

## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — User flagged class sizes as too sparse vs. French's ~100+/class (Swahili was n=7-25). Expanded the lexicon to 319 words (n=22-57/class) via the same empirical probe; the within-class signal got STRONGER with more data while the between-class null stayed essentially unchanged across three different sample sizes -- evidence this is a real finding, not underpowered noise.

- **User's exact question**: "How many nouns did we have for each
  class... In the French example we had about 100 for each class. how
  about here?" Direct comparison: French had 231 nouns / 2 classes
  (108-123 each); the agreement-based Swahili lexicon had 144 nouns / 11
  classes (7-25 each, mean ~13) -- roughly 8-17x fewer per class, spread
  across 11 classes (55 pairwise comparisons) instead of 1. User chose
  "expand the lexicon substantially" over the cheaper targeted or
  do-nothing options.
- **Built `swahili_noun_lexicon_expansion.py`**: 229 new candidate
  nouns (verified zero overlap with the original 159), deliberately
  loading up class 9/10 with ~40 words (21 animals + 19 abstract/
  inanimate) since that split is simultaneously the best test of
  whether the animacy-override finding generalizes further AND a way to
  grow the still-thin true-9/10 inanimate remainder.
- **Ran the same two-frame probe** (`swahili_agreement_probe_expansion.py`,
  the "-ko" frame then a "my X" retry for flags, combined into one
  script this time): 175/229 (76%) resolved -- a notably higher
  first-pass-inclusive resolution rate than the original batch's 55%,
  consistent with the possessive frame now being applied automatically
  rather than as a separate manual step.
- **Clean, unplanned corroboration of the animacy finding**: within the
  SAME old shape-tag "9/10" bucket, the split was perfect -- all 4
  animals that resolved via the possessive frame (twiga/giraffe,
  chura/frog, pomboo/dolphin, nyati/buffalo) got "wangu" (the animate
  possessive form), while EVERY inanimate/abstract 9/10 noun that
  resolved (barua, sauti, kazi, dawa, hadithi, lugha, huduma, amani,
  haki, hasira, furaha, elimu, afya, bei, siku -- 15 words) got iko/yangu
  (the N-class forms) instead. Zero contamination either direction.
- **Caught and fixed a real bug in my own classifier before merging,
  not after**: `build_swahili_agreement_lexicon.py`'s (v1) tie-break for
  the genuine 3-vs-11 concord homophony used a HARDCODED word list
  (only the original 15 ambiguous words) -- any NEW inanimate class-3/
  4/6/11 word hitting an ambiguous marker (uko/wangu/yangu) would have
  silently defaulted to ANIMATE. Rewrote as `build_swahili_agreement_lexicon_v2.py`,
  using each word's OWN shape tag directly to break the tie whenever
  applicable (legitimate -- resolving a real structural homophony, not
  assuming shape determines agreement) and only falling through to the
  ANIMATE reading when a word's shape tag is OUTSIDE the homophonous set
  for its observed marker, which is exactly the animacy-override case.
- **Merged lexicon: 319 words, 11 classes, n=22-57 each (mean ~29)** --
  roughly 2.2x the previous sample and, critically, MUCH more evenly
  distributed (old range 7-25, new range 22-57). Still well short of
  French's 108-123/class, but a substantial, credible improvement.
  Counts: ANIMATE-SG=57, ANIMATE-PL=35, 3=27, 4=22, 5=22, 6=28, 7=25,
  8=26, 9/10=30, 11=25, 15=22.
- **Centroid analysis rerun on the 319-word lexicon**
  (`swahili_noun_centroid_analysis_agreement_v2.py`) -- **the two halves
  of the finding diverged in an informative way**:
  - **WITHIN-class cohesion got MORE convincing, not less**: real=0.3707
    (n=319) vs. 0.3807 (n=144) vs. 0.3878 (n=159, shape-based) -- stays
    in the same tight band regardless of sample size, i.e. genuinely
    stable. But the RANDOM-RELABELING CONTROL's cohesion fell
    substantially as n grew: 0.1798 (n=319) vs. 0.2727 (n=144) vs. 0.2518
    (n=159) -- expected statistically (larger random groups' centroids
    converge toward the generic global-mean direction, leaving less
    spurious alignment for individual members). Net effect: the
    real-vs-control GAP nearly DOUBLED, 0.108 -> 0.191, as n increased.
    This is what a genuine effect looks like under more data, not what
    noise looks like.
  - **BETWEEN-class separation stayed a genuine, stable null**:
    real=-0.0901 vs. control=-0.0977 (n=319) -- essentially the SAME
    tiny, inconclusive gap as n=144's -0.0927/-0.0971 and n=159's
    -0.0951/-0.0989. Unchanged across a ~2.2x increase in sample size.
    If this were a statistical-power problem (too little data to detect
    a real but modest effect), more data should have started closing or
    at least visibly narrowing that gap. It didn't move at all across
    three independent sample sizes. **This is now much stronger evidence
    that the lack of between-class separation is a genuine property of
    the raw embedding space, not an artifact of the sparsity the user
    correctly flagged.**
  - **The class-3-vs-ANIMATE-SG shape-prefix artifact intensified with
    more data**: cos=0.7091 (n=319) vs. 0.5382 (n=144) vs. 0.6120 (n=159)
    -- still by far the single largest pairwise similarity in the whole
    matrix (next-highest, at n=319, is 5-vs-9/10 at only 0.2032 -- see
    below). Getting STRONGER rather than washing out with more data is
    itself informative: a spurious small-n coincidence would be expected
    to shrink toward zero as n grows; this one grew. Reinforces (does
    not newly discover) the m-/mw--shared-prefix tokenization-artifact
    reading from two entries ago.
  - **A second candidate surface-artifact pair emerged with the larger
    lexicon, not visible before**: class 5 vs. class 9/10, cos=0.2032 --
    both classes are heavily zero/no-overt-prefix in their singular
    surface form (many class-5 nouns like gari/duka/shamba/jicho have no
    audible ji- prefix; nearly all class-9/10 nouns like nyumba/paka/
    nguo are prefixless by definition), a plausible same-shape-of-
    tokenization-artifact as the 3/ANIMATE-SG case, not yet confirmed
    the same rigorous way (checking whether it holds for OTHER same-
    prefix-pattern pairs, not just this one).
- **Overall verdict, updated again**: expanding the lexicon did what
  good power analysis should -- it didn't just add more noise around
  the same conclusion, it let the two halves of the finding separate
  cleanly. The within-class signal is real and now well-evidenced
  across three sample sizes with a widening real-vs-control gap. The
  between-class null is now well-evidenced too, in the opposite
  direction -- three sample sizes, no movement, not what an
  underpowered test looks like. Sparsity was a reasonable, well-founded
  concern to raise, but it turns out NOT to be the explanation for the
  lack of separation. Per the null-hypothesis rule, raw embedding
  centroids still do not license a steering attempt.
- Saved: `swahili_noun_lexicon_expansion.py` (229 new candidates),
  `swahili_agreement_probe_expansion_results.json`,
  `swahili_noun_lexicon_agreement_v2.py` (319-word merged lexicon,
  supersedes the 144-word v1), `swahili_class_centroids_agreement_v2.pt`,
  `swahili_noun_centroid_analysis_agreement_v2_results.json`.
- **Not yet done**: same three follow-ups as before, now on firmer
  footing to actually resolve rather than merely suspect -- (1)
  semantic-domain-controlled check (still not run); (2) systematic
  shared-prefix control, now with a SECOND candidate pair (5/9-10) to
  test alongside 3/ANIMATE-SG -- does pairwise similarity correlate
  with shared-prefix-pattern generally, across many pairs, not just
  these two; (3) whole-word (not first-subword) pooling -- fragmentation
  got WORSE at this lexicon size (199/319 = 62% multi-subword, vs.
  87/159 = 55% before), so this is now a larger, not smaller, potential
  confound than when first flagged.

## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — User asked to see the clusters visually (PCA plot). While preparing the data, caught a real confound: first-subword-only pooling collapses 125/319 words (39%) onto just 35 identical embedding vectors. Fixed with whole-word mean-pooling; core conclusions replicate, and the class-3/ANIMATE-SG confound roughly halved once the collision artifact was removed.

- **User asked two things**: (1) could the between-class null be explained by
  NLLB's 200-language embedding space being generically "crowded" rather than
  by a genuine absence of structure, and could a modest-but-real separation
  still be functionally sufficient even if it doesn't beat the random-
  relabeling control on this coarse metric; (2) show the clusters visually.
  On (1): the random-relabeling control already holds the embedding space,
  dimensionality, and noise floor constant, so "real ~= control" does mean the
  raw pairwise centroid distance isn't beating chance -- but a coarse
  aggregate metric could still miss a real, exploitable, low-variance signal a
  TRAINED PROBE would find, exactly as happened on the French track
  (`mmt_noun_gender_probe.py`: 82.2% real vs. 51% control CV accuracy, well
  beyond what the naive centroid showed). Noted as the natural next check
  regardless of what the plot shows.
- **While preparing the PCA data for the plot, caught a real, previously
  unnoticed confound**: `swahili_class_pca_projection.py` (first-subword-only,
  same convention used throughout this session and inherited from the French
  track) produced 35 groups of words sharing IDENTICAL (x, y) PCA coordinates
  -- 125/319 words (39%) collapse onto just 35 distinct points, because their
  FIRST SUBWORD TOKEN happens to coincide even though the words themselves
  are unrelated (e.g. mchakato/mchuzi/mguu/mlima/mto/mzizi -- 6 semantically
  and grammatically unrelated words -- all share one first-subword id and are
  therefore the exact same embedding vector). This directly inflates every
  within-class cohesion number reported in the last two entries (any class
  containing 2+ colliding words gets a free cos=1.0 pair) and would have made
  a plot show artificial clumps that are a tokenization artifact, not
  structure. This is the "whole-word pooling" item already queued as a
  future check in the previous entry's "not yet done" -- turned out on
  inspection to be a live, severe confound (39% collision rate), not a minor
  refinement.
- **Fixed with whole-word mean-pooling** (`swahili_wholeword_recheck.py`:
  average ALL subword rows per word instead of using the first one only) --
  confirmed 0/319 collisions remain. Recomputed BOTH the centroid/selectivity
  analysis and the PCA projection under the fix, for direct comparison
  against every first-subword number already logged:

  | metric | first-subword (n=319) | whole-word pooled (n=319) |
  |---|---|---|
  | within-class cohesion, real | 0.3707 | 0.3085 |
  | within-class cohesion, control | 0.1798 | 0.1798 |
  | between-class similarity, real | -0.0901 | -0.0965 |
  | between-class similarity, control | -0.0977 | -0.0980 |
  | class-3 vs ANIMATE-SG cosine (largest pair) | 0.7091 | 0.3824 |

- **The core conclusions replicate under the more rigorous method**: real
  within-class cohesion still clearly exceeds the random-relabeling control
  (0.31 vs 0.18); between-class separation is still a genuine, essentially
  exact tie with the control (-0.097 vs -0.098) -- the null holds up, not an
  artifact of the collision bug. **The class-3/ANIMATE-SG confound roughly
  HALVED** (0.71 -> 0.38) once the collision artifact was removed -- still by
  far the largest pairwise similarity in the matrix (next-highest, 4-6, is
  only 0.11), so a real residual shared-surface-form effect likely remains
  (m-/mw--initial words plausibly still share elevated similarity across
  MULTIPLE subwords, not just the first), but roughly half of what was
  measured before was specifically the raw token-collision bug, not even a
  softer "shared prefix" effect. **This whole-word-pooled run now supersedes
  every first-subword-based number in the two prior entries as the
  canonical figures.**
- Saved: `swahili_class_pca_projection_wholeword.json` (corrected PCA data,
  used for the plot below), `swahili_wholeword_recheck_results.json` (full
  corrected centroid/selectivity numbers).
- Interactive PCA visualization published (see chat for link) -- small
  multiples by class plus an "Animate vs Inanimate" and a "3 vs ANIMATE-SG
  confound spotlight" panel, built from the corrected whole-word data. Top-2-PC
  explained variance is low (~5%, down further from the first-subword
  version's ~10.6% -- the collision clusters had been artificially
  concentrating variance) -- flagged prominently on the page itself, since a
  2D picture of this space necessarily misses most of its structure either
  way.
- **User's verdict after seeing the plot**: "I still feel like there could be
  [a] direction... Let's put a break on embedding layer steering and see if
  we can do stream level steering in the layers." Correct call given this
  project's own French precedent -- gender was NOT cleanly separable in
  mBART's raw embedding geometry either, yet noun-side gender was still
  causally steerable via a stream-level push (`mmt_encoder_prenominal_steering.py`
  and everything downstream of it). No embedding-space finding, weak or
  strong, settles whether a LAYER push works -- this had not actually been
  tested for Swahili yet.

## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — First causal steering attempt on Swahili noun classes: stream-level-only (no embedding-table edit), layer swept at 6/12/18 of NLLB's 24 encoder layers. Layer 12 alone produces a real, control-validated agreement flip (class 1 -> class 4/9-10) with the noun's own spelling preserved -- layers 6 and 18 are flat nulls. Did not land on the specifically-targeted class 7, but this is Swahili's first demonstrated causal class-agreement steering in this project.

- **Explicit design choice, per the user**: no permanent embedding-table
  edit this round (that piece of the mechanism is deliberately switched
  off) -- test the encoder-push/stream component ALONE. This is also a
  real ablation the fleur/table NLLB pilot never isolated: that pilot's
  own diagnostic (embed_alpha=0, encoder-only, alpha=500) flipped the
  determiner but SUBSTITUTED the noun ("fleuriste" for "fleur") rather
  than preserving it -- open question whether that failure mode is
  general or specific to pushing at the EMBEDDING layer specifically
  (encoder.embed_tokens output) rather than a deeper transformer layer.
- **Target changed from a binary flip to a specific class target, per the
  user**: steer "mtu" (person, empirically ANIMATE-SG) toward CLASS 7
  (ki-/vi-) agreement, e.g. producing forms like "kinaitwa" (ki-na-itwa,
  "is called") in place of "anaitwa" (a-na-itwa). Test sentence, after
  back-and-forth on phrasing: "A person of cooking is called a cook." ->
  baseline `"Mtu anayejua kupika anaitwa mpishi."` -- two class-1 markers
  riding on "mtu": "anayejua" (a-na-ye-, subject+relative concord) and
  "anaitwa" (a-na-, subject concord).
- **Residual-stream norm diagnostic run FIRST, before picking alpha**
  (lesson learned from the fleur/table pilot's mis-scaled first grid):
  mean position norm at encoder layer 0 ~426, layer 6 ~1946, layer 12
  ~3279, layer 18 ~4393, layer 23 ~5222 on this test sentence -- grows
  roughly linearly with depth, confirming alpha cannot be reused across
  layers and must be recalibrated per layer (each layer's grid set to
  roughly 15%/45%/90% of that layer's own mean norm).
- **Fit recipe**: same established encoder-side margin-objective recipe
  used throughout this project (`GradientPatch`/`FixedPatch`, 25 Adam
  steps, 2 fit sentences), re-targeted to the existential-frame class
  flip yuko [ANIMATE-SG, gold] -> kiko [class 7, flip target], fit
  separately at each of 3 candidate layers (`model.model.encoder.layers[i]`
  for i in {6, 12, 18} -- roughly 25%/50%/75% depth of NLLB's 24-layer
  encoder, the 50% point chosen to match mBART's own L6-of-12 that
  worked for French).
- **Layer 6: clean null across the full alpha grid** (300, 900, 1800) --
  byte-identical baseline output at every alpha, matching layer 6's
  earlier null in the fleur/table debugging history (that pilot's own
  working layer was deeper).
- **Layer 12: a real, alpha-dependent, non-null effect** -- did NOT land
  on the fit-targeted class 7, but did produce a genuine class change:
  - alpha=500: `"Mtu wa kupika anaitwa mpishi."` -- the relative clause
    "anayejua" (who knows) simplifies to the associative construction
    "wa" (of); still class-1 concord throughout, a construction-level
    change, not yet an agreement-class flip.
  - alpha=1500 and alpha=3000 (identical, plateaued): `"Mtu wa kupika
    inaitwa mpishi."` -- "anaitwa" (a-na-, class 1) flips to "inaitwa"
    (i-na-, the class 4/9-10 subject-prefix group) -- a real, stable,
    reproducible agreement-class change on the SAME noun the direction
    was fit for. **"Mtu" itself stays spelled correctly at every
    alpha level tested, with zero embedding-table edit** -- directly
    answers the open question above: a DEEPER stream-layer push (layer
    12, vs. the embedding-layer push that caused substitution in the
    fleur/table diagnostic) can flip agreement while preserving the
    word on its own, no embedding-edit crutch needed.
  - No repetition-collapse or degeneration at any alpha tested, up to
    3000 -- an orderly, interpretable progression from "no effect" to
    "construction simplifies" to "verb agreement flips," not a jump to
    gibberish.
- **Layer 18: clean null across the full alpha grid** (700, 2000, 4000)
  -- same flat-baseline pattern as layer 6, despite alphas calibrated to
  layer 18's own (larger) residual-stream norm. **Layer 12 specifically
  is causally live for this mechanism; layers on either side of it, at
  comparable proportional alpha magnitudes, are not** -- a real,
  non-monotonic layer-susceptibility finding, not "more alpha always
  helps."
- **Controls at layer 12, alpha=1500** (`nllb_swahili_layer12_controls.log`,
  ad hoc, not saved as a separate script): 3 random-direction seeds AND
  the orthogonal-null direction ALL reproduce the exact unsteered
  baseline (`"Mtu anayejua kupika anaitwa mpishi."`), byte-for-byte, at
  the identical alpha that flips cleanly under the real fitted
  direction. **4/4 clean controls** -- tighter than the fleur/table
  pilot's own control (which had 1/20 random-direction hits) or the
  original mBART book/livre control (4/4 real vs. 19/20 random). This
  is the cleanest control result of any steering experiment in this
  project so far.
- **Standing interpretation**: this is Swahili's first demonstrated
  causal, control-validated noun-class agreement steering in this
  project -- real, reproducible, word-preserving, and direction-specific.
  It does NOT yet hit the user's specifically-requested class 7 target;
  it lands on the 4/9-10 group instead, most likely because the fit
  objective (existential-frame yuko->kiko margin) optimizes for "beat
  class 1 on this one downstream marker in this one frame," not
  "become class 7 specifically" -- the direction may be closer to a
  general "push away from class 1" axis than a precise class-7 axis,
  and/or class 7 and class 4/9-10 are not cleanly separated at layer 12
  the way the fit procedure implicitly assumes. Directly parallels this
  project's own French finding that fit-frame/test-frame mismatches
  (there: Cette/Ce-fit vs. La/Le-test) still transfer but imperfectly.
- **Not yet done**: refit directly against a class-7 marker in the SAME
  frame family as the test sentence (rather than the existential frame)
  to check whether that closes the class-7-vs-4/9-10 gap; sweep alpha
  more finely between 500 and 1500 at layer 12 to see whether the
  construction-simplification and verb-flip effects are two points on
  one continuum or genuinely separate thresholds; test generalization to
  a second animate noun (not just "mtu") and a second target class; test
  whether layer 12 is specifically privileged or whether a finer sweep
  (9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15) reveals a wider live band around it now that
  6 and 18 are confirmed dead.

## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — Optimization attempt #1 (fit directly on the class-7 marker pair, not a proxy frame): did NOT close the class-7 gap. Lands on the identical class-4/9-10 flip, then degrades. Real evidence the bottleneck isn't fit-objective mismatch.

- **User's framing, verbatim**: "how do we learn the steering? I suspect
  there is room to optimize here." Explained the current recipe in full
  (margin objective, 25-step Adam, unit-normalize then grid-search alpha
  separately, deliberately NOT learning magnitude jointly given this
  project's own French-track finding that more optimizer freedom
  monotonically hurt or did nothing at small fit-set sizes) and laid out
  3 concrete, differently-motivated optimizations: (1) fit directly
  against the class-7 marker instead of the generic existential-frame
  proxy; (2) more fit sentences/frames per noun; (3) a probe-style
  direction (regularized classifier across many noun/class pairs)
  instead of a 2-example gradient fit -- an item already logged as an
  open decision in CLAUDE.md. User chose to start with (1).
- **`nllb_swahili_class7_refit.py`**: refit at layer 12 (the only live
  layer) directly against `anaitwa` [class 1, gold] -> `kinaitwa`
  [class 7, flip] -- the EXACT verb pair from the test sentence itself,
  not a different frame's proxy pair. Fit sentences use the same verb
  ("kuitwa") with fillers independently verified to produce the clean
  class-1 form (`"The person is called a farmer/king."` ->
  `"Mtu huyo anaitwa mkulima/mfalme."`) rather than the unmarked
  habitual `"huitwa"` several other fillers produced unpredictably.
- **Result: the class-7-targeted fit reproduces the IDENTICAL wrong
  answer as the generic-frame fit, then degrades, and never once
  produces "kinaitwa" at any alpha tested (500-4000)**:
  - alpha=500: no flip yet (`"Mtu wa kupika anaitwa mpishi."`)
  - alpha=1000: **`"Mtu wa kupika inaitwa mpishi."`** -- "inaitwa"
    (class 4/9-10), the exact same flip target as the OLD
    existential-frame-fit direction from the prior entry, despite this
    direction being fit on a completely different, precisely-matched
    objective.
  - alpha=1500-3000 (plateaued): repetition-collapse -- `"mpishi"`
    (the actual target word, "cook") gets replaced by a repeated
    `"kupika"` (`"...inaitwa kupika."`).
  - alpha=4000: degrades further to an invariant, non-class-marked
    construction (`"Mtu wa kupika ni kuitwa mpishi."`, "ni kuitwa" =
    bare copula + infinitive, no subject-class marking at all -- the
    same "give up on class marking entirely" pattern seen in the
    agreement-class probing sessions' "ni hapa" flagged entries).
- **This is a real, informative negative result, not just "try harder
  alpha"**: two independently-fit directions, from two different frames,
  targeting two different specific marker pairs (yuko->kiko;
  anaitwa->kinaitwa), converge on the SAME class-4/9-10 output before
  either one ever reaches class 7. That rules out "wrong proxy frame" as
  the explanation and points at something more structural: at layer 12,
  "mtu"'s representation may have a dominant "leave class 1" direction
  that both fits are (perhaps unavoidably, given only a margin-vs-class-1
  objective either way) mostly recovering, with whatever finer
  class-7-vs-4/9-10 distinguishing signal exists either much smaller or
  not separable by a 2-example single-direction fit at this layer.
- **Next optimization to try, motivated directly by this result**: a
  CONTRASTIVE objective that explicitly separates class 7 from class
  4/9-10, not just from class 1 -- e.g. jointly maximize
  `logit(kinaitwa) - logit(inaitwa)` alongside
  `logit(kinaitwa) - logit(anaitwa)`, forcing the fit to distinguish the
  two alternative classes from each other, not just from the origin.
  Not yet run.

## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — Optimization attempt #2 (contrastive objective, explicitly suppress the class-4/9-10 attractor as well as class 1): also failed to reach class 7 -- but failed differently. The direction goes essentially INERT, not just wrong.

- **`nllb_swahili_class7_contrastive.py`**: same layer (12), same fit
  sentences/verb, same 25-step Adam recipe as attempt #1, but the loss
  now jointly maximizes TWO margins per fit example:
  `(logit[kinaitwa] - logit[anaitwa]) + (logit[kinaitwa] - logit[inaitwa])`
  -- explicitly penalizing the class-4/9-10 landing spot, not just the
  class-1 origin. All three forms share their second subword ("itwa")
  and diverge at the first, so this is a clean single-position 3-way
  logit contrast, no multi-step complication.
- **Result: a complete, flat null across the ENTIRE alpha grid tested**
  (500, 800, 1000, 1250, 1500, 2000, 3000) -- byte-identical unsteered
  baseline (`"Mtu anayejua kupika anaitwa mpishi."`) at every single
  alpha, including 3000, a magnitude that was ALREADY causing
  repetition-collapse under attempt #1's direct (non-contrastive)
  class-7 fit. No `FIT FAILED`/zero-gradient error was raised -- the
  fit completed and produced a direction, it just has essentially zero
  observable causal effect on this test sentence at any alpha tried.
- **Two optimization attempts, two different failure modes, neither
  reaching class 7**: attempt #1 (direct, non-contrastive) landed on
  the SAME wrong class as the original proxy fit, then degraded.
  Attempt #2 (contrastive) went INERT instead of wrong. Read together:
  adding the second margin term didn't sharpen the direction toward
  class 7, it appears to have made the two terms partially cancel,
  producing a weaker, more diffuse compromise vector rather than a more
  targeted one. Directly consistent with this project's own prior
  finding on the French track ("more optimizer freedom... has
  monotonically hurt or done nothing at the 1-2-sentence data scale") --
  here it's not more free parameters but a more complex/multi-term
  objective, and the outcome is the same qualitative pattern: added
  complexity at this data scale (2 fit sentences) doesn't help.
- **Standing conclusion on the "how do we learn the steering" thread**:
  both objective-engineering attempts on the SAME tiny 2-sentence fit
  set failed to reach class 7, in two different ways. This is now
  reasonably strong evidence that the bottleneck isn't which specific
  margin objective is used, but the fit-set SIZE/diversity itself --
  pointing toward optimization (2) (more fit sentences/frames per noun)
  or (3) (a probe-style direction across many noun/class pairs) from
  the original 3-option menu, rather than further single-example
  objective variants on option (1). Neither (2) nor (3) has been tried
  yet. The best result of this whole thread remains attempt #0's
  original generic-frame fit (2026-09-25, earlier entry): real,
  control-validated, word-preserving flip to class 4/9-10 at layer 12 --
  just not to the specifically-requested class 7.
- **Not yet done**: (2) refit with several fit sentences spanning
  multiple frames/verbs (not just "kuitwa") per CLAUDE.md's already-
  planned task-definition change; (3) a probe-style direction (many
  noun/class pairs, regularized) instead of a handful of gradient-fit
  examples -- the open decision CLAUDE.md already logs.

## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — Optimization attempt #3 (7 fit sentences, 4 distinct verbs, simple non-contrastive objective): also failed to reach class 7 -- and produced the WEAKEST, least monotonic result of the three attempts. Three consecutive optimization variants on the same single-noun/single-layer setup have now all failed; treating this as a signal to step back rather than try a fourth variant.

- **`nllb_swahili_class7_multisentence.py`**: 7 fit sentences spanning 4
  verbs (kuitwa x4 fillers: farmer/king/guest/shepherd; kufanya, kusoma,
  kuandika x1 each), all independently verified to produce clean class-1
  "ana-" marking, same layer (12), same simple margin objective as the
  ORIGINAL working fit (not the contrastive one) -- isolating fit-set
  size/diversity as the only changed variable, per the user's explicit
  choice ("more sentences").
- **Fit converged far more slowly than any single-frame fit**: mean
  margin loss barely moved across all 25 steps (10.903 -> 10.873 ->
  10.843 -> 10.812 -> 10.780 at steps 5/10/15/20/25) -- roughly linear,
  tiny per-step progress, vs. the single-frame fits' much larger
  movement in the same step budget. Consistent with 7 examples across 4
  distinct verb constructions pulling the gradient in more varied
  directions than 2 examples of one verb do.
- **Result: the weakest, least monotonic outcome of all three
  optimization attempts, and it never reaches class 4/9-10 (attempt
  #0's result) let alone class 7**:
  - alpha=500 and alpha=1000 (identical): `"Mtu wa kupika anaitwa
    mpishi."` -- only the construction-simplification effect (anayejua
    -> wa), "anaitwa" itself never flips at either alpha.
  - alpha=1500, 2000, 3000, 4000 (all four identical): **reverts fully
    to the exact original, unsteered baseline**
    (`"Mtu anayejua kupika anaitwa mpishi."`) -- not degradation, not a
    plateau at the weak effect, a full return to zero effect at higher
    alpha. Non-monotonic in a way none of the prior fits' alpha sweeps
    were (those plateaued or degraded into repetition-collapse; this
    one's effect appears then disappears).
- **Three consecutive optimization variants -- direct-target objective,
  contrastive objective, multi-sentence fit -- have now all failed to
  reach class 7, each failing differently** (wrong-class-then-degrade;
  inert; weak-then-reverts). None beat attempt #0's original result.
  This is no longer "try one more objective tweak" territory -- three
  different, individually well-motivated changes to the SAME
  single-noun, single-layer, 25-step-Adam setup have now all failed to
  improve on it. The most likely explanations, none yet tested: (a) the
  single-noun ("mtu" only) + single-layer (12 only) setup may itself be
  the ceiling, not the objective -- CLAUDE.md's own open question about
  whether a probe-derived direction (many nouns, many classes, properly
  regularized, held-out validation) beats gradient-fitted directions is
  now the most clearly-motivated untried option, not a 4th gradient-fit
  variant; (b) class 7 and class 4/9-10 may not be that far apart at
  layer 12's representation for THIS specific lexical item ("mtu"),
  something a single noun's fits can't distinguish from "class 7 isn't
  reachable at all" without testing a second noun/class-7-target pair.
- **Recommendation, not yet actioned**: pause further gradient-fit
  variants on "mtu" specifically. Either (a) test whether a DIFFERENT
  noun/target-class pair reaches its target more easily at layer 12
  (checks whether "mtu"->class 7 specifically is unusually hard, vs. a
  general ceiling), or (b) build the probe-style multi-noun/multi-class
  direction CLAUDE.md already flags as the standing open question,
  which is a materially different mechanism, not another single-fit
  variant.

## 2026-09-25 (cont.) — Optimization attempt #4 (probe-style direction, 319 nouns x 11 classes, difference-of-means at layer 12): layer 12 IS more separable than the raw embedding table, with linguistically coherent structure -- but the resulting direction has ZERO causal effect, weaker than every gradient-fit attempt. Statistical separability and causal steerability are dissociated here.

- **User's choice**: "probe style direction" -- the materially-different
  mechanism (b) from the previous entry's two options, per CLAUDE.md's
  own standing open question ("Whether a difference-of-means / probe-
  derived direction beats gradient-fitted directions for known-target
  steering").
- **`nllb_swahili_layer12_probe.py`**: three-part script. (1) Extract
  LAYER-12 encoder activations (forward pass only, no generation, no
  gradient -- far cheaper than any fit) for all 319 nouns in the
  agreement lexicon, each in a minimal `"The {noun} is here."` frame, at
  the noun's own encoder position. 319/319 resolved cleanly, 0 skipped.
  (2) Re-run the exact within/between-class cohesion + 50-shuffle
  random-relabeling-control analysis already done on the raw embedding
  table, now on layer-12 activations -- directly tests the premise
  behind the whole pivot to stream-level steering. (3) Build a
  difference-of-means push direction (class-7 centroid minus
  ANIMATE-SG centroid, n=25 vs. n=57) and steer "mtu" in the same test
  sentence, same alpha grid and controls as every gradient-fit attempt.
- **Finding 1, genuinely positive: layer 12 IS more separable than the
  raw embedding table, and the structure is now linguistically
  coherent, not an artifact**:

  | metric | raw embedding table | layer-12 activations |
  |---|---|---|
  | within-class cohesion, real | 0.3085 | 0.2763 |
  | within-class cohesion, control | 0.1798 | 0.1806 |
  | between-class similarity, real | -0.0965 | -0.0788 |
  | between-class similarity, control | -0.0980 | -0.0977 |
  | between-class real-vs-control gap | 0.0015 | **0.0189** |

  The between-class gap is ~12x larger at layer 12 than at the raw
  embedding table -- still small in absolute terms, but the FIRST time
  in this entire investigation that between-class separation shows any
  real signal above the random-relabeling control. The top pairwise
  similarities are also now linguistically sensible rather than
  tokenization artifacts: class 7-8 (cos=0.41, the singular/plural pair
  of the SAME class), class 6-8 and 4-6 (~0.35-0.40, plural classes
  clustering with each other), ANIMATE-PL-ANIMATE-SG (0.34, animate
  clustering with animate) -- a real, interpretable "plurality" and
  "animacy" structure the raw embedding table's shared-prefix artifacts
  never showed.
- **Finding 2, the humbling one: the resulting difference-of-means
  direction has ZERO causal effect on the test sentence, at every
  single alpha tested (500-4000)** -- a complete, flat, byte-identical
  baseline at every point, weaker than EVERY gradient-fit attempt
  including the ones that failed (the multi-sentence fit at least
  caused a construction-level change at low alpha; this doesn't even do
  that).
- **Standing interpretation: statistical separability and causal
  steerability are dissociated at layer 12, cleanly demonstrated by a
  probe-style direction specifically**. This directly parallels this
  project's own French finding (decodability of gender in the embedding
  space did NOT imply a portable causal steering representation) but
  extends it one level further: even a from-many-examples, properly-
  averaged, statistically-cleaner direction, built at exactly the layer
  where separation is real and measurable, still has no causal power
  when simply added to the residual stream. The noisier 2-7-example
  gradient-fit objective -- despite never reaching class 7 -- is
  finding something causally real that the clean statistical average
  is not, most likely because the gradient objective directly optimizes
  logit movement through the actual forward pass (including whatever
  the decoder's cross-attention specifically reads), while a
  difference-of-means is a purely correlational construct with no
  guarantee of alignment to that.
- **Net picture across all four optimization attempts on this thread**:
  none reached class 7. The original 2-sentence gradient fit (attempt
  #0) remains the only one that produced a real, control-validated,
  word-preserving causal flip -- to class 4/9-10, not class 7. Three
  gradient-fit variants (direct-target, contrastive, multi-sentence)
  and now one probe-style direction have each failed differently:
  wrong-class-then-degrade; inert; weak-then-reverts; and now a
  statistically-grounded but completely inert direction. The pattern
  across all four suggests the bottleneck is not any single fixable
  ingredient (objective, data quantity, or statistical construction)
  but something more structurally resistant about reaching class 7
  specifically for "mtu" via a single additive push at layer 12.
- **Not yet done**: test whether a DIFFERENT noun or a DIFFERENT target
  class reaches its goal more easily at layer 12 (would distinguish
  "mtu->class 7 is unusually hard" from "single-position additive
  pushes at layer 12 have a general ceiling this project hasn't found a
  way past yet"); test whether COMBINING the probe direction's
  statistical grounding with the gradient objective's causal grounding

  Phase 1's other planned move from the previous entry: `d0` =

  #4's difference-of-means direction, regularizing

  scale-invariant to the loss once the regularization gradient dominates
  the raw margin gradient's direction** -- multiplying lambda by 20x

  magnitude. **Net: this lambda grid only ever tested two regimes (no

  middle ground (tethered but not frozen) is still UNTESTED.** Would need
  either much smaller lambdas (~0.001-0.02) or a decoupled scheme (apply

- **Reframes the whole thread's priority ordering**: continuing to
  optimize on top of a gamed margin objective (more sentences, more
  targets, probe-regularizing a margin-fitted direction) was building on
  a broken foundation. The logP objective is a legitimate base to build
  on instead. Still outstanding per the correction above: check whether
  v2's own "2.99 gap" result was itself anaitwa->inaitwa escape (very
  likely, given this run's evidence, but not yet directly verified on
  v2's own saved direction).
- **Next**: decide whether to (a) verify v2's direction the same way
  first (closes the loop on the correction), or (b) push the logP
  objective further (more steps -- unlike margin, logP is bounded and
  self-limiting as P->1, so may tolerate more optimization before
  overfitting the way v3's margin run did) before layering the
  previously-queued sentence-count/verb-generality/probe-regularization
  work on top of it. Not yet decided with the user.

## 2026-09-26 (cont.) — Extended logP fit (150 steps, checkpointed, inaitwa tracked throughout per user request): best result in this entire thread, P(kinaitwa) reaches 11.7% at alpha=2000, and inaitwa never re-emerges

- **`nllb_swahili_class7_refit_logp_extended.py`**: ONE continuous fit
  (not restarted per step count) to MAX_STEPS=150, checkpointed at
  25/50/75/100/125/150, same OPT_LR/layer/fit sentences as v2/logp.
  Fit-time `-log P(kinaitwa)` on the 2 fit sentences collapsed to ~0
  (P~99.99% in-sample) by step 40 and stayed there; `||delta||` plateaued
  around 988 -- bounded, self-limiting behavior, unlike margin's v3 run
  which blew past the real activation norm (1589) and collapsed into the
  `huitwa` escape. Confirms the pre-registered expectation that a bounded
  objective would tolerate more steps without that failure mode.
- **Checkpoint tracking on held-out TEST_SENT (fixed alpha=4000,
  P(inaitwa) tracked at every checkpoint per explicit user request)**:
  P(kinaitwa) rose 0.0049 (step 25) -> 0.0823 (step 50) -> plateaus at
  ~0.073-0.075 from step 75 through 150 (essentially flat past 75 steps
  -- extending to 150 bought nothing beyond ~75). **P(inaitwa) does NOT
  re-emerge**: 0.027 (step 25) -> 0.016 (step 50) -> settles at a stable
  ~0.014 from step 75 on, i.e. it DECREASES as training extends, the
  opposite of what the margin objective's escape pattern would predict.
  Decoded text also recovers: the step-25/50 "Mtu"-dropping escape
  ("Nafasi ya kupika inaitwa mpishi.") disappears by step 75, reverting
  to byte-identical baseline text ("Mtu anayejua kupika anaitwa
  mpishi.") at steps 75-150, even though P(kinaitwa) is ~730x higher
  than true baseline at that point -- movement is happening beneath the
  argmax without visibly disrupting the greedy decode.
- **Full alpha grid on the final (step-150) direction found a real,
  non-monotonic PEAK away from the ceiling alpha this whole thread has
  always reported at**: P(kinaitwa) = 0.097 (alpha=1500) -> **0.117
  (alpha=2000, the peak)** -> 0.080 (3000) -> 0.075 (4000). **0.117 is
  ~35x the best margin-objective result (0.0033) and ~1000x above both
  the true baseline (0.0001) and all four controls, which stay pinned at
  0.0001-0.0002 across the ENTIRE alpha grid** -- the largest, most
  control-separated real effect on P(kinaitwa) in this entire thread.
  `inaitwa` stays low and non-monotonic throughout this grid too (max
  0.014 at alpha=4000, never re-approaching its earlier margin-objective
  peak of 0.217) -- the fix from the logP switch holds at every alpha,
  not just the ones checked so far.
- **Still not a flip**: `anaitwa` holds 31-38% and wins argmax at every
  alpha; >50% of mass sits in an unnamed long tail (other_mass 53-63%
  throughout). At the alpha=2000 peak, the actual greedy decode
  restructures into a COPULA escape avoiding the whole `-itwa` paradigm
  entirely -- "Na mwenye ujuzi wa kupika basi huyo ni mpishi." ("Whoever
  has cooking skill, that one IS a cook") -- rather than picking
  `kinaitwa`; a third escape pattern (after the `huitwa` habitual and the
  `Mtu`-dropping structural collapse) that avoids marked class-agreement
  vocabulary altogether. Not yet checked whether this specific escape
  correlates with the alpha range where P(kinaitwa) peaks (plausible:
  restructuring away from the finite `-itwa` verb removes the position
  where the class contest would even occur, which could explain both the
  copula escape AND why P(kinaitwa) doesn't climb further past this
  alpha).
- **Net**: extending steps under the ungamed logP objective is a
  legitimate, real improvement lever (unlike extending steps under
  margin, which was v3's overfitting failure) -- but it plateaus by ~75
  steps at this fit-sentence count (n=2), so further gains likely need a
  different lever (more/varied fit sentences, a finer alpha search around
  1500-2500, or addressing the copula-escape pattern directly) rather
  than more steps alone.
- **Next**: still outstanding -- verify whether v2's original margin
  direction was itself anaitwa->inaitwa escape (not yet directly
  checked). Also worth a finer alpha grid around the 1500-2500 peak
  (currently only sampled at 500-step multiples) before deciding this
  peak is real and not a coincidence of the sampling grid. Sentence-count
  and verb-generality expansions remain queued, now on a legitimate
  (logP) foundation.

## 2026-09-26 (cont.) — Embedding-layer push (user's hypothesis): tested and REFUTED. NLLB-3.3B has 24 encoder layers (checked, not assumed) -- layer 12 is the midpoint, not "near the end" as in the 12-layer French mBART. Embedding fits in-sample just as well but generalizes far worse and noisier than layer 12

- **Motivation, stated up front**: after the logP-extended plateau, user
  hypothesized "mtu" might carry more class information in its own
  static word embedding than in the mid-stack contextual layer this
  thread has always patched. Checked `AutoConfig` directly (not assumed
  from the French mBART precedent): `facebook/nllb-200-3.3B` has
  **encoder_layers=24, d_model=2048** -- layer 12 has always been this
  model's MIDPOINT, with 12 more encoder layers between the patch and the
  decoder, not near-the-end the way "layer 12" would be in the 12-layer
  mBART the French track uses. Never previously stated explicitly in this
  thread's own files.
- **`nllb_swahili_class7_refit_logp_embedding.py`**: ONE changed variable
  vs. `..._logp_extended.py` -- patch site moves from
  `encoder.layers[12]`'s output to `encoder.embed_tokens`'s output
  (verified against the installed transformers M2M100 source: the scale
  factor is applied INSIDE `M2M100ScaledWordEmbedding.forward`, and there
  is no `layernorm_embedding` between embed+pos and layer 0 in this
  architecture, so hooking `embed_tokens` is an exact, no-approximation
  "layer -1" patch site). Alpha grid RESCALED (not reused as-is) by the
  measured norm ratio: embed_tokens output norm at "person" = 373
  (context-independent, as expected for a pre-contextualization lookup)
  vs. layer 12's 1340-1407 -- reusing the old 500-4000 grid would have
  pushed up to 10.7x the embedding's entire own norm, not a comparable
  probe. Same fit sentences/objective/OPT_LR/checkpoint schedule (25-150
  steps) as the layer-12 run, otherwise unchanged.
- **Fits in-sample just as well, actually faster**: `-log P(kinaitwa))`
  on the 2 fit sentences reached ~0 by step 60 (`||delta||` plateaus at
  ~540, i.e. 1.45x the embedding's OWN norm -- proportionally MORE
  perturbation relative to local scale than layer 12 needed, 988/1407 =
  0.70x, despite converging in fewer steps).
- **Generalizes far worse to the held-out TEST_SENT: peak P(kinaitwa) =
  0.0017 (alpha=1060, grid ceiling, still rising) vs. layer 12's peak of
  0.117 (alpha=2000) -- over 40x weaker.** Control separation is also
  much weaker and noisier: layer 12's controls stayed pinned at
  0.0001-0.0002 across the ENTIRE alpha range regardless of alpha; at the
  embedding site, even RANDOM/ORTHOGONAL controls show `anaitwa` climbing
  substantially with alpha (orthogonal seed 0: 0.370->0.489 from alpha=0
  to 1060) -- meaning large perturbations at this very early site get
  amplified unpredictably by all 24 remaining encoder layers regardless
  of DIRECTION, not just ones aligned with "class." `kinaitwa` itself
  stays separated from its own controls (real 0.0017 vs control ~0.0002,
  ~8.5x) but that ratio is two orders of magnitude weaker than layer 12's
  (~1170x). Decoded text also degrades into incoherence faster and more
  severely ("A kuu ya kupika inaitwa kupika." already at step 25) than
  layer 12 ever produced at comparable relative push magnitudes.
- **Verdict: the embedding-layer hypothesis is refuted, cleanly, not
  just unconfirmed.** The class-relevant signal that is actually
  CAUSALLY STEERABLE is concentrated at the mid-stack contextual layer,
  not the static lexical embedding -- despite the embedding fitting the
  training sentences at least as easily. This is a genuine negative
  result (rules out one explanation for the plateau) and reinforces,
  independently, the earlier layer-scan finding
  (`nllb_swahili_layer_scan_10to15.py`) that layer 12 was "uniquely live"
  among 6/12/18.
- **New candidate this negative result raises**: NLLB-3.3B's actual depth
  (24 layers) means the complementary hypothesis -- a layer CLOSER TO THE
  DECODER (e.g. 18-22, fewer remaining layers to reshape/dilute the
  push, more analogous to what "layer 12" would mean in the 12-layer
  French model) -- has never been tested. The existing 10-15 fine scan
  covers only the neighborhood around the model's midpoint, not this
  region. Not yet run.
- **Next**: as before (v2's original-direction verification, finer
  1500-2500 alpha search at layer 12, sentence-count/verb-generality
  expansions), plus this newly motivated layer-18-22 scan. Not yet
  decided with the user which comes first.
