## 2026-09-28 — Layer scan (14-23) finds layer 20 as a strong candidate, full treatment reveals it games the objective via REFERENT SUBSTITUTION, not a genuine flip -- retracting the "first real kinaitwa success" claims made in chat

- **NOTE**: this entry was written late -- the layer-scan, layer-20 full
  treatment, and fine-scan runs below were reported to the user in chat
  as they completed but NOT logged here at the time, against this
  project's own working convention (CLAUDE.md section 7: "Log every
  session's results in status.md"). Reconstructed now, in order.
- **`nllb_swahili_class7_layer_scan_14to23.py`**: coarse screen (25
  steps, logP objective, farmer/king fit sentences, real direction only,
  no controls -- matching `nllb_swahili_layer_scan_10to15.py`'s own
  screening methodology) across layers [14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 23], each
  with an alpha grid rescaled to that layer's own measured activation
  norm at "person" (same proportional coverage as the layer-12 grid).
  Peak P(kinaitwa) per layer: **layer 20 = 0.167** (alpha=7020), layer
  22 = 0.027, layer 18 = 0.023, layer 23 = 0.014, layer 16 = 0.006, layer
  14 = 0.005 -- layer 20 beat layer 12's 150-step peak (0.117) at just
  25 steps. Layers 22-23 showed early signs of catastrophic collapse
  (layer 23: literal "Person Person Person..." repetition by alpha=2112,
  the English source word repeating -- a distinct, more brittle failure
  mode than anything layers <=20 showed). Not a monotonic "later is
  better" trend -- 20 is a local peak, not an endpoint.
- **`nllb_swahili_class7_refit_logp_layer20.py`**: full treatment (150
  steps, checkpointed 25/50/75/100/125/150, same recipe as layer 12's
  extended run, alpha grid rescaled to layer 20's measured norm 2469.68).
  Fit-time loss saturated by step 50 (`||delta||` plateaus at 1648, 0.67x
  local norm). **Checkpoint trace at alpha=3509.9 (the alpha screening
  flagged as producing a complete sentence)**:
  - step 25: P(kinaitwa)=0.040, text ends "...kinachomhusu **kinaitwa**
    mpishi." -- a complete, non-repetitive sentence.
  - step 50: P(kinaitwa)=0.168, text degrades into repetitive "Kina
    kirefu cha kina kirefu cha jina la mtu..." -- still control-separated
    (see below) but linguistically empty.
  - step 150: P(kinaitwa)=**0.285** (~2850x baseline 0.0001, the largest
    number in this entire thread), text is PURE REPETITION: "Kina kirefu
    cha kina kina kuhusu: mtu kina kirefu cha kina kina katika lugha ya
    Kiingereza ni: mtu kina kirefu cha kina kina" (mentions "Kiingereza"
    ["English"] and "Mungu" ["God"] at various steps -- semantically
    empty token cycling, not meaningful text).
  - **Final-checkpoint full alpha grid + controls confirm the collapse is
    specific to the REAL direction, not alpha or scale in general**: all
    four controls (random/orthogonal, seeds 0/1) stay at P(kinaitwa)
    <=0.0001 and byte-identical baseline text across the ENTIRE alpha
    grid (877.5-7019.8) -- the repetition collapse is a genuine property
    of the fitted direction at high step counts, not generic large-alpha
    noise. **New failure mode, distinct from margin's word-escape and the
    embedding site's noisy controls: at this later layer, extended
    optimization games the bounded logP objective via REPETITION
    ("flood the context with ki-/kina- prefixed tokens, which generically
    raises P(kinaitwa) in the teacher-forced position without producing
    anything coherent")**, not via suppressing a competitor. Confirms
    (again) that raw target-token probability, even under an ungamed
    objective, is not sufficient on its own without checking decoded
    coherence.
- **User's suspicion after seeing this: step 25 might ALREADY be
  over-pushing.** `nllb_swahili_class7_refit_logp_layer20_finescan.py`:
  every single step 20-30 checkpointed (same layer/objective/recipe,
  CHECK_ALPHA=3509.9 fixed so step count is the only variable). Result:
  **20-30 is NOT where the repetition collapse happens** -- every step in
  this range is a single well-formed, non-repetitive clause; the
  repetition collapse seen at step 50 must emerge somewhere between 30
  and 50, not below 25. P(kinaitwa) climbs steadily: 0.015 (step 20) ->
  0.040 (25, first kinaitwa appearance) -> 0.075 (step 30, still
  non-repetitive, nearly double step 25's number). Full trace:
  step 20/21: "Mtu ambaye anajua/ana ujuzi wa kupika anaitwa mpishi."
  (Mtu preserved, not flipped); step 22-24: "Mtu" dropped, replaced by
  "Ambaye" (itself class-1-marked), still "anaitwa" (not flipped); step
  25-26: "chakula" ("food") introduced, "kinaitwa" first appears; step
  27-30: "chakula" replaced by "Kina kirefu cha mtu" ("the great
  height/depth of a person" -- semantically odd), "kinaitwa" persists.
- **CORRECTION (user's direct semantic read, confirmed against the data):
  the "kinaitwa" appearances at steps 25-30 are NOT a genuine flip of
  "mtu"/the steering target -- retracting the "first real kinaitwa
  success" language used in chat for this whole thread.** The user
  pointed out that in "chakula kinachohusiana naye kibinafsi,
  kinachomhusu kinaitwa mpishi", the subject and any human referent
  ("mtu"/"ambaye") are both LOST, and the new "subject" ("kina kirefu")
  doesn't semantically connect to the rest of the sentence -- grammatical
  concord chains (kinachohusiana/kinachomhusu/kinaitwa, all ki-/kina-
  prefixed) are self-consistent, but the SENTENCE reads as nonsense
  ("food... which concerns him, is-called a cook" / "the height of a
  person... is-called a cook"), not as "the person is called (class 7) a
  cook." **Checked directly against the data: `kinaitwa` NEVER appears
  in ANY checkpoint (20-30, or the earlier 50/150 steps) without an
  alternate class-7-eligible noun phrase ALSO appearing immediately
  before it** ("chakula" at 25-26, "kina kirefu" at 27+) -- steps 20-24,
  which keep "Mtu"/"Ambaye" as an intact referent and never introduce an
  alternate class-7 noun, NEVER produce "kinaitwa" either (stay
  "anaitwa"). This is a strong, direct correlation, not a coincidence:
  **the actual mechanism the optimizer found is "drift the sentence
  content until some other class-7-eligible noun exists nearby, then
  produce ordinary agreement with THAT noun" -- not "override mtu's own
  class."** A new, more specific failure mode than the repetition
  collapse: REFERENT SUBSTITUTION. This directly validates why CLAUDE.md's
  already-planned sentence-level metric ("success = every agreement
  target of THAT noun flipped... AND all non-agreeing tokens unchanged")
  is necessary and not just extra rigor -- a looser "does the target
  word appear anywhere in the decoded string" check is gameable exactly
  this way, as now directly demonstrated.
- **Net state of the whole class-7 thread after this correction: there
  is still no example anywhere in this project of a genuine, clean
  class-7 flip** (target noun preserved as subject, agreement chain
  pointing AT it changes class, nothing else drifts). Every apparent
  "success" so far (margin-based partial movement, logP's probability
  gains, layer 20's kinaitwa appearances) has turned out on close
  inspection to be either (a) movement toward an unrelated word/class,
  (b) repetition collapse, or (c) referent substitution -- three
  different gaming mechanisms across three different objective/layer
  combinations, not three different partial successes.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. Candidate directions: (a) add
  an automatic check for referent preservation (does "mtu" or a
  class-1-consistent anaphor referring to it survive, with NO alternate
  class-7 noun introduced) before crediting any future decode as
  progress, operationalizing CLAUDE.md's planned sentence-level metric
  now rather than later; (b) investigate why "mtu" specifically resists
  reclassification so strongly (durable finding candidate: human/animate
  referents may carry a much stronger class-1 prior than arbitrary
  lexical gender assignment in French, making noun-side class override
  fundamentally harder than the French gender-flip task this project is
  modeled on); (c) the still-queued finer 1500-2500 alpha search at
  layer 12, sentence-count/verb-generality expansions.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Combined embed+layer20 push (user's proposal): dramatically bigger numbers, same failure modes arriving much faster. Fine scan confirms no window exists where the target referent survives AND real kinaitwa movement is happening. Settled: this direction is worse than layer 20 alone

- **Motivation**: layer 20 alone showed "a more significant impact on
  the sentence" than layer 12 or the embedding did individually --
  hypothesis was that an embedding push (broad, reshaped by all 24
  layers) and a layer-20 push (direct, late, little further reshaping)
  could be complementary. Known prior against this class of change
  (French durable finding: "more optimizer freedom... multi-position...
  has monotonically hurt or done nothing") -- tested rather than assumed
  to fail, since this specific combination was never tried.
- **`nllb_swahili_class7_combined_embed_layer20.py`**: two simultaneously
  patched sites (`encoder.embed_tokens` + `encoder.layers[20]`, both at
  "person"'s position), jointly optimized under one Adam optimizer, same
  logP objective, farmer/king fit sentences. Checkpointed at
  5/10/15/20/25/30/40/50, each deltas applied at their OWN trained
  magnitude (no separate alpha scaling, to avoid a 2D alpha search).
- **P(kinaitwa) reaches 0.878 by step 50 and wins ARGMAX outright from
  step 25 onward -- by far the largest number anywhere in this project.**
  But applying the referent-preservation check from the immediately
  preceding correction: "Mtu" survives only through step 10 ("Mtu
  anayefanya kazi ya kupika anaitwa mpishi.", unflipped); by step 15 it
  is GONE, replaced by "A kina ya kupika inaitwa kupika." (nonsensical);
  by step 20-25, "kina-binadamu" appears (literally "depth-human", not a
  real Swahili word -- plausibly the model grafting "binadamu"
  [human being] onto the hallucinated "kina" referent, but still
  ungrammatical); "kinaitwa" itself doesn't appear until step 30 ("kina
  kina-binadamu cha kupika kinaitwa mpishi."), by which point "Mtu" has
  long since been abandoned; by step 50, full repetition collapse
  ("kina kina cha kupika kinaitwa mpishi.", echoing the same "kina"
  repetition pattern layer 20 alone reached at step 150).
- **Fine scan, steps 11-14** (user's request, checking the exact
  transition): steps 11-13 are unchanged from step 10 ("Mtu anayefanya
  kazi ya kupika anaitwa mpishi.", P(kinaitwa) still 0.0004-0.0006,
  negligible). **Step 14 is a cliff, not a gradient**: "Mtu" is abandoned
  abruptly via a THIRD, previously-unseen escape -- "Mwili wa kupika
  huitwa mpishi." ("Mwili" = body, replacing "Mtu" entirely; "huitwa" is
  the unmarked-habitual escape valve, not even inaitwa/kinaitwa).
  **Confirmed: there is no step anywhere in the combined trajectory where
  the target referent survives AND real kinaitwa-family movement is
  simultaneously happening** -- the transition is binary (intact-but-
  static, then immediately lost to an unrelated escape), not a narrow
  window this scan could have missed by being too coarse.
- **Verdict: combining embed+layer20 does not unlock a new capability --
  it compresses the SAME known failure modes (referent substitution,
  then repetition collapse) into roughly a third the step count layer 20
  alone needed** ("Mtu" lost by step 14 here vs. ~step 22-24 for layer 20
  alone; full collapse by step 50 here vs. step 150 there). This is a
  direct, specific confirmation of the project's own standing finding
  about multi-position optimizer freedom, not just an assumption carried
  over from the French track. **Settled: this direction is worse than
  layer 20 alone, not better, despite far larger raw P(kinaitwa)
  numbers** -- raw target-token probability continues to be an
  unreliable proxy for real progress on its own, exactly as the
  referent-substitution correction already established.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. Remaining candidates: the
  automatic referent-preservation check (still not built -- would have
  caught both this and the earlier correction automatically), the
  "why does mtu resist reclassification" investigation, the finer
  1500-2500 alpha search at layer 12, sentence-count/verb-generality
  expansions.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Probe-guided objective (user's follow-up to the probe check): works exactly as designed on the 2 fit sentences, but the improvement is INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM CONTROL NOISE on the held-out sentence. Reframes the bottleneck as fit-data scale, not the objective

- **Motivation**: the probe check just found layer 20's representation
  frozen (class-7 cosine ~0.227 unchanged across 25-150 steps) despite a
  huge decoder-side effect -- direct evidence pure decoder-logit
  optimization doesn't move the representation. This script puts the
  probe's class-7 direction INTO the objective (not a fixed post-hoc
  regularization anchor like the earlier, Adam-insensitive lambda
  attempt): `loss = -log P(kinaitwa) + lambda * (1 - cos(h+delta-mean,
  c7_centroid))`, both terms sharing one delta, one Adam optimizer.
- **`nllb_swahili_class7_refit_probe_guided.py`**: rebuilt (and cached to
  `nllb_swahili_layer20_centroids.pt` for reuse) the layer-20
  nearest-centroid probe over the same 319-noun/11-class lexicon.
  lambda=0.0 (sanity check) and lambda=5.0 (roughly balances the two
  terms' initial magnitudes), checkpointed every 5 steps to 50.
- **On the FIT sentences (farmer/king, what's actually in the loss):
  lambda=5.0 works exactly as designed** -- cos to class-7 centroid
  climbs from -0.086 (step 10) to +0.302 (step 50), real and
  substantial, vs. lambda=0.0 staying frozen near -0.04 throughout.
- **On the HELD-OUT TEST_SENT, checked at every checkpoint: the
  improvement is tiny (0.227->0.233 over 50 steps) and, checked against
  controls at the final checkpoint, INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM NOISE** --
  random seed 0 = 0.2270, **orthogonal seed 0 = 0.2332 (identical to the
  real direction's own 0.2332 to four decimal places)**, random seed 1 =
  0.2268, orthogonal seed 1 = 0.2228. The real direction's entire
  held-out movement sits inside the spread of random/orthogonal controls
  at the same magnitude -- not a real, control-separated effect.
- **Cost, not just a null result**: lambda=5.0's decoded text stays
  BYTE-IDENTICAL to baseline at every single checkpoint through step 50
  ("Mtu anayejua kupika anaitwa mpishi." unchanged) -- the probe term
  didn't just fail to generalize, it slowed the decoder-side effect too
  (lambda=0.0 at least shows text drift by step 50, "Mtu anayetumia
  lugha ya Kiingereza anayetegemea sana mambo ya kupikia anaitwa
  mpishi.", still preserving "Mtu").
- **Verdict: the probe-guided objective does exactly what it is asked
  to do on the 2 fit sentences, but that improvement does not transfer
  to new sentences at all** -- a clean, direct instance of this
  project's own oldest, most durable finding ("gradient-fitted
  directions are dominated by a word-specific component... different
  words ~=0.03 [cosine]"), now demonstrated for the probe-cosine
  objective specifically, not just the original margin objective it was
  first observed with. **This means the bottleneck this whole session
  has been circling (margin's gaming, logP's representation-freeze,
  now probe-guidance's overfitting) is not really about WHICH objective
  is used at all -- every objective tried so far overfits hard to
  whichever 2 sentences are in the fit set, in its own different way.**
  The fit-data SCALE (n=2) is the more likely common root cause, not any
  single objective's specific flaw.
- **Reprioritization**: the sentence-count expansion (queued early this
  session -- 34 validated `-itwa` sentences already sitting ready,
  `class7_fit_sentence_validation_results.json` -- then set aside for
  the huyo/lambda/layer/probe threads) now looks like the load-bearing
  missing piece, not a secondary nice-to-have, given every objective
  fix tried on top of the SAME 2-sentence fit has independently failed
  to generalize.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. The 34-sentence expansion
  (using whichever recipe -- likely logP, given its cleaner non-gamed
  behavior -- and now checkable against the probe as well as decoder
  probability) is the best-motivated candidate given today's findings.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — 34-sentence layer-20 run: sentence-scale hypothesis REFUTED (probe stays exactly as frozen as with 2 sentences), and the apparent decoder-side gain turns out to be a generic magnitude-triggered collapse, not gaming specific to the fitted direction -- a random ORTHOGONAL direction reproduces the identical decoded sentence

- **`nllb_swahili_class7_refit_logp_layer20_34sentences.py`**: ONE
  changed variable vs. the layer-20 full treatment -- fit sentences
  34 (validated `-itwa` set) instead of 2 (farmer/king), same layer,
  same plain logP objective (dropped the probe-guided term -- it added
  cost without generalization benefit last entry). All 34 built
  successfully. Checkpointed 5-50 steps, tracking BOTH decoder
  P(kinaitwa) and probe cosine-to-class7 (reusing the cached
  `nllb_swahili_layer20_centroids.pt`).
- **Probe cosine stays frozen at 0.2270-0.2271 across the ENTIRE 5-50
  step range -- unchanged to four decimal places, identical to the
  2-sentence run's frozen value.** More fit-sentence diversity did
  nothing to move the representation toward class 7. **Refutes the
  fit-data-scale hypothesis directly** -- it was not, in fact, "just a
  data scale problem."
- Decoder P(kinaitwa) does climb (0.0001->0.0885 by step 50), with text
  staying byte-identical to baseline through step 40, then degrading at
  step 50 into the same repetitive "kina kirefu cha kina kina" pattern
  already seen in the 2-sentence run's later steps (just reached in 50
  steps here instead of ~150 there -- more data made the SAME collapse
  arrive faster, not a different, better outcome).
- **User's direct question: "is it still gaming the objective?"
  Checked precisely with `nllb_swahili_class7_check_gaming.py`** (the
  saved control numbers only logged teacher-forced probabilities, not
  decoded text, so this was verified rather than assumed): decoded text
  at the same norm (1607) for the real direction vs. its own control
  seeds. **`ORTHOGONAL seed=0` -- a random direction with ~zero cosine
  to the real fitted direction -- produces the IDENTICAL decoded
  sentence, character-for-character**: "Mtu kina kirefu cha kina kina
  kinachomhusu mtu wa kimwili ni mtu anayejua kupika." (random seed=0,
  random seed=1, and orthogonal seed=1 all stay at clean baseline text).
- **This is a stronger finding than the earlier referent-substitution
  gaming, not just a repeat of it: the collapse at this magnitude is not
  even specific to the fitted direction's content.** At norm~1607
  (~65% of layer 20's own activation norm), the model's generation
  appears to have a generic instability/attractor state that at least
  one other, UNRELATED direction also falls into at the same magnitude.
  P(kinaitwa)=0.0885 and the "kina kirefu" text are therefore not
  evidence the fitted direction is doing anything distinguishable from
  noise AT THIS SCALE -- confirmed, not inferred.
- **Net state, updated**: every lever tried today -- 3 objectives
  (margin, logP, probe-guided-logP), 4 site configurations (layer 12,
  embedding, layer 20, combined), 2 fit-data scales (2 vs. 34
  sentences) -- has independently failed, via a different specific
  mechanism each time (word-escape, representation-freeze, in-sample-
  only overfitting, referent-substitution, magnitude-triggered generic
  collapse). No genuine, clean, control-separated class-7 flip exists
  anywhere in this project as of this entry.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. Candidate: consolidate
  today's findings into `CLAUDE.md`'s durable-findings section (a lot
  was learned today that should inform future sessions, not stay buried
  in dated status.md entries) before choosing a new direction, rather
  than immediately trying another variant of the same gradient-fit
  approach.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Reset to clean, unfitted observation (user's request): embedding push toward the class-7 centroid produces a real, interpretable pattern (Mtu -> mnyama/mlinzi/mchungaji, then Ki/kiziwi), but a translation check reveals the "class-7 direction" is semantically confounded, not a clean grammatical-class axis

- **Mask-infill check (user's question: could we use `<mask>` instead of
  full translation for evaluation?)**: `nllb_swahili_mask_infill_check.py`.
  NLLB's tokenizer does encode `<mask>` as a real single token (id
  256203, verified against the tokenized ids, not assumed), but the
  model does nothing meaningful with it -- "Mtu <mask>" -> "Mtu Mtu Man"
  (garbage, includes a stray ENGLISH word); "Mtu huyo <mask> mpishi." ->
  "Mtu huyu ni mkali." (ignores "mpishi" entirely, generates an
  unrelated sentence); others default to generic fillers ("mmoja"/"one",
  "fulani"/"a certain"). **Unlike French mBART-large-50 (denoising-
  pretrained, 9/9 correct gender agreement under mask infill per
  `mask_infill_steering_critique_prompt.md`), NLLB is a pure translation-
  finetuned model with no denoising pretraining -- `<mask>` in its
  vocabulary is inherited artifact, not a working capability. Do not
  build evaluation on this for NLLB.**
- **Embedding push toward the class-7 centroid, no fitting, no decoder
  objective** (`nllb_swahili_embedding_push_toward_class7_centroid.py`):
  push_vec = class7_raw_centroid - mtu_raw_embedding (both un-centered
  embed_tokens outputs), alpha=1.0 means mtu's embedding exactly reaches
  the centroid. Clean 3-stage pattern across 4/5 test sentences (TEST_SENT
  itself never responded at all, even at alpha=2.0):
  - alpha 0->1.0 (up to and including sitting exactly at the centroid):
    no effect, text stays byte-identical to baseline.
  - alpha=1.25: "Mtu" replaced by a DIFFERENT, specific class-1 noun --
    "Mnyama" (animal), "Mlinzi" (guard), "Mchungaji" (shepherd) -- not a
    class-7 flip, all class-1 concord (huyo, ana, hu-) stays unchanged.
  - alpha 1.5-2.0: class-7 material finally appears, but degenerate
    (bare, unattached "Ki" prefix fragment, not a real word) except for
    ONE case: "Kiziwi ni mrefu." (alpha=1.5) -- a real, grammatical
    Swahili sentence. At the time, read as "kiziwi" being a genuine
    class-7 HUMAN-referent noun, motivating a hypothesis (below) that
    Swahili class-7 human reference is lexically restricted to
    disability terms. **CORRECTION (user's catch, 2026-09-28, same
    session): kiziwi/kipofu/kilema are absent from this project's own
    agreement-validated lexicon (`swahili_noun_lexicon_agreement_v2.py`)
    entirely -- the "genuine class-7 noun" claim was asserted from
    outside knowledge, never checked against this project's own
    methodology.** Checked directly with the SAME existential-frame test
    the lexicon itself was built with
    (`nllb_swahili_kiziwi_agreement_check.py`): **"Kiziwi yuko hapa."
    and "Kipofu yuko hapa." -- both take `yuko` (the ANIMATE-SG
    override marker), NOT `kiko`.** Both behave as ANIMATE-SG by real
    agreement, exactly like mtu/kipepeo in this project's own original
    2026-09-25 finding, despite their ki- surface shape. **The disability-
    lexical-restriction hypothesis is RETRACTED.** "Kiziwi" was never a
    class-7 success -- it is grammatically identical in class to "mtu"
    itself. Every substitution the sweep produced (mnyama/mlinzi/
    mchungaji/kiziwi) is the SAME phenomenon: mtu replaced by a
    DIFFERENT animate/class-1-agreeing noun, not movement toward class 7
    in any real sense. Only the bare "Ki" fragments even attempted
    something class-7-shaped, and those are degenerate, not real words.
    **This observational sweep therefore found ZERO genuine instances of
    class-7 agreement, not even a partial one** -- a stronger, more
    negative reading than originally logged.
- **User's suspicion, directly tested: "the directions we are moving
  aren't what we think they are."** Multi-centroid push
  (`nllb_swahili_embedding_push_multi_centroid.py`, ANIMATE-PL/9-10/8/7,
  interrupted partway through -- ANIMATE-PL and part of 9/10 completed)
  and, more decisively, a TRANSLATION check
  (`nllb_swahili_mtu_translation_check.py`, SW->EN, "mtu" patched at ITS
  OWN position this time -- see bug note below) confirm it.
- **Bug found and fixed while building the translation check**: the
  earlier embedding-push scripts computed push_vec from SWAHILI word
  embeddings (mtu and the class centroids, looked up via Swahili tokens)
  but APPLIED it at the position of the ENGLISH word "person" in an
  English-source sentence, since all EN->SW generation encoded English.
  NLLB shares ONE embedding table across all 200 languages -- "person"
  (English) and "mtu" (Swahili) are different tokens with different
  embeddings. Those earlier EN->SW push experiments were never literally
  pushing "mtu"'s own embedding; they were pushing "person" by a delta
  vector computed from a different word's relationships. The translation
  check fixes this: SW source, "mtu" patched at its own position.
  (Separately: sentence-initial capitalized "Mtu" tokenizes to a
  DIFFERENT token than lowercase "mtu" -- also caught directly, by a
  `mtu_ids[0] not in enc_seq` skip on the first run, not assumed;
  lowercased the test sentences to match the token the centroid was
  built from.)
- **Result: as mtu's OWN embedding is pushed toward the class-7
  centroid, SW->EN translation shows a clean semantic breakdown, but
  NOT toward anything resembling "class 7" in English terms.** Baseline
  (alpha<=0.5): "the man"/"the person"/"he", stable. At alpha=1.0
  (exactly at the centroid): "mtu huyo ni mrefu." -> **"That's a long
  one."** (complete loss of personhood -- now reads as describing an
  object); "mtu huyo hutembea kila siku." -> **"The kitten walks every
  day."** (shifts to a non-human animal); other sentences shift to "The
  kid..." (younger human). At alpha 1.25-2.0: fluctuates between "He"
  and "The kid," never resolving to anything class-7-like in English.
- **Diagnosis: the "class-7 direction" this entire session has been
  built on is not a clean, isolated grammatical-class axis -- it is
  confounded with whatever semantic content is enriched in our class-7
  noun lexicon (skewing toward small/young/non-human referents, based on
  this evidence).** Pushing along it doesn't preserve "mtu's personhood
  while changing its grammatical class" -- it drags the REFERENT's
  meaning toward that confounded semantic neighborhood instead. This is
  the same class of problem the French track already diagnosed and
  fixed once, using a DIFFERENT method: `build_centroid_gender_direction.py`'s
  `ANIMATE_BLOCKLIST`, built specifically because an unfiltered gender
  centroid showed identical lexical-drift contamination (chanteurs->
  fans/artistes, etudiants->etudes/candidat) there too. This is a more
  precise, more actionable diagnosis than anything found earlier this
  session -- gaming, representation-freezing, and referent-substitution
  were downstream SYMPTOMS of this same underlying confound, not
  separate problems each needing their own fix.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. Best-motivated candidate:
  build a semantically-controlled class-7 direction (e.g. restricted to
  human-referent class-7 words specifically, mirroring the French
  track's inanimate/animate-filtering precedent) rather than a raw
  class-7-vs-everything centroid dominated by non-human semantic
  content. The interrupted multi-centroid push
  (`nllb_swahili_embedding_push_multi_centroid.py`) can be resumed/rerun
  separately if still useful once a cleaner direction exists.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Corrected multi-centroid push (embedding, then layer 20): embedding-level confirms semantic-confound diagnosis even for the ANIMATE-PL positive control; LAYER-20 push is dramatically cleaner and reframes the whole difficulty as a real linguistic fact, not just a confound

- **Fixed the mismatch found last entry and reran properly**:
  `nllb_swahili_mtu_multi_centroid_translation_check.py` -- "mtu"
  (lowercase, matching the token the centroids were built from) patched
  at its OWN position in SWAHILI-source sentences, read out via SW->EN
  translation, across ANIMATE-PL/9-10/8/7.
- **Even the positive control (ANIMATE-PL, mtu's own plural, cos=0.168)
  failed at the embedding level**: never produces "people"/"they" --
  holds onto singular human reference (he/man/son) longer than the
  other classes, then breaks down the SAME way at alpha>=1.0 ("mtu huyo
  ni mrefu." -> "That's a long one.", identical to class 7's result on
  the same sentence). **Each class showed its own distinct, non-
  grammatical "flavor" of drift**: 9/10 -> consistently BIRDS (bird,
  owl, seagull, sparrow); 8 (lowest cosine to mtu, 0.092, most
  orthogonal) -> most degenerate, literal Swahili morpheme "vi" (the
  class-8 plural prefix itself) leaking untranslated into English
  output; 7 -> consistently young/small (kid, kitten, matching the
  previous entry). Confirms the embedding layer alone cannot do this
  cleanly for ANY target, not just class 7.
- **User's diagnosis: this is expected, and matches a prior French-track
  lesson -- a pure embedding-space push has no "stream." The model
  never runs its contextual layers over the new location, so neither
  language has any grounding for what it means; a complete test needs
  the push to be at a site the model's own contextual processing
  produces, not just the input lookup table.**
- **`nllb_swahili_mtu_layer20_multi_centroid_translation_check.py`**:
  same method, LAYER 20 instead of the embedding layer. Required fresh
  layer-20 centroids built from bare SWAHILI single-word inputs (the
  existing cached `nllb_swahili_layer20_centroids.pt` was built from
  ENGLISH context frames, the same EN/SW mismatch already found and
  fixed for the embedding layer -- caught and avoided this time, not
  repeated). Cosines to mtu are much higher here (0.77-0.82) than at the
  embedding layer (0.09-0.27) -- contextual layer-20 representations
  compress toward a shared "subject-position noun" signal, with
  class-specific content a smaller component on top.
- **Result: dramatically more coherent than the embedding-level push.
  ANIMATE-PL now produces genuinely CORRECT results**: "mtu huyo ni
  mrefu." -> "the men are tall." (alpha 1.0-1.5); "mtu huyo yuko hapa."
  -> "The people are here." (alpha 1.0-1.25) -- clean, correct
  pluralization (mtu->watu), the first unambiguous success in this
  entire session's observational work.
- **Classes 7/8/9-10 drift toward INANIMATE OBJECTS, not random
  animals**: "the height of the building.", "The boxes are here.", "the
  length of the paper.", "The door is here." -- no bird/kitten/octopus
  chaos, no morpheme leakage. Coherent, grammatical English throughout,
  just a different referent.
  | class | cos(mtu) | drift |
  |---|---|---|
  | ANIMATE-PL | 0.805 | stays human, correctly pluralizes |
  | 9/10 | 0.817 (highest) | paper, answer, news |
  | 8 | 0.771 (lowest) | boxes, building |
  | 7 | 0.797 | door, box, building |
- **Reframing: this is not just a confound, it may be a real linguistic
  fact the model has correctly learned.** Classes 7/8/9-10 are, in
  actual Swahili, overwhelmingly populated by inanimate objects (tools,
  containers, household items); genuine class-7/8 human reference is the
  rare exception (confirmed directly this session: kiziwi/kipofu take
  ANIMATE-SG's `yuko`, not class-7's `kiko`, despite their ki- shape --
  see the retraction two entries above). Pushing mtu toward these
  classes' average isn't dragging it toward arbitrary noise -- it is
  dragging it toward what those classes statistically ARE. A model that
  has faithfully learned Swahili's noun-class distribution would
  reasonably resist "personhood + class 7" as a combination, because
  that combination is close to linguistically non-existent in the
  language it was trained on. This reframes the project's core
  difficulty: it may not be that steering CAN'T do this -- it may be
  that the model is correctly representing a target that barely exists
  in the language, and any successful steering will need to fight that,
  not just find a better direction/objective/layer.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. Worth considering: (a) random/
  orthogonal-direction controls at layer 20 for this same sweep, to
  confirm the "objects" drift is specific to these centroids and not a
  generic large-push effect (per the earlier gaming-check precedent);
  (b) revisit whether "steer mtu to class 7" is even the right target
  given this finding, versus e.g. testing the steering mechanism on a
  noun/class pair that DOES productively exist in Swahili (mirroring how
  ANIMATE-PL just worked cleanly) before returning to the harder,
  possibly not fully well-posed class-7 case.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Layer-12 rerun of the multi-centroid translation check: user's diagnosis refined, not confirmed as stated -- the "lands on an existing word" failure mode is depth-independent, not specific to layer 20

- **User's read of the layer-20 result**: the push doesn't create a
  coherent "mtu-but-reclassed" representation -- it lands near an
  EXISTING word's natural contextual location (paper/boxes/building/
  door) and gets decoded via THAT word's own learned associations, not
  anything that maps back to "person." Proposed testing a lower layer to
  see if this is layer-20-specific.
- **`nllb_swahili_mtu_layer12_multi_centroid_translation_check.py`**:
  identical method, LAYER 12 instead of 20 (the most extensively studied
  layer in this whole project, chosen for direct comparability). Fresh
  layer-12 raw centroids built the same way (bare SW single-word input).
- **ANIMATE-PL still works, even slightly MORE consistently than at
  layer 20**: "The men are tall." (alpha>=1.5), "The people are here."
  (alpha>=1.0), "The walkers walk every day." (alpha>=1.0 -- this exact
  sentence was completely flat/unresponsive at layer 20; here it
  responds correctly), "the owners of the house." All 4 test sentences
  now show correct human pluralization, vs. layer 20's one non-responder.
- **But classes 7/8/9-10 show the SAME "lands on an existing word"
  pattern, with remarkably consistent SPECIFIC words across both
  layers**: class 8 -> "boxes"/"box" at BOTH layer 20 and layer 12;
  class 7 -> "box" at BOTH layers; class 9/10 -> "answer" at BOTH
  layers (plus patient/staff/plan at 12, paper/news at 20 -- same
  abstract/institutional flavor, not identical words but the same kind
  of content). This consistency across two different depths is itself
  informative: it suggests these are stable properties of what is
  actually semantically enriched in these classes in our lexicon, not a
  layer-20-specific geometric artifact.
- **Verdict: the user's hypothesis is refined, not confirmed as
  stated.** Going to a shallower layer does NOT escape the "landing on
  an existing word" failure mode -- it is the same problem one layer
  earlier, not a layer-20 quirk. This is a stronger, more general
  negative result than "layer 20 has a problem" would have been: it
  rules out depth as the explanation and points toward something more
  fundamental about how these dense contextual representation spaces get
  decoded, independent of which layer is probed.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. The ANIMATE-PL success now
  replicates cleanly at two different layers, strengthening it as a
  genuine positive result and a natural mechanism-understanding
  baseline. Still open: random/orthogonal controls for this whole
  sweep (never yet run for the observational centroid-push work); testing
  whether even-shallower layers change anything; or accepting the
  depth-independence finding and moving to a different investigative
  angle for class 7 specifically.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Nearest-neighbor check: steered vector lands in the RIGHT semantic neighborhood, not on a specific word -- but the real finding is that SW and EN decoders disagree about what the same steered vector means

- **User's question**: does the layer-20 push land on (near-identical
  to) an EXISTING lexicon word, or just near a similar one?
  `nllb_swahili_nearest_neighbor_check.py`: cached per-word (not just
  per-class-mean) raw layer-20 vectors for all 319 nouns, then for four
  representative (class, sentence, alpha) cases, ranked the steered
  vector's cosine similarity against every individual word.
- **Sanity check**: mtu's own top neighbors are watu (people, 0.836),
  mchezaji (player, 0.785), mwanamke (woman, 0.785), mvulana (boy,
  0.784) -- sensible, confirms the method.
- **Answer: lands in the correct semantic CLUSTER, not on a specific
  word.** Class-7 case (alpha=1.5): top 5 neighbors are kikapu
  (basket), kitanzi (loop), kifuniko (lid), kigae (tile), kitambaa
  (cloth) -- ALL genuinely class 7, ALL small household objects, a
  coherent group -- but similarities only 0.86-0.88, well below the
  ~1.0 "same word" would show (and even below mtu's own top neighbor,
  0.836). Class 8 case: vifurushi/vikapu/vigae/vitambaa (packages/
  baskets/tiles/cloths), same pattern. Class 9/10: kazi/njia/mambo/nchi
  (work/road/matters/country), similarly a coherent but non-identical
  cluster. So the steered vector genuinely moves into the right region
  of the target class's real semantic content, but does not collapse
  onto any single existing word.
- **More important finding, surfaced while checking this: SW->SW and
  SW->EN outputs for the SAME steered vector DISAGREE substantially.**
  | case | SW->SW | SW->EN |
  |---|---|---|
  | class 7, alpha=1.5 | "Mchungaji huyo yuko hapa." (shepherd) | "The box is here." |
  | class 8, alpha=1.25 | "Mchungaji huyo yuko hapa." (shepherd) | "The boxes are here." |
  | class 9/10, alpha=1.25 | "Yeye yuko hapa." (he/she, a PRONOUN) | "The answer is here." |
  | class 7, alpha=2.0 | "Mzee huyo ni mrefu." (elder) | "the height of the building." |

  The Swahili decoder consistently keeps this as a DIFFERENT PERSON
  (shepherd, elder, or a personal pronoun) -- never an object. The
  English decoder, reading the exact same internal representation,
  consistently drops personhood entirely. Same vector, two different
  interpretations depending on which language decodes it.
- **This corrects, not just adds to, the earlier "semantic breakdown
  toward inanimate objects" diagnosis (two entries above): that finding
  was specific to the ENGLISH decoding pathway.** The Swahili pathway --
  the one this project actually needs -- never gives up personhood at
  this magnitude; it substitutes a DIFFERENT human noun, echoing the
  very first (uncorrected) embedding-push result (mnyama/mlinzi/
  mchungaji) rather than confirming the "drifts to objects" story. The
  EN translation check was a genuinely useful, correct diagnostic for
  what it measured, but it was never measuring the pathway that matters
  for the actual deployment goal -- SW/Kitaita output specifically.
- **Practical implication for future checks**: SW surface output must be
  read in parallel with any translation-based check from now on, not
  substituted for it -- the two can and do diverge substantially, and
  relying on EN translation alone would have kept pointing this
  investigation at the wrong failure mode (object-drift) instead of the
  real one in the language that matters (person-substitution).
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — First properly-powered noun-class direction: built from ~1500 sentences (57 animate + 25 class-7 nouns, 18 varied templates each, noun-disjoint split), real selectivity +0.299 at layer 12. Steered mtu with it -- still never reaches class 7

- **User's request**: stop fitting on 2-34 sentences of a single noun
  (mtu); build a general noun-class direction from MANY nouns x MANY
  contexts first, then steer with THAT.
- **Data build, efficiently** (`nllb_swahili_animate_1000sentences_extract.py`,
  `nllb_swahili_class7_450sentences_extract.py`): sentences built by
  STRING TEMPLATE, not translation -- all ANIMATE-SG nouns share one
  validated agreement pattern (huyo/ana-/hu-/yuko), so grammatically
  correct Swahili could be constructed directly and extracted via cheap
  single forward passes (no generation), making ~1500 examples tractable
  in minutes. 57 ANIMATE-SG nouns x 18 templates = 1026 sentences (0
  skipped); 25 class-7 nouns x 18 templates (class-7 agreement:
  hicho/kina-/kiko, kirefu/kizuri adjective concord) = 450 sentences (0
  skipped). Two template families flagged as compositional-by-analogy,
  not independently verified ("kina X" possessive, "hutembea" habitual
  invariance) -- noted, not silently assumed correct. Incidental finding:
  "kina" (depth) is ITSELF a real class-7 word in our lexicon, retroactively
  explaining the "kina kirefu cha..." repetition seen in earlier
  gradient-fit runs -- not random morpheme leakage, a real nearest word.
- **`nllb_swahili_animate_vs_class7_direction.py`**: first genuine
  Hewitt & Liang style probe for Swahili class in this project --
  noun-disjoint train/test split (16 nouns held out entirely, including
  several that kept appearing as drift attractors: mchungaji, mzee,
  mtoto), discriminative logistic-regression probe AND a difference-of-
  means centroid, both compared against a noun-type-shuffled control.
  **Layer 12: real accuracy 93.75%, control 63.9%, selectivity +0.299**
  -- the first non-trivial, properly-validated selectivity number this
  project has ever produced for Swahili class (smaller than French
  gender's +0.45, but real). Layer 20: same real accuracy, but
  selectivity only +0.163 (control accuracy jumps to 77.4%) -- layer 20
  is statistically less separable even though it showed stronger causal
  effects all session, the same separability/steerability dissociation
  as Optimization attempt #4, now with the opposite asymmetry. Probe and
  centroid directions agree well (cosine 0.89 at layer 12); the simple
  centroid slightly OUTPERFORMS the trained probe (95.8% vs 93.75%).
- **`nllb_swahili_mtu_layer12_learned_direction_steer.py`**: pushed
  mtu's OWN mean vector (averaged across its 18 contexts in the animate
  dataset, not a single bare-word lookup) toward the class7_mean from
  this new dataset, at layer 12, on the 4 established SW test sentences,
  reading out BOTH SW and EN, with full random/orthogonal controls.
  **Class 7 NEVER appears, at any alpha, on any sentence.** Instead:
  substitution to a DIFFERENT animate noun ("Mume wake" -- her husband;
  "Mnyama" -- animal), OR a genuine grammatical class shift but to the
  WRONG class ("Mchoro huo **uko** hapa" -- the drawing is here, class 3,
  not 7 -- notably the agreement marker DID correctly flip yuko->uko,
  confirming this is a real class change, just to the wrong target), OR
  the subject dropping out entirely ("ana nyumba." with no noun at all).
- **Controls: 3 of 4 clean, 1 exactly replicates the real direction --
  the same "generic collapse basin" phenomenon already found once this
  session** (layer 20, 34-sentence run): random seed 0/1 and orthogonal
  seed 0 stay flat/inert (clearly distinguishable from the real
  direction's drift); orthogonal seed 1 reproduces the real direction's
  output CHARACTER-FOR-CHARACTER across all 4 sentences and 6 alphas,
  including identical odd mistranslations ("The cage is tall.", "the
  cat has a home."). Confirms this is a real, reproducible model
  phenomenon (already validated once with a dedicated check script), not
  a new bug -- at sufficient magnitude, some unrelated directions land in
  the same attractor as the real one. 3/4 control separation means the
  real direction's effect is still mostly genuine, just not clean.
- **Verdict: a properly-powered, statistically-validated direction
  (highest selectivity yet, noun-disjoint accuracy 93.75%) behaves
  QUALITATIVELY DIFFERENTLY from every prior under-powered attempt --
  it triggers a real class change in one case, not just word-escape or
  representation-freezing -- but it OVERSHOOTS PAST class 7 into
  neighboring territory (another animate noun, or class 3) rather than
  landing on it.** This is new, real information: the direction from
  mtu toward "generic other class" is apparently easier for this
  mechanism to find/trigger than the direction specifically to class 7 --
  the target is not just hard to reach, it may be a narrow target
  surrounded by easier-to-reach alternatives in the same general
  direction.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Discriminative PROBE direction (not the centroid): first clean, control-separated, grammatically consistent class-7 output in this entire session -- "Kifaa hicho kiko hapa." (device, cl.7, correct concord throughout). Still substitutes a different word, not mtu itself, but the target is now demonstrably reachable

- **`nllb_swahili_mtu_layer12_probe_direction_steer.py`**: same test
  sentences/magnitude scale/controls as the centroid-direction run, ONE
  changed variable -- applies the DISCRIMINATIVE PROBE direction
  (logistic-regression weight vector) instead of class7_mean-mtu_mean.
  Notably cos(probe_direction, mtu-specific centroid-diff direction) =
  only 0.48 (vs. 0.89 against the POPULATION-level animate-vs-class7
  centroid direction reported earlier) -- mtu's own path to class7
  diverges more from the probe direction than the population average
  does, confirming this is a meaningfully different direction, not a
  minor variant.
- **3 of 4 sentences ("ni mrefu", "ana nyumba") stay surface-level FLAT
  across every alpha, in BOTH the real direction and all four
  controls** -- uninformative either way, not evidence for or against.
  "hutembea" shows MORE surface movement in controls than in the real
  direction -- also not supportive.
- **"yuko hapa" gives a clean, fully control-separated positive result:
  at alpha=2.0, the real probe direction produces "Kifaa hicho kiko
  hapa."** ("That device is here.") -- a fully grammatical, INTERNALLY
  CONSISTENT class-7 sentence: kifaa (device, class 7), hicho (class-7
  anaphoric demonstrative, correct), kiko (class-7 existential,
  correct). Every agreement marker matches class 7. **All four controls
  (random seed 0/1, orthogonal seed 0/1) stay at "mtu huyo yuko hapa."
  unchanged for this exact same sentence/alpha** -- unlike the centroid-
  direction run, where orthogonal seed 1 coincidentally replicated the
  real result, here NONE of the controls replicate it. Fully
  control-separated, not a generic-magnitude artifact.
- **Caveat, stated plainly: this is not "mtu reclassified."** The output
  substitutes a DIFFERENT lexical item (kifaa, "device/tool") for mtu,
  not "mtu" itself surviving with flipped class. Does not yet achieve
  the project's actual target (preserve referent, change class) -- but
  it is the first clean, grammatically consistent, control-validated
  class-7 output produced by ANY method this entire session (margin,
  logP, probe-guided-logP, embedding push, layer-12/20 centroid push,
  now layer-12 discriminative probe). Real evidence the target region is
  reachable via this general mechanism, even though the specific path
  that keeps mtu as the referent hasn't been found yet.
- **Read together with the centroid-direction result**: the probe
  direction is MUCH more conservative (3/4 sentences never move at all,
  vs. the centroid direction moving 3/4 sentences by alpha=1.0-1.25) but
  when it does move, it lands cleanly on class 7 rather than overshooting
  to a different class (3, "Mchoro") or a different animate noun. This
  suggests the probe direction, fitted specifically to discriminate
  class-7 from animate (not just "away from animate" like the centroid

- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. Natural candidates: finer

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Combined embedding + layer-12 probe push: TWO clean, fully control-separated class-7 outputs (up from one), confirming the user's mechanistic hypothesis -- but "mtu" itself still never survives, always a different real class-7 word

- **User's hypothesis, precisely stated**: the layer-12 probe push alone
  has to fight 12 layers' worth of already-baked-in "mtu-ness" (the
  embedding and layers 0-11 are completely unmodified by a layer-12-only
  patch), which plausibly explains why it needs a huge push and lands on
  a DIFFERENT word (kifaa) rather than "mtu, reclassified." Testing
  whether ALSO removing the identity signal at the embedding source
  changes this.
- **`nllb_swahili_mtu_combined_embed_layer12probe_steer.py`**: embedding
  push (mtu's own raw embedding -> class-7 centroid from the full
  319-noun lexicon, `nllb_swahili_embedding_raw_class_centroids.pt`) AND
  the layer-12 discriminative PROBE direction (selectivity +0.299),
  applied SIMULTANEOUSLY at mtu's position, each scaled by its own
  natural distance (309.32 embedding, 811.49 layer 12) at the same alpha
  fraction. Same 4 SW sentences, dual SW+EN readout, full random/
  orthogonal controls at both sites together.
- **Two clean, fully control-separated class-7 outputs, not one:**
  - "yuko hapa" at alpha=1.0: **"Kifaa hicho kiko hapa."** (device is
    here) -- the SAME clean result as the layer-12-alone run, but now
    reached at HALF the alpha (1.0 vs. 2.0). All four controls stay at
    "mtu huyo yuko hapa." unchanged, verbatim, at this exact alpha --
    fully control-separated.
  - "ni mrefu" at alpha=2.0 (new, did not appear in the layer-12-alone
    run): **"Kioo hicho ni kirefu."** (that mirror/glass is tall) --
    kioo is a real class-7 noun in our own lexicon; hicho and kirefu
    both correctly class-7. All four controls give different, non-
    class-7 results ("Yeye ni mrefu.", "Mnyama huyo ni mrefu.",
    "Huyo ni mrefu.", "Hakika yeye ni mrefu.") -- also fully separated.
- **Confirms the hypothesis directly: combining sites makes class-7
  easier and more frequent to reach, not just faster at one sentence.**
  Both new-word substitutes (kifaa "device", kioo "mirror/glass") are
  genuine physical objects, consistent with everything else this session
  has found about class 7's dominant semantic content in our lexicon.
- **The core pattern still holds, though: "mtu" itself never survives
  as the referent in either clean hit.** This is real, measurable
  progress toward reliably reaching the target region (2 clean hits
  instead of 1, at a lower alpha) -- but not yet the project's actual
  goal (preserve the referent, change only its class). Every clean
  class-7 output found so far, across every method this session, has
  been a word SUBSTITUTION, never mtu with flipped agreement.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. Natural candidates: check
  whether the two "winning" alphas (1.0 for yuko hapa, 2.0 for ni mrefu)
  generalize to the other 2 sentences with finer search; check via
  nearest-neighbor (mirroring the earlier layer-20 check) whether kifaa/
  kioo are literally the closest lexicon words to where these pushes
  land, to understand why THESE two words specifically keep recurring.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Probability check reveals a tokenization confound, then a full rebuild for class 9/10 (cleanest class by tokenization) reveals a DEEPER obstacle: animacy overrides class label even under steering

- **User's precise question**: at the exact pushes that produced clean
  class-7 hits, how high is P(mtu) really? Checked via full-word joint
  probability (chain rule across subwords, not just the first-subword
  softmax, which was initially checked with a bug -- the manual
  decoder_input_ids omitted `decoder_start_token_id` (2, == eos_token_id),
  verified directly against `model.config` and fixed before trusting any
  number).
- **Finding: "Mtu" is not straightforwardly losing to "Kifaa"/"Kioo"
  specifically.** Case 1 (yuko hapa): P(Mtu)=0.77% > P(Kifaa)=0.50% --
  Mtu individually beats the word that actually got generated. Case 2
  (ni mrefu): P(Kioo)=0.71% > P(Mtu)=0.17% -- here Kioo genuinely wins.
  **The mechanism in case 1: "Kifaa"/"Kioo"/"Kikapu" etc. all share the
  first subword `_Ki`, which collectively totals 3.56% -- greedy decoding
  picks the best FIRST TOKEN, not the best full word, so it commits to
  "some Ki- word" before knowing which one, purely because the whole
  family outweighs "Mtu" as a single first-token choice.** Mtu has
  definitely lost its dominant position (baseline ~100% for this
  template; here under 1%), but not necessarily to any specific rival --
  to the aggregate pull of an entire tokenization-sharing family.
- **User's hypothesis, tested quantitatively first**: class 7 might be
  disadvantaged BECAUSE so many of its nouns share first subwords.
  `check_class_tokenization_sharing.py`: class 7 has 60% first-subword
  sharing (25 nouns, 10 unique first subwords), class 8 is worse at 65%
  -- the two classes targeted all session are literally the two worst by
  this measure. **Class 9/10 has 0% sharing** (30 nouns, all 30 unique
  first subwords) -- the cleanest candidate in the entire lexicon.
- **Full rebuild for class 9/10, per the user's request** ("steering
  only one of the items does not help"): first verified its agreement
  markers empirically rather than assuming
  (`nllb_swahili_9_10_agreement_check.py`) -- found the existential
  frame ("iko hapa") used for animate/class-7 templates is UNRELIABLE
  here (several nouns escape to the generic "ni" copula: "Kazi ni
  hapa.", "njia ni hapa.", "Barua ni hapa."), so templates instead use
  three patterns confirmed reliable: `hiyo` (demonstrative), `ndefu`
  (adjective concord, 3/3 confirmed), `ina-` (SP+TAM prefix, confirmed
  via "Nyumba hiyo ina paa."). Built 540 sentences (30 class-9/10 nouns
  x 18 templates, 0 skipped) the same efficient way as before (string
  templates, no translation, cheap forward-pass extraction) --
  `nllb_swahili_class9_10_540sentences_extract.py`.
- **`nllb_swahili_animate_vs_class9_10_direction.py`**: same Hewitt &
  Liang methodology as class 7 (noun-disjoint split, control task).
  Layer 12 selectivity +0.297 (nearly identical to class 7's +0.299).
  **Layer 20 selectivity +0.467** (control accuracy drops to near-chance
  46.7%) -- dramatically higher than class 7's layer-20 selectivity of
  +0.163, and the best statistical separability found anywhere this
  session, comparable to the French gender track's own +0.45 benchmark.
- **`nllb_swahili_mtu_combined_embed_layer12probe_9_10_steer.py`**: same
  combined embedding+layer-12-probe method as the class-7 version.
  **Real direction reliably lands on "Ndege" (bird/plane, a genuine
  class-9/10 lexicon noun) across ALL 4 sentences at alpha>=1.0** --
  "Ndege huyo ni mrefu.", "Ndege huyo yuko hapa.", "Ndege huyo husafiri
  kila siku.", "Ndege huyo ana nyumba." -- far more consistent than
  class 7's combined result (2/4 sentences, different alphas each).
  Fully control-separated: all four controls either stay completely
  unchanged or drop to a generic pronoun ("Yeye"/"Huyo") -- NONE ever
  introduce a new content noun, unlike the real direction's consistent
  "Ndege." At alpha=2.0 "ni mrefu" shifts further to "Mti huo ni mrefu."
  (tree, class 3, `huo` concord) -- a third class again, echoing class
  7's "Mchoro" excursion.
- **But the agreement markers are `huyo`/`yuko` (ANIMATE), never `hiyo`
  (the class-9/10 form actually validated for this exact word list).**
  Our lexicon's own gloss for ndege is "bird(s)/plane(s)" -- genuinely
  ambiguous, and here the model is consistently choosing the ANIMATE
  ("bird") reading over the class-9/10 ("plane"/shape-class) reading,
  triggering animate-override agreement -- the SAME phenomenon this
  entire Swahili track started from (mtu/kipepeo: animate referents
  override shape-class regardless of lexical/shape label,
  `swahili_agreement_class_probe.py`, 2026-09-25).
- **Verdict: the tokenization fix worked exactly as hypothesized (4/4
  sentences hit the SAME lexical target reliably, vs. class 7's 2/4 at
  different alphas each) -- but this surfaced a DEEPER obstacle than
  tokenization.** When steering lands near a word with ANY plausible
  animate reading, the grammar reverts to animate agreement regardless
  of that word's nominal class label. This is not a new problem
  invented by steering -- it is the project's own founding finding about
  Swahili agreement, now shown to hold even under aggressive artificial
  intervention, not just in natural unsteered usage. Tokenization was a
  real, fixable confound; animacy-override appears to be a much more
  fundamental property of how this model represents Swahili grammar.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. Candidate: repeat this same
  combined test on a class-9/10 SEMANTICALLY DISAMBIGUATED noun (one
  with no plausible animate reading at all, e.g. nyumba/house or
  pesa/money) to test whether avoiding "ndege"'s inherent animacy
  ambiguity produces genuine class-9/10 concord this time.

## 2026-09-28 (cont.) — Probability check on the class-9/10 combined push: "Ndege" wins decisively (30-70%, not a close fight), which makes the animacy-override finding sharper, not weaker

- **`nllb_swahili_mtu_probability_9_10_clean_hits.py`**: same rigorous
  full-word joint-probability method as the class-7 check, applied to
  the class-9/10 combined embedding+layer-12-probe push at alpha=1.0
  (where "Ndege" appeared reliably across all 4 sentences).
- **P(Ndege) massively dominates P(Mtu) individually, in every
  sentence** -- ni mrefu: 69.9% vs. 0.033% (~2000x); yuko hapa: 29.8%
  vs. 0.13% (~224x); hutembea: 56.1% vs. 0.044% (~1266x); ana nyumba:
  66.5% vs. 0.040% (~1665x). **This is qualitatively different from the
  class-7 case, where "Mtu" sometimes individually outscored the word
  that actually got generated (Kifaa) and only lost via a first-subword-
  family aggregation effect.** Here there is no such ambiguity -- "Ndege"
  wins outright and overwhelmingly on its own.
- **This makes the animacy-override finding sharper, not weaker: even
  with this much certainty about WHICH noun gets chosen (Ndege locked in
  at 30-70%), the model still confidently applies ANIMATE agreement
  (huyo/yuko), not class-9/10 agreement (hiyo/ina-).** Not a marginal
  effect losing a close fight against the steering -- the data is
  consistent with two separate, largely independent decisions: the
  steering has enormous, confident control over WHICH noun gets
  generated, but negligible effect on the AGREEMENT PATTERN applied to
  it, which appears to be governed by a separate, animacy-driven
  judgment made regardless of how the noun itself was selected.
- **Next**: not yet decided with the user. The nyumba/pesa (animacy-
  unambiguous) test proposed in the previous entry remains the natural
  way to check whether this separate agreement-judgment mechanism can
  ever be moved, or whether it is animacy-locked regardless of which
  inanimate-only noun is targeted.

## 2026-09-28

- **User suspicion: "mtu did not move."** Built
  `nllb_swahili_verify_mtu_actually_moved.py` -- direct before/after
  measurement of mtu's own hidden vector at both push sites, on
  `"mtu huyo yuko hapa."`, at the same alpha=1.0 combined push used in
  the 9/10 probability-check runs above. **Confirmed mtu unambiguously
  moved**: `||after - before||` matches the intended push magnitude
  exactly at both sites (embed: 269.59 vs 269.59; layer12's own
  contribution: 508.79 vs 508.79 -- the hooks are not silently
  attenuated or no-op'ing), and the directional change is large, not
  cosmetic: cos(before, after) = **0.27** at the embedding layer,
  cos(unsteered, final) = **0.37** at layer 12 (0.50 from the embedding
  push alone, before layer 12's own push is even added). The embedding
  push (269.59) is comparable in size to mtu's own baseline norm
  (278.66) -- this is already a large-magnitude intervention, not a
  small one. **This rules out "the intervention isn't really applying"
  as the explanation for the animate-override behavior in the 9/10
  results above; the representation change is real and substantial.**
- **Follow-up user question: try a stronger alpha?** Recommended against
  it before testing anything else: the embedding push is already ~the
  same size as mtu's own vector norm, and the project's own prior
  finding (layer-20 alpha scan, `nllb_swahili_class7_check_gaming.py`)
  is that past some magnitude, even an ORTHOGONAL unrelated direction
  reproduces the same collapsed output as the real one -- a bigger win
  at higher alpha would not be distinguishable from generic collapse.
  Proposed testing the "unpatched context anchoring" hypothesis instead
  (decoder copying huyo/ana straight from their own, un-steered encoder
  positions in the source sentence) -- user agreed.
- **`nllb_swahili_context_anchor_check.py`**: patches the SAME
  class-9/10 direction (identical alpha=1.0, embed+layer12 combined,
  per the established recipe) at mtu's position AND the agreement
  marker's own position (huyo or ana), vs. the established mtu-only
  baseline -- one change per experiment: only WHICH positions get
  patched differs between conditions. Noun choice held constant by
  teacher-forcing "Ndege" (the noun that dominates at alpha=1.0 across
  all sentences) as the decoder prefix, isolating the marker-choice
  question from the already-answered noun-choice question. Markers
  checked are the ones independently verified in
  `nllb_swahili_9_10_agreement_check.py` (hiyo/ndefu/ina-), not the
  unreliable existential "iko".
  - `"mtu huyo ni mrefu."`, huyo/hiyo: ratio class910/animate 0.031 ->
    0.093 when marker position is also patched (P(huyo) drops
    0.758->0.396) -- the one case with a real, if small, effect in the
    predicted direction.
  - `"mtu huyo ana nyumba."`, huyo/hiyo: ratio 0.011 -> 0.007 -- moved
    the WRONG way when the marker position was also patched.
  - `"mtu huyo ana nyumba."`, ana/ina: ratio 0.0087 -> 0.0096 --
    negligible change.
  - **Verdict: weak, inconsistent support for the context-anchoring
    hypothesis.** Even directly patching the exact token position that
    decides the marker's own surface form, with the same push that
    demonstrably moves mtu's representation, leaves the animate form
    10-100x more likely than the class-9/10 form in every case tested.
    Simple copy-through from an unpatched position is NOT the primary
    explanation. Consistent with the standing framing: agreement-marker
    choice looks like a separate, animacy-driven judgment largely
    decoupled from which specific encoder positions are patched, not an
    artifact fixable by patching more positions.
- **Next**: the nyumba/pesa (animacy-unambiguous target) test from the
  previous entry is still the natural way to check whether this
  agreement-judgment mechanism is animacy-locked regardless of target,
  or whether it can move for a genuinely inanimate-only noun with no
  plausible animate reading (unlike ndege, which is ambiguous
  bird/plane and lets the animate reading win by default).

  3. **Natural (unsteered!) agreement preference already splits by

    the earlier context-anchoring result better than the anchoring
    hypothesis itself did.** All of this session's class-9/10 steering
    sentences are animate-noun templates with mtu's surface form
    swapped in ("mtu huyo ni mrefu.", "mtu huyo ana nyumba.") -- the
    PREDICATES (is tall, has a house, is here) are things said about
    people, not airplanes. When steering lands the noun on "Ndege"
    inside one of these sentences, the surrounding predicate content is
    already disambiguating it toward the bird sense, which the base
    model treats as animate-concord-eligible on its own, independent of
    any push. This is a property of sentence CONTENT, not of any single
    marker token's position -- explaining why directly patching huyo/ana's
    own encoder position (previous entry) only had a weak, inconsistent
    effect: patching a token doesn't change what the rest of the
    sentence is semantically about.

- **Phase 0a/0b: the decisive sense-vs-concord check.** Built

  sub-tests with the same alpha grid and controls as Test 3.
  - **Sub-test A (translation drift)**: applied the direction to `ndege
    ametua.` and translated SW->EN at each alpha. Baseline (alpha=0):
    "The bird has landed." At alpha>=0.5: **"The plane has landed."**
    at every alpha tested. **Confirms Claude/ChatGPT's sense-swap
    component is real** -- when a plausible reinterpretation exists,
    the model takes it.
  - **Sub-test B (the decisive one): same direction applied to `ndege
    ameimba.`** ("the bird has sung" -- kuimba/"to sing" is
    BIRD-EXCLUSIVE, no plausible airplane reading, closing off the
    sense-swap escape route). Baseline translation confirms
    bird-exclusivity: "The bird has sung." Baseline P('imeimba')/
    P('ameimba') = 0.0111 (strongly animate, as expected for a genuinely
    bird-only sentence).
    | condition | baseline ratio | peak ratio (alpha) |
    |---|---|---|
    | REAL (layer-17 pair direction) | 0.0111 | **199.4** (alpha=1.5) |
    | random seed 0 | 0.0111 | 0.067 (alpha=2.0) |
    | random seed 1 | 0.0111 | 0.103 (alpha=2.0) |
    | orthogonal-null seed 0 | 0.0111 | 0.120 (alpha=2.0) |
    | orthogonal-null seed 1 | 0.0111 | 0.059 (alpha=2.0) |
    **Real peak / best control peak = 199.4/0.12 = 1665x separation** --
    over 200x LARGER than Test 3's own 7.89x separation on the
    sense-ambiguous verb (ametua/imetua: real peak 92.3, best control
    peak 11.7). The ratio doesn't just move, it undergoes a clean
    crossover (0.011 -> 199, i.e. imeimba goes from ~90x less likely to
    ~200x MORE likely than ameimba) on a verb where "the plane has sung"
    is semantically nonsensical.
  - **Verdict: the pure sense-swap hypothesis (Claude's Q1, ChatGPT's
    hypothesis #9) is falsified by this test, in the specific form
    proposed.** The mechanism is not merely riding along on a bird->
    plane reinterpretation -- it forces class-9/10 CONCORD onto the verb
    even when the referent cannot plausibly be reinterpreted, and does
    so more cleanly (bigger, more control-separated effect) than in the
    sense-ambiguous case. Combined with sub-test A, the more accurate
    picture is: **the direction pushes toward "class-9/10 concord
    commitment," and the model resolves that pressure via WHICHEVER
    route is available** -- reinterpreting the noun's sense when one
    exists (ametua/ndege, sub-test A), or forcing unusual/marked concord
    onto a sense-fixed referent when no reinterpretation route exists
    (ameimba, sub-test B). This is genuinely a concord-control
    mechanism, not a disguised sense-swap -- though sub-test A shows it
    is also willing to "cheat" via sense-swap when that's available and
    presumably cheaper. **Not yet checked**: what the actual translated
    OUTPUT of steered `ndege ameimba.` looks like under generate() (does
    it produce something like "The plane has sung" -- accepting
    incoherence -- or dodge into a different, coherent sentence?) --
    worth a quick follow-up translation check, not yet run.

    ndege mechanism is more likely to generalize to a genuinely

    search) than the critiques' central hypothesis suggested -- worth
