## 2026-09-30 — Phase 2 (new target): family-averaged direction transfer test

**Motivating observation**: Phase 1's completed 25/25 causal transfer
matrix (2026-09-29) found two clean FAMILIES, not one universal
direction and not pure noun-specificity — Family A = {ndege, nyumba}
(class-9/10-adjacent) and Family B = {mtu, mwalimu, mtoto} (genuinely
class-1). All 6 within-family off-diagonal cells cleared the target's
own control peak; all 8 cross-family cells failed. This motivates the
specific follow-up flagged in that entry's "Next" and promoted to
Phase 2 in `cross_noun_class_signal_roadmap.md`: **does a single
FAMILY-AVERAGED direction (not per-noun) transfer within its family
about as well as the individually fitted per-noun directions did?**
If so, deployment may need only ~2 shared directions (one per family)
rather than a fit per noun.

**Failure criterion (stated before running)**: if the family-averaged
direction's peak ratio falls below the target noun's own control peak
for most within-family members, the per-family-shared-direction
hypothesis fails and per-noun fitting remains necessary.

Built `nllb_swahili_family_averaged_direction_transfer_check.py`,
extending the canonical `nllb_swahili_multi_noun_fit_and_transfer_matrix_check.py`
pipeline (CLAUDE.md hard rule #10) rather than forking it: identical
audit/fit/eval recipe (layer 17, 25 Adam steps, OPT_LR=1.0,
amefika/imefika, same 5 nouns), but this run persists each noun's
fitted direction to disk for the first time (the original run never
saved them, only summary stats), adds per-noun resume-from-checkpoint
(load an existing `_direction.pt` instead of refitting) per the
long-run checkpointing convention, then:
1. builds the full-family average for each family and evaluates it on
   every member's own test sentence against that member's own control
   peak (already established, no new controls needed);
2. for Family B only (n=3, so the leave-one-out average of the other 2
   is genuinely new information, unlike Family A's n=2 case where LOO
   collapses to an already-measured single-noun transfer cell), builds
   3 leave-one-out family averages and tests each on its held-out
   member;
3. extends the geometric matrix with cosine(family-avg direction, each
   individual member direction).

Launched as a background run (~60-90 min expected, same cost as
Phase 1's fit stage); results pending.

**Results (complete): the per-family-shared-direction hypothesis
SURVIVES — not just "as well as," in three cases the family average
beats the individual per-noun fit outright.**

All 5 individually-refit directions reproduced the exact Phase 1
numbers (confirms the rerun is faithful, not a different result by
accident): ndege 1.163e10/2.141, nyumba 4.104e9/2.030, mtu
112.6/0.0223, mwalimu 0.666/0.0117, mtoto 5.029e10/0.0345
(real_peak/best_control_peak).

**Full-family average, tested on every member's own test sentence —
5/5 clear their own control peak:**

| target | family-avg peak_ratio | own control peak | own individual peak | vs. individual |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ndege (A) | 1.31e8 | 2.14 | 1.16e10 | below (expected, avg dilutes) |
| nyumba (A) | 2.16e8 | 2.03 | 4.10e9 | below (expected) |
| mtu (B) | 4811 | 0.0223 | 112.6 | **ABOVE individual** |
| mwalimu (B) | **8.67** | 0.0117 | 0.666 | **crosses ratio=1 -- individual never did** |
| mtoto (B) | 4.60e4 | 0.0345 | 5.03e10 | below (individual's own peak is at alpha=3000, outside the 3-point transfer grid {500,1000,2000} used here -- not a clean apples-to-apples comparison) |

**The mwalimu result directly resolves the open question from this
session's discussion of it**: mwalimu's individual fit topped out at
0.666 (never crossing 1) across the full alpha grid up to 3000, which
looked like it could be either a genuine ceiling or an under-pushed
curve (the ratio was still climbing at alpha=3000, no plateau). The
family-B-averaged direction reaches 8.67 -- decisively above 1 -- at
alpha<=2000, i.e. *less* pushing than mwalimu's own fit used. This
means mwalimu's difficulty was a property of its own noisy 3-sentence
fit, not a hard barrier in the model.

**Leave-one-out family-B average (n=3, so this is a genuine 2-noun
average that never sees the held-out target's own data) -- all 3
cells clear control, and mwalimu's LOO result (10.25) is even better
than the full-family-average result (8.67) that included mwalimu's
own direction:**

| held-out | others averaged | peak_ratio | own control peak | own individual peak |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| mtu | mwalimu+mtoto | 1.82e4 | 0.0223 | 112.6 (LOO beats individual) |
| mwalimu | mtu+mtoto | **10.25** | 0.0117 | 0.666 (LOO beats individual AND crosses 1) |
| mtoto | mtu+mwalimu | 34.2 | 0.0345 | 5.03e10 (LOO far below individual, but still ~1000x control) |

This is genuine held-out generalization within Family B, not just
curve-fitting on already-seen directions -- two of three cases the
2-noun leave-one-out average outperforms the target's own individual
per-noun fit.

**Geometric matrix (cosine of family-avg direction vs. every
individual member) confirms the same block structure Phase 1 found,
now from the average's perspective:**
```
                 ndege    nyumba       mtu   mwalimu     mtoto
familyA_avg     0.8389    0.8389    0.1907    0.0946    0.1658
familyB_avg     0.1535    0.1845    0.7862    0.7530    0.6998
```
(familyA_avg's identical 0.8389 cosine to both ndege and nyumba is a
geometric necessity of averaging exactly 2 unit vectors -- not itself
evidence of anything -- but the sharp within-family/cross-family
split, echoed in familyB_avg's 0.70-0.79 vs 0.15-0.18, is the same
real structure as Phase 1's per-noun cosine matrix.)

**Verdict**: the failure criterion stated above (family-average peak
below the target's own control for most within-family members) did
NOT trigger -- the opposite happened. **Deployment implication
upgraded from "plausible" to "supported by held-out evidence": ~2
shared directions (one per family) may be usable in place of a
per-noun fit**, and for at least mwalimu, the shared direction is
actively better than trying to fit that specific noun alone. Caveats
before generalizing further: (a) n=5 nouns across 2 families is still
a small sample -- Phase 1's roadmap item about testing whether more
families emerge with more nouns is now higher priority, since the
practical payoff (replace N fits with ~2) is now empirically
motivated, not just plausible; (b) the transfer-matrix alphas here
only went to 2000, one step short of the full grid's 3000, so mtoto's
"below individual" comparisons above are not fully matched-alpha; (c)
this only tests the SAME verb pair (amefika/imefika) used throughout
Phase 0/1 -- generalization to other class-pair transitions and other
verbs is untested.

**Next**: extend mwalimu's own alpha grid past 3000 (queued, per this
session's discussion, alongside a control check at the same higher
alpha to rule out the known magnitude-triggered-collapse failure
mode); then decide whether to extend the noun set to look for a third
family or test whether the two found families are the whole story.

**CORRECTION (same day, 2026-09-30): free-generation check reveals the
verdict above overstates usability. Per-noun teacher-forced ratio is
NOT a valid proxy for "the sentence is actually usable" -- this
project has hit this exact trap before (2026-09-28's referent-
substitution and magnitude-collapse findings) and it recurred here,
undetected until checked directly, exactly the kind of gap CLAUDE.md's
planned Stage 2 sentence-level metric (section 3, item 2) exists to
close.** Built `nllb_swahili_family_averaged_generation_check.py`:
free-generation (greedy, forced Swahili-target, NOT teacher-forced)
of each noun's own test sentence under baseline / own individual
direction (at its reported peak alpha) / family-average direction
(alpha=2000) / leave-one-out family-B average (alpha=2000, for
mtu/mwalimu/mtoto).

| noun | own individual fit | family-average | leave-one-out |
|---|---|---|---|
| ndege | `Ndege imeanza safari.` -- clean, noun kept, correct concord | `Ndege imeanza kupaa.` -- clean, same | n/a (family A) |
| nyumba | `HABARI KUU Moto wa Msiba Wazuka Nyumbani` -- **complete derailment, not a sentence about nyumba at all** | `Nyumba Inatetemeka.` -- clean, coherent, correct concord | n/a (family A) |
| mtu | `Yetu imefika.` -- **noun replaced by a pronoun (referent substitution)** | `mtu wako imewasili.` -- noun kept, main verb flips correctly, but possessive `wako` stays class-1 (partial/inconsistent) | identical to family-average |
| mwalimu | `mwalimu wako ni hapa.` -- **evades the test via a copula that carries no class marking, never actually flips anything** | `Mwalimu imefika.` -- **perfect minimal pair, exactly one token changed, exactly the target form** | `Mwalimu imefika.` -- same perfect result, genuinely held-out |
| mtoto | `imefikia imefika.` -- **garbled, not a sentence** | `Yetu imefika.` -- **noun replaced by a pronoun** | `Mtoto imefika.` -- perfect minimal pair, held-out |

**This flips which mechanism looks best.** The individually-fitted
per-noun directions -- the ones with the most extreme probability
ratios -- are usable in only 1/5 cases (ndege); the other 4 achieved
their high ratio via collapse, evasion, or substituting the noun away,
none of which is fixable downstream (there is no noun left for
dictionary substitution to act on in the mtu/mtoto substitution
cases). The full family-average is usable in 3/5 (ndege, nyumba,
mwalimu) with mtu partially usable (internal disagreement) and mtoto
failing the same way its individual fit's neighbor did. **The
leave-one-out family-B average is the most reliable of everything
tested: 2/3 cases (mwalimu, mtoto) are perfect, minimal, deployment-
ready flips, and the third (mtu) is the same partial result as the
full average, not worse.**

**Revised verdict**: the "per-family direction can replace per-noun
fitting" conclusion is not just supported, it looks like the *better*
mechanism on a dimension the ratio metric couldn't see -- the shared
direction avoids the individual fits' overfit-to-3-sentences failure
modes (collapse, evasion) more often than it introduces new ones. But
"deployment-ready" still overstates it: mtu's possessive-disagreement
problem recurs in both the family-average and leave-one-out versions,
so it's a property of the mtu/class-1-possessive interaction, not
something averaging fixes. n=1 sentence per noun here (the same
"{noun} amefika." test sentence throughout) -- this is a single-
sentence spot check, not a powered generation-quality result, and
should not be treated as more than a caveat + direction-finder for
Phase 3's already-planned sentence-level metric work.

**Next (revised)**: before extending the noun set (previous "Next"),
Phase 3's sentence-level metric (CLAUDE.md section 3, item 2 -- check
EVERY agreement target flips, not just the main verb) should move up
in priority -- mtu's possessive-disagreement failure is exactly the
multi-target case that metric is designed to catch and the current
single-verb ratio metric cannot. Also worth a quick multi-sentence
generation check (not just one templated test sentence) before
trusting the mwalimu/mtoto leave-one-out "perfect" results as
general, since n=1 sentence could itself be a lucky draw.

## 2026-09-30 (cont.) — Two follow-ups requested by the user: multi-target (possessive+verb) fitting, and a scaled-up noun set at a lower alpha

**Motivating observations**: (1) the generation-check correction above
found mtu's steered sentence flips the main verb but leaves the
possessive `wako` (class-1 form) unflipped -- exactly the multi-target
gap CLAUDE.md's planned sentence-level metric is meant to catch, and
directly fixable by adding the possessive as a second fit target. (2)
alpha=3000 was where nyumba's individual fit derailed into an unrelated
news-headline fragment in that same check -- alpha=1500 (never yet
tried as a primary evaluation point, only as one grid value among many)
is a plausible sweet spot: enough push for a real flip, less risk of
the magnitude-triggered collapse documented on 2026-09-28.

**Failure criteria (stated before running)**: for (1), failure is
"the multi-target fit still doesn't flip the possessive in free
generation" -- would mean the objective wasn't the bottleneck. For (2),
failure is "the new nouns don't reproduce the two-family split, or
alpha=1500 doesn't clear each noun's own control peak" -- would mean
either family generalization was a 5-noun coincidence, or alpha=1500 is
too weak to be useful.

Built `nllb_swahili_family_scaled_multitarget_fit_check.py`, extending
the canonical pipeline (not forking, hard rule #10): reuses
`audit_candidates`/`build_decoder_prefix`/`encode`/`evaluate_direction`
unchanged; adds a new `fit_direction_multi_target` that generalizes the
existing single-target margin objective to a list of (decoder_prefix,
orig_id, flip_id) targets per fit sentence (single-target sentences are
a strict special case, so Family-A nouns' math is unchanged from
before).

- **Scaled noun set**: Family A grows from {ndege, nyumba} to {ndege,
  nyumba, barua/letter, kalamu/pen} -- the two additions pulled from
  this project's own empirically-labeled `swahili_noun_lexicon_agreement_v2.py`
  (both independently labeled class "9/10" there, not asserted by this
  session). Family B grows from {mtu, mwalimu, mtoto} to add
  {mwanafunzi/student, mkulima/farmer, mgeni/guest} -- all three labeled
  "ANIMATE-SG" in that same lexicon, the same empirical class as
  mtu/mwalimu/mtoto. Total 10 nouns, up from 5.
- **Multi-target fit for Family B only**: each Family-B noun's fit data
  is its usual 3 audited verb-only templates PLUS one new combined
  sentence `"{noun} wako amefika."`, fit toward BOTH targets at once
  (possessive `wako`->`yako` right after the noun, verb `amefika`-
  >`imefika` right after "{noun} wako"). Family-A nouns are NOT given
  this template -- forcing `wako` on an already-class-9/10 noun would
  push it the wrong way; their possessive is only monitored (via a
  poss_peak metric using their existing verb-only direction), not
  fit toward, as a check that the verb push doesn't collaterally break
  their already-correct "yako".
- Tokenization verified before running (not assumed): `wako`/`yako` are
  each single, distinct-first-token subwords (ids 21197/13817,
  first_divergence=0) -- a clean minimal pair exactly like
  amefika/imefika.
- **ALPHA_GRID changed to [0, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000]** -- dropped 3000
  (the documented collapse-risk zone) from the default grid; 1500 is
  the user-requested headline point, kept alongside 2000 for context
  rather than reported alone.
- Leave-one-out family averaging now runs for BOTH families (Family A
  grew to n=4, past the n>=3 threshold where LOO stops being trivial).
- Per-noun checkpointing (resume from an existing `_direction.pt`)
  kept, using NEW filenames (`nllb_swahili_family_scaled_*`, not the
  earlier run's `nllb_swahili_family_avg_*`) since Family B's fit
  recipe changed (multi-target) -- reusing the old single-target
  files would have silently skipped the whole point of this run.

Launched as a background run. Expected cost is higher than the
previous 5-noun run: Family B's fit step now does 5 forward+backward
passes per step (3 single-target + 2 for the combined sentence) vs 3
before, and there are 10 nouns instead of 5 -- roughly 2.5-3x the

sentence for Family B so both targets are visible at once) is planned
once fitting completes.

**Results (ratio metrics, complete): both extensions cleared their
stated failure criteria on the teacher-forced ratio metric.**

Per-noun multi-target fit (Family B), verb_peak / poss_peak / verb-
given-original-possessive_peak / best_control_peak:
| noun | verb_peak | poss_peak | verb\|orig_poss_peak | control_peak | pattern |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mtu | 8843 | 52.0 (crosses 1) | 1.18e4 | 0.0213 | BOTH targets flip |
| mkulima | 4.60e4 | 4.26 (crosses 1) | 1.83e4 | 0.00387 | BOTH targets flip |
| mtoto | 2.20e10 | 0.380 (fails) | 1.84e8 | 0.0345 | verb flips, independent of possessive |
| mwanafunzi | 1.08e5 | 0.373 (fails) | 7446 | 0.00564 | verb flips, independent |
| mgeni | 351 | 0.722 (fails, closest) | 3381 | 0.00750 | verb flips, independent |
| mwalimu | 0.938 (fails) | 0.630 (fails) | 0.105 (COLLAPSES) | 0.00948 | neither flips; verb flip is COUPLED to (weakened by) forcing the original possessive as context |

mtu's multi-target fit is a large improvement over its old single-
target fit (verb_peak 112.6 -> 8843, ~78x), not just an addition of a
new capability -- richer fit data helped the original objective too.
mwalimu's coupling finding is new and mechanistically informative: for
most of Family B the verb flip doesn't care what the possessive is
doing, but for mwalimu, committing to the OLD class-1 possessive
actively drags the verb back toward the old form -- a real per-noun
difference in how tightly the agreement targets are bound together,
not just a difference in how hard each one is to move individually.

Scaled noun set + full/leave-one-out family averaging (both families,
verb-only metric): **all 10/10 nouns cleared their own control peak
under the full-family average, and all 10/10 cleared it again under
leave-one-out** (Family A's LOO is now meaningful with n=4, unlike the
5-noun run where n=2 made it trivial). Several LOO/full-average cells
again beat the individual fit outright (ndege, kalamu, mtu, mkulima
under full-average; mtu under LOO), and mwalimu's LOO result (1739)
again dramatically beats its own individual fit (0.938) and even beats
the full-family-average (286.4) -- replicating the original 5-noun
run's most striking finding on a larger, partially new noun set.
Family A's two new members (barua, kalamu) reproduce the same
qualitative pattern as ndege/nyumba, but with a notable difference:
their own best_control_peak is 2-3 orders of magnitude higher (553,
623 vs 1.27, 1.45) -- random/orthogonal directions swing much harder
on these two nouns at the same alphas. Real separation ratios stay
enormous regardless, but this is a genuine, unexplained per-noun
difference worth remembering before assuming "high control peak" means
something is wrong.

**Failure criteria did not trigger for either extension** -- neither
"multi-target fit still doesn't flip the possessive" (2/6 nouns fully
succeeded, a real if partial win) nor "new nouns break the two-family
split or alpha=1500 doesn't clear control" (it generalized cleanly).

**CORRECTION (same day): the long-sentence generation check the user
requested next reveals this ratio-metric success is again a poor proxy
for deployment usability once the sentence is longer than the 2-4 word
test template -- the SAME trap as the first generation-check
correction above, now recurring at a different sentence length, not a
one-off.** Built `nllb_swahili_family_scaled_long_sentence_generation_check.py`:
free-generation (same methodology as before) on two long, multi-target
sentences ("{noun} wako mzuri amefika nyumbani jana usiku." for Family
B; "barua yako ndefu imefika salama asubuhi hii." for Family A,
monitoring case) that add a THIRD agreement target (the adjective
mzuri/nzuri) never included in any fit, across mtu/mwalimu/mtoto/barua
at alpha=1500/2000, individual/family-average/leave-one-out.

**No case produced a fully clean multi-target flip with everything
else preserved.** Concrete outcomes:
- **mtu**: individual direction gives a garbled partial flip (adjective
  flips to nzuri unprompted, but wako drifts to "Yetu", verb doesn't
  flip, noun reordered). Family-average AND leave-one-out at BOTH
  alphas produce literally NO change at all (byte-identical to
  baseline except adverb order) -- alpha=1500/2000, which overwhelmed
  control by orders of magnitude on the short test sentence, does
  nothing here. Confirms alpha requirements are sentence-length-
  dependent, not a fixed property of the direction.
- **mwalimu**: all three steered conditions (individual, full-average,
  LOO) converge on the SAME clean partial flip -- mzuri->nzuri (the
  UNFIT adjective target flips!) while wako and the verb both stay
  class-1. Stable across alpha 1500/2000 and across which direction is
  used. Grammatical and coherent, just internally mixed-class.
- **mtoto**: a NEW failure mode not previously documented in this
  project -- CODE-MIXING. Family-average@1500 inserts the English word
  "favorite" into the adjective slot ("Yetu favorite mtoto alikuja...");
  leave-one-out@1500 inserts "lovely" in the same slot. Both are
  semantically on-topic (positive-quality adjectives, matching mzuri's
  meaning) but in the wrong language entirely. Family-average@2000 and
  the individual direction both instead produce a clean concord flip
  (yako, imefika) but DROP THE NOUN mtoto entirely -- the referent-
  substitution failure mode from the first generation check, recurring
  here specifically for mtoto under stronger pushes.
- **barua** (Family A, "should already be correct" case): individual
  direction and family-average@2000 converge on the IDENTICAL derailed
  output ('Barua imeandikwa kwa njia ya moja kwa moja asubuhi ya leo.'
  -- "has been WRITTEN", wrong verb meaning, yako/ndefu both dropped) --
  this convergence across different directions at the same alpha is
  the signature of the already-documented magnitude-triggered-collapse
  failure mode (2026-09-28), recurring here, not a new problem.
  Family-average@1500 and LOO@1500 are milder but still not clean:
  both drop yako AND ndefu and add an invented "bila X" ("without X")
  clause not in the source sentence.

**Revised understanding**: the two-family / shared-direction mechanism
is real and reproducible (confirmed again on 5 new nouns), but its
demonstrated success is specifically WITHIN the narrow sentence shape
and alpha range it was measured on. Extending sentence length surfaces
at least three distinct failure modes -- (1) alpha that worked at one
sentence length can do literally nothing at another (mtu), (2) partial,
stable, grammatical-but-mixed-concord flips can be the actual ceiling
for a given noun regardless of which shared direction is used
(mwalimu), (3) a previously undocumented code-mixing failure mode
alongside the already-known referent-substitution and magnitude-
collapse ones (mtoto). None of this invalidates the ratio-metric
results themselves -- they are still real, correctly-computed measures
of what they measure -- but it sharpens exactly why CLAUDE.md's planned
sentence-level metric (check every target AND that non-agreeing
content is unchanged) is necessary before any ratio number should be
read as "this works for deployment," even a family-averaged/leave-one-
out one that looked strong on a short sentence.

**Next**: (a) queued from before -- 3f, the amefika-direction's
cross-marker-type transfer to yuko/iko, added to
`cross_noun_class_signal_roadmap.md`; (b) worth adding an alpha SWEEP
(not just 1500/2000) specifically on long sentences before concluding
anything is a hard ceiling -- mtu's "zero effect" result was only
checked at 2 points; (c) mwalimu's stable adjective-only partial flip
across every condition suggests trying the SAME multi-target trick
that fixed part of the short-sentence case (add the adjective as an
explicit third fit target, not just possessive+verb) -- it already
flips on its own here, so making it an explicit target plus the
existing two might close mwalimu's gap the way the possessive target
helped mtu; (d) the new code-mixing failure mode (mtoto) has only 2
data points -- worth a quick dedicated check (does it recur on other
Family-B nouns / other adjectives) before treating it as a real,
general phenomenon rather than a fluke of this one sentence.

## 2026-09-30 (cont.) — Embedding-layer version of the same methodology (user's "is the stream correcting the nudge" hypothesis)

**Motivating observation**: the long-sentence check above found alpha
values that overwhelmed control at the short test sentence did nothing
at all for mtu on a longer one, and mwalimu/mtoto/barua all showed
partial or collapsed flips. User hypothesis: patching encoder layer 17
gives the remaining layers (18-23) and/or surrounding context room to
correct the perturbation before the decoder sees it, and wants the
identical methodology tried at the embedding layer instead, to see if
patching before any encoder processing behaves differently.

**Noted before running**: this mechanically cuts both ways -- an
embedding-level change gets MORE downstream layers to be corrected by
(24, not 7), which argues against the hypothesis; but it also gets
integrated into every layer's attention computation from the start
rather than arriving "late," which could argue for it. Also on record:
a DIFFERENT, non-gradient-fitted embedding method (bare centroid push)
was already tried early in this project (2026-09-26) and found to
generalize worse/noisier than the encoder-layer approach -- that does
NOT settle this question, since this is the current best (multi-
target, family-averaged, gradient-fitted) recipe's embedding analogue,
not the old method, so it's being checked directly rather than assumed
to transfer.

**Alpha recalibration (measured, not assumed)**: a norm check at the
"mtu" position in the long test sentence found embed_tokens' raw
output norm ~=279 vs. layer 17's output norm ~=1381 at the same
position -- ~4.95x smaller. ALPHA_GRID scaled down accordingly to
[0, 100, 200, 300, 400, 600] (the old grid divided by ~5, with a bit of
headroom at the top) to keep the push comparable in RELATIVE terms,
not raw units.

Built `nllb_swahili_family_scaled_multitarget_embedding_fit_check.py`,
reusing (not reforking) the fitting/averaging/LOO code from the
layer-17 script unchanged -- it already takes `layer_module` as a
parameter, so only the patch site and the alpha grid differ. Launched
as a background run; results pending.

**Results (complete): the hypothesis is NOT supported -- embedding-
layer steering is clearly weaker and noisier than layer 17 across the
board, not more robust.** User's own read while results were still
coming in ("I think results of embedding layer are clearly subpar to
those of layer 17") is confirmed by the full data.

Per-noun individual fits (verb_peak / best_control_peak), compared to
the layer-17 run's numbers:
| noun | embedding verb_peak | embedding control | layer17 verb_peak | layer17 control |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ndege | 378 | 174.7 (2.2x sep.) | 9.469e8 | 1.271 (7.4e8x sep.) |
| nyumba | 730.2 | 19.13 (38x) | 1.993e9 | 1.449 |
| barua | 5379 | 2417 (2.2x) | 1.467e13 | 553 |
| kalamu | 683.1 | 684.2 (FAILS, <1x) | 4.476e6 | 623.1 |
| mtu | 1.936 (crosses 1, weak) | 0.04423 | 8843 | 0.0213 |
| mwalimu | 0.1142 (fails) | 0.006616 | 0.9382 (also fails, but closer) | 0.009482 |
| mtoto | 1.907e6 (strong) | 0.04483 | 2.199e10 | 0.03448 |
| mwanafunzi | 0.4462 (fails) | 0.01007 | 1.08e5 | 0.00564 |
| mkulima | 0.6039 (fails) | 0.005834 | 4.604e4 | 0.003866 |
| mgeni | 0.1651 (fails) | 0.02229 | 351.1 | 0.00750 |

Two systematic differences from layer 17, both working against the
hypothesis: (1) control peaks are consistently 10-1000x higher at the
embedding layer -- random/orthogonal noise has a much bigger effect
when it gets to propagate through all 24 encoder layers instead of
just the last 7, eating most of the separation budget; (2) even before
controls, raw verb_peak is smaller for 8 of 10 nouns.

Full-family-average (10 cells): kalamu FAILS outright (592.8 vs
control 684.2) -- the first full-average control failure seen in
either run; layer 17's family averages cleared control in all 10/10
cases. Family B only crosses the ratio=1 "real flip" threshold in 2/6
cases (mwalimu 2.911, mtoto 2.564) vs layer 17's 6/6.

Leave-one-out (10 cells): 2/4 Family A cells FAIL outright (ndege
34.31 < control 174.7; kalamu 592.8 < control 684.2, identical to its
full-average value) vs layer 17's 4/4 clean passes. Family B: only
mwalimu (2.609) and mgeni (1.505) cross 1 under genuine leave-one-out;
mtu/mtoto/mwanafunzi/mkulima all clear control but stay below 1.

**One real, replicated positive finding, smaller but consistent with
layer 17**: the "family averaging specifically rescues mwalimu" effect
reproduces at the embedding layer too -- mwalimu's own individual fit
fails badly (0.1142) but both the full-average (2.911) and the
genuinely-held-out leave-one-out (2.609) cross 1. Weaker in magnitude
than layer 17's (0.9382 individual -> 1739 LOO) but the same
qualitative pattern, on a different noun set's worth of averaging
partners. This is the one place the two layers agree.

**Verdict**: layer 17 remains the better site by a wide margin on
every metric that was compared head-to-head. The "correction" framing
(does patching later give less opportunity for downstream layers to
undo the change) is not supported by this result -- if that were the
main effect, embedding (more downstream layers = more correction
opportunity) should have done worse, which it did, but the SIZE of the
gap and the much-higher control-noise floor point more to "less of the
model's actual class-relevant computation has happened yet at the
embedding" than to "more correction happens." Matches and reinforces
the project's earlier (2026-09-26), differently-methodized finding
that embedding-level steering generalizes worse than encoder-layer
steering -- now confirmed with the current best (multi-target, family-
averaged) recipe too, not just the old centroid-push method.

## 2026-09-30 (cont.) — Set-margin objective over the whole TAM paradigm (user's fix for the escape-route failure), verb switched to "ondoka"

**Motivating observation**: the top-k diagnostic (this session, layer
17) found mwalimu's steering genuinely suppresses amefika's
probability, but the freed mass flows mostly into class-NEUTRAL escape
tokens (hapa, ni) at low-to-mid alpha, not into imefika -- because the
fit/eval objective only ever compared two single words, with no term
that competes against anything else. **User's proposed fix**: maximize
P(any class-9/10 TAM marker) vs P(any class-1 TAM marker), aggregated
over the whole tense-aspect-mood paradigm via a logsumexp margin --
raising this necessarily competes against ALL remaining mass,
including escape routes, unlike comparing two single words.

**Verified before building (not assumed)**: audited 9 candidate verb
roots x 5 TAM prefixes each for clean tokenization. The project's usual
verb, "fika", does NOT split cleanly for ame-/aki- (fuses to "▁am"/
"▁ak"). "ondoka" (to leave/depart) is one of a handful that splits
perfectly cleanly on all 5 markers both sides, giving two clean,
non-overlapping 5-token sets: class-1 {ana,ali,ame,ata,aki} -> tokens
{'▁ana','▁ali','▁ame','▁ata','▁aki'}; class-9 {ina,ili,ime,ita,iki} ->
{'▁ina','▁ili','▁ime','▁ita','▁iki'}.

Built `nllb_swahili_family_set_margin_ondoka_fit_check.py` at layer 17
(the site where the failure was diagnosed), reusing FAMILY_A/FAMILY_B/
FAMILY_OF/NOUNS/ORIG_POSS/FLIP_POSS/N_AUDITED_FIT_SENTENCES/
CONTROL_SEEDS/average_direction/build_fit_example from the layer-17
multitarget script unchanged; new `fit_direction_set_margin`
(logsumexp over token sets instead of a single pair) and
`evaluate_set_ratio` (same generalization for eval, plus an
`in_set_mass` diagnostic -- the direct test of whether escape-route
leakage actually shrinks, which is the whole point of this change).
Reports both the new SET-ratio metric and the legacy single-pair
(ameondoka/imeondoka) ratio for comparability of shape. Launched
immediately after the embedding run's `done.`; results pending.

**Results (complete): real progress on the ratio metric (mwalimu's
individual fit crosses 1 for the first time in this entire project),
but the escape-route hypothesis is only partially confirmed -- for the
genuinely-hard nouns, leakage got WORSE, not better, even as the
ratio improved.**

Per-noun individual fits (SET_ratio_peak / set_control_peak /
in_set_mass baseline->peak):
| noun | SET_ratio_peak | control | separation | in_set_mass: baseline -> peak |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ndege | 3.993e5 | 3.361 | 1.19e5x | 0.541 -> 0.746 (leakage SHRINKS) |
| nyumba | 6.987e6 | 1.662 | 4.2e6x | 0.274 -> 0.590 (shrinks) |
| barua | 6.078e8 | 15.02 | 4.0e7x | 0.237 -> 0.977 (shrinks dramatically) |
| kalamu | 1.133e8 | 524.1 | 2.2e5x | 0.279 -> 0.251 (flat/slight grow) |
| mtu | 9.577 (crosses 1) | 0.0577 | 166x | 0.346 -> 0.052 (leakage GROWS a lot) |
| mwalimu | 1.778 (crosses 1 -- FIRST TIME for an individual fit) | 0.00237 | 749x | 0.428 -> 0.318 (grows some) |
| mtoto | 5.062 (crosses 1) | 0.00458 | 1105x | 0.481 -> 0.343 (grows some) |
| mwanafunzi | 9.922 (crosses 1) | 0.00321 | 3095x | 0.514 -> 0.354 (grows some) |
| mkulima | 5.572 (crosses 1) | 0.00504 | 1106x | 0.402 -> 0.182 (grows more) |
| mgeni | 3.860 (crosses 1) | 0.00942 | 410x | 0.550 -> 0.499 (grows slightly) |

**All 6/6 Family B individual fits now cross the ratio=1 threshold**
-- most notably mwalimu, which never managed this with ANY fika-based
recipe (single-target: 0.666; multi-target+possessive: 0.938 --
always short). This is genuine, real progress directly attributable
to the set-margin objective and/or the verb switch (the two changed
together here, so which one specifically helped is not yet isolated --
see Next).

**But the in_set_mass pattern is the opposite of what the escape-route
hypothesis predicted for the hard cases.** For Family A (already
close to class 9/10), pushing harder genuinely shrinks escape-route
leakage -- exactly as hoped. For EVERY Family B noun (genuine class-1
-> class-9/10 flip), in_set_mass DECREASES from baseline to peak --
escape leakage gets WORSE, not better, even as the ratio between the
two target sets improves enough to cross 1. mtu is the extreme case:
94.8% of probability mass has fled outside both marker sets by the
alpha that maximizes its ratio, so its "9.577 crosses 1" result
represents a preference within a shrinking 5% sliver of the
distribution, not a broad commitment to the target class. Honest
characterization: the set-margin objective makes the model's
CONDITIONAL preference (given it picks one of the two classes) more
reliably correct, but does not by itself stop the model from
increasingly preferring to pick neither as alpha rises for the nouns
that need a genuine class change. It fixed the metric more than it
fixed the underlying escape behavior for the hard family.

Full-family-average and leave-one-out (20 cells total): **all 20/20
clear their own control peak**, and critically, **all 6/6 Family B
LOO cells cross ratio=1**, including mtu's genuinely-held-out LOO
(2.407) despite its individual fit's severe leakage problem -- shared
directions again outperform several individual fits outright (nyumba,
kalamu, mwalimu, mtoto, mkulima, mgeni all beat their own individual
peak under either full-average or LOO). mwalimu's LOO (3.312) again
beats both its individual fit (1.778) and the full-average (2.8) --
the "shared direction specifically rescues mwalimu" finding has now
replicated on THREE separate occasions today (fika layer-17, fika
embedding, and now set-margin-ondoka layer-17), across three different
objectives/verbs/sites. This is the most robust single finding of the
whole session.

**Verdict**: promoted from "plausible fix" to "partial fix, correctly
diagnosed mechanism but doesn't fully resolve it." The ratio-metric
numbers are genuinely better and mwalimu's individual-fit barrier is
broken for the first time -- real, usable progress. But the in_set_mass
diagnostic (built specifically to test whether escape-route leakage
shrinks) shows it does NOT shrink for the hard nouns -- if anything it
grows. Whether this translates to better or worse FREE-GENERATION
behavior (the thing that actually matters for deployment, per this
session's earlier generation-check corrections) is untested -- the
free-generation check that caught the escape-route problem in the
first place has not yet been rerun with these new directions.

**Next (queued for tomorrow, per user's request to pause here)**:
1. Rerun the free-generation check (same methodology as earlier today)
   with these set-margin-ondoka directions, especially mwalimu and
   mtu, to see whether the ratio-metric progress shows up as real
   output quality or whether the growing escape-route leakage means
   generation is just as unreliable as before, just differently so.
2. Isolate which change actually helped mwalimu cross 1 for the first
   time -- the set-margin objective, or simply switching the verb from
   fika to ondoka (a confound not yet controlled for: could rerun the
   OLD single-pair fika-style objective but on ondoka, or the NEW
   set-margin objective but restricted to just amefika/imefika's own
   markers, to separate the two factors).
3. For mtu specifically (severe leakage despite crossing 1): investigate
   what the escaped 94.8% of mass actually is (a top-k diagnostic like
   the one used for mwalimu earlier today) -- is it a DIFFERENT escape
   route than mwalimu's hapa/ni, or degenerate/off-topic completions.
4. Still open from earlier: item 3f (yuko/iko cross-marker-type
   transfer check) and the long-sentence alpha sweep, both queued
   before this set-margin work started and not yet done.

## 2026-10-01 — mtu top-k diagnostic (queued item 1): where does the escaped 94.8% in-set-mass actually go

**Motivating observation**: yesterday's set-margin-ondoka fit check found
mtu's SET_ratio crosses 1 (9.577 at alpha=2000) but in_set_mass collapses
from 0.3462 (baseline) to 0.0515 at that same alpha -- 94.8% of
probability mass flees OUTSIDE both the class-1 and class-9 ondoka
TAM-marker sets at the exact alpha that "wins" on the ratio metric.
Queued question: is the escaped mass the same kind of neutral token
mwalimu's earlier diagnostic found (hapa/ni), a different escape route,
or degenerate/off-topic completions?

**Method**: mirrored `nllb_swahili_mwalimu_topk_diagnostic.py` exactly
(full top-10 next-token distribution at two probe positions, across
alpha in [0,500,1000,1500,2000]), new script
`nllb_swahili_mtu_topk_diagnostic.py`, against the set-margin-ondoka
artifacts (own individual direction, familyB average, and familyB LOO
holding mtu out -- LOO added beyond what the mwalimu script checked,
since it's the deployment-realistic case). Purely a read-out, nothing
refit.

**Clarification on probe position**: confirmed the formal SET_ratio /
in_set_mass numbers in yesterday's fit-check are scored at the position
right after the BARE noun (decoder_prefix with no "wako"), not after
"{noun} wako" -- the FIRST probe position in both this script and the
inherited mwalimu script, despite its docstring label ("predicting the
possessive wako/yako"), which is stale: neither test sentence ("mtu
ameondoka." / "mwalimu amefika.") actually contains "wako" at that
position, so wako/yako never appear as candidates there in either
script's output. Not fixed (out of scope here, and the mwalimu script
carries the same stale label) -- flagging so it isn't mistaken for a
new bug later.

**Results at the alpha that actually sets the metric (alpha=2000,
bare-noun position)**:

- **Own individual direction**: dominated by a SINGLE escape token,
  '▁ni' (copula "is"), at **50.2%** of total probability -- far more
  extreme than anything seen in mwalimu's diagnostic (no single
  non-target token there exceeded ~22.7%). Remaining mass splits across
  function words ('▁kwa' 7.4%, '▁na' 1.9%, '▁ya' 1.4%) and, notably, two
  competing WHOLE VERB lexemes rather than just TAM-prefix noise:
  '▁kwenda' ("to go", 2.4%) and '▁kuwa'/'▁imekuwa' ("to be"/"has been",
  1.2%+1.3%). No class-1 marker appears in the top 10 at all at this
  alpha -- the original class is fully suppressed, but almost none of
  the freed mass reaches the intended class-9 set either ('▁ime' 2.7% +
  '▁ina' 1.8%, matching in_set_mass's own p9).
- **FamilyB average direction**: 'ni' drops to 17.9% (vs 50.2%
  individual) and both class markers stay in the top 3 ('▁ime' 19.8%,
  '▁ame' 7.5%) -- consistent with the project's recurring finding that
  shared/averaged directions generalize better than individual fits
  (mwalimu LOO finding, fika-embedding finding; this is a third
  replication).
- **FamilyB LOO (holding mtu out -- the deployment-realistic case)**: a
  QUALITATIVELY DIFFERENT failure mode from the individual fit. 'ni' is
  now a minor player (7.1%), but the ORIGINAL class-1 marker '▁ame'
  (13.7%) stays nearly as strong as the target '▁ime' (17.8%) -- LOO's
  problem isn't escaping to a neutral word, it's incomplete suppression
  of the source class. **Individual fit over-escapes to "ni"; LOO
  under-suppresses "ame".** Two different failure modes depending on
  whether the direction was fit on mtu itself or transferred from its
  family -- not visible in the aggregate ratio number alone.

**Secondary position** (after "{noun} wako" already committed -- not
what the formal metric scores, but relevant to full free-generation):
own-individual alpha=2000 shows an actual degenerate completion in the
top-10 -- the literal English token "gone" at 1.7% probability, a
genuine code-switch artifact. Also echoes mwalimu's earlier finding
that part of the escape takes the form of the verb's own INFINITIVE
('▁ku', ambiguous here between the preposition "ku" and the start of
"kuondoka" -- not disambiguated) rather than any finite TAM-marked form,
same pattern as mwalimu's 'kuja'/'kufika' escape at the analogous
position.

**Verdict**: partially answers the queued question. The escaped mass is
not a novel token type -- 'ni' is the same lead escape route mwalimu's
diagnostic found -- but it is far more dominant in degree for mtu (50%
vs mwalimu's largest single share ~18-23%), and surfaces a component
mwalimu's diagnostic didn't show as clearly: competing whole-verb
lexemes (kwenda, kuwa) in direct competition with the TAM-marker sets,
not just function-word noise. Crucially, the LOO/deployment-realistic
direction has a DIFFERENT dominant failure mode (under-suppression of
the source class) than the individual fit (over-escape to "ni") --
"escape-route leakage" is not one phenomenon to fix with one loss term;
a fix needs to address over-escape and under-suppression separately.

**Next**:
1. Item 3 from yesterday's queue (isolate set-margin objective vs.
   fika->ondoka verb-switch confound) still open, and now more clearly
   load-bearing: unclear whether a 'ni'-suppression term would fix the
   individual-fit failure without affecting the LOO under-suppression
   failure differently.
2. Consider an explicit penalty on the identified escape tokens ('ni',
   'kwa', 'kwenda', 'kuwa'/'imekuwa') added to the fit objective, now
   that they're identified concretely rather than guessed at.
3. Item 2 from yesterday's queue (rerun free-generation check with the
   set-margin-ondoka directions) still not done -- would show whether
   this 50%/18%/7% 'ni'-mass split actually shows up as broken vs.
   acceptable generations.
