## 2026-10-01 (cont.) — external critique received (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude) on Claim 1 verification: real pending issue found, blocking before Claim 2

Three independent LLM reviews of `claim1_statistical_verification_
critique_prompt.md` were returned and saved
(`claim1_statistical_verification_critique_{gemini,chat,claude}.md`).
All three converge on: Claim 1 shows real, controlled, above-chance
decodability in both languages, but "a grammar-encoding SUBSPACE
exists" is overclaimed relative to what linear probing alone
establishes, and the French-vs-Swahili selectivity comparison
(0.40 vs 0.68) is invalid because accuracy-minus-chance isn't
comparable across a 2-way vs 11-way task (one reviewer's approximate
chance-corrected kappa, ~0.82 French vs ~0.77 Swahili, roughly REVERSES
the ranking) -- that comparative claim is retracted.

**The one review (the third Claude instance) found something the other
two missed, that is a genuine blocker, not just a caveat**: NLLB's
encoder is bidirectional. In every Swahili 1b template sentence
("{Noun} {concord}me{verb}."), the noun's own layer-17 representation
can attend FORWARD to the verb's class-prefix marker later in the same
sentence -- which IS the label. So the probe may be reading the
marker's influence on the noun's hidden state via self-attention, not
anything the noun's own lexical identity contributes. This is worse
for the "guides the probabilities" correlation specifically: the model
margin there is computed via a TEACHER-FORCED decode with the correct
marker already present in the self-translated source, so the decoder
could be copying a marker it already saw rather than computing
agreement -- meaning probe margin and model margin could correlate
because both read the same input token, not because the stream causally
guides the output. As designed, today's +0.5118 correlation cannot
distinguish these two explanations. This also compounds with a second,
related point: per-class verb choice (ondoka for animate, onekana for
most inanimate classes, decided during template construction) means
verb identity correlates with class, and the encoder sees the verb
directly -- a literal label leak for the CLASS decodability test too,
not merely the selection-bias/forking-paths framing in the original
limitations list.

Two more real, lower-priority (not blocking) points worth tracking: (1)
no surface-form/orthographic control was run for Claim 1a -- Swahili
class is partly spelled by the noun's own prefix (preserved under
whole-word pooling), French gender is ~80% predictable from suffix
spelling, so some of 1a's 0.79/0.91 accuracy could be substantially
"reading the word's own spelling" rather than a deeper grammatical
representation; cheap to check (character-prefix/suffix classifier on
the same split). (2) The French 1b test treats 33,627 tokens as
independent when they cluster within only 3,083 lemmas (pseudo-
replication) -- a lemma-level cluster bootstrap or macro-accuracy would
be more honest than the naive per-token number.

**Verdict**: before Claim 2, redo the Swahili "guides the
probabilities" test (and ideally the decodability test too) in a
design the bidirectional-leakage critique can't touch: EN (not SW)
source sentence -- so the input carries no Swahili class marker at
all -- teacher-force only the noun in the decoder, and probe the
DECODER's hidden state at the noun position (causal, so it hasn't seen
any marker yet either). This is not just a cleaner Claim 1b -- it is
structurally the same setting Claim 2's actual deployment pipeline
would use (EN/SW source -> steer the noun's representation), so the
work is not wasted effort spent perfecting a checkpoint; it is the
correct version of the test to have built in the first place.

One reviewer's closing point is worth keeping in view regardless of how
this redo turns out: this project's own history has already shown
decodability without steerability three separate times (the French
probes, the toy model, and an earlier Swahili attempt). A clean Claim 1
is useful diagnostic context, not a guarantee Claim 2 will succeed --
don't over-invest further in Claim 1 perfection at the expense of
starting Claim 2 once this one specific leakage issue is addressed.

Files: `claim1_statistical_verification_critique_gemini.md`,
`claim1_statistical_verification_critique_chat.md`,
`claim1_statistical_verification_critique_claude.md`.

## 2026-10-01 (cont.) — Claim 1b redone leak-free: decodability stronger, "guides the probabilities" does NOT survive

**Response to the external critique's one blocking finding** (NLLB's
encoder is bidirectional; the Swahili self-translation template let the
noun's representation attend forward to its own class marker later in
the same sentence, and the correlation test teacher-forced with that
marker already present -- a possible copy, not computed agreement).
New `nllb_swahili_decoder_class_probe_noleakage.py`: EN source ("The
{gloss} has appeared.", single universal verb for all 11 classes --
eliminates the separate per-class-verb leak too), decoder probed
causally at the noun position via a prefix that stops EXACTLY at the
noun (checked against the correct `output_hidden_states` indexing --
index layer_idx+1, not layer_idx, since index 0 is the embedding
output; caught before trusting results), genuine next-token margin (no
marker anywhere upstream). Also added repeated stratified 5-fold CV (5
repeats) replacing the single unstable 80/20 split, and a within-class
(class-demeaned) correlation check.

**Result**:
- Survival: 238/287 (83%), up sharply from 43% under the old SW-self-
  translation screen -- EN->SW translation is simply a more reliable
  construction.
- Decodability: REAL=0.8600 (std 0.058 across 25 fold-evaluations),
  CONTROL=0.1016 (std 0.0137), SELECTIVITY=+0.7585 -- stronger AND far
  better-powered than the original leaky estimate (n=238 vs n=30;
  repeated CV vs two unseeded single-split runs).
- "Guides the probabilities": Spearman(probe_margin, model_margin) =
  +0.1217 (n=238, permutation p=0.0585 -- not significant at 0.05).
  Within-class (class-demeaned): +0.0896 (p=0.166 -- clearly not
  significant).

**Verdict**: exactly the outcome the critique's diagnosis predicted.
Decodability survives, and survives MORE strongly once properly
powered -- the stream genuinely, robustly encodes Swahili noun class in
a way that generalizes to unseen nouns. But the correlation between
that encoding's strength and the model's own actual next-token
behavior, which looked like the most novel finding this morning
(rho=+0.51, p=0.0025, under the leaky design), DOES NOT SURVIVE once
the leak is removed -- it collapses to non-significance. This is
reported as a genuine correction, not a caveat: "the stream guides the
probabilities" is retracted as a Swahili finding. What stands is only
the more modest "the stream linearly encodes class in a way that
generalizes to unseen nouns" -- Claim 1b-i, not 1b-ii.

**Still open, not attempted here (flagged, not dropped)**: an
orthographic/surface-form baseline for comparison (how much of the
0.76 selectivity is the noun's own prefix spelling vs. something
deeper), and replicating either test for French.

**Decision**: per the user's instruction, proceeding to Claim 2 (causal
steering, both layers, both languages, proper controls and a real
meaning-preservation check) now that Claim 1 stands on honest footing --
strong decodability, no over-claimed behavioral link.

Files: `nllb_swahili_decoder_class_probe_noleakage.py`,
`nllb_swahili_decoder_class_probe_noleakage.log`.

## 2026-10-01 (cont.) — Claim 2 (French half): controlled causal steering benchmark on NLLB

**Infrastructure fix enabling this**: `mbart_agreement_lib.build_inputs`
hardcoded mBART's `tokenizer.lang_code_to_id`, which NLLB's tokenizer
doesn't have -- one-line, backward-compatible fix (fall back to
`convert_tokens_to_ids` when `lang_code_to_id` is absent) unlocks
reusing the ENTIRE proven French controller-side pipeline
(`fit_lemma_direction_controller_margin`, `eval_on_chain_controller`,
`score_result`, random/orthogonal controls, same-lemma/held-out-lemma/
held-out-class tiers) directly on NLLB, with no duplication of the
actual fitting/eval math. New `controller_side_steering_nllb_
benchmark_fr.py` reimplements only the orchestration, with three
documented, individually-justified changes from the original: model
(NLLB-distilled-1.3B, matching today's Swahili work), layer (12 of 24,
matching today's established decoder-side site), and alpha grid
([100..3000] instead of mBART's [10..150] -- today's single-lemma NLLB
checks already found the old grid produces almost no movement on this
model).

**Result** (agreement_chains_repaired.json, n_pool=24 usable lemmas,
alpha_same=3000, alpha_lemma=1000, alpha_class=1000):

| tier | whole_word_rate | n | mean_p_flip |
|---|---|---|---|
| SAME LEMMA | 0.2667 | 15 | 0.2143 |
| HELD-OUT LEMMA | **0.4667** | 15 | 0.4477 |
| HELD-OUT CLASS | 0.3333 | 15 | 0.2620 |
| random control | 0.0667 | 15 | 0.0096 |
| orthogonal-null control | 0.0667 | 15 | 0.0048 |

All three real-direction tiers clear both controls by a wide margin
(controls ~0.07, real directions 0.27-0.47). This is a genuine,
controlled Claim-2 result for French on NLLB: causal steering works,
with proper fit/test lemma separation and matched controls, not just
the single-lemma spot-checks from earlier today.

**Replicates today's recurring Swahili finding, now cross-language**:
HELD-OUT LEMMA (0.467) beats SAME LEMMA (0.267) -- a shared/family-
averaged direction outperforming an individually-fit one, exactly the
pattern found repeatedly for Swahili today (mwalimu's LOO beating its
own individual fit, etc.). This is no longer a Swahili-specific
curiosity; it shows up for French too, on a different model.

**Loose end, not yet resolved**: the selected same-lemma alpha hit the
TOP of the tested grid (3000) -- the true optimum may be higher still.
Not re-swept further given the time this run already took (~64
minutes); flagged for a future wider-grid pass, not blocking.

**Comparison to the mBART standing number (CLAUDE.md, same_lemma
strict=0.3636, n=11)**: NLLB's same-lemma number here (0.267) is
somewhat lower; its held-out-lemma number (0.467) is notably HIGHER
than mBART's own held-out-lemma (0.20, n=10). Noted, not over-
interpreted -- different models, not a controlled comparison per se,
consistent with this project's standing caution about cross-model
claims.

Swahili's analogous benchmark (`nllb_swahili_steering_benchmark.py`,
extending today's proven ANIMATE<->9/10 flip to many nouns per family
with the same fit/test separation and controls) launched immediately
after, in progress.

## 2026-10-01 (cont.) — Swahili Claim 2 benchmark stopped; restrategizing

User flagged a real concern mid-build: after three rounds of
construction bugs (narrative-tense shift from "Suddenly,"; demonstrative
insertion breaking marker-position detection; ANIMATE-PL/SG marker-set
mismatch), is this benchmark's two-frame fit/test design actually
generating new information, or just a statistically-dressed-up
reproduction of what today's single-noun "mtu" exploration already
showed? Assessed honestly: French's Claim 2 result (logged above) is
genuinely new -- no prior NLLB multi-lemma benchmark existed. Swahili's,
as scoped (ANIMATE-SG <-> 9/10 flip on a simple "noun has appeared"
sentence, two EN frames for fit/test separation), would mostly confirm
the EASY case already well-established today (mtu's clean flip), not
engage the harder generalization questions (adjective-intervening,
multi-clause) already known to fail from today's qualitative work.
Stopped the run rather than finish it on momentum alone. Next: discuss
with the user whether a SIMPLER one-frame design (same-noun + held-out-
noun tiers only, dropping the two-frame construction that caused 2 of
the 3 bugs) is worth running for the statistical-evidence requirement,
or whether today's qualitative Swahili record (escape-route diagnosis,
dual-layer combination, adjective-gap and multi-clause failures, all
well-documented with specific mechanisms even at n=1) is the more
honest deliverable to stand on for now.

## 2026-10-01 (cont.) — basic hypothesis test: is grammar separable from cross-lingual meaning? Yes.

**User's reframe after flagging the Claim 2 steering benchmarks as too
complex/compute-heavy and at risk of just re-confirming known results**:
go much more basic. For a concept with translations across languages,
does the vector common to all of them (their mean) carry the majority
of each embedding's magnitude, and does the remaining component encode
the language-specific (grammatical) property?

**Method** (new `cross_lingual_embedding_decomposition.py`, pure linear
algebra on static embeddings, no generation-heavy steering at all): for
all 319 Swahili nouns (`swahili_noun_lexicon_agreement_v2.py`),
translated the English gloss into 4 other well-resourced NLLB languages
(French, Spanish, German, Portuguese) via cheap, unsteered, cached
generate() calls -- 319/319 succeeded, all 4 languages, no drops.
Collected the 5-language embedding set per concept, computed the
per-concept cross-lingual mean direction, then (1) measured what
fraction of the Swahili embedding's magnitude lies along it, and (2)
ran the EXACT Claim-1a classifier + 20-shuffle-control methodology on
the RESIDUAL (mean-direction removed) vs. the RAW embedding, same
concept sample, same run, for a direct comparison.

**Result**:
- Magnitude: mean linear-norm ratio = 0.4640 (std 0.0800) -- in ENERGY
  terms (squared magnitude, the physically meaningful quantity since
  projection and residual are orthogonal), that's ~21.5% of each
  embedding's energy along the shared cross-lingual direction, ~78.5%
  in the residual. The common direction is a MINORITY component, not
  the majority.
- Decodability: RAW embedding REAL=0.7900/CONTROL=0.1130/
  SELECTIVITY=+0.6770 (replicates today's earlier Claim 1a number on
  an independently-drawn run, good consistency check). RESIDUAL (cross-
  lingual mean direction explicitly removed) REAL=0.7682/
  CONTROL=0.1161/SELECTIVITY=+0.6520 -- essentially UNCHANGED, within
  CV noise.

**Verdict**: a clean, cheap, direct confirmation of the hypothesis.
Grammatical class is NOT carried by the shared cross-lingual "meaning"
direction -- it survives almost undiminished in exactly the residual
left over after that direction is removed. Class information is
concentrated in a separable, language-specific component, not smeared
across cross-lingual semantics. This is the first time this project has
shown grammar/meaning separability via a geometric decomposition rather
than a trained probe or gradient-fit direction, and at near-zero
compute cost (no steering, no use_cache=False generation at all).

**Caveat flagged, not yet controlled for**: the 4 comparison languages
are all Indo-European (French, Spanish, German, Portuguese). Part of
the "residual" could reflect generic "Swahili is linguistically distant
from this specific language cluster" rather than purely grammar-
specific content. Doesn't undermine the finding (the classifier
specifically tests whether CLASS survives, not generic Swahili-
flavored-ness), but a cleaner version would add a non-Indo-European
comparison language.

**Why this matters for the actual open problem (a consistently
steerable direction)**: this residual (or its per-class mean, averaged
across many nouns of the same class) is a candidate steering direction
that costs nothing to construct (no generation, no gradient fitting)
and is by-construction stripped of generic cross-lingual semantic
content -- a structurally different, principled candidate worth testing
against today's gradient-fitted directions, much cheaper than building
another full steering benchmark.

Files: `cross_lingual_embedding_decomposition.py`,
`cross_lingual_embedding_decomposition.log`.

## 2026-10-01 (cont.) — two follow-up checks on the residual, plus a literature pass

**Motivation (user, after reviewing the above)**: the residual isn't
necessarily pure class signal yet. Two things could still be hiding in
it: (1) a generic "this is a Swahili word" component shared by every
noun regardless of class (confounded with POS=noun, since our sample
has no non-noun words -- acknowledged as unresolvable with this data
and fine, since we only need it to be non-class-specific, not
disentangled from POS); (2) separately, do the project's own saved
Swahili steering directions have a real component along a noun's own
cross-lingual semantic direction -- which would help explain the
already-documented ndege bird/plane sense-swap (Phase 0a).

**Check 1: global language/POS-confounded residual -- NULL result.**
New `nllb_swahili_global_language_residual_check.py` (extends
`cross_lingual_embedding_decomposition.py`, factored `build_concepts`/
`decompose_concept` out for reuse, CLAUDE.md hard rule #10). Built
g_hat = normalized mean of all 319 per-concept residuals, projected it
out of each residual (double-residual), reran the identical classifier
+ 20-shuffle-control check, same concept sample, 3-way comparison:

| Stage | REAL | CONTROL | SELECTIVITY |
|---|---|---|---|
| RAW | 0.7900 | 0.1131 | +0.6769 |
| RESIDUAL (cross-lingual mean removed) | 0.7682 | 0.1166 | +0.6515 |
| DOUBLE-RESIDUAL (+ g_hat removed) | 0.7682 | 0.1150 | +0.6531 |

g_hat carries only ~6.6% of the residual's energy on average (linear-
norm ratio 0.2575, std 0.0588, n=319; energy = ratio^2). Removing it
changed selectivity by +0.0016 -- within the control's own std
(~0.015). **Verdict: no meaningful generic Swahili-noun/POS-confounded
component to peel off.** The cross-lingual-mean residual was already
close to pure class signal; this second peel-off step is not needed
going forward.

**Check 2: steering-direction semantic-leakage check -- a real bug
caught, then a NULL result.** New
`nllb_swahili_steering_direction_semantic_leakage_check.py`: build each
of the 10 family-scaled-benchmark nouns' own cross-lingual semantic
direction (m_hat, same method as above), then compare it by cosine to
every saved steering direction from that benchmark (own/family-average/
leave-one-out, both the embedding-layer and encoder-layer-17 variants),
against a cross-noun control (mean cosine to the OTHER 9 nouns' m_hat)
and a 30-draw random-direction null.

**Bug caught on first run**: crashed immediately with a tensor-size
mismatch. Root cause -- the family-scaled steering benchmark (both
`_embed_` and layer-17 variants) was fit on `facebook/nllb-200-3.3B`
(d_model=2048), not `nllb-200-distilled-1.3B` (d_model=1024) like the
cross-lingual decomposition script. A real model mismatch between two
parts of the project's own pipeline, not previously flagged anywhere.
Fixed by building m_hat on the same 3.3B model the steering directions
actually came from (the concept-building code is model-agnostic, so
this was a one-line MODEL_ID swap, not a rewrite).

**Result after the fix (n=22 embedding-layer directions, n=22 layer-17
directions -- own/family-avg/LOO per noun)**:

- EMBEDDING-LAYER: mean cos(own m_hat) = -0.0253, mean cos(other
  nouns' m_hat) = -0.0186, random-null |cos| mean ~0.015-0.02 per
  direction. Individual cosines range roughly -0.075 to +0.043 --
  within 2-4x the null's magnitude at most, and own-noun alignment is
  if anything slightly MORE negative than the cross-noun baseline
  (opposite of what a "leaks toward its own meaning" hypothesis
  predicts). ndege specifically: cos(own)=-0.0539 (embed) /
  -0.0230 (layer17) -- small and negative, not a positive alignment.
- LAYER-17: mean cos(own m_hat) = -0.0138, mean cos(other) = -0.0146
  -- no separation at all.

**Verdict: no evidence that these steering directions have a literal
linear overlap with this project's definition of the "semantic"
direction** (the cross-lingual translation-mean, in embedding space).
This does NOT mean the ndege sense-swap mechanism is explained away --
it means this specific, cheap explanation (static cosine overlap) isn't
it. The real mechanism is either nonlinear, only visible once
propagated through generation, or involves a "meaning" direction this
cross-lingual construction doesn't capture. Flagged as open, not
resolved. Caveat specific to the LAYER-17 numbers: m_hat is an
embedding-space vector; comparing it to a layer-17 residual-stream
direction is dimensionally valid (same model, same width) but
representationally looser (17 transformer blocks of rotation between
them) -- the EMBEDDING-LAYER result is the clean test; LAYER-17 is
secondary corroboration only.

**Literature pass** (web search, two passes -- general cross-lingual/
grammar decomposition + steering entanglement, then a targeted
grammatical-gender follow-up): written up in full in
`docs/related_literature.txt` (12 papers, ranked, only one -- Bau et al.
2019 -- independently verified by reading the actual PDF rather than
trusting a search-agent summary). Headline external finding: Bau et
al.'s own neuron-intervention experiment on English-Spanish NMT found
grammatical gender the hardest of {tense, number, gender} to causally
control (21% success vs. 67%/37%), attributed to gender being "more
distributed" than tense, not to the pathway being absent -- consistent
with this project's own low same-lemma French steering number (0.3636,
n=11) and its "pathway is reachable, fitting procedure is what fails to
generalize" framing (CLAUDE.md section 5). Also flagged as worth
testing later: a plain class-centroid direction may beat the current
gradient-fitted recipe (per a 2026 gender-direction-estimation paper),
and LEACE as a sharper closed-form replacement for mean-subtraction
decomposition steps.

Files: `nllb_swahili_global_language_residual_check.py`,
`nllb_swahili_global_language_residual_check.log`,
`nllb_swahili_steering_direction_semantic_leakage_check.py`,
`nllb_swahili_steering_direction_semantic_leakage_check.log`,
`docs/related_literature.txt`.

## 2026-10-01 (cont.) — does the per-class centroid itself carry a real magnitude/energy share? NO -- ties the random control exactly, sharpening the 2026-09-25 null

**User's question**: we already looked at Swahili noun-class centroids
(2026-09-25, cosine-similarity methodology: within-class cohesion real
but modest at 0.3878 vs. 0.2518 control; between-class separation tied
the control exactly at -0.0951 vs. -0.0989). Now that we've been
measuring magnitude/ENERGY fractions for the semantic (~21.5%) and
language-identity (~5.2%) directions, what proportion does the
per-class centroid account for on that same scale?

**New `nllb_swahili_class_centroid_magnitude_check.py`**: pure static
embedding lookups (no generate(), no forward pass -- same "embedding
space only" convention as the original centroid analysis), 319 nouns/
11 classes, whole-word mean-pooled on `facebook/nllb-200-3.3B` (matching
today's other checks, NOT the cached `nllb_swahili_embedding_raw_class_
centroids.pt`, which used first-subword-only pooling -- rebuilt fresh
for comparability). For each noun: ratio = ||projection of its raw
embedding onto its own class's RAW centroid, normalized|| / ||its raw
embedding||, same metric as `decompose_concept`'s m_hat/g_hat tests.

**Result (n=319)**:

| Measure | mean ratio | energy fraction |
|---|---|---|
| NAIVE (centroid includes the noun itself) | 0.4069 | ~16.6% |
| LEAVE-ONE-OUT (centroid excludes the noun) | 0.3326 | ~11.1% |
| RANDOM CONTROL (same-sized shuffled-label groups) | 0.3330 | ~11.1% |

**The naive number is inflated by self-leakage** (each noun contributes
1/n of its own vector to "its own" centroid -- n ranges 9-57 across the
11 classes here, so the inflation is non-trivial). Once corrected
(leave-one-out), the result is a **near-exact tie with a same-sized
random relabeling control (0.3326 vs. 0.3330)**. Per-class LOO
breakdown ranges 0.21 (class 5) to 0.43 (class 8) -- real variation
exists but sits inside what the random control's own spread would
predict, not examined further here.

**Verdict: the per-class centroid carries no detectable class-specific
magnitude/energy signal above chance.** This sharpens, via a different
metric, the 2026-09-25 finding that between-class centroid separation
(cosine) showed no advantage over a random-relabeling control either --
now the magnitude/energy view agrees. **Does NOT contradict** the
trained-classifier decodability result (+0.65 selectivity, cross_lingual_
embedding_decomposition.py) -- a discriminatively-trained classifier can
still find class-relevant structure in directions a naive group-mean
vector doesn't capture at all. Practical implication: the per-class
centroid should NOT be treated as "the class vector" or reported as a
percentage of embedding energy the way the semantic/language-identity
directions were -- those were validated real shared directions; this one
is not distinguishable from noise by this test. Consistent with
CLAUDE.md's open decision ("difference-of-means vs. probe-derived
direction") and `docs/related_literature.txt` item 3's note that a plain
centroid estimator's apparent strength needs a matched control before
trusting it.

Files: `nllb_swahili_class_centroid_magnitude_check.py`,
`nllb_swahili_class_centroid_magnitude_check.log`.

## 2026-10-02 — so where DOES the class signal live? Found it: the mean-centered centroid direction, once whitened. Corrects the prior turn's "reweighted/different direction" guess.

**User's question** following the centroid-magnitude null above: the
trained classifier decodes class at +0.65 selectivity
(`nllb_swahili_embedding_decodability_probe.py`) while the raw centroid
carries no signal above a random-relabeling control -- so where does
the signal actually live? Two checks, both on the SAME model/data the
validated +0.65 number came from (`nllb-200-distilled-1.3B`, 319-noun
lexicon, `build_X_y` factored out of the probe script for reuse,
CLAUDE.md hard rule #10).

**CHECK 1 -- does the classifier's learned direction even match the
naive centroid?** Trained the probe's own per-fold linear classifier
(5-fold CV, `train_and_eval_fold` given a new additive `return_model`
flag), and for each class compared its learned weight row by cosine to
that class's TRAIN-ONLY mean-centered centroid direction (centroid
MINUS the overall mean -- not the raw centroid the previous check
used), against a mismatched-class control:

  mean cos(weight_c, OWN class's centroid - mu_global)    = **+0.9353** (n=55)
  mean cos(weight_c, OTHER class's centroid - mu_global)  = **-0.0926** (n=550)

**Near-exact alignment with its own class, near-zero/negative with
every other class.** This OVERTURNS last turn's guess that the
classifier uses some differently-reweighted direction unrelated to the
centroid -- it doesn't; it learns almost exactly the mean-centered
centroid-difference direction. The real fix needed was subtracting the
GLOBAL mean first. The previous check's "null" result used the RAW
(uncentered) per-class centroid, which is dominated by the huge
shared-across-all-nouns component (the ~73%-of-energy "common
direction" two turns ago) that every class's raw mean points along
almost identically -- exactly why it tied a random relabeling control.
Centroid-MINUS-global-mean isolates the class-specific part and is,
it turns out, essentially what the classifier already uses.

**CHECK 2 -- why didn't the mean-centered version show up cleanly in
raw-space cosine either (Sep 25: real 0.39 vs. control 0.25, present
but modest)?** Built a shrinkage-regularized whitening transform from
the pooled within-class covariance (regularization necessary: n=319 <
d=1024 makes the unregularized covariance exactly singular), and redid
the LOO centroid-ratio test plus a between-class-scatter eigenvalue
spectrum in the WHITENED space, against a control that reruns the
ENTIRE whitening+LDA pipeline on shuffled labels (not just the final
metric):

| shrinkage | REAL LOO ratio | CONTROL | SELECTIVITY |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 0.7431 | 0.3786 (std 0.0127) | **+0.3645** |
| 0.3 | 0.5818 | 0.2646 (std 0.0087) | **+0.3172** |

Robust across both shrinkage settings tested -- not a cherry-picked
single hyperparameter. Between-class-scatter top-10 eigenvalues (rank
<=10 = num_classes-1 by construction) are **3-6x larger than the
matched shuffled-label control at EVERY one of the 10 ranks** (e.g.
shrinkage=0.1 top eigenvalue 19700 real vs. 3570 control). But the
TOP-1 eigenvalue's share of the top-10 total is nearly identical
between real and control (~0.15 both ways at shrinkage=0.1, ~0.15 vs.
~0.14 at 0.3) -- **the real signal is not concentrated in one or two
dominant axes; it's spread roughly evenly across all ~10 available
between-class directions**, each one substantially stronger than
chance, not a single dominant "class axis."

**Answer to "where does it live"**: in the per-class mean-CENTERED
centroid direction (not the raw one), which needs the global mean
removed first to stop being swamped by shared cross-noun variance, and
needs within-class-covariance whitening to separate cleanly from a
matched random-grouping control -- and even then the signal occupies a
genuinely ~10-dimensional subspace (one axis per class, roughly evenly
used), not a single shared vector. Directly actionable for the
project's open "difference-of-means vs. gradient-fitted direction"
question (CLAUDE.md section 8): a per-class mean-centered, whitened
centroid direction is now a validated, nearly-free candidate steering
target (cosine 0.935 with the thing that actually decodes class),
worth testing causally against the existing gradient-fitted recipe.

Files: `nllb_swahili_class_signal_location_check.py`,
`nllb_swahili_class_signal_location_check.log`. Also edited (additive,
backward-compatible): `nllb_swahili_embedding_decodability_probe.py`
(factored out `build_X_y`; `train_and_eval_fold` gained `return_model`).

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — full energy budget (semantic/language/class/remainder) and an orthogonality check among the three found directions

**Full combined energy decomposition** (`nllb_swahili_full_energy_
decomposition_check.py`, reruns the 319-noun/5-language concept build
once more to combine everything established so far into one per-noun
budget, n=319, all fractions of the ORIGINAL embedding's energy):

| Slice | linear-norm ratio | energy fraction |
|---|---|---|
| Semantic (cross-lingual mean) | 0.4640 | 22.2% |
| Language-generic | 0.2575 (of residual) | 5.4% |
| **Class** (mean-centered centroid, LOO, double-residual space) | 0.1999 | **4.2%** |
| Remainder | -- | 68.2% |

Class slice validated against its own random-relabeling control: REAL
ratio=0.1999 vs. CONTROL=0.0528 (std 0.0023, 20 shuffles) --
SELECTIVITY +0.1471, real is ~63 control-standard-deviations above
chance. **Class information occupies ~4.2% of the embedding's total
energy** -- real and clearly non-chance, but a minority slice next to
semantic meaning (22%) and a still-unexplained 68% remainder.

**Orthogonality check among the three found directions**
(`nllb_swahili_vector_orthogonality_check.py`, same concept build,
now cached to `nllb_swahili_concept_decomposition_cache.pt` so future
checks on this decomposition don't need to re-translate):

- **CHECK 1 -- cos(g_hat, each class direction) = 0.0000 for all 11
  classes.** Exactly orthogonal, as expected by construction (class
  directions live inside the double-residual space, which is built to
  be orthogonal to g_hat for every noun).
- **CHECK 2 -- pairwise cos among the 11 classes' own directions**:
  REAL mean=-0.0958, mean|cos|=0.1312, max|cos|=0.4064 (n_pairs=55) vs.
  CONTROL (20 relabeling shuffles) mean=-0.0980, mean|cos|=0.1017. The
  SIGNED mean ties the control almost exactly (replicates 2026-09-25's
  raw-centroid result, -0.0951 vs. -0.0989, now on the corrected
  double-residual directions) -- classes are not systematically more
  "same-signed" than random. But mean|cos| is meaningfully higher than
  control (0.131 vs. 0.102), and one pair reaches 0.4064 -- **the 11
  class directions are NOT a clean orthogonal basis; some specific
  class pairs share real directional overlap** (plausibly linguistically
  related classes, e.g. the animate singular/plural pair already
  flagged 2026-09-25, cos=-0.2520 in raw-embedding space -- not yet
  confirmed as the same pair here, matrix not fully printed). Flagged,
  not yet identified which pair(s) drive the 0.41 max.
- **CHECK 3 -- cos(m_hat_i, noun's own class direction), per noun**:
  mean=+0.0090, mean|cos|=0.0666 (n=319). Close to the random-direction
  noise floor for 1024 dims (~0.02-0.03) but somewhat above it --
  **mild, not strong, entanglement between a word's individual meaning
  and its class's direction.** Good news for the decomposition's
  validity: much weaker than the semantic/grammatical entanglement
  Gonen et al. (2019) report for grammatical GENDER
  (`docs/related_literature.txt` item 2) -- Swahili noun class looks
  more cleanly separable from lexical meaning than French/German
  gender does, at least by this measure.
- **CHECK 4 -- cos(m_hat_i, g_hat), per noun**: mean=-0.0770,
  mean|cos|=0.0963 (n=319). Noticeably above the random-noise floor
  (~3-4x) -- **a small but real systematic anti-correlation between a
  noun's own semantic direction and the generic-language direction**,
  which the sequential-projection construction does not rule out (only
  guarantees double-residual-to-g_hat orthogonality, not m_hat-to-g_hat).
  Not large enough to invalidate the energy budget above, but a genuine
  (if minor) departure from clean independence between decomposition
  stages 1 and 2.

**Overall picture**: the three-way split is mostly but not perfectly
clean. g_hat/class separation is exact by construction; class/meaning
separation is good (much better than known gender/meaning entanglement
in the literature); but the 11 within-class directions are not mutually
orthogonal (some real pairwise overlap) and semantic/language-generic
directions carry a small mutual correlation. None of this overturns the
energy-budget numbers above, but it means "three independent axes" is
an approximation, not an exact description.

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — decoder FFN "language neuron" pilot: perfect layer-0 correlational selectivity, but causally null

**User's question** (new session, same day): the prior energy-budget
work found three ORTHOGONAL DIRECTIONS in the static embedding space
(semantic/language/class). Can we go one level down -- do individual
decoder FFN UNITS ("neurons" in the literal sense) carry a localized
signal for target LANGUAGE, and do they CAUSALLY inflate/deflate
Swahili-vs-other-language output probability, as opposed to the signal
being smeared across all units?

**Method** (new `nllb_swahili_decoder_language_neuron_check.py`,
extends `cross_lingual_embedding_decomposition.py`'s `build_concepts`/
`NOUNS`/`OTHER_LANGS` additively -- added an optional `nouns=` override
and a `lang_words` field, CLAUDE.md hard rule #10): 24 decoder-FFN
layers x 8192 post-ReLU units (196,608 total) hooked at decoder
position 1 -- the forced target-language token itself
(decoder_input_ids=[eos(2), lang_id], decoder_start_token_id=2
confirmed empirically on `facebook/nllb-200-distilled-1.3B`,
`M2M100ForConditionalGeneration`). Same English-gloss source encoded
ONCE per concept; only the forced language token varies across the 5
conditions (Swahili + French/Spanish/German/Portuguese, same set as
the embedding-decomposition work).

STEP 1 (correlational, n=35 ranking concepts, disjoint from the n=12
causal concepts): per-neuron AUC/common-language effect size (Swahili
activation vs. pooled other-4-language activation across concepts),
control = random per-concept relabeling (20 shuffles), with the SAME
top-k selection procedure applied to both real and control data --
this is what correctly handles the 196,608-way multiple-comparisons
problem (comparing "best of 196,608 under the real labeling" against
"best of 196,608 under a random labeling," not a per-neuron p-value).

STEP 2 (causal, disjoint n=12, never used for ranking): zero-ablate the
step-1 top-40 units during the Swahili forward pass; metric =
logit(own Swahili noun's first subword id) minus mean logit(its 4
translations' first subword ids) -- a margin objective in the same
spirit as `mbart_agreement_lib.py`'s gradient-fit margin -- shift vs.
baseline, compared to 10 random same-size-unit-set ablation draws.

**Two real bugs caught and fixed during smoke-testing, before trusting
any number** (both on record in the script's own docstring): (1) the
activation-recording hooks were registered before the translation step,
which internally calls `model.generate()` -- its later autoregressive
steps run with KV-cache seq_len=1 and crashed a hook hardcoded to read
position 1; fixed by only attaching hooks after the (hook-free)
translation step completes. (2) The first version used Cohen's d, which
exploded to ~90-160 at small n because many post-ReLU units have
near-zero WITHIN-GROUP variance by chance (not globally dead -- a
floor-based dead-unit filter, tried first, did not fix it either);
switched to a bounded AUC/common-language effect size, where a fully
dead/constant unit self-excludes at exactly 0.5 with no explosion.

**Result**:

| Step | Metric | Value | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 correlational | REAL top-40 mean\|AUC-0.5\| | 0.5000 (= AUC 1.0, perfect) | 35 concepts |
| 1 correlational | CONTROL (20 shuffles) | 0.1366 (std 0.0339) | 35 concepts |
| 1 correlational | SELECTIVITY | +0.3634 (~10.7 control-std) | |
| 2 causal | baseline margin | +9.3644 (std 1.07) | 12 concepts |
| 2 causal | REAL top-40 ablation SHIFT | -0.0101 (std 0.207) | 12 concepts |
| 2 causal | RANDOM ablation SHIFT (10 draws) | -0.0006 (std across draws 0.0104) | 12 concepts |
| 2 causal | SELECTIVITY | -0.0095 (-0.92 control-std) | |

**Verdict -- two findings pulling in different directions**:
- CORRELATIONAL: yes -- individual decoder FFN units exist that
  PERFECTLY (AUC=1.0, ~10.7 control-std above a 20-shuffle null)
  separate "target=Swahili" from "target=one of 4 other languages"
  across 35 different noun concepts. All 40 top units are in decoder
  LAYER 0.
- CAUSAL: ablating exactly those units produces a margin shift
  statistically indistinguishable from ablating random same-size unit
  sets (-0.92 control-std). **The pre-registered failure criterion
  ("no evidence of localized causal language neurons at this site" if
  the real shift isn't distinguishable from the random-set control) is
  met.**
- **Important caveat on the correlational result, not yet resolved**:
  layer 0 is the very first decoder layer, immediately downstream of
  the forced language token's own input embedding -- a unit scoring
  AUC=1.0 there may simply be reflecting "which literal token id was
  fed in" (near-tautological: of course an early layer can tell
  swh_Latn's embedding from fra_Latn's) rather than anything about the
  model's actual language-GENERATION behavior. This plausibly explains
  the causal null: a unit that only encodes "which token came in" has
  no obvious reason to causally drive what comes out several layers
  later. Also: all 40 winners tied at the exact ceiling (AUC=1.0) --
  likely many more than 40 layer-0 units hit this ceiling (exact count
  not run this session), so "top-40" was an arbitrary slice of a much
  larger tied set, not a sharply distinguished result.
- **Not yet tested**: units in layers 1-23 only (excludes the trivial
  layer-0 token-identity signal), and whether a MUCH larger ablated set
  (not just top-40) produces a causal effect -- either would help
  distinguish "distributed across many units" from "a few localized
  ones," the same conclusion pattern Bau et al. (2019) report for
  grammatical gender specifically (`docs/related_literature.txt`).

**Open threads for next session**:
- Rerun STEP 1 restricted to layers 1-23, to separate "reflects input
  token identity" from "causally drives language of generation."
- Count how many layer-0 units actually hit the AUC=1.0 ceiling (tie
  diagnostic not run this session).
- Scale n up further (35/12 is still a pilot) if layers 1-23 show a
  weaker but real correlational signal -- will need more concepts for
  stable ranking at a less saturated effect size.
- The same two-step recipe (correlational AUC scan + disjoint causal
  ablation) is reusable for the project's other two established
  directions (semantic, noun-class) per the user's original
  three-aspect framing -- not run yet.

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — decoder FFN write-vector geometry: no population-level language alignment anywhere, but a real sparse tail concentrated at the first and last layers

**User's question**, after asking for an architecture walkthrough of how
a single FFN neuron relates to the embedding space (a neuron = one READ
row of `fc1`'s weight matrix + one WRITE column of `fc2`'s weight
matrix, a rank-1 operation, not a full matrix -- the full FFN sublayer
is what reconstructs a matrix-like map): start at the LAST decoder
layer and work backwards -- is there a segment of a layer's weight
matrix (a set of neurons) whose WRITE direction works almost
exclusively on the language subspace, rather than relying on the noisy,
indirect ablation test from the previous entry?

**Architecture fact verified first, since the whole approach depends on
it**: `facebook/nllb-200-distilled-1.3B` TIES input embeddings and the
unembedding projection -- `model.config.tie_word_embeddings=True`,
`model.lm_head.weight IS model.model.shared.weight` (literally the same
tensor, confirmed `max abs diff: 0.0`). This means the cached g_hat /
per-noun m_hat / per-class directions (all built directly from that
same weight matrix's rows in the embedding-decomposition work, 2026-
10-01/02) live in the EXACT space the model dots a final hidden state
against to produce every vocab token's logit -- so a decoder FFN
neuron's WRITE vector (one column of `fc2.weight`) can be compared BY
COSINE directly against those cached directions, no forward pass or
generation needed at all. Also confirmed: `model.model.decoder.
layer_norm` exists (a final LayerNorm after all 24 decoder layers,
before `lm_head`) -- for layer 23 this makes the raw-cosine comparison
only an approximation; for every earlier layer, 1-23 more full decoder
blocks sit in between, a much larger approximation gap (same
"representationally looser" caveat as the 2026-10-01 layer-17 note).

**Method** (new `nllb_swahili_decoder_write_vector_language_subspace_
check.py`, reuses the existing `nllb_swahili_concept_decomposition_
cache.pt` and `class_directions`/`build_or_load_concepts` from
`nllb_swahili_vector_orthogonality_check.py` unchanged -- CLAUDE.md hard
rule #10, zero new generation): for each of the 24 decoder layers,
normalized `fc2.weight` columns (8192 write vectors, 1024-dim) scored
by (1) signed cosine with g_hat ("lang"), (2) max \|cosine\| over the 11
class directions ("class entanglement"), (3) mean \|cosine\| over all
319 per-noun m_hats ("semantic entanglement"). Control: 50,000 random
unit vectors in the same 1024 dims, scored on the SAME three
statistics (matching each one's own aggregation -- max-of-11,
mean-of-319 -- not a generic single-draw null). Threshold set
EMPIRICALLY from the control's own tail (not an assumed-Gaussian
mean+3*std -- a first attempt at that was replaced once it was clear a
2000-draw sample can't reliably support a 1-in-8192 quantile; redone at
n=50,000 draws) so that ~1.0 random unit out of 8192 is expected to
clear each threshold by chance alone, per layer -- a direct,
assumption-free "expected by chance" baseline per CLAUDE.md hard rule
#7. For layer 23 specifically, also computed a LayerNorm-corrected
version (write vector multiplied elementwise by `layer_norm.weight`) to
check how much the one intervening operation changes the picture.

**Result**:
- **Population level (mean\|lang score\| over all 8192 units, every
  layer): flat, within +/-0.3 control-std of the random-direction null
  EVERYWHERE** -- no layer's write vectors are, on average, more
  aligned with g_hat than chance. Layer 23 raw vs. LN-corrected: 0.0304
  vs. 0.0290, correlation +0.9975 -- the final LayerNorm barely changes
  which units look language-aligned, so the uncorrected approximation
  used for every other layer is a reasonable proxy, at least by this
  check.
- **Tail level (units clearing the empirical ~1-in-8192 threshold):
  real and consistent excess everywhere, but sharply peaked at the two
  ends of the stack, not uniform:**

  | Layer | clears LANG threshold | also clears BOTH entanglement thresholds |
  |---|---|---|
  | 23 (last) | 53 | **30** |
  | 22 | 39 | 27 |
  | 1-21 (middle) | 7-20 | 4-15 |
  | 0 (first) | 35 | **19** |

  (~1.0 expected by chance alone, per threshold, per layer, of 8192
  units -- every layer's count is well above that, but layers 22-23 and
  0 stand out well above the middle-layer baseline too.)
- **Connects directly to the previous entry's causal null**: the
  layer-0 units that had PERFECT activation-level AUC selectivity in
  the ablation pilot are, by this write-vector-geometry test,
  unremarkable -- only 19 "exclusive" candidates at layer 0, no better
  than the modest middle-layer baseline (7-15). Consistent with that
  entry's hypothesis: those units are plausibly a READ-side phenomenon
  (detecting which token came in, via `fc1`'s rows) rather than a
  WRITE-side one (pushing the output toward Swahili, via `fc2`'s
  columns) -- geometrically unremarkable write vectors would explain
  why ablating them didn't move the output margin. **Layer 23 is the
  more promising candidate population**: largest tail (30 "exclusive"
  units after both entanglement filters), closest to the unembedding
  matrix (one LayerNorm, confirmed to barely matter), best-motivated
  site for an actual causal test.
- Top layer-23 candidates (e.g. unit 5063 lang=-0.19, unit 4543
  lang=+0.18, unit 1458 lang=+0.18) have class_entangle in the
  0.04-0.12 range and sem_mean 0.02-0.05 -- clearly below their own
  empirical ~1-in-8192 ceilings, but NOT literally zero / orthogonal;
  "exclusive" here means relatively more lang-aligned than class- or
  semantic-aligned, not perfectly separated from those subspaces.

**Not yet done**: a causal ablation test on this specific, geometrically-
motivated layer-23 candidate set (would reuse
`nllb_swahili_decoder_language_neuron_check.py`'s causal-ablation
machinery, swapping in these 30 units instead of the AUC-activation-
selected ones) -- explicitly deferred, the user wants to keep working
backwards through more layers / understanding the geometry further
before spending another causal-ablation run.

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — closed-form logit-shift prediction vs. real ablation: r=0.9945, the single-axis projection story is the actual mechanism

**User's question**, after a conversation walkthrough of the
architecture (a neuron = one READ row of `fc1` + one WRITE column of
`fc2`, a rank-1 op; `logit(v) = ev . u_v`, computed separately per
candidate token then softmax, not a sum of vectors): for ANY single
axis `L_hat`, splitting `ev = ev_par + ev_perp` (parallel/orthogonal to
`L_hat`) gives `logit(v) = (ev.L_hat)(u_v.L_hat) + (ev_perp . u_v_perp)`
with the two cross terms EXACTLY zero, always, by construction (not an
approximation -- `ev_par` is a multiple of `L_hat`, `u_v_perp` has zero
component along `L_hat` by definition, so their dot product is
identically 0). Does this give a genuine closed-form PREDICTION of what
ablating a layer-23 "language-exclusive" write-vector candidate
actually does to the output, and does it match reality?

**Method** (new `nllb_swahili_layer23_closed_form_vs_ablation_check.py`,
reuses the previous entry's functions for candidate regeneration and
the causal-pilot entry's `NeuronRecorder`/`forward_at_lang`/`build_pool`
unchanged -- CLAUDE.md hard rule #10): for each of the SAME 30 layer-23
"language-exclusive" candidates (regenerated deterministically, not
hardcoded) plus 20 random non-candidate layer-23 neurons as a
comparison group, across 8 fresh concepts (no disjointness requirement
needed -- candidate selection depends only on the global 319-noun
cache, not on these concepts):

  predicted_shift = -a_i * (gamma ⊙ w_i) . (u_sw - mean(u_other))

  a_i = the neuron's OWN observed baseline activation (not
  hypothetical) at decoder position 1; w_i = `fc2.weight`'s column i;
  gamma = `model.model.decoder.layer_norm.weight` (the one operation
  between layer 23's output and the TIED unembedding matrix -- `model.
  lm_head.weight IS model.model.shared.weight`, confirmed 2026-10-02
  earlier today); u_v = token v's row of that same tied matrix. The
  gamma multiply is the linear part of LayerNorm's effect; its mean-
  centering/std-division is deliberately left uncorrected (flagged as a
  known, minor-to-moderate approximation up front). actual_shift: a
  real teacher-forced forward pass, zero-ablating neuron i alone,
  measuring the same margin metric as the causal-ablation pilot, minus
  baseline. Control: a shuffled-pairing null (predicted re-paired with
  a random permutation of actual, 200 shuffles) per hard rule #7.

**Result (n=400 (neuron, concept) pairs: 240 candidate, 160 random)**:

| | ALL | CANDIDATES | RANDOM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pearson r (predicted vs actual) | **+0.9945** | +0.9960 | +0.9828 |
| mean\|predicted shift\| | -- | 0.4826 | 0.2319 |
| mean\|actual shift\| | -- | 0.0035 | 0.0016 |

SHUFFLE-PAIRING CONTROL (200 shuffles): mean r=+0.0089, std=0.0549 --
**the real r is +17.95 control-std from the shuffle null.** A smaller
n=2-concept smoke test gave an even tighter r=+0.9989 (+27.5 control-
std) on 66 pairs, confirming the result isn't an artifact of the larger
run's specific sample.

**Verdict**: the simple single-axis projection identity is not just a
plausible mental model -- **it is the actual mechanism**, verified down
to individual neurons: sign and relative magnitude of the real ablation
effect are predicted almost perfectly from pure linear algebra on
already-trained weights, no forward pass needed for the prediction
itself (only to obtain each neuron's own baseline activation `a_i`,
and to measure the real ablation effect for validation). The
correlation holds about equally well for candidates (r=0.996) and
random neurons (r=0.983) -- exactly as expected, since the FORMULA
should be a good local approximation for ANY layer-23 neuron's marginal
contribution, not something special to language-aligned ones; what
differs between the groups is effect SIZE (candidates ~2x larger mean
|predicted| and |actual| shift than random), which is the thing
"language-exclusive" selection was supposed to predict. A consistent
~100-130x gap between predicted and actual MAGNITUDE (seen on the two
nonzero-activation units in the n=2 smoke test: ratios 134.2 and 114.9)
is exactly what the deliberately-uncorrected LayerNorm std-division
would produce -- a roughly constant missing scale factor, not a sign of
the mechanism being wrong.

**Not yet done**: correcting for the LayerNorm's std-division exactly
(would need the actual pre-LN hidden state's norm at that position, one
more hook away) to close the remaining magnitude gap; testing whether
the same closed-form approach predicts ablation effects at EARLIER
layers as well as it does at layer 23 (expected to degrade, since
earlier layers must additionally survive the intervening decoder
blocks' nonlinear transformations that this formula doesn't model at
all -- layer 23 was the best case by construction, only one LayerNorm
in the way).

Files: `nllb_swahili_layer23_closed_form_vs_ablation_check.py` (new),
`nllb_swahili_layer23_closed_form_vs_ablation_check.log`.

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — cross-language steering: amplifying 12 layer-23 neurons makes Swahili beat the FORCED target language up to 95.8% of the time

**User's question**: forget prediction -- can we actually TRICK the
model? Given a forced target language A (what the decoder is literally
told to generate), can modifying the layer-23 "language-exclusive"
neurons' activations make a DIFFERENT language B (Swahili) win the
next-token competition over A? No grammar/fluency bar -- success is
purely P(B's word) > P(A's word) at the position right after the forced
language token.

**Method** (new `nllb_swahili_layer23_cross_language_steering_check.py`;
additive extension to the shared `NeuronRecorder`
(`nllb_swahili_decoder_language_neuron_check.py`) -- a new `set_values`
dict that pushes a unit to an ARBITRARY value, not just zero, existing
`ablate`-only callers unaffected; everything else reused unchanged,
CLAUDE.md hard rule #10): A = each of the 4 OTHER_LANGS in turn
(French/Spanish/German/Portuguese), B = Swahili (fixed -- the only
language `g_hat` represents), decoder forced to A throughout exactly as
if actually asked for language A. Metric = logit(B's first subword) -
logit(A's first subword) right after the forced language token.

Of the 30 regenerated layer-23 candidates, 12 have POSITIVE lang score
(their write vector points toward g_hat) and 18 negative. A ReLU
activation can only be >= 0, so a negative-lang neuron can be ablated to
stop it pushing AWAY from Swahili but can never be driven negative to
push toward it -- only the 12 positive-lang neurons can be amplified.
Intervention: the 12 positive-lang units SET to a calibrated value
alpha (`NeuronRecorder.set_values`, new capability); the 18 negative-
lang units zeroed (`ablate`, as before). Alpha grid was NOT a guess:
built from the positive candidates' own observed baseline activation
scale across the actual concepts/languages tested (max observed x
small multiples), logged explicitly (hard rule #4). CONTROL (hard rule
#7): the IDENTICAL intervention shape (12 amplified + 18 ablated) on a
random, non-candidate, size-matched layer-23 neuron set instead.

**Result (n=24 (concept, target-language-A) pairs per alpha, 6
concepts x 4 languages; baseline/no-intervention flip rate = 0.0% --
the forced language always wins naturally)**:

| alpha (x observed max activation) | REAL flip rate | REAL mean shift | RANDOM flip rate | RANDOM mean shift |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10x (116.1) | 16.7% | 6.15 | 0.0% | 1.68 |
| 30x (348.3) | 66.7% | 13.66 | 8.3% | 5.18 |
| 100x (1161.1) | **91.7%** | 18.63 | 41.7% | 8.92 |
| 300x (3483.3) | **95.8%** | 20.05 | 54.2% | 10.35 |

A smaller n=2-concept (8-pair) pilot at a wider alpha range showed the
same pattern (REAL reaches 100% at alpha=903.7 while RANDOM is still at
25%; REAL 50% at alpha=271.1 while RANDOM is 0%), confirming this isn't
an artifact of the specific 6-concept sample.

**Verdict**: yes -- the model can genuinely be tricked. Amplifying just
12 specific neurons (out of 196,608 across the decoder) at a single
layer and position, while zeroing 18 others, makes Swahili's token
outscore the LITERALLY-REQUESTED language's own token in up to 95.8% of
tested cases. The real-vs-random gap is largest at moderate alpha
(66.7% vs 8.3% at 30x) and narrows but never closes even at extreme
alpha (95.8% vs 54.2% at 300x) -- real candidates are doing something
qualitatively more efficient than "any sufficiently large push in some
direction," not merely benefiting from a bigger perturbation norm. This
is the first genuinely CONSTRUCTIVE/causal-sufficiency result in the
language-neuron thread (the ablation pilot was a null at layer 0; the
closed-form check validated PREDICTION at layer 23; this is the first
successful STEERING demonstration) -- directly relevant to the
project's core deployment mechanism (CLAUDE.md section 1: steer a
noun's representation so its agreement class matches the target), now
shown concretely for the language axis specifically, at the neuron
level, with a working controls-and-alpha-grid recipe that could be
reused for the class axis.

**Caveats, stated plainly**: (1) no grammar/fluency check at all -- this
tests whether a Swahili SUBWORD TOKEN'S logit exceeds the forced
language's own token's logit at one position, not whether a full,
fluent Swahili sentence is produced; (2) the random control also climbs
substantially at high alpha (54.2%), so "trick the model" becomes
possible via brute-force perturbation eventually regardless of which
units are hit -- the REAL finding is the efficiency/specificity gap at
moderate alpha, not that random intervention never works at all; (3)
alpha values needed are large relative to natural activation scale
(30-300x the observed max) -- whether this generalizes to a
PERCEPTIBLE, generation-level effect (not just a single logit
comparison) is not yet tested.

**Not yet done**: checking whether this logit-level flip survives into
actual multi-token GENERATION (does the model go on to produce a
recognizably Swahili word, or does the flip only win the very first
subword before reverting); the same recipe for OTHER target-B languages
(is Swahili special because `g_hat` was built from it, or would e.g. a
French-specific direction work just as well); repeating at other layers
now that the mechanism is understood.

neuron_check.py`'s `NeuronRecorder` -- added `set_values` dict

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — does the pairwise-margin flip survive real generation? No: 0% Swahili at every alpha tested, after catching two real bugs in the test itself

**User's question**: the previous entry's pairwise-margin "flip" (up to
95.8%) only raced Swahili's token against the ONE forced language's own
token. Free-running `generate()` picks the greedy argmax over the
entire ~256k-token vocabulary -- a much harder bar. Does the effect
survive into actual generation?

**Method** (new `nllb_swahili_layer23_generation_steering_check.py`):
same 30 layer-23 candidates (12 positive-lang amplified via a new
`AllPositionSteerer` hook, 18 negative-lang zeroed), same random-control
design, now applied through real `model.generate()` calls
(`forced_bos_token_id`, greedy, `max_new_tokens=6`) instead of a single
teacher-forced forward pass. Success checked two ways: a strict token-id
match (does the argmax first generated token exactly equal the
concept's Swahili word's first subword id?) and the full decoded text,
printed for every example.

**Two real bugs caught and fixed BEFORE trusting any number** (both
would have produced a false negative or an uninterpretable result if
missed):
1. **Hook-timing/scope bug**: an initial version applied the
   intervention at EVERY position of every forward call throughout
   generation (necessary in spirit -- KV-caching means each
   autoregressive step is its own call at a different absolute
   position, so `NeuronRecorder`'s single fixed `pos` doesn't apply --
   but applying it literally everywhere, including the `decoder_start`
   token's own processing, over-disrupts the model long before any
   clean word-level effect could appear: both REAL and RANDOM collapsed
   into repeated-token gibberish ("mada mada mada...", "im im im...")
   at the SAME alpha that gave a 91.7% pairwise flip in the previous
   entry's single-position test.
2. **Wrong-call and wrong-position bugs, found by direct empirical
   verification, not assumption** (the project's own hard-won lesson --
   CLAUDE.md hard rule #2's "verify propagation before trusting a run"
   applied here to generation mechanics instead of layer choice): (a) a
   first attempt to restrict the intervention to "the first call only"
   actually targeted call index 0, which processes `decoder_start_
   token_id` ALONE -- `forced_bos_token_id`'s own override/discard
   mechanism (`ForcedBOSTokenLogitsProcessor`) means the language token
   is only ever fed as actual model INPUT on call index 1, confirmed by
   directly inspecting hook call shapes and the generated id sequence
   (`[2, 256168('swh_Latn'), 26328('nyumba'), 2]` for 3 total calls).
   Fixed by targeting call index 1. (b) Separately, the script's
   extracted "first generated token" was read from `out[0, 1]` --
   **also wrong**: `forced_bos_token_id` makes position 1 of the output
   sequence literally, unconditionally, equal to the requested
   language's own code token id, regardless of ANY intervention (direct
   check: `out[0]=[2, 256057('fra_Latn'), 236130('vêtements'), 2]`) --
   that position can never move. The real first FREELY generated
   content token is position 2. Before this fix, even the unintervened
   BASELINE showed 0% "correctly matches language A" (100% "OTHER"),
   which was the tell that the metric itself, not the model, was wrong
   -- confirmed fixed when baseline flipped to the expected 100% "A".

**Result, after both fixes (n=20 (concept, target-language-A) pairs per
alpha, 5 concepts x 4 languages; baseline/no-intervention: 100% A, 0%
SW, 0% OTHER -- the correctness sanity check passes)**:

| alpha (x observed max activation) | REAL: correct-A | REAL: OTHER | RANDOM: correct-A | RANDOM: OTHER |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10x (116.1) | 10.0% | 90.0% | 40.0% | 60.0% |
| 30x (348.3) | 0.0% | 100.0% | 5.0% | 95.0% |
| 100x (1161.1) | 0.0% | 100.0% | 0.0% | 100.0% |
| 300x (3483.3) | 0.0% | 100.0% | 0.0% | 100.0% |

**SW (Swahili) = 0.0% at EVERY alpha tested, for BOTH real and random
interventions, across all 80 generations run.** Amplification
progressively destroys the ability to produce the CORRECT forced-
language word (REAL degrades faster -- already 0% correct-A at 30x vs.
RANDOM's 40%/5%/0% schedule) and replaces it with unrelated,
NON-SWAHILI output. Qualitatively (from the printed examples), the two
groups fail in recognizably different ways: REAL's broken output
converges toward a small set of largely CONCEPT-INDEPENDENT fragments
("muka", "madais", "madache" appear across different source concepts
and target languages alike), while RANDOM's broken output stays closer
to real words IN THE FORCED LANGUAGE itself but semantically wrong
("immeubles"/"impresión"/"imóveis" -- all coincidentally share an
"im-"-prefixed real word in their respective language). Neither pattern
is Swahili.

**Verdict**: the pairwise-margin success from the previous entry does
NOT survive into free-running generation. It was a genuine, correctly-
measured result for the question it actually asked (does Swahili's
token's logit exceed this ONE specific competitor's logit) but that
question is a much narrower bar than "does the model generate Swahili,"
and conflating the two would be a real overclaim. This directly
qualifies the previous entry's practical relevance to the project's
deployment goal (CLAUDE.md section 1: steering a noun's representation
for deployment-time generation) -- the mechanism is real and
causally verified at the single-comparison level (closed-form r=0.9945,
pairwise flip up to 95.8%), but "trick the model into generating
Swahili via this specific neuron-amplification recipe" is, on this
evidence, a NULL result, not yet a success story.

**Not yet done**: a narrower alpha scan between 10x and 30x (where the
transition from "intact" to "fully broken, still non-Swahili" happens)
to see whether any alpha window exists where REAL output is partially
disrupted toward something Swahili-recognizable rather than jumping
straight to unrelated garbage; testing whether a DIFFERENT, non-
amplification-based intervention (e.g. directly setting the stream's
g_hat-component to a value matched to real Swahili activations, rather
than driving 12 individual units to an arbitrary large constant) fares
better, since the arbitrary-constant approach may be an unnecessarily
blunt choice of intervention shape.

Files: `nllb_swahili_layer23_generation_steering_check.py` (new),
