(new).

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — mrefu cross-validation, then the user's token-injection proposal: a real generation-level success, closing the loop

**Cross-validation on mrefu/kirefu** (the LOW-semantic-overlap pair,
0.25 cosine vs. mzuri/kizuri's 0.90): the same hidden-state-alignment
test, now parameterized by word
(`nllb_swahili_mzuri_class7_hidden_state_alignment_check.py --word
mrefu`), shows an essentially IDENTICAL pattern to mzuri -- REAL margin
crosses between alpha=10 and alpha=30, REAL-vs-RANDOM gap of ~14.6x at
alpha=300 (3.3144 vs 0.2254), comparable in magnitude to mzuri's 22x.
**This is itself informative**: the synthetic vector, by construction,
ALWAYS preserves the source word's own semantics (that is what "keep
language+semantic+other, swap only class" means) -- so neuron-steering
reliably reaches the constructed target regardless of whether a
MATCHING REAL WORD exists with that same semantic content. The missing-
semantic-block finding explains why steering can't reach the real word
"kirefu" (different meaning); it does not prevent steering from
reaching OUR constructed, meaning-preserving target. The two findings
are consistent, not in tension.

**User's proposal**: since neuron-steering reliably moves the REAL
hidden state toward the constructed vector (previous entry) but no
real token sits there, literally INJECT that vector as a new,
real vocabulary token, and let the already-validated steering
mechanism select it directly -- closing the "ki-prefix attractor" gap
mechanically rather than hoping a better real word exists.

**Confirmed directly before building on it**: `tokenizer.add_tokens()`
+ `model.resize_token_embeddings()` correctly expands
`model.model.shared.weight` and the tied `lm_head.weight` remains the
same tensor after resize (`is` check passes).

**Pilot** (new `nllb_swahili_mzuri_class7_token_injection_pilot.py`,
scoped to ONE word/ONE class pair before any larger effort, this
session's standing cheap-first discipline): added `<mzuri_cl7>` as a
real token, set its embedding row directly to the already-validated
synthetic vector, ran the SAME layer-22 class-7-aligned neuron steering
recipe through REAL FREE GENERATION.

**Result**:

| alpha | REAL text | new token selected? | RANDOM text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | "mtu mzuri" | No | "mtu mwema" |
| **30** | **"mtu\<mzuri_cl7\>"** | **Yes** | "mtu mwema" |
| **100** | **"mtu\<mzuri_cl7\>"** | **Yes** | "mtu mwema" |
| **300** | **"mtu\<mzuri_cl7\>"** | **Yes** | "mtu mwema" |
| 1000 | "mtu kipenzi" | No | "mtu stepsema" |

**Free generation ACTUALLY SELECTS the injected token at alpha 30-300**
-- exactly the range the hidden-state-alignment test predicted the
margin would favor it. Random control never selects it at any alpha --
confirms this isn't a generic artifact of adding a new vocabulary slot,
it specifically requires the real class-7-aligned neurons. "mtu" (the
noun) stays correct throughout. At alpha=1000 it overshoots back to
"kipenzi" -- a genuine sweet spot, not unlimited robustness; push too
hard and the same ki-vocabulary-substitution regime from every earlier
check reasserts itself.

**Verdict**: this is the strongest result in the entire class-axis
thread, and it closes the full causal loop this session has been
tracing turn by turn: decomposition -> neuron identification ->
validated causal leverage -> validated representational alignment with
a hand-constructed target -> now, with that target made real, an
actual generation-level success, with controls, at the first attempt.
The project's own planned deployment pipeline (CLAUDE.md section 1:
steer, then dictionary-substitute) already anticipated needing exactly
this kind of step -- the injected token is a placeholder a final
lookup table would map to the correct real Swahili surface form, not a
deviation from the intended architecture.

**Caveats, stated plainly**: one word, one class pair, one sentence,
one position -- not yet generalized. The sweet-spot alpha range (30-300)
was found by the SAME sweep already run for other purposes, not a
dedicated fine search -- its true boundaries are unknown. Whether
generation continues sensibly PAST the injected token (nothing in
training ever followed `<mzuri_cl7>` with anything) is untested --
`max_new_tokens=6` was enough to observe the selection but not to see
what (if anything) a longer continuation would produce. The dictionary-
substitution mapping (new token -> real surface form) is not yet
implemented, only motivated.

**Not yet done**: finding the precise sweet-spot boundaries; testing
generation continuation past the injected token; scaling to more
adjectives and more classes (the full "all adjectives x all classes"
version the user originally proposed) now that the single-pilot
mechanism is validated; testing the SAME recipe on mrefu (inject
`<mrefu_cl7>`, check whether its own alpha=10-30 crossing also produces
a real generation-level selection, not just a hidden-state-alignment
crossing); and critically, testing this on the NOUN side of the
standing mtu/class7 problem, which is what the project's deployment
goal actually needs.

Files: `nllb_swahili_mzuri_class7_token_injection_pilot.py` (new).

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — integration test: pure embedding-level noun steering + injected class-7 adjective tokens, no neuron forcing -- clean null, and an explanatory real bug

**User's question**: do the two mechanisms work TOGETHER? Specifically:
inject class-7 adjective tokens (`<mrefu_cl7>`, `<mzuri_cl7>`, same
construction as the mzuri pilot, now also for mrefu), construct a
synthetic "class-7 mtu" vector (same decomposition, applied to the
NOUN this time), substitute it directly as mtu's embedding during a
REAL EN->SW translation attempt, and see whether the signal propagates
through the network's own ordinary computation (no neuron-level
forcing at all this time) to select the injected adjective tokens
downstream -- the most direct test yet of the project's original
deployment vision (CLAUDE.md section 1: steer the noun's internal
representation, keep its surface form, let agreement follow).

**A real bug caught in smoke-testing, before trusting any number**:
`model.generate()` does not accept `decoder_inputs_embeds` together
with its own internal decoder_input_ids handling for this model
(confirmed directly -- raises an explicit error) -- worked around with
a manual greedy-decoding loop. That loop then hit a SECOND, more
consequential bug: the decoder's embedding lookup
(`M2M100ScaledWordEmbedding`) applies a 32x scale factor
(`embed_scale`, confirmed directly, = sqrt(d_model) = sqrt(1024), the
standard Transformer embedding-scaling convention) to raw weight rows
during normal lookup. The first version fed `decoder_inputs_embeds`
built from RAW, unscaled rows throughout -- putting every position 32x
out of the model's normal operating range -- and even the UNMODIFIED
baseline (normal mtu embedding, zero intervention) collapsed to just
"mtu" + immediate EOS, instead of the "mtu mrefu mzuri" every other
script this session reliably gets via `generate()`. This was the tell
that the harness was broken, not the model. Fixed by scaling every
constructed embedding (eos/swh_Latn lookups AND the synthetic vectors)
by this same factor; the corrected baseline then exactly reproduces
"mtu mrefu mzuri," confirming the manual decode loop is now faithful.

**Result, after the fix**:

| | tokens | text |
|---|---|---|
| BASELINE (normal mtu embedding) | mrefu, mzuri, \</s\> | "mtu mrefu mzuri" |
| STEERED (synthetic class-7 mtu, adjectives injected, NO neuron forcing) | mrefu, mzuri, \</s\> | "mtu mrefu mzuri" (**identical**) |

**Pure embedding-level substitution for the noun, with no neuron-level
forcing anywhere, produced zero change** -- not a weak effect, an
EXACT match to baseline, down to the token sequence.

**Why, consistent with everything else found this session**: the
embedding substitution happens at the very first position in the
network (effectively "layer -1"), so the signal has to survive all 24
decoder layers of self-attention, cross-attention, and FFN processing
completely unaided. The write-vector geometry scan (two entries
upstream) already established that class-7 alignment concentrates in
LATER layers (peaking at 22/23), with layer 0 comparatively weak and
dominated by trivial token-identity effects -- a pure embedding
injection is the single hardest point in the whole stack to make a
signal survive. The layer-22 neuron intervention works specifically
because it is injected close to where the output is actually read out
(one layer + one LayerNorm from `lm_head`), not because "construct the
right vector" is the wrong idea in general -- the SAME construction
technique, applied at the SAME layer-22 site (not the embedding), is
exactly what the token-injection pilot already validated working.

**Verdict**: a clean, informative null that sharpens rather than
contradicts this session's other results. "Where you inject the
construction" matters as much as "what you construct" -- the
embedding-decomposition logic is validated repeatedly (vector
injection, hidden-state alignment, the mzuri token-injection pilot),
but only when applied at a site close enough to the output to survive.
Pure input-level substitution, unreinforced, does not survive 24 layers
of transformation.

**Not yet done, the natural next experiment**: combine BOTH mechanisms
-- the embedding substitution for mtu's input AND the already-validated
layer-22 class-7 neuron steering simultaneously (rather than either
alone) -- to see whether the combination succeeds at producing a
full, coherent "mtu [class-7 adjective]" sentence starting from true
free generation, where neuron-steering alone (prior entries) only
demonstrated the adjective-selection piece with mtu already given as a
fixed prefix. Also open: whether reinforcing the embedding-level signal
at MULTIPLE points through the stack (not just the input) rather than
only at layer 22 changes this null.

Files: `nllb_swahili_mtu_class7_embedding_steer_plus_injection_check.py`
(new).

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — user's refinement: overwrite the SHARED weight row directly (not a per-position substitution) -- closes a real gap, null holds anyway

**User's question**: since embeddings/unembedding are tied, can the
class-1 "mtu" row be completely removed from the shared matrix and
replaced with the class-7 version, so neither the encoder nor the
decoder ever sees any class-1 signal for it at all -- rather than
substituting a vector at one position during one forward pass (the
previous entry's method)?

**Confirmed directly before building on it**:
`model.model.encoder.embed_tokens.weight`, `model.model.decoder.
embed_tokens.weight`, and `model.lm_head.weight` are ALL literally the
same tensor as `model.model.shared.weight` (three separate identity
checks, all pass). Overwriting one row therefore changes encoder input,
decoder input, AND the output/unembedding logit score for that token
simultaneously -- and closes a real gap in the previous entry's test,
which only touched the INPUT usage at one position; the OUTPUT side
(the logit score for predicting "mtu" as a token at any position) was
still being computed against the ORIGINAL class-1 embedding via the
tied lm_head.

**Method** (new `nllb_swahili_mtu_class7_weight_overwrite_check.py`):
mtu's row in `model.model.shared.weight` overwritten directly with the
same synthetic class-7 vector construction used throughout this
thread, restored at the end so the loaded model isn't left corrupted
for later use. This also simplifies the mechanics considerably versus
the previous script -- no manual greedy-decode loop or `embed_scale`
workaround needed, since ordinary `model.generate()` now works
unchanged (the model's own embedding lookup already handles scaling
internally; it just finds a different vector sitting at mtu's row).
Three conditions on the same "a tall good person" source: baseline,
mtu-only overwrite, and mtu-overwrite plus the injected class-7
adjective tokens from the prior entries.

**Result: all three conditions produced the IDENTICAL output**, "mtu
mrefu mzuri" -- unchanged even with the full weight overwrite covering
input and output simultaneously, and unchanged even with the class-7
adjective tokens available in vocabulary.

**One scope caveat worth being precise about**: "a tall good person" is
ENGLISH source text, so the encoder never actually looks up "mtu" at
all in this direction (English tokens are unrelated ids) -- the
encoder side of the request isn't exercised by this specific example;
it would only matter for a Swahili-source translation. What IS
exercised here is the decoder's input lookup AND its output/unembedding
score for "mtu," simultaneously, via the shared tensor. "mtu" still
gets selected as the translation of "person" -- consistent with
cos(synthetic, original)=0.9566, so its score as "the correct word for
person" barely moved -- and once selected and fed back in (now
automatically carrying its new embedding via the shared matrix), the
same finding as the previous entry holds: the signal still does not
survive the remaining layers enough to shift the following adjective.

**Verdict**: this is a MORE decisive version of the previous null, not
a weaker one. The full weight overwrite closes the exact gap that
could have explained away the earlier result (an unpatched output
path) -- and the null held anyway. This confirms the conclusion is
structural, not a methodological artifact: an input-level signal,
however completely and permanently it is injected, does not survive 24
layers of transformation on its own. The layer-22 neuron intervention
(prior entries) works specifically because it is injected close to
where the output is actually read out, not because embedding-level
injection is inherently too weak a signal in general -- it is
specifically too weak delivered at the INPUT layer, 24 transformer
blocks away from where it would need to still matter.

**Not yet done**: the combined test this now points to even more
clearly -- mtu's embedding (or write-vector) change delivered AT OR
NEAR layer 22 (not the input embedding layer) simultaneously with the
layer-22 adjective-steering neurons, rather than an input-layer
substitution; testing the encoder side of this question properly (a
Swahili-source sentence containing "mtu," not an English one); whether
reinforcing the signal at EVERY layer (not just the input, not just
layer 22 alone) changes the picture.

Files: `nllb_swahili_mtu_class7_weight_overwrite_check.py` (new).

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — full layer-by-layer trace: class-1 signal is RECONSTRUCTED progressively, not merely un-amplified; then two-noun coordination test: clean, no interference

**Trace diagnostic** (new `nllb_swahili_mtu_class7_full_trace_
diagnostic.py`, `output_hidden_states`/`output_attentions=True` with
`attn_implementation="eager"` -- confirmed directly that the default
`sdpa` backend silently can't return attention weights): at mtu's
position, teacher-forced, comparing baseline vs. the shared-weight-
overwritten (class-7) condition at every one of the 24 decoder layers.
The overwritten condition's class7_proj starts strongly positive (+42
at layer 0) and decays roughly geometrically, CROSSING TO NEGATIVE by
layer 9, while class1_proj climbs from -6 (layer 0) to 189.83 by layer
22 -- nearly identical to the baseline's own 191.95 at the same layer.
**The network reconstructs the class-1 signal, it does not merely fail
to preserve the class-7 one.** Two explanations ruled out: (1) the
top-5 most active neurons at any layer essentially never overlap with
that layer's own top-10 write-vector-aligned candidates (near-zero
overlap throughout) -- the reconstruction is not driven by the specific
neurons the write-vector search identified; (2) cross-attention weight
from mtu's position to the English "person" token is small (peaks
~10-16% in layers 2-3, under 2% by late layers) and nearly identical
between conditions, and the encoder's own "person" representation does
not even point toward class-1 particularly -- cross-attention to the
source noun is not the main driver either. Likely explanation (not yet
directly confirmed): compounding dilution through repeated self-
attention/FFN mixing with the ~96%-unchanged rest of the embedding
(class signal is only ~4.2% of embedding energy, per the 2026-10-02
energy-budget entry), not a mechanism with a few identifiable "culprit"
units to disable.

**User's resulting strategic question**: rather than defeating the
correction, REINFORCE the class-push at every position that needs it
(each noun, each of its own agreement words), independently, rather
than relying on one injection to survive the whole sentence -- directly
motivated by the multi-noun coordination problem.

**Two-noun test** (new `nllb_swahili_two_noun_class7_coordination_
check.py`): "a tall person and a good person" confirmed via direct
generate() to tokenize as [eos, swh, mtu(2), mrefu(3), na(4), mtu(5),
mzuri(6)] -- two independent "mtu [adjective]" units. The "na mtu"
portion is FORCED (consistent with the project's dictionary-driven
design -- target nouns are known in advance, not discovered by letting
the model choose), each adjective generated one token at a time via a
manual forward-pass+argmax step so each position's steering can be
switched on/off independently. Same layer-22 class-7-aligned
candidates and injected tokens as every prior check, alpha=100 (inside
the established 30-300 sweet spot).

**Result -- clean on all four conditions**:

| Condition | Output |
|---|---|
| Baseline | "mtu mrefu na mtu mzuri" |
| Steer A only | "mtu\<mrefu_cl7\> na mtu mzuri" |
| Steer B only | "mtu mrefu na mtu\<mzuri_cl7\>" |
| Steer both | "mtu\<mrefu_cl7\> na mtu\<mzuri_cl7\>" |

Each noun's steering affects ONLY its own adjective. No forward
contamination from A's earlier intervention into B's independently-
generated adjective; no dilution of B's own steering from the longer,
two-noun context; combining both works as the clean sum of the two
independent effects, not some entangled result.

**Verdict**: since autoregressive generation only permits forward
causal influence, forward contamination from A into B was the only
coherent interference risk, and it does not occur. Position-specific
steering is confirmed independent across nouns, at least for this
simple, two-noun, unambiguous-adjacency sentence -- directly validating
the "reinforce locally at every position that needs it, rather than
hoping one injection survives the whole sentence" architecture.

**User's immediate follow-up, a real and still-open gap**: this test
deliberately used a sentence where each adjective is immediately
adjacent to its own noun, with the positions to steer specified BY
HAND (we knew position 2 was noun A and position 5 was noun B because
we forced that structure ourselves via the prefix). The general
problem -- identifying, for an ARBITRARY sentence, which words agree
with which noun, especially with intervening material or long-distance
agreement (subject-verb across a clause, relative clauses, coordination
scope ambiguity) -- was not tested and is not solved by this result.
This is explicitly the open question CLAUDE.md section 8 already
flags as steering's claimed advantage over a rule-based baseline (using
the model's OWN knowledge of which words agree with which noun, not
external parsing) -- not yet demonstrated, only motivated.

Files: `nllb_swahili_mtu_class7_full_trace_diagnostic.py`,
`nllb_swahili_two_noun_class7_coordination_check.py` (both new).

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — extending to VERBS: same recipe generalizes mechanistically, but no sweet spot without token injection

**User's redirect**: cache the Hewitt-et-al.-structural-probe fallback
idea (recovering a learned syntactic tree to find agreement targets at
arbitrary distance) for much later; for now, test VERBS with simple
sentences, before tackling the general position-identification problem.

**A real confound caught before building on it**: a first attempt
translated "a thing likes to sing" EN->SW and got "kitu hupenda" --
"hu-" turned out to be Swahili's INVARIANT HABITUAL TENSE marker, not
a noun-class prefix, so this wasn't the clean minimal pair it looked
like. Confirmed directly via SW->EN: "Mtu anafanya kazi." = "A man is
working," "Kitu kinafanya kazi." = "Something is working" -- both
valid, recognized, parallel present-tense constructions. Tokenization
confirmed directly: "anafanya" -> ["_ana","fanya"], "kinafanya" ->
["_kina","fanya"] -- IDENTICAL second subword, differing only in the
first. Unlike every adjective tested this session, no token injection
should be structurally necessary: if "_kina" beats "_ana" at the one
position where the verb's first subword is predicted, the model should
naturally continue with the shared "fanya".

**Method** (new `nllb_swahili_verb_class7_steer_check.py`): SAME
layer-22 class-7-aligned candidates as every adjective check (found
via write-vector geometry on NOUN embeddings, never retuned for verbs)
and random control, same alpha grid, on "mtu anafanya kazi" ("a man is
working").

**Result**: REAL margin (logit "_ana" minus logit "_kina") moves
monotonically toward class-7 at every alpha (+9.1685 -> +7.13 -> ...
-> -2.61 at alpha=1000, an actual crossing) with real-vs-random
separation at every step, confirming the SAME generic class-7 neurons
causally affect a completely different part of speech with no
retuning. **But the generated text shows no sweet spot at all**: a
finer sweep (120,150,180,210,250) found REAL output stays exactly
"mtu anafanya kazi" (unchanged) through alpha=180, then jumps straight
to "mtu kijijini" ("in the village," yet another real, unrelated
ki-prefixed word -- joining kipaji/kilele/kizima/kipenzi in the
project's running list of this exact attractor pattern) at alpha=210 --
no intermediate alpha, at this or the coarser grid tested, ever
produces "kinafanya."

**Why this differs from the successful mzuri/mrefu cases, a specific
and testable hypothesis**: those worked because we INJECTED a
hand-constructed token sitting at the EXACT point the steered
hidden state was shown (hidden-state-alignment entry) to reliably move
toward. Here, "_kina" is a REAL, PRE-EXISTING token with its own
independent history and usage across many Swahili words -- its
embedding was never placed with that same surgical precision, so it
carries its own baggage the way "kirefu" (meaning "deep," not "tall")
did for the adjective case before injection fixed it. The fix this
predicts: construct and inject a dedicated `<anafanya_cl7>` token the
same way as the adjective pilot, rather than relying on a real,
independently-trained token to happen to win.

**Verdict**: the MECHANISM (generic class-7 neurons causally move a
real margin, with clean real-vs-random separation) generalizes cleanly
across parts of speech with zero retuning -- a genuinely reassuring
sign for the project's broader goal. The LIMITATION (no sweet spot
without injection) also generalizes, in a predictable, falsifiable way
-- not yet tested whether injecting `<anafanya_cl7>` closes this gap the
same way it did for mzuri.

**Not yet done**: injecting `<anafanya_cl7>` and rerunning the same
sweep to test the hypothesis directly; the Hewitt-et-al. structural-
probe idea (cached, not started); testing verb agreement at a REAL
distance from its subject (not immediately adjacent, as this test
still was).

Files: `nllb_swahili_verb_class7_steer_check.py` (new).

## 2026-10-02 (cont.) — user's refinement confirmed: inject a PREFIX-level token, not a whole-word or real-token one -- clean success, and a more scalable architecture than per-word injection

**User's refinement**: the previous entry's hypothesis was right in
spirit (inject, don't rely on a real pre-existing token) but should be
applied at the PREFIX level, not the whole verb -- construct the
synthetic vector FROM "_ana" (the subword that actually carries class
information) and inject that, rather than either the real "_kina"
token or a whole-word "<anafanya_cl7>" placeholder. The stem "fanya" is
IDENTICAL between class-1 and class-7 forms (confirmed via
tokenization, previous entry) and needs no transformation at all -- so
this targets exactly the unit that differs.

**Method** (new `nllb_swahili_verb_prefix_class7_injection_check.py`):
same construction recipe as every injected token this session, applied
to "_ana" specifically: keep its language+semantic+other components,
swap only its class component to class7_hat (cos with the real "_ana"
= +0.9792). Injected as `<kina_cl7>`. Same layer-22 candidates, random
control, and sentence ("mtu anafanya kazi") as the previous entry.

**Result**:

| alpha | REAL text | new token selected? | RANDOM text |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | **"mtu\<kina_cl7\>fanya kazi"** | Yes | "mtu anafanya kazi" |
| 30 | **"mtu\<kina_cl7\>fanya kazi"** | Yes | "mtu anafanya kazi" |
| 100 | **"mtu\<kina_cl7\>fanya kazi"** | Yes | "mtu anatumika" |
| 300 | "mtu kijijini" | No | "mtu anashiriki kazi" |
| 1000 | "mtu kijijini" | No | "mtu steps" |

**Clean success across a WIDE sweet spot (10-100, wider than the
single-word mzuri case's 30-300), and the result is genuinely
compositional, not just a token substitution**: the model selects the
injected prefix token and then CONTINUES ON ITS OWN with the unchanged
stem "fanya kazi" -- no further intervention needed at that position.
This is the first result in the entire class-axis thread where an
injected unit correctly composes with surrounding REAL, untouched
material to produce a structurally well-formed continuation, rather
than either failing to change anything or replacing the whole
utterance with an unrelated real word.

**Why this likely matters beyond fixing this one verb**: Bantu
agreement morphology is PREFIX-based across the board (the same class
markers recur as noun prefixes, adjective prefixes, subject-marker
verb prefixes, etc.). If prefix-level injection reliably composes with
unchanged stems the way this result suggests, the architecture needed
for "all adjectives x all classes" (the user's original token-injection
proposal, several entries back) does NOT require injecting one token
per word per class -- a combinatorial blow-up -- it could instead
require only ONE SET of class-marking prefix tokens per agreement-slot
TYPE (noun-class prefix, adjective-concord prefix, subject-marker
prefix, etc.), reused compositionally across every stem. This is a
substantially more scalable proposal than per-word injection, though
it rests on ONE example at this point and needs direct testing before
being trusted as a general pattern.

**Not yet done**: testing whether this compositional pattern holds for
OTHER stems/verbs (is "fanya" special, or does any class-1/class-7
minimal pair with a shared stem behave this way); testing prefix-level
injection on the ADJECTIVE side too (would "<ki_cl7>" + stem "-refu"
compose into something usable, rather than needing the whole-word
mrefu_cl7/mzuri_cl7 tokens used so far); the Hewitt-et-al. structural-
probe idea (still cached); verb agreement at real distance from its
subject.

Files: `nllb_swahili_verb_prefix_class7_injection_check.py` (new).

## 2026-10-03 — multi-class generalization: prefix-level injection works cleanly across 3 classes, each with its own distinct neurons and sweet spot

**User's request**: test other classes, varied sentences, and
paragraphs, scaling well beyond the single class-7 verb example.

**Subject-prefix forms verified directly via SW->EN translation before
use** (not assumed): class 5 "Gari linafanya kazi."/"Jiwe linafanya
kazi." -> "The car/stone is working."; class 7 "Kiti kinafanya
kazi." -> "The chair works." (already on record); class 8 "Vitu
vinafanya kazi." -> "Things are working." **Class 9 ("nyumba
inafanya") checked and explicitly excluded**: its tokenization splits
as ["_inaf","anya"], not sharing "fanya" as a clean second subword the
way the other three do -- the prefix-injection recipe depends on an
unchanged, shared stem token, so it doesn't cleanly apply here with
this particular verb. Flagged rather than silently skipped.

**Method** (new `nllb_swahili_verb_prefix_multiclass_check.py`, a
single class-parametrized script, not three near-duplicates): for each
of classes 5, 7, 8, constructs the synthetic prefix vector from "_ana"
(cos with real "_ana" = 0.987/0.979/0.969 respectively), injects it as
`<{prefix}_cl{class}>`, and -- critically -- finds THAT class's own
top-10 layer-22-aligned neurons via write-vector geometry rather than
reusing class 7's units. Same "mtu anafanya kazi" sentence, same
margin/generation sweep as every check this session.

**Result -- clean compositional success for all three classes, each
with a DIFFERENT neuron population and a DIFFERENT sweet spot**:

| Class | Neurons (pos/neg) | Sweet-spot alpha | Output at sweet spot |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 8 / 2 | 30-100 | "mtu\<lina_cl5\>fanya kazi" |
| 7 | 5 / 5 | 10-100 (widest) | "mtu\<kina_cl7\>fanya kazi" |
| 8 | 3 / 7 | 100 only (narrowest) | "mtu\<vina_cl8\>fanya kazi" |

Every class shows the SAME clean pattern at its own sweet spot (select
the injected prefix, then continue on its own with the unchanged
stem), and RANDOM never selects any injected token at any alpha, for
any class. Each class's candidate neuron SET is genuinely distinct
(different units, different positive/negative counts) -- not a shared
"generic push" mechanism, a real per-class population found
independently each time. Every class breaks down into an unrelated
real word or gibberish at alpha=300 (SHAKILI / kijijini / vidole),
consistent with the attractor-overshoot pattern documented throughout
this thread.

**Verdict**: this is no longer a single-class result. Three
independently-verified classes, three independently-discovered neuron
populations, the same recipe, the same clean compositional outcome --
real evidence this generalizes across the class system, not a property
of class 7 or of "fanya" specifically. The DIFFERING sweet-spot widths
across classes (class 8's is far narrower than class 7's) is itself
worth noting for any future automated pipeline -- a single fixed alpha
will not work for every class.

**Not yet done, the remaining parts of the user's request**: varied
SENTENCES (different stems, different subject nouns, different
structures -- this entry still only tests "fanya kazi") and
PARAGRAPH-length text (every test this session has been a single short

## 2026-10-03 (cont.) — a different verb stem: caught a real construction bug (uncontrolled baseline overshoot), fixed with an automatic safety check, then clean replication

**Testing "kusoma" (to read) instead of "kufanya"** to check whether
the verb-prefix recipe generalizes across stems, not just classes.
Subject-prefix forms verified directly first (same discipline as
always): "Mtu anasoma kitabu."="A person is reading a book.",
tokenizes ["_anas","oma"]; class-7 "kinasoma" tokenizes
["_kinas","oma"] -- same shared-stem pattern as "fanya". (Also checked
and excluded: "kuona"/"to see" -- "anaona" is a SINGLE token while
"kinaona" splits as ["_kina","ona"], not a parallel structure --
flagged, not forced.)

**A real bug caught before trusting any result**: reusing the SAME
"noun-average" alpha_construction (1.6143, calibrated from class-7
nouns, reused unchanged across every injected token so far) produced a
synthetic `<kina_cl7>` that beat the REAL "_anas" token with ZERO
intervention -- baseline (no steering at all) and even RANDOM steering
both showed the injected token winning. This passed silently at first
because the printed baseline text looked plausible; the tell was
RANDOM selecting the new token too, which should never happen if the
construction itself isn't already overpowering. Verified directly:
margin(real-synthetic) crosses from positive to negative somewhere
between alpha=0.5 and 0.8, far below the reused 1.6143 -- the
"noun-average" calibration is NOT reliably transferable across words,
confirmed concretely rather than assumed. All PRIOR results this
session were checked and are unaffected -- every earlier baseline
explicitly showed the correct, real-word output before any steering,
which is itself now understood to be the thing that must always be
verified, not just hoped for.

**Fix, now built into `nllb_swahili_verb_prefix_multiclass_check.py`
for every future run**: an automatic per-word, per-class safety check
-- before injecting, compute the real token's baseline logit and the
would-be synthetic logit against the actual final hidden state; if the
synthetic already wins, halve alpha_construction and retry (up to 10
backoffs) until the real token safely wins unsteered. For "anasoma"/
class 7 this converged to alpha=0.4036 (2 backoffs from 1.6143),
baseline margin +0.0995 -- small but genuinely positive.

**Result after the fix**: baseline correctly "mtu anasoma kitabu"
(unchanged); REAL steering at alpha=30,100 cleanly produces
"mtu\<kina_cl7\>oma kitabu" -- the same compositional pattern as every
other successful check, now on a second, independent stem; RANDOM
never selects the injected token at alpha<=100. At alpha=300, REAL
shows a milder degradation than previous overshoots: "mtu
kiume\<kina_cl7\>oma kitabu" -- an extra spurious word inserted before
the injected prefix, but the injected token AND its correct stem
continuation both survive, unlike the complete substitutions seen
before (kijijini, vidole, SHAKILI).

**Verdict**: the recipe generalizes across stems, not just classes --
now confirmed on 2 independent verbs (fanya, soma) across 3 classes (5,
7, 8) = effectively a 2x3 grid of independent confirmations (not all
cells run, but the pattern holds everywhere tested). The caught-and-
fixed construction-overshoot bug is arguably as important as the
positive result: it's a concrete reminder that "a recipe that worked
for one word" does not mean the SAME numeric calibration transfers
unchanged to the next, and the fix (an automatic, per-instance safety
check) should be considered a standing requirement for this recipe
going forward, not a one-off patch.

**Not yet done**: PARAGRAPH-length text (every test this session
remains a single short sentence); varied SUBJECT NOUNS (every test
still uses "mtu"); the adjective-side prefix-injection idea
("\<ki_cl7\>" + stem "-refu", flagged two entries ago, not yet tried).

Files: `nllb_swahili_verb_prefix_multiclass_check.py` (updated,
additive safety-check logic).

## 2026-10-03 — Paragraph-scale, mixed-class coordination test: clean when steering sentence 1, broken when steering sentence 2 (root-caused to class-5 neuron weakness, not a mechanism bug)

Motivated by: "Let's test other classes as well and multiple varied
sentences and paragraphs" -- the first test of the recipe beyond a
single short sentence, and the first test with TWO DIFFERENT target
classes present in one generated context.

Script: `nllb_swahili_paragraph_multiclass_check.py`. Task: "Mtu
[PREFIX1]fanya kazi. Mtu [PREFIX2]fanya kazi. Mtu [PREFIX3]fanya kazi."
-- sentence 1's prefix steered toward class 7, sentence 2's toward
class 5, sentence 3 always left unsteered. Entire verb stem forced
(only the prefix slot is freely generated/steered) after an earlier
design bug (letting the stem vary freely gave the model no reason to
pick a different verb for sentence 2, producing nonsense "mtu hufanya
kitabu"). Source sentence changed from "a man works" to "a man is
working" -- the simple-present English primes Swahili's invariant
HABITUAL "hu-" construction, not the progressive "ana-" the whole
recipe assumes; caught directly, not assumed.

**Condition 1 (baseline, no steering)**: `'mtu anafanya kazi . mtu
anafanya kazi . mtu anafanya kazi .'` -- correct throughout.

**Condition 2 (steer sentence 1 only, class 7)**: `'mtu<kina_cl7_para>
fanya kazi . mtu anafanya kazi . mtu anafanya kazi .'` -- clean. The
injected token appears exactly where intended; sentences 2 and 3 are
completely unaffected (no forward contamination from steering earlier
in the same generated sequence).

**Conditions 3 and 4 (steer sentence 2, class 5) looked broken at
first**: sentence 2 rendered as `'mtufanya kazi'` (nothing between
"mtu" and "fanya"), and sentence 3 -- which is NEVER steered in any
condition -- showed `<kina_cl7_para>` (sentence 1's class-7 token, not
even class 5) instead of "anafanya".

**Diagnosis (direct, not guessed)**: re-ran condition 3's exact
decoder context in isolation and printed top-5 logits at sentence 2's
position under class-5 steering (alpha=100, the established class-5
candidates [4459, 6360, 3907, 888, 3132, 221, 4125, 7364] amplified,
[6670, 40] zeroed). Result: `</s>` (EOS) wins outright (logit 11.08),
with `<lina_cl5_para>` a close but clear second (10.40). The script has
no EOS check and force-continues regardless, so the real decoded
sequence contains a mid-paragraph EOS token, which `skip_special_tokens
=True` silently deletes -- producing the "mtufanya" artifact. Raising
alpha (300, 1000, 3000, 10000) does NOT make `<lina_cl5_para>` win --
it overshoots straight past the target into generic, semantically
unrelated high-frequency noise ("▁S"), never landing on it at any alpha
tried.

**Control check -- is this a general "later position is harder"
problem, or specific to class 5?** Built a fresh class-7 synthetic
token calibrated at sentence 2's own context (not reused from sentence
1) and tested the already-established class-7 candidates
([488,6108,6191,7659,1502]/[2888,3618,662,7473,6148]) at sentence 2's
position. Result: **clean win**, alpha 10-100, injected token on top by
a wide margin at every alpha tested (e.g. alpha=100: injected token
16.89 vs `</s>` 13.46). This rules out "later position in a paragraph
is inherently harder" -- class 7's neurons generalize across position
fine. The weakness is specific to class 5's write-vector-aligned
candidate set (or possibly to this specific position+class
combination), not to the steering mechanism or to paragraph position in
general.

**The hook/state mechanism itself was independently verified correct**:
traced `armed`/`position`/`amplify`/`zero` state through
`gen_one_token()` call-by-call; each call correctly arms, applies at
its own absolute position, then resets to empty/False before the next
call. No cross-talk between sentence 1's and sentence 2's steering
calls. Sentence 3's stray class-7 token is a downstream consequence of
feeding an anomalous mid-sequence EOS token as context (out-of-
distribution input), not a steering leak or state bug.

**Verdict**: the cross-sentence coordination mechanism itself is sound
-- condition 2 (steer sentence 1, class 7) replicates the two-noun,
same-sentence clean result at paragraph scale with zero forward
contamination. The condition-3/4 breakage is a **per-class neuron-set
strength issue**, not a flaw in the approach: class 7's candidates are
robust enough to win across both sentence 1 and sentence 2 positions;
class 5's candidates, found via the identical write-vector-geometry
procedure, are not strong enough to beat EOS at sentence 2's position,
and blind alpha escalation does not fix this (it overshoots into
unrelated garbage instead of ever selecting the target). This echoes,
at the class level, the same lesson as the earlier per-word alpha-
construction bug: a recipe validated on one instance (here, one class)
does not automatically transfer to another (a different class) without
its own calibration/verification.

**Not yet done**: find out why class 5's candidates are comparatively
weak (fewer candidates found by the write-vector scan for class 5 at
layer 22? worth comparing candidate-set sizes/cosines side by side with
class 7's); whether a different layer or a larger k for class 5
specifically fixes this; re-running the full paragraph script with an
EOS-aware guard (so a losing condition fails loudly/visibly instead of
silently decoding as an empty gap); varied subject nouns (still only
"mtu" tested); the adjective-side prefix-injection idea (still not
tried).

Files: `nllb_swahili_paragraph_multiclass_check.py` (written this
session, surfaced the above; not yet fixed/finalized -- the class-5
weakness needs to be resolved or the test redesigned around classes
known to be robust before the paragraph-level claim can be trusted).

## 2026-10-03 (continued) — Root cause found and fixed: paragraph coordination is clean at alpha=30

Follow-up to the entry above. Root cause of class 5's breakage at
sentence 2's position: **alpha=100 (the script's then-default)
overshoots class 5's sweet spot**, which is narrower and lower than
assumed. Swept alpha directly at sentence 2's exact context:

```
alpha=5-25:  '_ana' wins (understeered)
alpha=30-50: <lina_cl5_para> wins cleanly (sweet spot)
alpha=60+:   </s> (EOS) wins, then generic noise at higher alpha
```

(Widening the candidate set, k=10->20->40->80, made things WORSE, not
better -- more candidates diluted the effect at every alpha tested.
The fix is a smaller alpha, not more neurons.) Class 7 was independently
confirmed to also win cleanly at alpha=30 at BOTH sentence positions, so
a single shared alpha=30 works for this specific pairing.

**Re-ran the full 4-condition paragraph script at `--alpha 30`:**

```
[1. BASELINE]              'mtu anafanya kazi . mtu anafanya kazi . mtu anafanya kazi .'
[2. STEER S1 ONLY (cl7)]   'mtu<kina_cl7_para>fanya kazi . mtu anafanya kazi . mtu anafanya kazi .'
[3. STEER S2 ONLY (cl5)]   'mtu anafanya kazi . mtu<lina_cl5_para>fanya kazi . mtu anafanya kazi .'
[4. STEER BOTH]            'mtu<kina_cl7_para>fanya kazi . mtu<lina_cl5_para>fanya kazi . mtu anafanya kazi .'
```

All four conditions clean. This is the target result: two DIFFERENT
classes steered at two DIFFERENT sentence positions within one
generated paragraph, independently and simultaneously, with the third
(always-unsteered) sentence staying correct in every condition --
including condition 4, where two prior steering events have already
fired earlier in the same context.

**Verdict, updated**: the coordination mechanism is confirmed clean at
paragraph scale for this noun/verb pairing. But the alpha=100->30 fix
is itself an important, generalizable caution: **alpha is not safely
transferable across class OR position** -- it must be swept per
(class, position) pair, the same way `alpha_construction` already is
per (word, class) via the existing backoff check. Fixed script default
changed to 30 with a comment explaining this is confirmed only for
classes 5/7 at these two specific positions, not a universal constant.

Files: `nllb_swahili_paragraph_multiclass_check.py` (default alpha
30.0, documented as pairing-specific, not universal).

## 2026-10-03 (continued) — First test on real, unscripted text; corrected a methodology deviation; built a class-9/class-10 split

User pasted a real BBC-style Swahili news article (about an onion-in-
socks home remedy claim) and asked to steer three real nouns within it
to different target classes: "njia" (currently 9/10) -> class 7,
"kitunguu" (currently class 7) -> class 9, "vitunguu" (currently class
8) -> class 10.

**Class 9/10 split, built fresh (`nllb_swahili_class9_class10_split_
build.py`)**: the existing concept decomposition only has ONE merged
"9/10" direction -- checked the lexicon directly
(`swahili_noun_lexicon_agreement_v2.py`): all 30 N-class nouns are
labeled "9/10" as a single category because Swahili N-class nouns use
the IDENTICAL surface form for singular and plural ("njia" = both
"road" and "roads"). The existing method (average isolated-word static
embeddings by class label) cannot split these -- there is no second
lexical form to pull a class-10-only set from; re-running it verbatim
cannot work. Adapted method: took the class-9 and class-10 PRESENT-
TENSE SUBJECT PREFIXES, which DO have distinct single-token static
embeddings ("ina" id=3668, "zina" id=11557, confirmed via direct
tokenization -- unlike "inafanya"'s own ["_inaf","anya"] split that
excluded class 9 from the earlier verb-prefix sweep), took their raw
embedding difference as a number-marking axis (confirmed near-
orthogonal to the general class_dir["9/10"], cos=-0.0060 -- a genuinely
independent signal, not redundant), and composed it with the general
"9/10" direction: `class9_hat = normalize(class_dir["9/10"] +
scale*axis)`, `class10_hat = normalize(class_dir["9/10"] - scale*axis)`
with scale = class_dir["9/10"].norm(). Result: class9_hat and
class10_hat come out EXACTLY orthogonal to each other by construction,
each still strongly correlated with the general 9/10 signal (+0.70,
+0.71), and uncorrelated with classes 7/8/1/2 (all |cos| < 0.2). Saved
to `nllb_swahili_class9_class10_split_cache.pt`.

**A real methodology deviation, caught by the user, not by me**: the
first attempt (`nllb_swahili_real_text_multinoun_steer_check.py`)
REPLACED each controlling noun itself with an injected synthetic token
(to sidestep kitunguu/vitunguu's multi-subword tokenization) -- a
deviation from the recipe validated all session (every noun check,
including the two-noun coordination test and the paragraph test): the
noun stays exactly as real text, UNCHANGED; only its layer-22 FFN
neurons are patched AT its own position so that what follows it shifts.
User caught this directly: "we don't steer the nouns we steer the
adjectives and prepositions etc. so kitunguu remains as is. just the
way mtu remained as is." This also fully dissolved the multi-subword-
pooling problem that attempt had hit (mean-pooling kitunguu's 3
subwords collapsed to an anomalously low norm, ~4.8 vs ~6-8.5 for real
single-token/subword embeddings, breaking the safety check) -- that
problem doesn't exist when the noun is never touched in the first
place. Corrected version:
`nllb_swahili_real_text_noun_position_steer_check.py`.

**Results (alpha=300 -- confirmed needed: alpha=30-100, which worked
throughout this session's toy templates, produced ZERO visible effect
in this much longer, richer real-text context; another confirmation
that alpha must be swept per-context, not assumed to transfer)**:

- **njia -> class 7**: real word "hiyo" (class 9/10 demonstrative)
  logit drops under steering (+15.567 -> +13.325, delta -2.243). Free
  generation: baseline `'njia hiyo kwa watoto wao wagonjwa, yak...'` ->
  steered `'njia kienyeji ya kupikia watoto wao...'` -- **"kienyeji"
  ("traditional/local") is a genuine, correctly-formed class-7 ki-
  adjective**, naturally selected by the model itself, replacing the
  original class-9/10 continuation. Clean qualitative success.

- **vitunguu -> class 10**: real word "vibichi" (class 8 concord,
  "raw/fresh") logit drops VERY sharply (+12.599 -> -5.468, delta
  -18.068 -- the strongest suppression of any real-text check so far).
  Free generation: baseline `'vitunguu vya kijani kibichi wa
  kuponya...'` -> steered `'vitunguu yasiyotiwa mafuta wa kuponya
  magonjwa'` ("that have no oil added") -- the original class-8
  adjective is strongly suppressed, but the model's own replacement is
  a negative relative-clause construction rather than an obviously
  class-10-concordant adjective, so this is a strong SUPPRESSION
  result without an equally clean POSITIVE replacement to point to.

- **kitunguu -> class 9**: real word "chekundu" (class 7 concord,
  "red") logit drops modestly (+13.052 -> +11.486, delta -1.567 -- the
  weakest effect of the three). Free generation: baseline `'kitunguu
  kikuu. Video hiyo ya mama...'` -> steered `'kitunguu inchi kavu.
  Video hiyo ya mama...'` -- some suppression, but "inchi kavu" is not
  a clearly class-9-concordant replacement either.

**Verdict**: the noun-position steering recipe DOES generalize to
real, unscripted, multi-paragraph text -- the clearest case (njia) is a
genuine, qualitatively correct class-shift with NO noun-side
modification at all, matching the project's actual deployment design
for the first time on authentic content rather than templates. Effect
strength varies a lot by noun/class pair (njia strongest/cleanest,
kitunguu weakest) at the same alpha=300 -- consistent with the
session's standing lesson that alpha (and apparently effect size in
general) is not a fixed, class-independent constant; a proper sweep per
noun, and a larger sample of real sentences, would be needed before
treating this as more than a promising first look.

**Not yet done**: alpha sweep for kitunguu/vitunguu specifically (only
njia was swept; 300 was carried over for the other two without
verifying it's their own optimum); testing whether EARLIER-occurring
injected/control tokens from one noun's test leak into a LATER noun's
free generation within the same run (observed once in the superseded
multinoun script, not yet checked in the corrected version); a larger
sample of real sentences/nouns beyond this one article.

Files: `nllb_swahili_class9_class10_split_build.py` (new),
`nllb_swahili_class9_class10_split_cache.pt` (new cache),
`nllb_swahili_real_text_multinoun_steer_check.py` (superseded --

rather than deleted per CLAUDE.md "add a correction section rather

check.py` (corrected, current version).

## 2026-10-03 (continued) — Full recipe (injection + neuron steering) on real text: njia still clean, kitunguu/vitunguu's class-9/10 candidates are too weak at layer 22

User's follow-up catch: the prior real-text check (njia/kitunguu/
vitunguu) applied neuron steering ALONE, with no injected target-class
adjective available -- a real gap versus every successful toy-sentence
check this session (mzuri_cl7, mrefu_cl7, kina_cl7, etc.), which always
paired steering WITH a purpose-built injected token. Built the missing
piece (`nllb_swahili_real_text_full_recipe_check.py`): "chekundu"
(class 7, "red") and "nyekundu" (class 9/10, "red") share the identical
final subword "undu"; "vibichi" (class 8, "raw/fresh") and "mbichi"
(class 9/10, "raw/fresh") share the identical final subword "chi" --
confirmed via direct tokenization, same style of shared-stem evidence
used for every verb-prefix injection this session. Injected
`<chekundu_cl9>` and `<vibichi_cl10>` from these shared final subwords,
class component swapped the same way as every other injected token.

**A real bug caught before trusting the first run**: initially
calibrated `alpha_construction` for the adjectives using the ADJECTIVE'S
OWN CURRENT class population (class 7's own nouns for chekundu, class
8's own nouns for vibichi) instead of the TARGET class's population --
produced nonsensical near-zero/negative alpha values (-0.0251, -0.0003)
that barely pushed toward class 9/10 at all. Fixed by calibrating
against the "9/10"-labeled noun population (the only real population
available for this target) instead.

**After the fix, the safety check passes cleanly** (margins +0.5912,
+0.4392) but **free generation still never selects either injected
token**, even at alpha=300. Swept alpha directly (100 up to 30000) to
find out why:

- **kitunguu (class 9 target)**: only 3 positive layer-22 candidates
  ([163, 4138, 3252], vs. class 7's 5) -- clearly a smaller, weaker set.
  Across the ENTIRE alpha range, the dominant competitor is a generic,
  semantically unrelated token ("▁in") whose logit climbs WITHOUT
  BOUND as alpha increases (14.71 -> 28.74) while the injected
  `<chekundu_cl9>` token barely moves (3.22 -> 4.01) and never comes
  remotely close. Not an alpha-tuning problem -- this candidate set is
  just too weak to compete at this site, at any strength.

- **vitunguu (class 10 target)**: 9 positive candidates (more than
  class 9's), but the failure mode is WORSE, not better: at every
  alpha from 100 to 10000, the top candidates collapse into completely
  incoherent, CROSS-SCRIPT garbage (Tibetan, Telugu, Hindi tokens:
  "སྤྱན་", "ఁ", "जाति" ...). Both the real adjective "vibichi" AND our
  injected `<vibichi_cl10>` lose badly throughout (both deeply
  negative, ~-9 to -12, versus winning candidates at +9 to +11) -- a
  total representational collapse, not a close contest with a wrong
  winner the way kitunguu's was.

**Verdict, updated and more cautious than the previous entry**: njia's
success remains the one clean, real-text result this session --
notably, it succeeded WITHOUT needing any adjective injection at all
(the model already had a naturally fitting real class-7 word,
"kienyeji", and selected it unassisted). kitunguu and vitunguu's
failures are NOT explained by missing injection (that gap is now
fixed) -- they're explained by the class-9/10 write-vector candidates
at layer 22 being too weak (kitunguu) or actively destabilizing
(vitunguu) in this richer, longer, real-text context. This may mean
the class9_hat/class10_hat split built this session (a composite,
derived direction -- see the entry above) is a noisier signal than the
directly-population-derived class directions (7, 8, ANIMATE-SG, etc.),
or that layer 22 specifically is a poor site for these two classes
regardless of direction quality, or both. Does NOT generalize the
"full recipe works on real text" claim beyond the one class (7) already
extensively validated all session -- class 9/10 need their own
dedicated diagnosis (candidate neurons at OTHER layers; whether the
composite split direction itself is the weak link, testable by
checking class9_hat/class10_hat's write-vector alignment quality at
several layers the way `nllb_swahili_decoder_write_vector_class_
subspace_check.py` did for class 7) before any claim is made about
them specifically.

Files: `nllb_swahili_real_text_full_recipe_check.py` (new, contains the
caught-and-fixed alpha-calibration bug and the full-recipe real-text
test, current best version of this check).

## 2026-10-03 (continued) — Kitunguu failure diagnosed: neither candidate-set balance nor alpha explains it; class 9/10 was never validated on a toy sentence before this real-text test

Follow-up to the full-trace diagnostic above. Tested the leading
hypothesis from that trace directly: that class 9's 3-positive/7-
negative candidate imbalance (vs. class 7's balanced 5/5, which worked
cleanly for njia) was driving the overshoot/collapse.

**Balance hypothesis, tested and REFUTED**: forced a balanced 5-
positive/5-negative class-9 set (found 2 additional genuine positive
candidates -- 2214, 3443 -- that existed but were crowded out of the
original top-10-by-absolute-cosine selection by stronger negative
candidates). Result: the overshoot got WORSE, not better -- class9_proj
at the steering site jumped to +1016.8 (vs. the original set's already-
large +658.2), and the top prediction became MORE incoherent, not less
("▁in" climbed to 14.67, plus new junk candidates "▁ina"/"▁iny"
appeared). Adding more amplified units just added more net force; it
did not stabilize anything. The balance/imbalance correlation with
njia's success was coincidental, not causal.

**Alpha hypothesis, tested and also REFUTED**: swept alpha 5->300 with
the ORIGINAL (unbalanced) candidate set. Found NO intermediate sweet
spot at any value: from alpha=5 to 100, the real adjective "chekundu"
barely moves at all (logit 14.23 -> 14.68, steering has essentially no
grip); from 150 to 300 it falls off a cliff straight into generic
garbage ("▁in" overtakes at alpha=300) with no window in between where
either the real class 9/10 word OR our injected synthetic ever leads.
This is qualitatively different from njia, which had a wide, stable
plateau (alpha 300-3000) with a coherent class-7 result throughout.

**Conclusion**: the failure is not a tuning problem (neither balance
nor alpha fixes it) -- the class-9 write-vector candidates at layer 22
simply do not form a working steering circuit for this noun/context,
full stop. The likely reason, in hindsight: class 9/10 is the ONE
class this entire session that went straight to the hardest test (a
167-token real news article) with NO prior validation on a controlled
toy sentence -- classes 5, 7, and 8 were all proven on simple templates
first before ever being tried on anything harder. class9_hat/
class10_hat are also the only COMPOSITE/derived directions in use
(built from class_dir["9/10"] + a number-marking axis from "ina"/
"zina", not a direct population average the way every other class
direction is) -- plausibly a noisier signal to begin with. Both
explanations point the same way: class 9/10 needs the same toy-sentence
validation ladder (clean minimal pair -> simple template -> real text)
that classes 5/7/8 already went through, rather than being judged on
its real-text debut.

**Not yet done**: a toy-sentence test for class 9/10 analogous to the
original mtu/mzuri/mrefu or verb-prefix checks, to establish whether
class9_hat/class10_hat work AT ALL in a controlled setting before
revisiting real text; the same diagnostic ladder for vitunguu/class10,
which showed an even more severe failure (full cross-script garbage
collapse, not just a wrong-but-coherent token).

Files: diagnostic code run inline, not yet saved as a standalone
script (ad hoc balance-test and alpha-sweep); worth promoting to a
proper script if the toy-sentence validation for class 9/10 is done
next.

## 2026-10-03 (continued) — Root cause found: the class 9/10 split direction is miscomputed, confirmed with a control

User's hypothesis, tested directly: "let's try to isolate and see if
it's a class 9 issue in general. Maybe we have miscomputed the class 9
direction." Three checks (`nllb_swahili_class9_class10_direction_
validity_check.py`), isolating the DIRECTION from both layer-22's
neurons (already shown broken at the real-text site) and from real-text
complexity (controlled toy items/sentences only):

1. **Tautological sanity** (the exact source tokens "ina"/"zina"):
   passes as expected, cos(ina,class9_hat)=+0.4520, cos(zina,
   class9_hat)=-0.3669, correctly opposite-signed. Necessary, not
   sufficient -- these are the tokens the axis was built FROM.

2. **Independent lexical check** (class-9/10 demonstratives "hii"/
   "hiyo" vs. "hizi"/"hizo" -- none used in construction): PASSES
   cleanly. hii/hiyo project higher on class9_hat than hizi/hizo do,
   and hizi/hizo project higher on class10_hat than hii/hiyo do, for
   BOTH pairs. Real evidence the direction captures something genuine
   about these words' STATIC embeddings.

3. **Contextual check** (24 different class-9/10 nouns, each in a
   minimal "noun ipo."/"noun zipo." singular/plural pair, encoder
   hidden state at the noun's own position, WITH a random-direction
   control): **FAILS outright**.
   ```
   mean(sg - pl) on class9_hat  = +0.0010   (16/24 correct-signed)
   mean(pl - sg) on class10_hat = -0.0044   (5/24 correct-signed)
   RANDOM-DIRECTION CONTROL     = -0.0020
   ```
   The "real" signal (+0.0010) is SMALLER in magnitude than the random
   control (-0.0020) -- indistinguishable from noise. class10_hat is
   actively backwards on the majority of nouns (only 5/24 correctly
   signed): plural contexts project LOWER than singular ones for most
   nouns, the opposite of what a working "plural" direction should do.

**Verdict**: the class9/10 split is miscomputed in the sense that
matters -- it captures a real property of a couple of specific lexical
items' STATIC embeddings (checks 1-2 pass), but does NOT correspond to
how the model actually represents singular-vs-plural N-class agreement
when PROCESSING a real sentence (check 3, the one with an actual
random-direction control, fails outright). This fully explains every
real-text steering failure logged above for kitunguu and vitunguu:
neither alpha tuning nor candidate-set balance could ever have fixed
it, because the TARGET direction itself does not correspond to the
thing the model uses for class 9/10 concord in context -- no amount of
better-aimed steering at the wrong target produces the right result.

**Why the construction likely failed despite looking clean on paper**:
"ina" vs "zina" are TWO SPECIFIC TOKENS, and a difference between two
single static embeddings can easily be dominated by OTHER idiosyncratic
properties of those two tokens (frequency, phonological neighbors,
unrelated collocations) rather than cleanly isolating "grammatical
number." The demonstrative check (2) passing is consistent with this --
demonstratives are STATIC, ISOLATED items too, so of course a direction
built to separate two OTHER static items can partially transfer to
other static items with a similar lexical/distributional profile. But
"real sentence processing" (check 3) is a different regime entirely,
and that is where it breaks.

**Open question, not yet resolved**: whether a genuinely working class-
9-vs-10 direction could be built from CONTEXTUAL hidden states directly
(e.g. the difference-of-means over the same 24 ipo/zipo sentence pairs
used in check 3, rather than composing with two isolated prefix
tokens) -- untested. If check 3's own contextual vectors themselves
show a usable mean difference even where cosine-per-noun is noisy, a
population-level difference-of-means built FROM them (rather than from
"ina"/"zina") might succeed where the current construction failed;
this has not been tried.

Files: `nllb_swahili_class9_class10_direction_validity_check.py` (new).
Supersedes trust in `nllb_swahili_class9_class10_split_cache.pt`'s
class9_hat/class10_hat for any further steering work -- flagged as
unreliable, not deleted, per CLAUDE.md's correction-section convention.

## 2026-10-03 (continued) — Contextual difference-of-means fixes the class 9/10 direction, confirmed on held-out nouns with a control

Follow-up to the direction-validity check above, which found the
static-token-based class9_hat/class10_hat (built from "ina" minus
"zina") carries no real contextual signal. Rebuilt the number-marking
axis from a DIFFERENCE-OF-MEANS over the SAME minimal singular/plural
sentence pairs ("noun ipo."/"noun zipo.") used in that check's
contextual test, instead of from two isolated static tokens -- the
genuine minimal-pair logic used throughout this project, applied here
for the first time to build a direction rather than just to test one.

Methodology (`nllb_swahili_class9_class10_contextual_rebuild.py`), with
a held-out split to avoid validating on the same data the direction was
built from: 16 of the 24 class-9/10 nouns used to build number_axis_v2
= normalize(mean over TRAIN nouns of [h_sg(noun) - h_pl(noun)]), the
other 8 held out purely for validation. Composed with the existing
general class_dir["9/10"] the same way as before (swapping ONLY the
axis source, CLAUDE.md hard rule #9 -- one change per experiment).

**Result, on the 8 HELD-OUT nouns (never seen during construction)**:
```
mean(sg - pl) on class9_hat_v2  = +0.1621   (7/8 correct-signed)
mean(pl - sg) on class10_hat_v2 = +0.1647   (8/8 correct-signed)
RANDOM-DIRECTION CONTROL        = -0.0032
```
The signal is ~50x the random control's magnitude, and the held-out
result (+0.1621) nearly matches the in-sample TRAIN result (+0.1593,
16/16 correct-signed) -- genuine generalization, not overfitting to the
16 training nouns. The new axis is nearly orthogonal to both the old,
invalidated "ina-zina" axis (cos=-0.0076) and to the general class_dir
["9/10"] (cos=+0.0262), confirming it is a genuinely different,
independent, and -- unlike the old one -- actually-working signal.

**Verdict**: this is now a trustworthy class 9/10 split, in sharp
contrast to the original. Saved to
`nllb_swahili_class9_class10_split_cache_v2.pt` (the original,
invalidated cache is kept, not overwritten, per the correction-section
convention). The natural next step is re-running the real-text
kitunguu->class9 / vitunguu->class10 steering checks with THIS
direction in place of the old one, to see whether the earlier failures
were entirely a direction-quality problem (in which case they should
now work, or at least behave very differently) or whether layer 22's
write-vector candidates for this corrected direction have their own,
separate problems still to diagnose.

Files: `nllb_swahili_class9_class10_contextual_rebuild.py` (new),
`nllb_swahili_class9_class10_split_cache_v2.pt` (new, validated cache
-- use this one going forward, not the original
`nllb_swahili_class9_class10_split_cache.pt`).

## 2026-10-03 (continued) — The direction fix was necessary but not sufficient: layer 22's neurons still too weak for class 9 on real text

Retested kitunguu->class9 real-text steering with the corrected,
held-out-validated class9_hat_v2 (previous entry) in place of the
broken static-token version.

**Improvement**: the write-vector candidate search at layer 22 now
naturally returns a BALANCED 5-positive/5-negative set ([7204, 5335,
1902, 6433, 743] / [4714, 2450, 6661, 1498, 3009]) -- unlike the old
direction's lopsided 3/7 split -- without needing to force balance by
hand. The safety-checked `<chekundu_cl9_v2>` injection (built the same
way as every other injected adjective this session, from "chekundu"'s
shared final subword "undu") now passes cleanly (alpha_construction=
0.9165, margin=+0.6198, no backoff needed) and its logit DOES overtake
the real "chekundu" around alpha=80-100 (synth 1.75 vs chekundu 1.67 at
alpha=80).

**Still fails**: neither the real adjective NOR the injected synthetic
one ever comes close to the position's actual top candidates at any
alpha from 10 to 300 -- the model just drifts toward punctuation and
generic filler (",", ".", "▁fulani"="certain/some") as alpha increases,
never toward a coherent class-9-concordant word. This is a DIFFERENT
failure mode than before (generic PUNCTUATION/FILLER, not a wrong-
language token like "▁in" or cross-script garbage) but equally not a
success.

**Conclusion**: the two problems were separate and both real. (1) The
class9/10 DIRECTION was genuinely miscomputed -- now fixed and
validated with a held-out set and a random-direction control. (2)
Layer 22's write-vector-selected neurons, EVEN FOR THE CORRECTED
direction, still do not produce enough causal force to win this real-
text position -- a separate, likely deeper limitation (cosine alignment
between a unit's write vector and a target direction does not
necessarily predict how much CAUSAL leverage amplifying that unit
actually has; this was validated for class 7 at this exact layer but
evidently does not automatically transfer to every class). Fixing the
direction was necessary but not sufficient.

**Not yet done**: scanning OTHER layers' write-vector alignment for
class9_hat_v2/class10_hat_v2, the same way `nllb_swahili_decoder_
write_vector_class_subspace_check.py` originally scanned all 24 layers
for class 7 (which is how layer 22 was chosen in the first place) --
it has never been run for the class 9/10 direction specifically, old or
new. Layer 22 may simply not be the right site for this class; this
has been assumed, not verified, every time class 9/10 was tested this
session.

## 2026-10-03 (continued) — 24-layer scan: class 9/10 has no strong neuron-level candidates ANYWHERE, not just at layer 22

Ran the full 24-layer write-vector-geometry scan
(`nllb_swahili_class9_10_write_vector_layer_scan.py`, same anisotropic-
control methodology as `nllb_swahili_decoder_write_vector_class_
subspace_check.py`, which is how layer 22 was originally chosen -- for
class 7, never re-verified for class 9/10) against the CORRECTED,
held-out-validated class9_hat_v2/class10_hat_v2.

**Result**: tail counts (units clearing the anisotropic empirical
threshold, ~1 expected by chance per layer) are weak at EVERY layer:
```
best layer, class9_v2:  layer 23, only 5 units clear threshold
best layer, class10_v2: layer 23, only 4 units clear threshold
layer 22 (used throughout this session's class9/10 tests): only
  1 unit (class9_v2) / 2 units (class10_v2) clear threshold
```
No layer comes close to the strength class 7 showed at layer 22
earlier this session (a clear, balanced 5-positive/5-negative set well
above chance). Every layer for class 9/10 sits in the 0-5 unit range,
barely distinguishable from the ~1-unit chance baseline.

**Layer 23 (the nominal best) is structurally disqualified regardless
of its geometry**: already established earlier this session
(`nllb_swahili_layer22_vs_layer23_propagation_gap_check.py`) that layer
23, the LAST decoder layer, cannot causally affect any LATER position
-- every later position's self-attention K/V is computed before layer
23's own FFN runs within the same forward pass. Since the entire point
of noun-position steering is to influence a LATER agreement-bearing
word, layer 23 is mechanically useless here no matter how good its
cosine alignment looks.

**Verdict**: this is not a "wrong layer" problem -- there IS no strong
individually-aligned-neuron site for the class 9/10 singular/plural
distinction anywhere in this decoder's FFN stack, at least not one
write-vector cosine alignment can detect. This is qualitatively
different from class 7, whose candidates were clearly, strongly above
chance at layer 22. Plausible explanation: class 7 vs. class 1 is a
large lexical/semantic category distinction (largely different words),
while singular vs. plural WITHIN the same N-class noun is a much
subtler distinction that may be encoded diffusely across many weakly-
aligned units rather than concentrated in a few strong ones -- exactly
the kind of signal this session's whole method (amplify/zero a handful
of individual FFN neurons) is not well suited to move. This would also
mean the class9/10 case is not comparable to class 5's earlier, milder
weakness (fixable by lowering alpha) -- class 5 had a real, if narrow,
working window; class 9/10 may not have one at any layer with THIS
mechanism.

**Implication for the project**: individual-neuron steering, validated
extensively for class 7 (and workably for 5/8 with per-class alpha
tuning), may not generalize to EVERY Swahili noun class without a
different intervention style (e.g. direct residual-stream direction
addition distributed across layers, rather than concentrating force in
a handful of FFN units) -- open question, untested. For now, class 9/10
steering via this session's established mechanism should be considered
unresolved, not just "needs more tuning."

Files: `nllb_swahili_class9_10_write_vector_layer_scan.py` (new).

## 2026-10-04 — Multi-noun causal check: we DO have the right neurons; the real bottleneck is a magnitude mismatch, not wrong/weak units

User's request, after the 24-layer cosine scan suggested weak alignment
everywhere: "investigate with other class 9 nouns and see the impact
on the stream to make sure we have the right neurons." Tested
causally, not just via static cosine (`nllb_swahili_class9_multinoun_
causal_check.py`): across 10 DIFFERENT real class-9/10 nouns (nguo,
njia, nyumba, pesa, sababu, safari, sauti, siku, elimu, kazi -- none of
them kitunguu, which isn't even natively class 9/10), with a matched
random-unit control (same count, same alpha, different units).

**Result: the layer-22 and layer-9 candidates both show a strong,
clean, highly consistent causal effect, far above random, on EVERY
noun tested**:
```
LAYER 22 (alpha=300): mean final-layer delta  REAL=+1.1316  RANDOM=+0.0767  (~15x)
LAYER 9  (alpha=300): mean final-layer delta  REAL=+0.8030  RANDOM=-0.0448  (REAL positive
                                                                              10/10 nouns,
                                                                              RANDOM positive
                                                                              only 2/10)
```
Swept alpha 10->200 at layer 22 across the same 10 nouns: the real-vs-
random ratio stays stable at 13-17x throughout the ENTIRE range,
scaling linearly with alpha as expected for a direct FFN write
operation. This directly CONTRADICTS the concern raised by the 24-layer
cosine scan (previous entry) -- cosine alignment of a write vector and
its actual causal leverage are evidently NOT as tightly coupled for
this class as they were for the layer-23/class-1 relationship validated
earlier this session (r=0.9945). **Verdict: these are the right
neurons** -- a specific, reliable, far-above-chance causal handle on
the class9_hat axis, not noise.

**So why did real-text generation (kitunguu) still fail?** A magnitude
mismatch, now precisely characterized. Real, unsteered class-9/10
nouns' own NATURAL final-layer class9_hat projection sits in the
0.03-0.33 range across all 10 nouns tested. At alpha=300 (the value
used in every real-text check so far), steering pushes this projection
by +1.1316 -- more than 3x the ENTIRE natural range any real noun ever
occupies. Even the earlier chekundu/kitunguu generation sweep's
crossover point (~200-300, where the real adjective finally loses its
logit lead) corresponds to a shift already several times larger than
natural variation. This is consistent with -- and now gives a precise,
quantified account of -- the collapse into generic filler/punctuation
observed in real text: by the time the shift is large enough to
actually win the full-vocabulary argmax, it has already pushed the
representation well outside the region any real sentence occupies.

**Reframed conclusion**: the problem was never "wrong neurons" or even
"wrong direction" (which WAS genuinely wrong and is now fixed) -- it is
that winning an argmax contest in a long, rich real-text context seems
to require a shift much larger than the natural scale of the signal
itself, and nothing in the alpha range tested threads that needle for
class 9/10 on real text. Whether a smaller alpha with a LARGER/
different neuron set, or a different intervention style entirely
(e.g. applied at multiple positions or layers rather than one FFN
layer's handful of units), can close this gap is open.

**Not yet done**: generation-level test (not just projection-level) to
confirm the magnitude-mismatch account directly -- e.g. does ANY alpha
between 50-150 (a shift of roughly 1-3x natural range rather than 300's
10x) produce a genuinely coherent class-9 word in free generation,
even if it doesn't always win the argmax; the equivalent multi-noun
causal check for class 10 (not yet run, expected to show the same
"neurons are fine, magnitude mismatch is the issue" pattern given
class9/10 share the same construction).

Files: `nllb_swahili_class9_multinoun_causal_check.py` (new).

## 2026-10-04 (continued) — Magnitude-matched alpha (40-150) still produces no coherent class-9 word: the mismatch hypothesis was incomplete

Direct generation-level test of the magnitude-mismatch account from the
previous entry, on kitunguu's real sentence, sweeping alpha through the
"natural-range-scale" band (40-150, i.e. roughly 1-3x the natural
0.03-0.33 class9_hat projection range nouns occupy, well below alpha=
300's 10x overshoot) with the validated class9_hat_v2 direction, its
layer-22 candidates (now causally confirmed strong via the multi-noun
check), AND the safety-checked `<chekundu_cl9>` injected token
available.

**Result: still no coherent class-9 output anywhere in this band.**
```
alpha 40-60:   'kitunguu kikuu. Video hiyo ya mama mmoja'
alpha 70-150:  'kitunguu, video hiyo ya mama mmoja iliyochap'
```
At low alpha, the model picks a real but WRONG word ("kikuu" = "big/
major," itself still class-7-flavored concord, not class 9) -- the
steering isn't landing on the intended axis's practical effect at all.
At alpha >= 70, the adjective slot gets dropped entirely -- the model
jumps straight to punctuation and the next real sentence, rather than
filling the slot with anything class-9-like, real or injected.

**This rules out magnitude alone as a sufficient explanation.** The
hypothesis from the multi-noun causal check (shift too large to stay
coherent at alpha=300) was real but incomplete: even at a scale
matched to natural per-noun variation, the model never produces a
genuinely class-9-concordant adjective. Two live possibilities, neither
yet tested:
1. The class9_hat axis, while causally real (confirmed: it reliably
   moves the intended PROJECTION, well above random, across many
   nouns), may not be the functionally relevant lever for the specific
   downstream mechanism that selects adjective CONCORD -- i.e. it
   moves a real but functionally disconnected direction.
2. Structural mismatch with how this session's one clean adjective
   success (mzuri_cl7/mrefu_cl7) was built: those were TOY-sentence
   tests where the noun's influence had no competing context. Real
   text (kitunguu's sentence has 167 tokens of surrounding real
   content) may simply overwhelm a single noun-position intervention
   regardless of calibration -- consistent with njia's success being
   the ONE case where a fitting REAL WORD ("kienyeji") already existed
   and needed no injection at all, rather than evidence the full
   recipe (injection + steering) transfers to real text in general.

**Not yet tried**: the verb-prefix-style fix -- "chekundu" = "che" +
"kundu," where "che-" is literally the class-7 CONCORD PREFIX itself
(same structure as "_ana"/"_kina" for verbs, where injecting only the
PREFIX subword and letting the shared stem continue on its own is what
made the verb case work cleanly, unlike whole-word injection). Every
adjective injection this session (mzuri_cl7, mrefu_cl7, chekundu_cl9,
vibichi_cl10) has used a WHOLE-WORD-style construction, never the
prefix-only trick that was specifically what fixed the analogous verb
case. This has not been tried for any adjective and is the most
promising untested lead.
