## 2026-10-05 — Toy-sentence baseline: class 9 steering works cleanly; the real-text failure was never about class 9/10 itself

The one untested baseline, finally run: the exact same class9_hat_v2
direction, the same layer-22 candidates (causally validated across 10
nouns in the previous entry), and the same safety-checked injection
recipe, tested on the SAME minimal toy sentence structure as the
session's original class-7 success ("a good person" -> "mtu mzuri",
steering mtu's position toward class 9, injected `<mzuri_cl9>`).

**Result: clean, wide, stable success.**
```
baseline:      top5 = mzuri(14.84), mw(14.81), <mzuri_cl9>(14.72) -- already near-tied
alpha=30-300:  <mzuri_cl9> wins outright at EVERY alpha in this range, no collapse
```
This is the widest, cleanest sweet spot seen for class 9/10 all
session -- as good as class 7's own toy-sentence result and, unlike
every real-text class-9/10 attempt, shows zero sign of the punctuation/
filler collapse seen on real text at the same alpha values.

**This overturns the framing of every entry since the direction fix.**
Four separate hypotheses were tested and individually ruled out against
kitunguu's real-text failure (wrong direction -- fixed; wrong/weak
neurons -- ruled out via multi-noun causal check; wrong magnitude --
tested, didn't fix it; wrong injection structure -- tested, didn't fix
it). None of them were the actual answer, because the premise was
wrong: class 9/10 steering is NOT fundamentally broken. It works
cleanly in a controlled setting, exactly like class 7 does. The failure
is specific to the REAL-TEXT context (167 tokens of dense, real
content), not to class 9/10 as a target.

**Reframed account of njia's earlier "success"**: njia likely succeeded
in real text not because class 7 steering specially survives real
text's complexity, but because njia needed NO INJECTION at all -- a
naturally fitting real class-7 word ("kienyeji") was already available
and simply won on its own merits once steering suppressed the
competing class-9/10 signal. Kitunguu and vitunguu both required an
injected token (no equally fitting real alternative existed), and an
injected, non-pretrained token apparently cannot compete against the
sheer weight of 167 tokens of real, rich surrounding context -- a
likely general limitation of the injection technique in long text,
not a class-9/10-specific problem. This reframes the earlier "class
7 generalizes, class 9/10 doesn't" conclusion: the real variable may be
"needed injection vs. didn't," not "which class."

**Open question, directly actionable next**: does an INJECTED class-7
token (e.g. re-testing mrefu_cl7 or a case where class 7 needs
injection, not a naturally-available real word) ALSO fail on real,
long-context text the way kitunguu/vitunguu's injected tokens did? If
yes, this confirms the real bottleneck is "injected tokens vs. long
real context" in general, not anything about class 9/10 specifically --
a much more important, generalizable finding for the project's actual
deployment goal (CLAUDE.md section 1), where EVERY Kitaita-target noun
will need dictionary substitution and most will likely need some form
of injection, not just the lucky cases where a fitting real word
happens to already exist.

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — Confirmed: it was never about class 9/10. Injected tokens lose to real text regardless of class.

Direct test of the question raised by the toy-sentence success: does
class 7 -- the single most validated, most robust class this entire
session -- ALSO fail to get an injected token to win in a real, long-
context article, the same way kitunguu/vitunguu's class 9/10 injections
did? Used "mwanamke" (a real class-1 ANIMATE-SG noun already in the
pasted article, single token), steered toward class 7 with the
ORIGINAL, most-validated layer-22 class-7 candidates ([488, 6108, 6191,
7659, 1502]/[2888, 3618, 662, 7473, 6148]), injected `<mzuri_cl7>`
built the same way as the session's very first successful pilot.

**Result: class 7's injection fails too, in the same way.**
```
alpha 10-200:  injected token never appears in top-5 at all; "mmoja"
               (the real, unsteered continuation) barely budges even
               at alpha=200
alpha=300:     "▁ki" wins -- the generic class-7 PREFIX FRAGMENT (the
               "ki-attractor" documented earlier this session, now
               confirmed to recur here too) -- NOT the injected token.
               Continuation: "mwanamke kipofu mwenye kitunguu nyek..."
               -- "kipofu" ("blind") is a genuine, real class-7 word,
               thematically unrelated to "good," not our constructed
               synthetic token.
```

**Verdict, now generalized beyond class 9/10**: the earlier framing
("class 7 generalizes to real text, class 9/10 doesn't") was wrong.
The real, generalizable finding is: an INJECTED, non-pretrained token
-- regardless of which class it represents, including the most
validated class in the whole session -- cannot compete against the
strong distributional pull of ~167 tokens of real, dense context. What
steering CAN reliably do in long real text is redirect the model
toward a DIFFERENT REAL, already-pretrained, class-concordant word
(njia -> "kienyeji" earlier; "mwanamke" -> "kipofu" here) -- never
toward an artificial vector, however carefully constructed, however
strong its validated causal effect on the stream in isolation.

**Implication for the project's deployment design (CLAUDE.md section
1)**: the pipeline currently imagines steering + dictionary
substitution working for ANY noun. This result suggests injection-
dependent steering (needed whenever no fitting real word already
exists for the target class -- which will be the common case, not the
exception, once Kitaita concord targets are involved) may not survive
real deployment-scale text at all. Steering that only ever succeeds by
redirecting among EXISTING real vocabulary (never injecting new
content) may be the only mode that survives contact with real text --
a significant, previously unrecognized constraint on the whole
approach, independent of which Swahili class is involved.

**Not yet done**: confirming whether a SHORTER real-text context (e.g.
a single real sentence in isolation, rather than the full 167-token
article) still shows this failure, to find out whether it's context
LENGTH specifically that defeats injection, or something else about
real text's density/distributional strength that even a short real
sentence would already exhibit.

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — Root cause isolated: it's the SOURCE class, not context length, multi-subword structure, or construction details

Follow-up to the user's "che_cl9" correction (chekundu's true morpheme
split is "che"+"kundu", not the tokenizer's BPE-merged "chek"+"undu")
and the short-context retest it prompted. Rebuilt the injection from
the correct token ("_che", id 854, confirmed via tokenization to be an
independent, freestanding token used across many words, not merged
with part of the root the way "_chek" was) -- STILL failed, with an
output pixel-identical to a completely different injection (`<mzuri_
cl9>` built from "mzuri", after kitunguu) -- revealing that in BOTH
cases the injected token never enters contention AT ALL; the output is
driven entirely by real-vocabulary competition under steering,
independent of which synthetic token is added.

This prompted a systematic isolation across FOUR candidate variables,
each tested while holding the others fixed:

1. **Context length**: ruled out. Re-ran kitunguu/chekundu_cl9 in a
   SHORT (5-token) context, mirroring the successful mtu/mzuri toy test
   exactly. Injection still failed identically to the 167-token real-
   article version.
2. **Multi-subword noun position**: ruled out, two ways. (a) Measured
   the actual CAUSAL effect on the stream at kitunguu's last-subword
   position vs. mtu's single-token position, same alpha: kitunguu's
   delta (+0.7281 at alpha=100) is if anything LARGER than mtu's
   (+0.6754) -- steering is not weaker at a multi-subword position. (b)
   Tested "kiti" (chair, class 7, SINGLE token) with the exact mtu-
   style recipe -- injection failed for kiti too, identically to
   kitunguu, even though kiti has no multi-subword structure at all.
3. **Which word the injection is built from**: ruled out. Tested
   `<chek_cl9>` (from the BPE-native "_chek"), `<che_cl9>` (from the
   true morpheme "_che"), and `<mzuri_cl9>` (from the independently-
   successful "mzuri") all after kitunguu/kiti -- all three fail
   identically.
4. **Source noun's starting class**: THIS is the variable that
   predicts the outcome, confirmed across 5 nouns:
   ```
   class 1 (ANIMATE-SG) -> class 9:  mtu, mwanamke, mtoto  -- ALL succeed
                                      cleanly, alpha 30-300, wide margin
   class 7 -> class 9:                kiti, kitunguu        -- ALL fail,
                                      injected token never enters top-5
                                      at any alpha tried
   ```
   Same target direction (class9_hat_v2), same layer-22 candidates,
   same injection recipe, same alpha range -- the ONLY thing that
   changes is the noun's OWN starting class, and that alone perfectly
   predicts success or failure across every noun tested.

**Working explanation**: this converges with a pattern that recurred
all session without being named as a single phenomenon -- the "ki-
attractor" (bare "ki-"-flavored fragments/tokens winning free-
generation collapse in multiple earlier, unrelated tests; "▁ki" as a
top candidate in the kitunguu/mwanamke real-text failures; "kipofu"
winning over an injected class-7 adjective in the class-7-injection-
fails-too test). Class 7's own class signal may simply be unusually
strong and deeply entrenched in this model's embedding geometry --
hard to override regardless of target class, while class 1's signal is
comparatively easy to displace. If so, the operative variable for this
whole session's steering work was never really "which target class,"
it is "how entrenched is the SOURCE class" -- a noun's resistance to
being steered AWAY, not a target's difficulty to steer TOWARD.

**Not yet done**: testing OTHER source classes (5, 8, 11, etc.) toward
class 9 to see if class 7 is uniquely "sticky" or if this is a more
general strength-ordering among all classes; a direct, quantified
measure of each class's "stickiness" (e.g. the same multi-noun causal
check style, but measuring how much FORCE is needed to move AWAY FROM
each class, not just toward class 9/10 specifically) -- would turn
this from a qualitative observation into the kind of controlled,
confidence-interval-backed number this project's other findings have.

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — Direction-quality audit refutes "more data = better direction"; real pattern is the ki-/vi- prefix family, not direction quality

User's hypothesis, tested directly: "I suspect we did not learn the
directions correctly for all the classes. Because surely class 1 has
more context." Checked the lexicon directly: ANIMATE-SG has 57 nouns
vs. class 7's 25 -- more than double, a real basis for the suspicion.

**Built a held-out + random-control validity audit for classes
ANIMATE-SG/5/7/8**(`nllb_swahili_class_direction_quality_audit.py`),
the same discipline that caught class 9/10's bug, adapted to verb-
prefix concord sentences ("<noun> <prefix>fanya kazi.", prefixes ana/
lina/kina/vina) since class1/5/7/8 nouns are different lexical items
per class (no same-noun minimal pair available the way 9/10 had).
80/20 train/test split per class, direction rebuilt from TRAIN only,
tested on HELD-OUT nouns via their CONTEXTUAL (encoder) representation.

**Result -- the opposite of the "more data" hypothesis**:
```
class ANIMATE-SG (57 nouns): own-class-wins 0/12 held-out nouns.
                              mean(own)=-0.0308 -- actually NEGATIVE.
class 5          (22 nouns): own-class-wins 4/5.
class 7          (25 nouns): own-class-wins 4/5.
class 8          (26 nouns): own-class-wins 0/6.
```
ANIMATE-SG -- the class with MORE THAN DOUBLE the raw data of class 7
-- has the WORST-validated direction of the four; class 7 -- the class
found hardest to steer away from -- has one of the BEST-validated
directions. More data did not produce a better direction here, and
direction quality does NOT predict ease-of-override in the way
hypothesized.

**Likely reason ANIMATE-SG fails this check specifically**: Swahili
class-1 nouns are morphologically HETEROGENEOUS in a way classes 5/7/8
are not -- many (mtu, mwalimu, mpishi) carry an overt "m-/mw-" prefix,
but many others in this lexicon (paka, tai, chui, mbwa -- animals
grammatically treated as class 1/2 by animacy, not morphology) carry
NO overt class marker at all. Classes 5/7/8 are uniformly, overtly
prefixed (ki-/vi- always present). This mixed-marking heterogeneity
plausibly makes class 1's own "class signal," as isolated by the
static-embedding residual method, inherently noisier/more diffuse --
independent of how much raw data went into it.

**Re-tested class5/class8 -> class9 injection directly, given this new
information (predicting class 5 "hard" like class 7, class 8 "easy"
like class 1, based on direction-quality alone) -- prediction FAILED
too**:
```
class 5 (gari, duka) -> class 9:  REAL vocabulary naturally shifts to
                                   "nzuri" (the CORRECT class-9/10
                                   word) within a few tokens at EVERY
                                   alpha tried, including 30 -- EASY,
                                   same as class 1.
class 8 (viti)       -> class 9:  stays on "vizuri" (class 8's OWN
                                   form) even at alpha=300, ZERO shift
                                   -- HARD, same as class 7.
```
Direction quality (4/5 for both 5 and 7; 0/6 and 0/12 for both 8 and 1)
does NOT separate along the same lines as ease-of-override (1 and 5
easy; 7 and 8 hard). Both hypotheses tested this session for WHY some
transitions are easy and others hard -- "source class is intrinsically
sticky" and "source direction is poorly learned" -- are now refuted as
the explanation on their own.

**What DOES separate cleanly along the observed easy/hard split**:
classes 7 and 8 are precisely the ki-/vi- PREFIX FAMILY (both
resistant); classes 1 and 5 carry neither prefix (both easy). This
lines up with the "ki-attractor" phenomenon documented much earlier
this session (2026-10-02/03 entries) -- the bare "ki-" fragment
winning full-vocabulary argmax over specific real/constructed words at
high alpha, demonstrated independently via BOTH live neuron steering
AND pure static-vector injection with no network involved at all,
suggesting "ki-"/"vi-" occupy an unusually large, dominant region of
this model's embedding/vocabulary space -- likely a property of their
extreme frequency and versatility as subwords across the ENTIRE
vocabulary (ki-/vi- appear as prefixes or fragments in enormously many
unrelated words), not a property of their GRAMMATICAL class signal
specifically. This would make classes 7/8 hard to leave for a reason
ORTHOGONAL to grammar -- a lexical/frequency dominance effect -- while
classes 1/5, lacking this prefix family's outsized footprint, are easy
to override.

**Not yet done**: directly testing whether "ki-"/"vi-" fragments have
unusually large AGGREGATE embedding-space presence (e.g. total
vocabulary mass of tokens starting with these prefixes, or their
write-vector norms/frequencies at layer 22) compared to other
classes' prefixes, which would confirm the frequency/dominance
explanation quantitatively rather than just by pattern-matching to the
earlier qualitative ki-attractor observations; testing classes 3/4/6/
11/15 to see if the ki-/vi- vs. other split holds beyond just these
four classes, or if there are OTHER resistant/easy classes not yet
identified.

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — Expanded 39-combination matrix: no clean source-class rule; mtu/ANIMATE-SG is the one decisive outlier

Following the pilot (4 nouns x 1 target x 3 adjectives,
`nllb_swahili_big_noun_adjective_class9_matrix_check.py`), user's
directive: "increase the number of nouns and target classes once this
test is done. treat it like a pilot." Expanded to 7 source-class nouns
(mtu=1, mchezo=3, gari=5, macho=6, kiti=7, viti=8, ukweli=11 -- all
single-token, every adjective's concord form per class verified via
direct SW->EN translation before use, not assumed) x 2 target classes
(9/10 and 7, the two with validated directions+candidates) x 3
adjectives (zuri/kubwa/dogo) = 39 valid combinations (3 degenerate
source==target cases skipped), each run both without injection
(tracking the real target word's rank trend) and with injection
(safety-checked synthetic from the noun's own source-class form).
Script: `nllb_swahili_expanded_noun_adjective_class_matrix_check.py`.

**Overall: injection succeeds in 22/39 (56%)** -- close to a coin
flip, not a hard rule in either direction.

**By source class (injection success rate)**:
```
mtu     (1):  6/6  = 100%
gari    (5):  5/6  =  83%
macho   (6):  4/6  =  67%
kiti    (7):  2/3  =  67%
viti    (8):  2/6  =  33%
ukweli (11):  2/6  =  33%
mchezo  (3):  1/6  =  17%   <-- WORST, and NOT a ki-/vi- class
```
This directly REFUTES the "ki-/vi- prefix family is the resistant
group" hypothesis from earlier entries: mchezo (class 3, "m-" concord,
sharing its surface form with class 1 and 11) has the WORST success
rate in the entire table -- worse than either ki-/vi- class (7, 8).
Meanwhile kiti (class 7) succeeds 2/3 of the time for target 9/10.
Source-class identity alone does not predict outcome.

**By target class**: 9/10 succeeds 57% (12/21), target 7 succeeds 56%
(10/18) -- statistically indistinguishable. Target class does not
predict outcome either.

**By adjective**: kubwa 69% (9/13), zuri 62% (8/13), dogo 38% (5/13) --
some spread, no clean rule.

**The one clean, decisive, reproducible pattern: mtu is 6/6, the only
noun with a perfect record**, regardless of target class or adjective.
This is consistent with the earlier finding (multi-noun causal check,
2026-10-04/05) that mtu's class-9 candidate neurons are ALREADY
naturally active before any steering, unlike class-7 nouns (kiti,
kitunguu) tested in that same check. **Correction (2026-10-05, caught
by external critique against this entry's own imprecise wording)**:
that pre-activation was NOT unique to mtu -- the same causal check also
measured mwanamke at the same units and found the same pattern (mtu
7.327, mwanamke 7.2174 at the same unit, both clearly active, vs. kiti/
kitunguu both ~0.0). The phrase "unlike every other noun ... including
other class-1 nouns" above conflated "the only class-1 noun in THIS
39-combo matrix" with "the only noun with this activation property" --
the second claim was wrong on this project's own existing data.
Whether this generalizes to "ANIMATE-SG in general" remains open, but
it is NOT mtu-specific -- it was already shown to hold for at least one
other class-1 noun before this matrix was even run.

**Catastrophic collapses are narrow, not categorical**: injected rank
blowing up to 5000+ (macho/dogo->910: 20591; viti/kubwa->910: 5081;
viti/dogo->910: 6736) happens ONLY at alpha=300, ONLY for target=9/10,
ONLY for kubwa/dogo (never zuri) on macho/viti specifically -- these
same pairs are FINE at alpha=100 (ranks 1-17). This is a per-pair
alpha-sensitivity/overshoot issue, not evidence that these pairs are
categorically blocked the way earlier framing suggested.

**Revised verdict**: there is no single decisive variable (source
class, target class, or adjective) that cleanly separates "works" from
"doesn't" across this broader sample. Success looks genuinely
multi-factorial / idiosyncratic to each specific (noun, adjective,
target) triple, with mtu as the one clear, reproducible exception
rather than a representative case for its whole class. Any future
claim about "which classes are hard to steer" should be checked
against this full matrix, not generalized from kiti/kitunguu alone as
earlier entries this session did.

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — Confirmed: ANIMATE-SG's advantage is a real class-level property, not mtu-specific

Follow-up to the 39-combination matrix, testing whether mtu's 6/6
(100%) injection-success record generalizes to ANIMATE-SG as a class
or is specific to mtu. Ran the same adjective (zuri/kubwa/dogo) x
target-class (9/10, 7) matrix on 3 MORE class-1 nouns (mwanamke, mtoto,
paka -- all single-token, confirmed earlier this session), 24 combos
total. Script: `nllb_swahili_animatesg_only_matrix_check.py`.

**Result**:
```
mtu:       6/6  = 100%
mwanamke:  5/6  =  83%   (only failure: dogo -> target class 7)
mtoto:     6/6  = 100%
paka:      5/6  =  83%   (only failure: dogo -> target class 9/10)
ANIMATE-SG total: 22/24 = 92%
```
Compare to the broader matrix's other classes: gari (5) 83%, macho (6)
67%, kiti (7) 67%, viti (8) 33%, ukweli (11) 33%, mchezo (3) 17%,
overall average across all 7 classes 56%.

**Verdict**: ANIMATE-SG's advantage is CONFIRMED as a genuine,
reproducible, class-level property -- not an artifact of mtu
specifically. 92% success across 4 different class-1 nouns is far
above every other class tested, including gari (class 5, the next-best
at 83%, but based on only 1 noun so far). This is now the most
solid, decisive, actionable finding from the whole steering-asymmetry
investigation: whatever makes ANIMATE-SG nouns easy to steer, it
operates at the CLASS level (consistent across 4 different lexical
items), not at the level of one lucky word. The two isolated failures
(mwanamke/dogo->7, paka/dogo->9-10) both involve "dogo" specifically,
suggesting "dogo" may be a weaker base word for injection in general
(consistent with the broader matrix's dogo=38% success rate, the
lowest of the three adjectives), not a noun-specific issue.

**Open, now the clear next step**: confirm whether OTHER classes also
show this kind of within-class consistency when sampled with 4 nouns
instead of 1 (gari was ANIMATE-SG's closest competitor at 83% but
based on a single noun) -- test 3-4 more class-5 nouns the same way,
to see if class 5 is ALSO a genuinely strong class (making ANIMATE-SG
not unique) or if gari was itself a lucky outlier (making ANIMATE-SG's
92% the standout).

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — External critique (ChatGPT/Gemini/Claude) on the ANIMATE-SG puzzle; one factual fix, one confound tested and ruled out

Sent `animate_sg_steering_advantage_critique_prompt.md` externally;
saved all three replies (`_chat.md`=ChatGPT, `_gemini.md`=Gemini,
`_claude.md`=an external Claude instance that reviewed the prompt
against this project's own status.md before answering, catching real
problems in the prompt itself, not just the underlying puzzle).

**Convergent recommendation across all three**: static write-vector
cosine selection (used for every candidate-neuron search this session)
conflates GEOMETRIC alignment with a class-mean direction and CAUSAL
relevance to a specific noun's own steering outcome -- all three
independently recommend replacing it with per-noun gradient/activation-
patching attribution (d(target-source logit difference)/d(activation))
as the next methodological upgrade, not another geometric scan.

**Leading reframing (ChatGPT, Gemini)**: class 1's advantage may not be
an intrinsic "class 1 is steerable" property at all -- it may be that
class-1 nouns' pre-intervention residual state happens to already sit
in a region compatible with this PARTICULAR actuator (the specific 5+5
units selected for THIS target class), given Test 7's finding that
steering suppresses the whole vocabulary distribution roughly uniformly
and winning is decided by baseline logit gap, not differential benefit
from steering. Both flag animacy/default-class-frequency as competing
explanations for WHY class 1 specifically would have this property,
distinct from its grammatical marking per se.

**External Claude's corrections, verified directly against this
project's own data**:

1. **Factual fix applied** (see correction inserted into the "mtu is
   6/6" entry above): that entry's wording claimed mtu's pre-activation
   was "unlike every other noun tested including other class-1 nouns,"
   contradicting the actual multi-noun causal check, which also
   measured mwanamke at the same units (7.2174, vs mtu's 7.327) --
   both clearly active, consistent with a class-1 property, not an
   mtu-specific one. The sloppy wording has been corrected in place.

2. **Most diagnostic existing data surfaced**: classes 1, 3, and 11 all
   share "m-" adjectival concord, so mtu/mchezo/ukweli were all
   injected from the IDENTICAL source word ("mzuri") toward the same
   target, yet scored 100%/17%/33% in the expanded matrix -- the
   closest thing to a controlled contrast already in the dataset.

3. **A specific, testable confound hypothesis (construction backoff
   correlating with class) -- tested directly and REFUTED**: re-ran the
   SAME "mzuri" injection with ONLY the current-class direction varied
   (ANIMATE-SG for mtu, class-3 for mchezo, class-11 for ukweli), same
   target direction, same base alpha_construction. Result:
   ```
   mtu (ANIMATE-SG):  margin=+0.12  backoff=0  wins at EVERY alpha (30/100/300)
   mchezo (class 3):  margin=+0.30  backoff=0  wins only at alpha=300
   ukweli (class 11): margin=+0.13  backoff=0  never wins (rank 2-3 throughout)
   ```
   Margins and backoff counts are similar across all three (no
   construction-quality gradient that tracks the outcome), and the
   injected token's OWN logit decays along nearly identical trajectories
   regardless of noun (13.3->6.7, 13.5->7.2, 13.3->6.8). **This rules
   out the safety-check-backoff confound as the explanation** -- the
   construction step itself is not what differs between these three
   cases. Whatever differs must be in each noun's own context/residual
   state producing a different landscape of COMPETING real words, not
   in how the injected token itself was built.

**Verdict**: this sharpens the puzzle exactly the way the external
critiques intended -- construction-level and candidate-selection-level
confounds are now substantially ruled out (the candidates are causally
real, Test 3; the construction recipe isn't the lever, just shown
above); what's left pointing at a real, unexplained property of each
noun's own pre-intervention representational state, consistent with
all three critiques' leading hypothesis.

**Not yet done, in priority order per the convergent critique
recommendations**: (1) the cheap logistic-regression reanalysis of all
combinations run so far (success ~ baseline logit gap + layer-22 input
projection onto target direction + class-1 indicator) to see if the
class-1 indicator's effect survives controlling for those; (2) the
animacy-vs-morphology test (plural animates class 2 "watu"; animate
class-7 nouns like "kijana"/"kiongozi" vs their inanimate class-7
counterparts) to separate animacy from grammatical class as the real
lever -- "paka" (an animal, grammatically class 1) already leans this
direction in the existing matrix; (3) per-noun gradient/activation-
patching attribution to replace global cosine-based candidate
selection, the one recommendation all three external responses
converged on independently.

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — Logistic reanalysis: the "class 1 advantage" is fully explained by baseline competitiveness, not class membership

External critique's recommended cheap reanalysis (Claude response to
the critique prompt), run before any new experiment. Reconstructed all
57 valid (noun, target_class, adjective) combinations from BOTH prior
matrices in one unified pass (10 nouns: mtu/mwanamke/mtoto/paka
[class 1], mchezo[3], gari[5], macho[6], kiti[7], viti[8], ukweli[11]),
this time ALSO capturing the noun's own layer-22 INPUT projection onto
the target direction (the residual stream BEFORE layer 22's FFN runs
-- not captured in any earlier script; earlier scripts only captured
the FINAL layer norm output after all 24 layers). Script:
`nllb_swahili_logistic_reanalysis.py`.

**Fit a logistic regression of success (injected token wins at any of
alpha=30/100/300) on: alpha_construction (after backoff), margin0
(construction-time real-vs-synthetic logit gap), target_rank0 and
inject_rank0 (baseline, alpha=0 ranks), layer-22 input projection onto
the target direction, and an is_class1 indicator.**

```
is_class1 ALONE:                    68.4% accuracy, coef=+1.2022
FULL model WITH is_class1:          89.47% accuracy, coef(is_class1)=-0.0175
FULL model WITHOUT is_class1:       89.47% accuracy  (IDENTICAL)
```

**Verdict: the apparent class-1 advantage is fully explained by these
confounds.** Adding is_class1 to the full model changes accuracy by
exactly zero (not even a small overfitting bump, which even a pure-
noise feature would typically produce) and its coefficient collapses
from a real, meaningful +1.20 (alone) to -0.02 (controlled) -- the
indicator carries no independent information once baseline
competitiveness is known. The dominant predictor is `inject_rank0`
(coef=-2.39, the single largest-magnitude coefficient): the injected
token's rank in the COMPLETELY UNSTEERED distribution predicts success
far better than anything about the noun's grammatical class. This
directly confirms Test 7's "race" framing from the external critique
round: class 1 succeeds because its injected tokens happen, across
this sample, to already be more competitive before any steering is
even applied -- a property of the specific word-in-context pairing,
not an independent causal effect of class membership layered on top
of it.

**This reframes the entire multi-week investigation's central
question.** "Why is class 1 special" was the wrong question from early
in this thread onward; the right question, per the external critique's
own reframing (independently proposed by two of the three responses),
is "what makes a noun's unsteered baseline state compatible with this
specific actuator" -- and this reanalysis shows that question is
already mostly answered by cheap, pre-computable quantities (baseline
rank, construction margin) rather than requiring any grammatical-class
reasoning at all.

**Caveat, stated plainly**: n=57 with 6 features is a small sample for
a 7-parameter logistic fit, and `success` is itself an operationalization
choice (injected token specifically winning, not "any correct class-
9/10 word winning," which Test 9's real-word-redirect cases like njia
-> kienyeji would score differently under a broader definition). The
zero-accuracy-change result is nonetheless a clean, hard-to-fake
signal regardless of sample-size concerns, since it would require the
confounding features to coincidentally and exactly saturate whatever
signal is_class1 carries -- a much stronger coincidence than ordinary
overfitting noise would produce.

**Not yet done**: the animacy-vs-morphology test (watu/kijana/kiongozi
vs inanimate counterparts) remains the next step to determine whether
inject_rank0 ITSELF correlates with animacy specifically, or with
something else (adjective-prediction tightness, word frequency) that
happens to correlate with class 1 in this particular sample.

Files: `nllb_swahili_logistic_reanalysis.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — Per-noun gradient attribution beats global cosine selection on all 3 cases tested

Direct test of the one recommendation all three external critiques
converged on independently: replace GLOBAL, static write-vector-cosine
candidate selection with PER-NOUN gradient attribution. Script:
`nllb_swahili_pernoun_gradient_attribution_check.py`.

**Method**: hook layer 22's activation_fn, replace its output at the
noun's own position with a fresh leaf tensor (requires_grad=True,
initialized to the natural value) so every one of the 8192 units is
treated as an independently settable free variable; forward, compute
`logit(target_word) - logit(source_word)`, backward, read the leaf's
gradient directly. Used PURE gradient, not gradient-times-activation
(Gemini's literal suggestion) -- gradient-times-activation would
structurally always score a naturally-dead unit as zero-importance
regardless of its gradient, which would defeat the purpose for exactly
the non-class-1 nouns whose candidate units were found dead at
baseline (2026-10-04/05 entries).

**Tested on 3 combinations, comparing OLD (global cosine) vs NEW
(per-noun gradient) candidates within the same script/conditions**:
```
mchezo -> class9/10, kubwa:  OLD best rank=3 (never 1).  NEW reaches rank=1 at alpha=100.
ukweli -> class9/10, zuri:   OLD best rank=4 (never 1).  NEW reaches rank=3 (closer, still no 1).
viti   -> class9/10, kubwa:  OLD reaches rank=1 at alpha=100-300.
                              NEW reaches rank=1 at alpha=30-100 (lower, SAFER alpha).
```
**Zero overlap between OLD and NEW candidate units in all 3 cases** --
confirms these are genuinely different, noun-specific unit sets, not a
relabeling of the same ones.

**Trade-off, consistent across all 3**: the new candidates overshoot
MORE SEVERELY at alpha=300 than the old ones did (ranks 35, 136, 11 at
alpha=300 vs milder degradation for the old candidates at the same
alpha) -- these are stronger, more concentrated per-noun actuators,
which narrows the safe operating window rather than eliminating the
overshoot problem. Per-noun alpha calibration would likely be needed
in any production use of this method, not a fixed global alpha.

**Verdict**: this is a real, if modest-n, confirmation that the
external critiques' top convergent recommendation has practical
value -- per-noun causal attribution outperforms global geometric
selection on every case tested, including unlocking one case (mchezo)
that never succeeded with the old method at any alpha. This is the
first methodological change this whole investigation has found that
demonstrably IMPROVES steering reliability rather than just explaining
why the old method sometimes works -- directly relevant to the actual
deployment goal (any dictionary-supplied noun needs to steer
reliably, not just the lucky ones).

**Caveat**: n=3 cases, all target class 9/10, all using the REAL
target word's rank as the success metric (not an injected token --
this script tests whether steering ALONE, no injection, can promote
the correct real word, a related but distinct question from the
earlier injection-based matrix). Not yet validated at the scale of the
57-combination matrix, nor against target class 7, nor combined with
the injection recipe.

**Not yet done**: scale this to the full matrix (replace global
candidates with per-noun gradient candidates for all 57 combinations)
to see if the overall success rate improves and whether the
"class-1 confound" from the logistic reanalysis changes shape;
per-noun alpha calibration (given the narrower safe window found
here); combining per-noun gradient candidates WITH the injection
recipe (not yet tried together).

Files: `nllb_swahili_pernoun_gradient_attribution_check.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — Per-noun gradient attribution scales: 2x success rate on the full matrix, and solves one of the session's longest-standing real-text failures

Following the 3-case pilot's success, user's directive: check whether
this generalizes (a) across the full matrix and (b) to longer, real-
text contexts specifically, since that is where every method tried
this session has been least consistent.

**(A) Full 57-combination matrix** (`nllb_swahili_pernoun_gradient_
full_matrix_check.py`, same 10 nouns x 2 target classes x 3 adjectives
as the logistic reanalysis, metric = does the REAL target word reach
rank 1 via steering alone, no injection, at any of alpha=
10/30/50/100/150/200):
```
OLD (global cosine) success:        11/57 (19.3%)
NEW (per-noun gradient) success:    25/57 (43.9%)
```
More than double the success rate, not a 3-case fluke. Improvement is
consistent across nearly every row (occasional exceptions, e.g.
gari->7/zuri got slightly worse: 12->17), and is LARGEST specifically
for target class 7 (previously the weakest target overall): e.g.
mtu->7/zuri 46->15, mwanamke->7/zuri 38->7, paka->7/kubwa 16->1,
mchezo->7/kubwa 30->3.

**(B) The 167-token real article** (`nllb_swahili_pernoun_gradient_
realtext_check.py`), the two cases that have failed under every method
tried since 2026-10-03/04 -- gradient computed DIRECTLY in this long
context, not a toy sentence:

```
kitunguu -> class 9 (chekundu -> nyekundu):
  OLD: best rank=2, NEVER reaches 1, across alpha 10-300
       (at alpha>=200 collapses to rank 132, then 36169 -- the
       familiar overshoot-into-garbage pattern)
  NEW: rank=1 at alpha=10 -- CLEAN WIN, first alpha tried.

mwanamke -> class 7 (mzuri -> kizuri):
  OLD: best rank=33,747 (catastrophic -- matches the earlier finding
       that even class 7's own injection collapses into "kipofu"
       garbage in this exact context, 2026-10-05 entry)
  NEW: best rank=7,138 -- a real ~4.7x improvement, but nowhere near
       winning.
```

**This is the first time ANY method has produced a clean win for
kitunguu->class 9 in this real article** -- the single most persistently
failing case of the entire session (tested via whole-word injection,
prefix-level injection built from "_che"/"_chek", classifier-derived
direction swaps, alpha sweeps from 10 to 1500, and the contextual
difference-of-means direction rebuild -- all of which either failed
outright or got stuck at rank 2-3 without ever reaching 1). Per-noun
gradient attribution, computed on the noun's own long-context
representation rather than a toy sentence or a global class-mean
direction, breaks through where nothing else did.

**mwanamke->class 7 remains unsolved** despite real improvement,
suggesting the method helps but does not uniformly fix every case --
consistent with (A)'s pattern of large gains concentrated on target
class 7 overall, but with this specific (noun, context) pairing still
far from competitive. Candidate units had near-zero overlap with the
old global selection in both cases (0/5 and 1/5 respectively),
confirming per-noun, per-context attribution finds genuinely different
levers than any global, static criterion would.

**Verdict**: per-noun gradient attribution is the clearest, most
broadly-validated methodological improvement this entire investigation
has produced -- it generalizes from 3 hand-picked cases to the full
matrix (2x success rate) AND to the long-text setting that previously
defeated every other method, including solving outright one of the
session's most stubborn individual failures. It does not solve
everything (mwanamke->7 remains far from success), so it is a real
improvement to the existing mechanism, not evidence the mechanism's
fundamental "suppression, not amplification" character (confirmed two
entries above) has changed.

**Not yet done**: understanding WHY mwanamke->7 improves so much less
than kitunguu->9 despite both being long-text, real-article cases;
testing per-noun gradient attribution combined with the injection
recipe (not yet tried together, only tested as a pure steering-alone
mechanism in both (A) and (B)); checking whether gradient-based
candidates computed in a SHORT context transfer to the LONG context as
well as context-matched gradients do, which would matter for making
this practical (recomputing gradients per-document rather than
per-noun-in-context would be much cheaper at deployment scale).
