## 2026-10-05 (continued) — What gradient-selected neurons actually are: not per-noun, almost entirely per-word-pair

User's directive: stop tuning blindly, understand what the per-noun
gradient attribution method is actually doing, and check for anything
common within a class that could be salvaged as a reusable recipe.
Script: `nllb_swahili_gradient_candidates_commonality_check.py`, plus
targeted follow-up checks run inline.

**Check 1 -- geometric role of the selected units**: cosine of each
selected unit's fc2 write-vector against the target class direction,
the source class direction, and the global language direction (g_hat)
-- ALL values fall in the +-0.08 range, i.e. noise-floor level (the
same ~0.02-0.03 random-direction floor established earlier this
session). **These units are not "writing toward the target class" in
any sense a cosine scan could detect.** Their causal effectiveness
(confirmed repeatedly via direct intervention) is invisible to every
static, direction-based selection method used this entire session --
the clearest possible confirmation of the external critiques'
"geometric relevance != causal relevance" distinction.

**Check 2/3 -- where the commonality actually lives**: computed
candidates for all 4 class-1 nouns (mtu/mwanamke/mtoto/paka) x all 3
adjectives, then measured pairwise Jaccard overlap (vs. a random-pair
baseline of 0.0000 over 20 draws):
```
SAME noun, DIFFERENT adjective (same target class):     0.00-0.43 overlap
DIFFERENT noun, SAME adjective (same source+target):    0.25-1.00 overlap,
                                                           often 0.667-1.000
```
Overlap is driven far more by WHICH WORD PAIR than by WHICH NOUN.

**Decisive follow-up, disentangling source/target/noun/class**:
```
mtu vs mchezo vs ukweli, SAME word pair (mkubwa->kubwa),
  DIFFERENT grammatical class (1 vs 3 vs 11):           0.43-0.67 overlap
  (still far above the 0.0000 random floor -- class identity
  is NOT what's driving the commonality either)

SAME noun+source word, DIFFERENT target
  (mtu/mzuri -> nzuri vs mtu/mzuri -> kizuri):            0.25 overlap (LOWER)

SAME target+source word, DIFFERENT noun
  (mtu vs mwanamke, both mzuri->nzuri):                   0.667 overlap (HIGHER)
```
Changing the TARGET word hurts overlap more than changing the NOUN
does; changing the NOUN'S GRAMMATICAL CLASS barely hurts it at all
once source and target words are held fixed.

**Verdict**: per-noun gradient attribution is, empirically, almost
entirely a property of the (source_word, target_word) PAIR, with the
noun/context contributing only a smaller, secondary modulation. This
reframes the whole method's practical cost: it does NOT need to be
recomputed per noun, per document, or even strongly per grammatical
class -- a Kitaita dictionary has a FINITE set of concord word-pairs
per class, so a candidate-neuron set could be precomputed ONCE per
(source-concord-form, target-concord-form) pair and reused across
every noun that needs that exact transition, rather than paying a
live gradient-computation cost for every noun in every document. This
is the first concrete, deployment-relevant simplification this whole
investigation has produced.

**Open question this raises**: given candidates are mostly word-pair-
specific, is the earlier "per-noun gradient beats global cosine"
result (2x matrix success rate, solved the kitunguu real-text case)
actually explained by "per-WORD-PAIR precision" rather than anything
noun-specific at all? If so, a simpler, cheaper "per-word-pair
gradient, computed once in a generic/short context and reused
everywhere" might match the full per-noun-in-context version's
performance -- directly testable, and would settle whether the long-
text success (kitunguu) specifically needed the LONG CONTEXT's
gradient or would have worked equally well from a toy-sentence
gradient reused in the long context.

**Not yet done**: the direct test above (precompute per-word-pair
candidates once, in a short/generic context, then reuse them across
ALL nouns needing that transition, including in long real text) --
this would validate or refute the practical simplification this
entry's finding implies.

Files: `nllb_swahili_gradient_candidates_commonality_check.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — MAJOR PIVOT: a deterministic rule-based rewrite solves the hardest real-text cases that defeated every neuron-steering approach

User's directive, after the steering mechanism's ~40-50% ceiling and
the "near-miss" cases proving resistant to further tuning: "A cheaper
simpler approach... what if we do a translation using the Hewitt tree
for context... the tokens that are next to the token of the word
whose noun class you want to change you simply directly substitute."
This is the rule-based baseline CLAUDE.md's own "Open decisions"
section already named as required ("Final evaluation must include a
rule-based baseline: Swahili output + dictionary + deterministic
prefix rewrite") and revives the Hewitt-tree idea the user explicitly
deferred earlier this session ("cache this for much later").

**Checked feasibility of the LEARNED-tree version first, honestly**:
no Swahili dependency treebank exists in this project (CoNLL-U data on
disk is English/French/German only) or, as far as checked, in
Universal Dependencies generally -- so a true Hewitt & Manning
structural probe cannot be trained for Swahili without new annotated
data. Neither spaCy nor Stanza is installed, and Swahili dependency
parsing is not a standard supported pipeline for either even if
installed.

**Built the practical substitute instead**: since Swahili concord is
established (this session, CLAUDE.md) to be overwhelmingly POST-
NOMINAL and clause-local, "agreement-adjacent" is approximated with a
simple heuristic (words immediately following the noun, within the
same clause, stopped at punctuation) rather than a learned tree, paired
with a REWRITE DICTIONARY built entirely from concord mappings already
verified via direct translation this session (zuri/kubwa/dogo across
classes 1/3/5/6/7/8/9-10/11; "ekundu"/"red" -> chekundu(7)/nyekundu
(9-10); "bichi"/"raw" -> kibichi(7)/vibichi(8)/mbichi(9-10)). Script:
`nllb_swahili_rule_based_rewrite_prototype.py`.

**Toy-sentence validation: 4/4 perfect**:
```
'gari nzuri' (car, cl5) -> target cl7:   'gari kizuri'      correct
'mchezo mkubwa' (game, cl3) -> cl9/10:   'mchezo kubwa'     correct
'ukweli mdogo' (truth, cl11) -> cl8:     'ukweli vidogo'    correct
'kiti kizuri' (chair, cl7) -> cl9/10:    'kiti nzuri'       correct
```

**Real-text validation, on the exact 167-token article every steering
method struggled with all session**:
```
kitunguu -> class 9/10:  "...ameshika kitunguu chekundu." ->
                          "...ameshika kitunguu nyekundu."
vitunguu -> class 9/10:  "...uwezo wa vitunguu vibichi..." ->
                          "...uwezo wa vitunguu mbichi..."
```
BOTH correct on first try. "kitunguu chekundu->nyekundu" was the single
most persistent failure of the entire session (never fully solved by
whole-word injection, prefix-level injection, classifier-derived
directions, alpha sweeps to 1500, or per-noun gradient attribution,
which got closest at rank 1 but only after extensive, specific tuning
in that one case). The rule-based rewrite solves it in one pass, with
zero model forward/backward computation for the rewrite step itself
(the translation is generated completely unsteered), and with no
exposure to the garbage-collapse failure mode that affected nearly
every neuron-level method tried this session.

**Known, honestly-stated limitations of this prototype, not yet
addressed**:
1. The adjacency heuristic (next ~4 words, stop at punctuation) will
   MISS genuine long-distance agreement across clause boundaries (e.g.
   a relative-clause verb agreeing with a noun several clauses back) --
   exactly the case the user's original full "Hewitt tree" idea was
   meant to handle, and exactly why it was deferred rather than
   abandoned.
2. The rewrite dictionary must be extended by hand (verified via
   translation, as done all session) for every new adjective/verb-
   prefix pattern encountered -- it is not automatically complete.
   Words not yet in the dictionary are silently skipped (confirmed:
   chekundu/vibichi produced NO change until explicitly added).
3. Not yet tested on sentences with MULTIPLE nouns needing
   DIFFERENT target classes in the same clause (the "coordination"
   question raised earlier this session, 2026-10-02/03) -- the
   adjacency heuristic as written does not yet guard against
   misattributing an agreement word to the WRONG nearby noun.
4. Only tested on adjective agreement so far, not verb subject-prefix
   or demonstrative agreement, though the dictionary already includes
   verb-prefix mappings (ana/kina/lina/vina) ready to extend to this.

**Verdict**: this is now the most promising, and by far the cheapest,
path to the project's actual deployment goal found this entire
session. It sidesteps every failure mode investigated across dozens of
entries (suppression-not-amplification dynamics, word-pair-specific
gradient requirements, per-class inconsistency, garbage-collapse at
high alpha, the ANIMATE-SG confound) because it does not touch the
model's internals at all -- it only requires (a) a working Swahili
MT system (already have: NLLB), (b) a lightweight agreement-adjacency
heuristic (built, validated on 6/6 cases so far), and (c) a verified
concord dictionary (already mostly built as a side effect of this
session's steering work). The neuron-steering investigation's main
remaining value is as a fallback for cases this heuristic's limitations
(long-distance agreement, multi-noun coordination) cannot reach --
not as the primary mechanism.

**Not yet done, natural next steps in priority order**: (1) extend the
adjacency heuristic to handle verb subject-prefix agreement (dictionary
already has ana/kina/lina/vina ready); (2) test on sentences with
multiple nouns/multiple target classes (the coordination case); (3)
test on a LARGER, more varied set of real sentences to find the actual
failure rate of the simple adjacency heuristic (how often does genuine
long-distance agreement actually occur in realistic text?) before
deciding whether the learned-tree version is worth pursuing despite the
missing-treebank problem (e.g. via synthetic/silver-standard Swahili
dependency data, or a different proxy signal).

Files: `nllb_swahili_rule_based_rewrite_prototype.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (continued) — Structural probe validated: cross-lingual transfer to real Swahili gold data beats both Spanish and Finnish

Following up the English->Spanish/Finnish cross-lingual validation
(previous entries) and CLAUDE.md's Stage C (which names Steimel &
Kuebler 2023's SWH_UDT as preferred training data): found and
confirmed this resource is LIVE (git.steimel.info/ksteimel/SWH_UDT),
with REAL, human-annotated Swahili CoNLL-U data (GlobalVoices news
sentences, standard UD format, noun-class features already annotated
per-token) under `data/global_voices/Anno/` -- downloaded 175
sentences (145 length-8-30 + 30 length-20-50).

**Scripts**: `nllb_structural_probe_crosslingual_check.py` (English/
Spanish/Finnish cross-lingual check, with the critical scale-mismatch
fix -- see below), `nllb_structural_probe_swahili_apply.py`
(qualitative check on 4 hand-picked Swahili sentences, superseded by
the quantified version), `nllb_structural_probe_swahili_gold_eval.py`
(real, quantified Swahili evaluation).

**Critical bug found and fixed before any of these numbers were
trustworthy**: `structural_probe.py`'s documented default (lr=1e-4)
was calibrated for "BERT-scale embedding norms (~20-25)" per its own
history comment -- but NLLB's RAW encoder hidden states run far
larger (confirmed directly: layer-12 mean norm ~1766, up to ~12,700).
Training with the unmodified default produced a probe that
underperformed a RANDOM, UNTRAINED control on ALL THREE languages
tested (English in-sample: 0.078 vs 0.115 random; a probe doing WORSE
than random on its own training language is a clear bug signal, not
noise). Fixed by rescaling every token embedding to a fixed target
norm (20.0) before training/eval -- after the fix, English in-sample
jumped to DSpr=+0.922, UUAS=0.816 (comparable to or better than Hewitt
& Manning's own published BERT numbers), confirming the extraction/
alignment/training pipeline is sound once the scale mismatch is
corrected.

**Cross-lingual transfer, English-trained probe (zero target-language
data) evaluated frozen on each language's own real gold trees**:
```
English (in-sample):          DSpr=+0.922  UUAS=0.816
Spanish (Indo-European):      DSpr=+0.546  UUAS=0.419   (random: 0.181 / 0.307)
Finnish (non-Indo-European):  DSpr=+0.495  UUAS=0.479   (random: 0.252 / 0.326)
Swahili (REAL gold, n=175):   DSpr=+0.587  UUAS=0.499   (random: 0.264 / 0.354)
```
Swahili transfer is AT LEAST AS STRONG AS, arguably stronger than,
both the Indo-European sanity check and the non-Indo-European stress
test -- on real, human-annotated dependency trees, not a hand-picked
example. This directly answers the user's original question (would a
probe trained on English, validated first on a typologically distant
language, transfer usefully to Swahili) with a real, quantified yes.

**Swahili-specific probe vs. English-transfer, head-to-head on the
SAME held-out Swahili test split (n=35)**:
```
Probe trained DIRECTLY on 140 Swahili sentences: DSpr=+0.568  UUAS=0.464
Probe trained on 373 English sentences (zero Swahili): DSpr=+0.599  UUAS=0.492
```
The English-trained probe slightly OUTPERFORMS the one trained
directly on Swahili -- almost certainly because 140 sentences is too
few to train a good probe from scratch (the English probe itself
needed ~373 sentences to reach strong performance). Practical
implication: the available real Swahili gold data (175 sentences) is
more valuable as an EVALUATION set than as training data on its own at
this scale; cross-lingual transfer from the much larger English
treebank is currently the stronger practical choice for Stage C.

**Qualitative spot-check (before the quantified gold-data check,
still useful as a sanity confirmation on hand-picked examples)**:
applied the frozen, English-trained probe to 4 Swahili sentences
including the user's own hard test case, "Kijana alikiokota kikombe"
(fused subject+object verb morphology -- a-...-ki-... = class-1
subject prefix "a-" for Kijana + class-7 object infix "-ki-" for
kikombe). Predicted root = alikiokota (the verb, correct); predicted
edges = Kijana--alikiokota (subject-verb, correct) and alikiokota--
kikombe (verb-object, correct) -- the probe correctly separated the
morphologically fused subject+object agreement using only NLLB's own
contextual signal, no Swahili training data at all. 3 of 4 test
sentences were essentially correct or had only one minor
mis-attachment; see conversation for full per-sentence detail.

**Important scope clarification, raised directly by the user and
confirmed by direct tokenization check**: the tree is built at the
WORD level, not subword/morpheme level -- "alikiokota" is ONE node
(its 3 subwords, confirmed via tokenization to be `['_ali','ki',
'okota']`, are mean-pooled into one vector). NLLB's own BPE split
happens to isolate the object-marker "ki" as its own subword here, but
does NOT separate the subject-prefix "a-" from the tense-marker "-li-"
(both fused into one "ali" piece) -- so tokenization only PARTIALLY,
coincidentally overlaps with true morpheme boundaries, and cannot be
relied on for full morphological segmentation. The word-level tree
tells us WHICH NOUNS relate to a verb and via WHICH RELATION TYPE
(nsubj vs obj, directly useful) but NOT which part of the verb's
surface form to rewrite for a given relation -- that still requires a
separate, rule-based Swahili verb-template model (subject-prefix +
tense + [object-infix] + root, fixed order) mapping relation-type to
surface position, exactly the gap CLAUDE.md's Stage D ("relation
probe... decide morpheme-level training targets") already names as
separate, not-yet-done work.

**Verdict**: Stage C's gate looks clearable with real evidence now,
not just a hand-picked example. The practical plan going forward:
(1) use the English-trained probe (373 sentences, cross-lingual
transfer) as the production structural probe rather than training
directly on the small Swahili gold set; (2) reserve the 175 real
Swahili sentences for evaluation/validation, exactly as just done;
(3) the remaining, separate problem (word-level tree -> morpheme-level
rewrite target) is Stage D/E's job, not something the structural probe
itself can solve.

**Not yet done**: Autoanno/ (the much larger, 43MB auto/rule-annotated
silver corpus in the same repo) was found but not yet used -- could
provide more Swahili-specific training volume if the English-transfer
approach needs improving later; a proper layer sweep (only layer 12
tested) per CLAUDE.md Stage C's own stated plan; the context-stability
check (sentence-alone vs. sentence-in-paragraph) also named in Stage C
but not yet run.

Files: `nllb_structural_probe_crosslingual_check.py`,
`nllb_structural_probe_swahili_apply.py`,
`nllb_structural_probe_swahili_gold_eval.py` (all new);
`Conlu/es_ancora-ud-{train,dev}.conllu`, `Conlu/fi_tdt-ud-{train,dev}.
conllu`, `Conlu/swahili_udt/GlobalVoices.ken.sw.{8_30,20_50}.filtered.
conllu` (new downloaded data).

## 2026-10-05 (cont.): raw NLLB-token (no pooling) probe distances -- object-marker signal mostly explained by word order, not morphology

Follow-up on the same-day "Not good enough, we need a tree that works
on the morpheme level" directive. Before building a from-scratch rule-
based Swahili verb segmenter (checked: SALAMA's parser was never
publicly released; Lipp 2011's XSMA has no available source/rules,
only the descriptive paper; `ksteimel/SwahiliMorphemeTagging` is an ML
classifier trained FROM XSMA's silver output, not a usable segmenter
itself -- none of the three external options are viable), tested
whether the English-trained structural probe, applied directly to RAW
NLLB subword tokens (no word-pooling) instead of word-level vectors,
already carries usable morpheme-level signal on its own.

**Single-sentence check** (`nllb_structural_probe_token_level_check.py`,
"Kijana alikiokota kikombe." -> pieces `_Ki jana _ali ki okota _kik
ombe .`): within-word BPE pieces are reliably each other's nearest
neighbours (e.g. d(_ana,imba)=1.21 in a different sentence). The
object-marker piece 'ki' sits closer to 'kikombe' (object) than to
'kijana' (subject): d(ki,kikombe) min 2.72 vs d(ki,kijana) min 3.26 --
right direction. But '_ali' (subject-prefix+tense fused) was, counter
to expectation, ALSO closer to 'kikombe' (2.42) than to 'kijana'
(3.10) -- wrong direction for a subject-agreement reading. Flagged
explicitly as n=1, not a result.

**Generalization across the real Swahili gold set**
(`nllb_morpheme_distance_object_subject_check.py`, SWH_UDT, 175
sentences): found 63 (verb, nsubj-NOUN, obj-NOUN) triples; 2 verbs are
single-BPE-piece (skipped), 0 alignment failures; n=61 usable multi-
piece verbs. Object-closer rate by piece position (Wilson 95% CI):
  - first piece:  n=61  rate=0.574  [0.449, 0.690]  -- NOT distinguishable from chance
  - middle piece: n=37  rate=0.784  [0.628, 0.886]
  - last piece:   n=61  rate=0.836  [0.724, 0.908]
So the single-example 'ki'-closer-to-object pattern partially
generalizes (middle/last pieces lean object), but the first-piece
subject-agreement reading does NOT replicate -- it's noise.

**Confound check (the important part)**: Swahili is SVO, so a
multi-piece verb sits physically between its subject (before) and
object (after) in the raw token stream -- "later piece closer to
object" could be pure linear-adjacency, nothing to do with agreement.
Stratified the same 61-verb sample by whether raw NLLB-token POSITION
distance alone already favors the object or the subject:
  - pieces where position favors object: n=125  probe object-closer rate=0.768  [0.687, 0.833]
  - pieces where position favors subject: n=34  probe object-closer rate=0.559  [0.395, 0.711]
When position does NOT favor the object, the probe's "object-closer"
rate collapses to within noise of chance. **Conclusion: the apparent
middle/last-piece object-marker signal is mostly a linear-position
artifact of SVO word order, not evidence that raw-token probe
distances recover real morpheme-level agreement structure.** This
downgrades (does not retract outright -- CI at n=34 is wide, a real
but weaker residual effect isn't ruled out) the earlier single-example
finding reported in the same day's "word-level tree is correct but
insufficient" entry.

**What this means for the morpheme-level-tree task**: raw NLLB subword
distances from a word-level-trained probe are not, on their own, a
reliable route to morpheme-level agreement-target identification.
Confirms (rather than undercuts) the standing plan: the word-level
tree supplies relation TYPE (nsubj/obj/amod/etc., CLAUDE.md pipeline
step 4) and a SEPARATE, explicit Swahili verb-template model (subject-
prefix + tense + [object-infix] + root, fixed order; concord prefixes
for adjectives/demonstratives already partly verified via
`CONCORD_REWRITE`) is still needed to map relation type -> surface
morpheme slot. This is CLAUDE.md Stage D's open problem, not yet
started; no shortcut via raw-token probe distances available.

**Not yet done**: re-run the same confound-stratified check restricted
to VERB-INITIAL or object-fronted sentences (if any exist in the 175-
sentence set) to see whether the residual signal in the
position-favors-subject stratum (n=34, rate 0.559) is more than noise
once position is fully disentangled from dependency structure, rather
than just partially controlled for as done here.

Files: `nllb_structural_probe_token_level_check.py`,
`nllb_morpheme_distance_object_subject_check.py` (both new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 2): hand-set morpheme-distance "mini-benchmark" -- trains to 100% in-sample, does NOT generalize (negative result)

User's proposal, directly tested: not a full treebank, just a small
set of hand-built Swahili sentences with REAL NLLB tokenization and
hand-specified target distances for the pairs we have a linguistic
reason to supervise (does this verb-internal BPE piece carry subject
or object agreement), training a Hewitt & Manning-style linear probe
(`StructuralProbe`) directly against those targets instead of a full
gold tree. `swahili_morpheme_distance_benchmark.py` (new).

**Setup**: 10 train + 10 held-out test sentences, SUBJ-VERB-OBJ, all
forms verified by direct NLLB translation before encoding (incl. the
class-1 object marker `-m-`/`-mw-`, confirmed distinct from the class-1
subject prefix `a-` -- conflating them would have silently mislabeled
every class-1-object sentence). Role labels (SUBJ/TENSE/OBJ/ROOT) are
assigned to each NLLB BPE piece automatically, by overlapping known
morpheme character-spans with each piece's character span within the
word (not hand-typed per piece -- removes a class of labeling error).
Target-pair rule: piece carries SUBJ only -> d(piece,subject)=1,
d(piece,object)=3; OBJ only -> reversed; pure ROOT -> d=1 to both
(matches real UD convention that nsubj/obj are both distance-1 from
their verb head); pure TENSE or ambiguous -> left unsupervised.
Test sentences reuse the same patterns with different nouns/one new
verb root (`-kumbuka`), so eval checks generalization, not memorization.

**First attempt used lr=1e-3 and produced a non-converging, oscillating
loss** (0.81->0.91->0.73->0.58->0.64 across 300 epochs) -- this is
exactly the failure mode `structural_probe.py`'s own docstring already
documents from this project's earlier history ("lr=1e-3... caused Adam
to overshoot and oscillate"); re-ran with the documented-safe lr=1e-4
and 2000 epochs, which converged smoothly (loss ~0.05-0.09, stable).

**Results** (Wilson 95% CI; TEST = held-out, the result that matters):
  - hand-trained probe, TRAIN (in-sample): SUBJ n=8 rate=1.000 [0.676,1.000]; OBJ n=12 rate=1.000 [0.757,1.000]
  - hand-trained probe, TEST (held-out):   SUBJ n=7 rate=0.857 [0.487,0.974]; OBJ n=12 rate=0.583 [0.320,0.807]
  - RANDOM untrained probe (rank 32), TEST: SUBJ n=7 rate=1.000 [0.646,1.000]; OBJ n=12 rate=0.750 [0.468,0.911]
  - RAW embeddings, no linear map, TEST:    SUBJ n=7 rate=0.571 [0.250,0.842]; OBJ n=12 rate=0.583 [0.320,0.807]

**Conclusion (negative result, not a success)**: the probe memorizes
the 10 training sentences perfectly but does not transfer to new
words -- on OBJ pieces specifically it ties the chance-level raw-
embedding control (0.583 both) and is clearly worse than even an
untrained random projection (0.750). The random probe's strong SUBJ
score (1.000) is a single seed at n=7 and should not be read as a real
effect without checking across seeds (not done). Raw, untransformed
NLLB geometry does NOT trivially separate subject-agreement from
object-agreement pieces on unseen words (0.571/0.583, indistinguishable
from chance) -- consistent with, and sharpening, the same-day finding
that the earlier apparent object-marker signal on the real gold corpus
was mostly a word-order artifact, not encoded agreement structure.

**What this means for the project**: 10 hand sentences is nowhere near
enough data for a learned probe to recover morpheme-agreement structure
that generalizes -- would need an order of magnitude more hand-labeled
sentences (or a different objective: margin/contrastive loss instead
of exact target distances, heavier regularization, lower rank) before
this route could be trusted. More importantly: the information this
probe is trying to learn (which verb slot marks the object, and its
surface form, for each noun class) is **already fully known and
rule-describable** -- it took direct lookup of regular Swahili verb-
template rules (subject-prefix + tense + [object-marker] + root, fixed
order, well-documented concord table) to hand-build this benchmark's
own supervision in the first place. That argues for building the
explicit rule-based Swahili verb-template segmenter (CLAUDE.md Stage
D's open problem) rather than trying to make a probe discover, from a
handful of examples, a correspondence we can already write down as a
lookup table.

**Not yet done**: average the random-probe control across multiple
seeds (currently one seed, n too small to trust); re-test at
meaningfully larger train-set scale (50-100+ hand sentences) before
concluding hand-supervision categorically doesn't work, vs. just
doesn't work at n=10; margin/contrastive-loss variant.

Files: `swahili_morpheme_distance_benchmark.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 3): encoder ATTENTION heads (not MLP, not embedding distance) -- a real, position-confound-surviving object-agreement signal

User's directive: "Instead of checking MLP maybe we can check
attention mechanism?" All prior steering work this session hooked
decoder layer22 FFN activations (the MLP sublayer); this checks
NLLB's encoder SELF-ATTENTION instead -- does any (layer, head)
already attend, with zero training, from an agreement-marking verb
piece to its correct controller noun? New: `nllb_attention_agreement_
check.py` (scan), `nllb_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py` (external
validation).

**Scan on the 20 hand-built, translation-verified benchmark sentences**
(same sentences as the just-logged failed probe-training attempt;
NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B encoder = 24 layers x 16 heads = 384 combos,
`attn_implementation="eager"` required -- the sdpa default silently
cannot return attention weights at all, raises IndexError on
`out.attentions`, not a soft failure): mean win-rate across all 384
heads combined = 0.567 (chance = 0.500, so attention carries signal on
average). Top head **L2H12**: combined SUBJ+OBJ win-rate 0.974 (38/39),
split-half consistent (TRAIN n=20 rate=0.950, TEST n=19 rate=1.000),
and balanced across roles (SUBJ n=15 rate=0.933, OBJ n=24 rate=1.000 --
not just one skewed role). Several other early-layer heads similarly
strong and split-half-consistent: L1H11 (0.923), L2H9 (0.923), L1H2
(0.872, OBJ-dominated), L3H12 (0.846), L5H10 (0.821). With 384
comparisons at n=39, a 38/39 result is still astronomically below any
reasonable significance threshold even after correction.

**External validation on the REAL Swahili UD gold corpus** (SWH_UDT,
175 sentences, same 63 (verb,nsubj-NOUN,obj-NOUN) triples as the
2026-10-05 embedding-distance check): bucketed by verb-piece position
(first/middle/last, since gold text has no hand-labeled morpheme
roles) and re-applied the SAME SVO-position-confound control that
fully explained away the earlier embedding-distance finding.
  - last-piece object-attends rate, all 6 heads: 0.951-1.000 (n=61)
  - **position-confound control, the critical number**: restricted to
    pieces where raw token position favors the SUBJECT (i.e. where
    pure linear proximity predicts "should attend to subject"), n=34:
      L2H12 0.676 [0.508,0.809]; L1H11 0.676 [0.508,0.809];
      L2H9 0.706 [0.538,0.832]; L1H2 0.794 [0.632,0.897];
      L3H12 0.735 [0.569,0.854]; L5H10 0.706 [0.538,0.832]
    **All six CIs sit clearly above 0.5** -- unlike the embedding-
    distance check, where the equivalent control (object-closer rate
    in the position-favors-subject stratum) was 0.559 [0.395,0.711],
    indistinguishable from chance. These attention heads are picking
    up something beyond linear word-order proximity.

**Read**: this is the first finding this session that (a) is strong on
a hand-built set, (b) replicates on real, naturally-occurring text,
AND (c) survives a confound control designed specifically to kill
spurious position-driven effects. It is a qualitatively different,
more promising signal than either the raw-embedding-distance route
(killed by the same confound) or the hand-trained probe route
(overfit at n=10, didn't generalize past memorization). Mechanistically
plausible too: attention is literally the mechanism by which one token
can read from another, so a head specializing in verb-argument binding
is a much more natural place for this information to live than a
generic linear subspace of the residual stream.

**Caveats, not yet resolved**: (1) gold-corpus validation only checked
the SUBJ-vs-OBJ binary via piece POSITION bucket, not hand-verified
morpheme roles (no gold morpheme labels exist for real text) -- a
"first piece" bucket result is still a position proxy, not a verified
SUBJ-marker check, same limitation flagged in the earlier embedding
check. (2) Both corpora are narrow: the hand-built set uses 3 verb
roots and 4 noun classes; the gold corpus is GlobalVoices news text
only, n=63 triples. (3) Have not yet checked whether the SAME heads
(or a parallel set) show an equivalent SUBJECT-attention effect, nor
tested adjective-concord agreement (amod) or other relation types --
only verb nsubj/obj tested so far. (4) attention weight is not the
same as causal effect -- a head attending to the right noun doesn't
by itself prove that information is read out and used downstream;
not yet tested with an ablation/patching check.

**Not yet done**: test the same candidate heads for subject-agreement
specifically (not just the object-vs-subject binary); extend to
amod/det/nmod:poss relations (the adjective/demonstrative/possessive
concord targets the deployment pipeline actually needs, per CLAUDE.md
step 4); causal check (ablate/zero the head, see if downstream
agreement-sensitive behavior changes) rather than relying on attention
weight alone as evidence of use.

Files: `nllb_attention_agreement_check.py`,
`nllb_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py` (both new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 4): bidirectional attention check at scale -- clean division of labor by relation type, both subject-verb AND adjective-concord, >90% at n=15-24 per cell

Direct follow-up to the single-sentence finding that attention is
sharply asymmetric ('Kijana'->'ali' 0.48-0.50 vs 'ali'->'Kijana' ~0).
Built `nllb_attention_bidirectional_check.py`: reuses the existing 20
nsubj/obj sentences unchanged, adds 9 NEW hand-built, translation-
verified adjective-concord (amod) sentences (concord/root forms reused
from the already-verified CONCORD_REWRITE: zuri/kubwa/dogo across
classes 1/7/8/5). For both relation types, measured BOTH attention
directions with a genuine specificity contrast (correct noun/piece vs.
the OTHER noun/piece in the same sentence), at the 6 candidate heads
found in the earlier 384-head scan.

**Result -- a clean, consistent division of labor by relation type**
(Wilson 95% CI; n=15 SUBJ / n=24 OBJ for verbs, n=16 for amod, pooled
over all sentences x all 6 heads' own per-head counts):
  - SUBJECT agreement (nsubj): reliable direction is NOUN -> PIECE
    (the subject noun attends to its verb's subject/tense piece).
    Rate = 1.000 [0.796,1.000] at 5/6 heads, 0.867 at the 6th (L5H10).
    The reverse (piece -> noun) is weaker and head-dependent: 0.600-
    0.933, degrading at the weaker heads.
  - OBJECT agreement (obj): reliable direction is PIECE -> NOUN (the
    object-marker piece attends to the object noun). Rate = 0.958-
    1.000 across all 6 heads. The reverse (noun -> piece) is not just
    weak but BELOW CHANCE at most heads (0.125-0.417) -- the object
    noun systematically prefers attending to something else (almost
    certainly the subject-side piece) over its own marker.
  - ADJECTIVE CONCORD (amod): matches the SUBJECT pattern exactly.
    Reliable direction is NOUN -> PIECE: 1.000 at 5/6 heads, 0.938 at
    the 6th. The reverse (piece -> noun) is weak/inconsistent: 0.250-
    0.562, several below chance.

**Read**: this is not "attention is generally informative" -- it is a
SPECIFIC, right-direction-dependent signal that is >90% reliable at
every head tested, for two independent relation types, each with its
own correct direction. Checking the WRONG direction for a relation
(e.g. piece->noun for subject agreement) gives mediocre-to-useless
results; checking the RIGHT direction gives near-ceiling reliability.
This explains why the original single-direction scan
(`nllb_attention_agreement_check.py`) found SUBJ noticeably weaker
than OBJ (93.3% vs 100% combined) -- it was only measuring the piece-
>noun direction, which is the WRONG direction for SUBJ specifically.

**Practical protocol this suggests** for morpheme-level agreement-
target identification (zero-shot, no training): for subject-agreement
and adjective-concord pieces, read off which NOUN attends most to a
given candidate piece; for object-agreement pieces, read off which
piece a given NOUN'S OBJECT MARKER attends to. Direction matters more
than which specific head you pick, among the 6 candidates.

**Not yet done / caveats**: (1) the amod sentences and the noun->piece
SUBJ direction have NOT yet been checked against the real gold corpus
(only the original piece->noun OBJ direction was externally validated
there, in the earlier position-confound check) -- needed before fully
trusting this past the hand-built set. (2) position-confound control
not yet re-run for amod or for the noun->piece direction specifically
-- though the sharp direction-dependent split itself is some evidence
against a pure generic-adjacency story (a pure position artifact
should not care about direction this cleanly). (3) still only 4 noun
classes (1/5/7/8) and 3 adjective roots (zuri/kubwa/dogo) covered.

Files: `nllb_attention_bidirectional_check.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 5): gold-corpus validation of the bidirectional finding -- 2 of 3 directions survive, SUBJ noun->piece does NOT

Extended `nllb_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py` (added
`validate_verb`'s reverse direction, `validate_amod`) to externally
validate the two untested legs of the bidirectional finding (cont. 4):
SUBJ noun->piece, and AMOD noun->piece, both against real SWH_UDT text
with position-confound stratification (same discipline as the already-
validated OBJ piece->noun check).

**AMOD noun->piece (head noun attends to its adjective's concord piece
more than a distractor noun does): confirmed, robustly.** 68 real
(adj, head-noun, distractor-noun) triples (51 single-piece adjectives
skipped, n too small to split). first/last bucket rates 0.824-1.000
across all 6 heads. Position-confound control, adversarial stratum
(distractor noun positionally CLOSER than the true head noun, n=8):
**0.750-1.000 across all 6 heads** -- survives cleanly, the strongest-
validated direction found so far.

**SUBJ noun->piece (subject noun attends to its verb piece more than
the object noun does): does NOT clearly survive.** Raw bucketed rates
looked reasonable (first/middle 0.557-0.892 across heads). But
position-confound control, adversarial stratum (OBJECT positionally
closer than the SUBJECT, n=125): **0.384-0.568 across all 6 heads,
every CI straddling or sitting at chance.** The dramatic single-
sentence result ('Kijana'->'ali' 0.48-0.50) does not replicate once
position is properly controlled on real, more complex text -- same
failure mode as the original embedding-distance check (cont. 1):
looked strong on a short, convenient example, collapses under the
confound that actually matters.

**Corrected picture (3 relation/direction pairs tested, real text,
position-controlled)**:
  - OBJECT agreement, piece->noun: SURVIVES (0.676-0.794 adversarial)
  - ADJECTIVE CONCORD, noun->piece: SURVIVES, most strongly (0.750-1.000 adversarial)
  - SUBJECT agreement, noun->piece: DOES NOT SURVIVE (0.384-0.568 adversarial, chance)

**Read**: do not generalize from the hand-built benchmark's SUBJ
numbers to real text -- that direction's apparent reliability was
mostly a product of the benchmark's own short, simple sentence
structure, not a property of the mechanism. Two directions remain
genuinely validated and usable without training: verb OBJECT marking
(read off which noun the marker piece attends to) and ADJECTIVE
CONCORD (read off which noun attends most to the concord piece).
Subject agreement still has no validated zero-shot attention signal;
falls back to the rule-based verb-template approach for that relation
until/unless a different signal is found.

Files: `nllb_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py` (extended, not forked).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 6): paragraph-context check -- the validated signals (OBJ piece->noun, AMOD noun->piece) are unaffected by surrounding context

User's directive: "work with longer pieces of text so that we see how
well it holds across paragraphs" -- CLAUDE.md Stage C's open "context-
stability check" (sentence alone vs. inside a paragraph), now done for
attention (not yet done for the structural probe). New:
`nllb_attention_paragraph_context_check.py`. Reuses the same 20 verb +
9 amod hand-built sentences unchanged, grouped into paragraphs (5
paragraphs of 4 verb-sentences; 3 paragraphs of 3 amod-sentences) and
re-encoded as continuous multi-sentence text instead of isolated
single sentences -- same words, same roles, same heads, only the
surrounding context changes.

Implementation bug caught and fixed before trusting any number: the
per-word alignment walk (reused unchanged from every earlier script)
assumes a sentence's trailing '.' is the harmless, unconsumed LAST
token -- true in isolation, but inside a paragraph each sentence's '.'
sits BETWEEN two sentences' words and silently desyncs every
downstream word span. Confirmed directly (not assumed) that '.'
always tokenizes as exactly one isolated BPE piece, mid-paragraph
included, then fixed by giving each sentence's period its own
placeholder entry in the word list.

**Result: paragraph context changes essentially nothing.** Comparing
directly to the isolated-sentence numbers already logged (cont. 4):
  - VERB OBJ piece->noun: 0.958-1.000 isolated -> 0.958-1.000 paragraph (identical)
  - VERB SUBJ noun->piece: 0.867-1.000 isolated -> 1.000-1.000 paragraph (if anything tighter)
  - AMOD noun->piece: 0.938-1.000 isolated -> **1.000 at all 6 heads** in paragraph context
  - The already-unreliable directions (VERB SUBJ piece->noun, VERB OBJ
    noun->piece, AMOD piece->noun) stay unreliable in paragraphs too,
    same pattern, no change.

**Caveat, important**: this is the hand-built benchmark, not gold
text. The SUBJ noun->piece number looking perfect in BOTH isolated and
paragraph settings here does NOT contradict cont. 5's finding that
this exact direction fails the position-confound control on real gold
corpus text (chance-level, 0.384-0.568) -- it just means the hand-
built sentences' own (likely still position-confounded) version of
the effect is stable across context length, not that the underlying
signal is suddenly trustworthy. For the two directions that DID pass
gold-corpus validation (OBJ piece->noun, AMOD noun->piece), this is
unambiguously good news: whatever these heads are doing, it is not
disrupted by longer, more realistic surrounding text.

Files: `nllb_attention_paragraph_context_check.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 7): correction -- OBJ piece->noun "survives position confound" is real but tiny; dominant attention is trivial same-word adjacency, not cross-sentence object-tracking

Direct follow-up to the user's question "where is the attention for
the subject pieces coming from if not the subject" -- answer, checked
directly: a "previous-token head" (attends almost unconditionally to
whatever token sits at position i-1, regardless of content -- in three
real examples this was the tail of an unrelated proper-noun compound,
a closing parenthesis, and a quote mark, never the actual subject).
This fully explains why that direction failed the position-confound
control (cont. 5): subject-identity and "immediately preceding token"
only coincide by construction in short hand-built sentences.

Asked to run the SAME direct check on the OBJ piece->noun direction
(the one direction that DID pass its confound control), since a
head/column inspection, not just the aggregate stratified rate, is the
only way to know what is actually driving a result. Found: **the same
kind of overwhelming low-level attention sink exists here too**, but
pointing WITHIN THE VERB WORD rather than to the preceding token --
90-99% of a verb piece's outgoing attention goes to its OWN next
subword piece (e.g. '_wana'->'zi', '_alit'->'embelea', '_kuk'->'osa',
all literally the next BPE piece of the same multi-piece verb), not to
either noun. Checked 6 real gold-corpus instances in the adversarial
stratum (piece positioned nearer the SUBJECT than the object) across
3 heads (18 cells): split exactly 9 SUBJ-wins / 9 OBJ-wins -- a coin
flip at this sample size, with several cells comparing two values that
round to 0.0000 at 4 decimal places (e.g. L2H12 on "Wanaharakati ...
wanaziomba ...": top target 'zi' at 0.991, mean_to_subj=0.0000,
mean_to_obj=0.0000, "SUBJ wins" by an unmeasurable margin).

**This does not retract the cont. 5 finding** -- the full n=34/n=125
aggregate statistics (Wilson CI excluding 0.5) are still a real,
above-chance signal, not noise; a 6-example spot check is far too
small to override that. But it DOES correct how that finding should be
weighted: the subject/object comparison lives in a tiny residual
sliver of attention mass left over after an overwhelming, trivial
same-word-adjacency pattern, not in a clean, dominant "look at the
object noun" signal. Statistically real at the population level is not
the same as reliable on any given sentence -- this is NOT, as currently
understood, a mechanism you could read off confidently per-sentence
for the deployment pipeline; it is at best a weak average tendency.

**Revised practical read**: neither attention direction tested so far
(SUBJ noun->piece: fails position control; OBJ piece->noun: passes
population-level but is a weak signal buried in trivial same-word
adjacency) is strong enough on its own to serve as a reliable, legible,
per-sentence morpheme-target-identification mechanism. AMOD noun->piece
has NOT yet been given this same head/column inspection -- it is the
only one of the three that passed its confound control with large
margins (0.75-1.00 in the adversarial stratum, not 0.68-0.79), so it
is the most likely to be a genuine signal rather than residual noise,
but this has not been directly verified the same way and should be
before trusting it either.

**Not yet done**: the same direct head/column inspection for AMOD
noun->piece, to check whether IT is also mostly trivial adjacency
(e.g. "noun attends to its own immediately-following word") with a
thin real signal on top, or whether it is actually attending
substantially (not just winning a near-zero comparison) to its
concord piece specifically.

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 8): AMOD noun->piece direct inspection -- the one signal that looks genuinely selective, not just a winning noise crumb

Completed the head/column inspection requested for AMOD (the direction
not yet checked in cont. 7). Pulled ALL 8 real adversarial instances
from SWH_UDT (distractor noun positioned closer than the true head
noun -- matches the n=8 from cont. 5's aggregate exactly) and printed
the full mean_head vs mean_distractor attention for each, all 6 heads.

Head-wins out of 8: L2H12 8/8, L1H11 8/8, L1H2 8/8, L2H9 7/8, L5H10 7/8,
L3H12 6/8 -- matches the earlier aggregate rate (0.75-1.00).

**The qualitative difference from the OBJ check (cont. 7) is the
important part.** For OBJ, many "wins" were two values that both
rounded to 0.0000 -- a coin flip. For AMOD, the pattern is different:
the DISTRACTOR is overwhelmingly exactly 0.00000 (not just smaller)
while the HEAD noun gets a small but clearly nonzero value -- e.g.
"jaji mwaminifu ... mtenda": head=0.13387, distractor=0.00000 (L1H2);
"Chuo Kikuu ... Peking": head=0.11844, distractor=0.00000 (L1H11).
Same-word BPE adjacency still absorbs most of the attention budget
(consistent with everything else found today -- this is universal,
not specific to any one relation), but within the small residual that
is NOT consumed by that, the model is doing something that looks
genuinely selective: allocating a real, specific, nonzero amount to
the correct controller noun and reliably suppressing the wrong one to
the floor, rather than arbitrarily favoring whichever of two near-
equal noise values happens to be marginally larger.

**Final, corrected ranking of the three signals tested today**:
  1. AMOD noun->piece: real and selective -- the distractor isn't just
     beaten, it's suppressed to ~zero. Most trustworthy of the three.
  2. OBJ piece->noun: real at the population level (Wilson CI excludes
     chance at n=34/125) but fragile -- frequently two near-zero values
     with no clear winner on any single sentence. Not something to read
     off reliably per-instance.
  3. SUBJ noun->piece: not real -- a previous-token attention-head
     artifact, confirmed by direct inspection (cont. 7) attending to
     whatever token sits immediately before it regardless of identity.
     Collapses to chance under position control (cont. 5).

**Practical implication**: of the two relation types investigated via
attention (verb argument marking, adjective concord), only adjective
concord currently has a signal worth building on without more work.
Object marking's signal is real but too weak/noisy to trust per-
sentence; subject marking has no attention-based signal at all and
should stay on the rule-based verb-template track.

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 9): correction -- "fall back to rules for verb agreement" is NOT a safe, simple plan either; coordination + a translation-verification blind spot

User's challenge, directly on the "Chama tawala cha PPP ... na kile cha PTI ... walilaumu
tukio hili" gold example used throughout cont. 1/5/7/8: "chama" is
class 7; there are TWO of them coordinated with "na"; shouldn't
agreement be plural "vililaumu" (vi-), not "walilaumu" (wa-, human
plural)? Checked directly rather than assumed.

**Finding #1 -- a real methodological gap in this session's own
verification method.** Tested "Chama {ki-/li-/wa-/a-}mefanya vizuri."
(four different, only-one-grammatical subject prefixes on the same
noun): NLLB's SW->EN translation returned the IDENTICAL "The party
has done well." for all four. SW->EN translation, used all session as
the verification tool, is blind to subject-prefix agreement errors --
it only checks gross meaning survives, never whether a specific
morpheme is grammatical. Every claim verified this session via SW->EN
translation should be read as "the gloss is right," never as "the
agreement morphology is right."

**Finding #2 -- coordination agreement has no single obvious answer,
even from the most relevant tool available.** EN->SW generation (the
more informative direction, since Swahili output quality is on the
line) for "The ruling party and the opposition party blamed this
incident" gave: "Chama cha serikali na chama cha upinzani
kilishutumu tukio hilo." -- SINGULAR ki- agreement on a two-party
coordinated subject (possibly closest-conjunct agreement, a real
attested strategy in some Bantu/African languages; possibly just
NLLB being unreliable on this construction -- not distinguished).
That is a THIRD distinct answer, agreeing with neither the gold
corpus's "wa-" nor the user's proposed "vi-". Three sources (gold
text, grammatical reasoning, NLLB's own generation), three different
answers, for what is nominally one construction.

**Read**: this overturns the implicit framing in cont. 8 ("subject/
object marking falls back to the rule-based verb-template approach,"
treated as the safe default once attention failed). A fixed Swahili
concord lookup table handles one simple noun controlling one verb
correctly, but: (a) coordinated-subject resolution (which class does
"NOUN_cl7 na NOUN_cl7" trigger -- plural of that class? closest-
conjunct? something else?) and (b) semantic/animacy-driven class
override (already logged as a durable finding: kipepeo/paka/nyoka
take class-1 concord despite lexical class; "chama" referring to a
group of people may license human wa- agreement the same way) are
BOTH open subproblems a simple table does not solve for free. Neither
the attention route nor the rule-based route is a complete, safe
answer once input goes beyond a single simple noun subject.

**Not yet done**: get an actual native Kitaita/Swahili speaker
judgment on the "Chama...na kile cha PTI walilaumu" sentence
specifically (is wa- acceptable human-collective agreement, a
coordination artifact, or a genuine error in the source article?)
before building ANY verb-template rule that assumes coordination
resolves to a simple plural-of-the-shared-class. Any rule-based
segmenter built next must explicitly flag (not silently guess)
coordinated subjects and known semantic-override nouns, pending that
verification, rather than assuming a default resolution.

## 2026-10-05: SESSION SUMMARY (end-of-session index, see cont. 1-9 above for full detail)

Pivoted this session's track from internal neuron steering (the
previous track -- see earlier entries, now superseded) to morpheme-
level agreement-target identification, driven by the user's directive
that word-level dependency trees are insufficient since morphemes,
not whole words, are the actual steering/rewrite targets. Tried, in
order, with honest retractions where warranted:

1. **Raw NLLB subword probe distances** (word-level-trained structural
   probe applied to individual BPE pieces, no pooling): looked
   promising on one example, DID NOT survive a position-confound
   control at scale on the real gold corpus -- mostly a word-order
   artifact. (cont. 1)
2. **Hand-set morpheme-distance "mini-benchmark"** (train a probe
   directly on 10 hand-labeled sentences' target distances, per the
   user's "not a full treebank, just a distance identifier" proposal):
   trains to 100% in-sample, does NOT generalize past memorization to
   10 held-out sentences -- a clean overfit, genuine negative result.
   (cont. 2)
3. **Encoder attention mechanism** (the user's "check attention
   instead of MLP" pivot): found 6 candidate heads (top: L2H12) with a
   striking, direction-dependent, relation-specific pattern -- subject
   agreement and adjective concord reliable via noun->piece attention,
   object agreement reliable via piece->noun attention, ~90-100% on a
   29-sentence hand-built benchmark, STABLE under paragraph-length
   context. (cont. 3, 4, 6)
4. **External validation on the real 175-sentence Swahili gold
   corpus, with position-confound controls**: only 2 of the 3 signals
   survived. Subject agreement (noun->piece) collapsed to chance --
   direct inspection showed this was a generic "previous-token head"
   (attends to whatever sits one position back, regardless of
   identity), not real agreement tracking; it only looked like subject
   tracking because short hand-built sentences put the subject right
   before the verb by construction. Object agreement (piece->noun)
   is statistically real at the population level but fragile -- direct
   inspection found the dominant pattern is trivial same-word BPE
   reconstruction, with subject/object comparison happening in a thin,
   often near-zero residual. Adjective concord (noun->piece) is the
   one signal that held up under direct inspection as genuinely
   selective -- it reliably suppresses the wrong noun to ~zero even
   when positionally closer, not just "wins" an ambiguous comparison.
   (cont. 5, 7, 8)
5. **User's coordination challenge** (the "Chama...na kile cha PTI
   walilaumu" example): exposed that SW->EN translation, this
   session's main verification tool throughout, is blind to agreement
   errors (translates 4 different, only-one-correct subject-prefix
   variants identically); and that coordinated-subject agreement
   resolution has no single obvious answer even from NLLB's own EN->SW
   generation (gave a THIRD different answer from both the gold text
   and the user's proposed rule). This overturns the assumption that
   "fall back to rule-based verb templates" is a safe, simple default
   for everything attention can't handle -- rules have their own real
   gaps (coordination, semantic/animacy class override) requiring
   native-speaker input, not just a fixed lookup table. (cont. 9)

**Net state going into the next session**: one validated, zero-shot,
training-free, context-robust mechanism exists -- adjective-concord
agreement via noun->piece attention at heads L2H12/L1H11/L1H2 (and to
a lesser extent L2H9/L3H12/L5H10). Nothing currently validated for
subject or object verb agreement; the planned rule-based fallback for
those needs to explicitly flag (not silently resolve) coordinated
subjects and known animacy-override nouns pending native-speaker
verification, rather than being treated as an automatically-safe
default. SW->EN translation checks done THIS session and in prior
sessions should be re-read as gloss-correctness checks only, not
morphology-correctness checks.

**Immediate next steps** (not yet started): (a) get native-speaker
judgment on the coordination/animacy-override question before writing
any verb-template agreement rule; (b) decide whether to extend the
concord-attention approach to other agreement-bearing relations
