## 2026-10-05 (cont. 10): encoder-decoder CROSS-attention tested as a second, independent mechanism for verb subject/object agreement -- fails the position-confound control the same way encoder self-attention's SUBJ direction did

New session, continuing same date. User's directive: encoder self-
attention gave exactly one validated signal (AMOD/adjective concord);
nothing validated for verb subject/object agreement, and rule-based
verb templates look like they'll accumulate too many edge cases
(coordination, animacy override, cont. 9) to be a safe default. Rather
than build the rule-based segmenter next, check a genuinely DIFFERENT
part of NLLB's architecture for a verb-agreement signal before falling
back to rules: encoder-DECODER cross-attention, not encoder self-
attention.

**Mechanism**: force NLLB to "translate" a Swahili sentence into
itself (src_lang = tgt_lang = swh_Latn, target text = source text,
teacher-forced via `decoder_input_ids = shift_tokens_right(labels, ...)`
with `transformers.models.m2m_100.modeling_m2m_100.shift_tokens_right`),
then read `output.cross_attentions` at the decoder row that produces
each verb piece. Checked and confirmed directly before trusting any
downstream number (not assumed): under this SRC==TGT setup, the
tokenized `labels` sequence is byte-identical to the encoder's
`input_ids` sequence (same text, same lang code, same tokenizer), so
cross-attention row i (query = decoder position producing `labels[i]`)
and the encoder's column positions can both be indexed with the SAME
word spans already used for self-attention -- no separate decoder-side
alignment walk needed. `tgt_lang` must be set as a tokenizer
**attribute** (`tokenizer.tgt_lang = ...`), not passed as a kwarg to
`__call__` -- passing it as a kwarg silently used the tokenizer's
default (`eng_Latn`) instead, caught by checking the decoded
`decoder_input_ids` tokens before relying on it (an easy, silent
correctness bug specific to this tokenizer, worth remembering as its
own lesson).

**Step 1 -- hand-built benchmark (`nllb_cross_attention_agreement_check.py`)**,
same 20 sentences / same train-test split / same automatic role
assignment as the self-attention script, unchanged (hard rule #10):
swept all 24 decoder layers x 16 heads = 384 combos. Found several
heads at 90-100% combined SUBJ+OBJ win-rate, train/test CONSISTENT --
top three: L12H15 (0.974), L12H11 (0.949), L15H7 (0.949), each doing
well on BOTH roles separately (not just a skewed base rate), with
comparatively low "trivial self-identity" attention (the piece
attending mostly to its own encoder-side span rather than either noun)
at these three heads specifically (0.28-0.44) versus other top-15
heads with that confound much higher (0.72-1.00).

**Step 2 -- gold corpus + position-confound control
(`nllb_cross_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py`)**, same SWH_UDT 175
sentences, same confound-control design as
`nllb_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py`: does raw token-position
proximity (Swahili SVO puts the object right after the verb) already
explain the apparent effect? Tested the top 6 candidates
(L12H11, L15H7, L12H15, L11H8, L9H5, L10H12) on n=63 real
(verb, nsubj-NOUN, obj-NOUN) triples (n=125 non-adversarial
pieces where the object IS positionally nearer; n=34 adversarial
pieces where the subject is positionally nearer instead).

**Result: fails, clearly, for all 6 heads.** In the non-adversarial
stratum all 6 heads look strong (object-attends rate 0.77-0.84). In
the ADVERSARIAL stratum -- the one that actually tests whether the
head tracks the true grammatical object independent of word order --
the object-attends rate does not just drop toward chance, it
**inverts below 0.5** for every single candidate: L12H11 0.441
[0.289,0.605], L15H7 0.324 [0.191,0.492], L12H15 0.382 [0.239,0.550],
L11H8 0.353 [0.215,0.521], L9H5 0.353 [0.215,0.521], L10H12 0.471
[0.315,0.633]. A real, position-independent object-tracking signal
should stay well above 0.5 in this stratum (c.f. AMOD's 0.75-1.00,
cont. 5/8); dropping below 0.5 consistently across every candidate
means the "win" in the easy stratum was explained by word-order
locality, not grammatical-role tracking -- the SAME failure mode
already diagnosed for self-attention's SUBJ noun->piece direction
(cont. 5/7, the "previous-token head" artifact), now showing up via a
completely different mechanism (cross-attention) and on the opposite
grammatical role (object).

**Step 3 -- direct inspection (`nllb_cross_attention_adversarial_inspection.py`)**,
same kind of qualitative check as cont. 7/8, run on L12H11's real
adversarial-stratum examples to see WHY, not just THAT. **Caught and
fixed a bug in the first draft before trusting it**: the filter
condition for "adversarial case: subject nearer by position" was
written inverted (`if tok_dist_obj >= tok_dist_subj: continue`, which
actually keeps the EASY/non-adversarial cases -- confirmed by the
printed count matching the non-adversarial n=125 exactly) -- fixed to
`if tok_dist_subj >= tok_dist_obj: continue` and re-run (counts differ
slightly from Step 2's n=34, 22 vs 34, because this script excludes
exact-distance ties that Step 2's `else`-branch folds into
"position_favors_subj" -- noted, not worth chasing further for a
qualitative check). Of the 22 adversarial pieces printed, the winner
matches whichever noun is positionally closer in 16/22 (73%) --
i.e. SUBJ wins most of the adversarial stratum simply because it's now
the nearer word, not because the head identifies it as the subject.
Also confirms the aggregate "self-dominant" statistic qualitatively:
attention to the verb's OWN encoder span is frequently the largest of
the three values (e.g. 0.157, 0.115, 0.071, 0.055, 0.053, 0.047 in
several rows) -- most attention mass never reaches either noun at all,
and the subj/obj comparison happens in whatever thin residual is left,
which is where the locality artifact lives.

**Conclusion**: cross-attention does not provide a validated,
position-independent verb subject/object agreement signal either.
This closes off a second, architecturally distinct avenue (after
encoder self-attention) for exactly the two relations (nsubj, obj)
that rule-based templates were going to need to cover -- AMOD/adjective
concord via encoder self-attention (L2H12/L1H11/L1H2) remains the ONLY
validated, zero-shot, training-free mechanism found so far in this
project, for any agreement relation.

**Reinforces an existing lesson, does not add a new one**: a strong
win-rate on the 20-sentence hand-built benchmark (90-100%, train/test
"CONSISTENT") was, again, not sufficient on its own -- short hand-built
sentences conflate grammatical role with linear position by
construction, so any position-sensitive mechanism will look like an
agreement-tracking mechanism there. Every zero-shot signal this project
has found "looking good" on the hand-built set required the same real-
corpus + position-confound step to find out whether it was real
(AMOD: survived; self-attention SUBJ: did not; cross-attention OBJ:
did not).

**Not yet done / open**: whether a PROPERLY trained structural probe
(Hewitt & Manning distance probe + Hewitt & Liang control task +
selectivity, per CLAUDE.md Stage C, on SWH_UDT) would do better than
either raw-attention mechanism tried so far for subject/object
agreement -- this is architecturally different (a trained linear map
over hidden states, not raw attention weights) and has NOT been tried
with full rigor yet; the two earlier attempts that used probes
(cont. 1-2, prior session) were shortcuts (word-level probe on raw
subwords; 10-sentence overfit benchmark) that skipped the control-task/
selectivity step CLAUDE.md actually calls for. With TWO mechanism-based
attention routes now ruled out for nsubj/obj specifically, the
remaining options are: (a) the proper Stage C probe, not yet tried
rigorously; (b) accept rule-based verb templates for nsubj/obj (with
explicit flagging, not silent guessing, for coordination and animacy-
override cases per cont. 9) while attention-based AMOD handles
adjective concord.

Files: `nllb_cross_attention_agreement_check.py` (new),
`nllb_cross_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py` (new),
`nllb_cross_attention_adversarial_inspection.py` (new, one inversion
bug fixed in-session before trusting its output).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 11): the LABELED relation probe (not the distance probe) succeeds at verb subject identification where both attention mechanisms failed -- first validated nsubj/obj signal, selectivity confirmed, object still needs more adversarial data before trusting it the same way

User's directive after cont. 10's negative cross-attention result:
"Go after the proper structural probe next." Before writing any code,
worked out which already-built component this actually means. The
distance/depth probe (`structural_probe.py`, Hewitt & Manning) is
UNLABELED -- it recovers tree GEOMETRY (how many edges apart), not
relation IDENTITY. A verb's nsubj and its obj are both direct
dependents (gold tree distance = 1) in virtually every real sentence,
so an unlabeled distance probe has no way, even in principle, to tell
"this is the subject" from "this is the object" -- that was never
going to solve this problem. The actual missing piece is
`relation_probe.py`: a LABELED relation classifier (nsubj/obj/amod/
det/...) given a (head, dependent) embedding pair, which ALREADY HAS a
proper Hewitt & Liang (2019) control task built in
(`build_control_labels` -- a fixed random label per (head_form,
dep_form) word-pair TYPE, matching this project's own top-level hard
rule "every probe needs a control task and selectivity"). Checked
directly: grepped the whole project for `relation_probe`/
`RelationProbe`/`find_argmax_candidates` outside its own definition and
`test_probes.py` -- **zero hits**. This component has never been run on
NLLB or on Swahili before this entry.

**Important distinction from every mechanism tried in cont. 3-10**:
this is NOT training-free. It requires the real SWH_UDT gold treebank
(already in use for every gold-corpus validation this project has
done) to train the linear probe. The self-/cross-attention routes
needed zero training; this trades that away for (per the results below)
actually working.

New: `nllb_relation_probe_swahili_gold_eval.py`, reusing
`relation_probe.py`, `structural_probe.py`'s sibling infrastructure,
`conllu_utils.py`, and `nllb_structural_probe_crosslingual_check.py`'s
`extract_embeddings` all unchanged (hard rule #10). NLLB encoder layer
12 (same baseline as `nllb_structural_probe_swahili_gold_eval.py`), all
175 SWH_UDT sentences.

**Part A -- real-vs-control selectivity, standard 80/20 Swahili split
(140 train / 35 test, 701 test head-dependent pairs, 21-label vocab)**:

  REAL    accuracy=0.8245  macro-F1=0.6935
  CONTROL accuracy=0.1384  macro-F1=0.0496
  SELECTIVITY (real - control): accuracy=+0.6862  macro-F1=+0.6438

Per-class F1 on the relations this project actually needs, REAL vs
CONTROL: nsubj 0.790 vs 0.048; obj 0.754 vs 0.000; amod 0.606 vs 0.000;
det 0.809 vs 0.000. The control task collapses to near-zero on every
target class (NOT just low -- the control probe, same architecture,
same embeddings, essentially cannot do this at all), while the real
probe is clearly above a trivial baseline. This is a real, selective
signal, not word-pair-identity memorization -- the first time any
probe/mechanism tried in this project has shown this combination for
nsubj or obj specifically.

**Part B -- head-to-head against the exact position-confound test that
sank both attention mechanisms**, on the SAME (verb, nsubj-NOUN,
obj-NOUN) triples (n=63) used in `nllb_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py`
/ `nllb_cross_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py`. 5-fold CV over
SENTENCES (not triples), so every triple is scored by a probe that
never saw its own sentence during training, while all 175 sentences
contribute training signal across folds. Question: does (verb, TRUE
subj) get labeled "nsubj", and (verb, TRUE obj) get labeled "obj",
stratified by whether the OTHER argument is positionally closer to the
verb (adversarial) or not (easy)?

  SUBJ (correct label = nsubj):
    non-adversarial  n=12  acc=0.917  [95% CI 0.646, 0.985]
    ADVERSARIAL      n=51  acc=0.941  [95% CI 0.841, 0.980]
    COMBINED         n=63  acc=0.937  [95% CI 0.848, 0.975]
  OBJ (correct label = obj):
    non-adversarial  n=61  acc=0.902  [95% CI 0.802, 0.954]
    ADVERSARIAL      n=2   acc=0.500  [95% CI 0.095, 0.905]
    COMBINED         n=63  acc=0.889  [95% CI 0.788, 0.945]

**SUBJ identification clearly survives the position confound** -- in
fact the adversarial stratum (n=51, the MAJORITY of real triples: most
real Swahili subjects have modifiers/relative clauses stretching them
farther from the verb than the object that follows it directly) scores
*higher* than the easy stratum (0.941 vs 0.917), the opposite of what a
locality artifact would produce. This is the exact test that collapsed
self-attention's SUBJ signal to a previous-token-head artifact (cont. 7)
and cross-attention's OBJ signal to a pure distance effect (cont. 10)
-- the relation probe does not show that failure mode.

**OBJ identification cannot be claimed as position-independent yet --
not because it failed, but because there isn't enough data to say
either way.** The adversarial stratum has n=2 (hard rule #5: no
selection or claims on n<8). This small-n problem is a property of the
corpus, not a bug: in real Swahili SVO text the object overwhelmingly
sits closer to the verb than the subject does (same asymmetry seen in
the attention validations' n=125 vs n=34 piece-level split, cont. 10),
so triples where the subject happens to be the CLOSER word are rare.
The non-adversarial OBJ number (0.902, n=61) is good but, on its own,
cannot rule out "this is partly riding on word order" the way the SUBJ
result does.

**Net read**: the labeled relation probe is the first mechanism in
this project to show a real, selective, non-trivial signal for BOTH
nsubj and obj -- succeeding specifically where two independent
training-free attention mechanisms failed under the same adversarial
test. SUBJ is validated to the same standard as AMOD's attention
signal (cont. 8: survives an adversarial position stratum with a
large, real margin). OBJ looks promising (strong non-adversarial
accuracy, real selectivity in Part A) but needs a larger or
differently-constructed adversarial test before being trusted at the
same level -- this project's own rules forbid calling it decided on
n=2.

**Not yet done / open next steps**: (a) get more OBJ-adversarial
coverage -- either a larger Swahili treebank slice, or relax the
"both nsubj and obj co-occur on the same verb" requirement (inherited
unchanged from the attention scripts for comparability) so OBJ can be
tested against ANY positionally-closer distractor noun, not only a
co-occurring subject; (b) this evaluation assumes gold (head,
dependent) PAIRS are already known -- the realistic deployment
pipeline still needs the candidate-shortlisting step
(`relation_probe.find_argmax_candidates`, built but never run, which
uses the distance probe to propose candidate dependents of a verb
before the relation probe labels them) wired up and evaluated
end-to-end, not just this controlled "given the true pair" check;
(c) amod's REAL F1 here (0.606) is well below attention's validated
AMOD signal (near-perfect, suppresses distractor to ~zero, cont. 8) --
the likely right production design is a HYBRID: attention for AMOD,
relation probe for nsubj/obj, not one mechanism for everything.

Files: `nllb_relation_probe_swahili_gold_eval.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 12): applying the ALREADY-TRAINED relation probe to NLLB's own BPE pieces (no rule-based morpheme segmenter) -- near-perfect discrimination, and the winning piece position matches real Swahili morphology without being told to

User's directive, in response to the kijana/alikiokota/kikombe demo's
scope caveat ("this is word-level, not morpheme-level -- locating the
specific subword slot still needs something"): explicitly reject a
rule-based morpheme segmenter as the next step. "Use the tokens of
NLLB to make the judgement/learning... avoid rule based approach until
we have exhausted NLLB's resources... rules might not segment cleanly
into what NLLB has as tokens."

Checked that claim directly before designing anything: NLLB's own BPE
for real gold-corpus verbs does NOT reliably respect Swahili morpheme
boundaries --
  alikiokota  -> ['_ali', 'ki', 'okota']   (a clean a-li | ki | okota)
  alimwamuru  -> ['_alim', 'wam', 'uru']   (NOT clean -- true split is
                                             a-li | mw | amuru)
confirming a hand-written segmenter would fight NLLB's own
tokenization on at least some real words. So: no segmenter. Instead,
added PART C to `nllb_relation_probe_swahili_gold_eval.py` (extended,
not forked -- hard rule #10): apply the SAME relation probe from cont.
11 -- already trained on whole-WORD-pooled vectors, already validated
for selectivity (Part A: +0.69) and position-independence on SUBJ
(Part B) -- directly to NLLB's own INDIVIDUAL BPE pieces of the verb.
No retraining, no new gold labels, no assumption about where a
morpheme "should" start or end -- NLLB's own tokenizer output is the
only thing defining the candidate units. This is a genuine out-of-
distribution generalization test (the probe has never seen a single
raw, un-pooled piece vector during training), reported honestly as
such regardless of outcome. Per-piece vectors rescaled to the same
norm=20 convention as the pooled training vectors (hard rule: "alphas/
scales never transfer... measure the activation norm first").

Same 5-fold CV as Part B (identical fold assignment), same n=63
(verb, nsubj-NOUN, obj-NOUN) triples. For each triple, for every piece
i in the verb's own NLLB tokenization: probe(piece_i, subj_vec) and
probe(piece_i, obj_vec), softmax probabilities for "nsubj" and "obj".
Metric: does the BEST piece's nsubj-probability against the TRUE
subject exceed the BEST piece's nsubj-probability against the
distractor object (symmetrically for obj)? 2/63 triples excluded
(single-piece verbs -- no within-word piece to localize to), n=61.

**Result:**

  SUBJ  COMBINED  n=61  win-rate=1.000  [95% CI 0.941, 1.000]
    winning piece=first   n=33 (54%)  win-rate=1.000
    winning piece=middle  n=12 (20%)  win-rate=1.000
    winning piece=last    n=16 (26%)  win-rate=1.000
  OBJ   COMBINED  n=61  win-rate=0.967  [95% CI 0.888, 0.991]
    winning piece=first   n=24 (39%)  win-rate=0.958
    winning piece=middle  n=12 (20%)  win-rate=1.000
    winning piece=last    n=25 (41%)  win-rate=0.960

Both relations discriminate the true controller from the distractor at
essentially every piece-position bucket -- no "easy" vs "hard" bucket
split the way position confounds did for both attention mechanisms.

**The winning-piece POSITION distribution is the actually interesting
part, since nothing told the model where to look.** The subject signal
concentrates at the verb's FIRST NLLB piece (54%, vs ~33% expected if
uniform across first/middle/last) -- matching real Swahili morphology,
where the subject-agreement prefix (a-/wa-/ki-/...) is word-initial.
The object signal is split roughly evenly between first (39%) and last
(41%), barely favoring middle (20%) -- also broadly consistent with
real morphology (the object marker sits after tense marking, i.e.
later in the word, but NLLB's own BPE boundaries don't always carve
exactly at that point, so "object piece" lands at different NLLB-token
positions depending on how a given verb happens to tokenize). This
pattern emerged purely from applying a probe trained on whole words to
individual pieces and watching where the signal landed -- no morpheme
rule was written or consulted to produce it.

**Caveats, stated plainly**: (a) this is a real out-of-distribution
generalization (pooled-vector-trained probe applied to raw single-piece
vectors) that happened to work far better than the distribution
mismatch alone would predict -- worth stress-testing on more data
before fully trusting the near-100% numbers, same caution this project
has applied to every other strong-looking result; (b) the "win"
metric compares the BEST piece for the true noun against the BEST
piece for the distractor -- these can be (and often are) different
piece positions within the same verb, so this establishes "somewhere
in this word, NLLB's own tokenization carries a piece that discriminates
the true controller," not yet "a single, nameable piece index is always
the right one to rewrite" -- the latter is what reinflection actually
needs and is the natural next check; (c) still 5-fold CV on only 175
sentences total -- the same small-corpus caveat that applies to every
SWH_UDT-based result in this project.

**Net read**: the user's instinct was right and is now checked, not
just argued for -- NLLB's own subword tokens, scored by the already-
validated relation probe with zero rule-writing, localize the
subject/object agreement signal within the verb word far more cleanly
than cont. 1/2's earlier (unlabeled, uncontrolled) attempts at the
same idea, and without needing to resolve NLLB's inconsistent BPE-vs-
morpheme alignment at all.

**Not yet done / open next steps**: (a) pin down, per triple, the
SINGLE best piece index for each role (not just "some piece beats some
piece") and check whether that piece, once identified, is a stable,
nameable target (e.g. "always the first piece for subj" vs "depends on
verb") -- needed before this can drive an actual rewrite; (b) stress
test on more than 175 sentences if a larger Swahili treebank slice can
be found, given how strong these numbers are relative to the small
corpus; (c) the object-adversarial small-n gap from cont. 11 Part B
(n=2) is still open and separate from this finding.

Files: `nllb_relation_probe_swahili_gold_eval.py` (extended with Part C).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 13): qualitative inspection of Part C -- the per-piece signal is NOT a sharp morpheme-level spike; it's the whole verb word knowing its controller nouns at nearly every piece

User's directive: "give me a few examples and the predictions so I can
see what it is doing. Particularly the long examples." New:
`nllb_relation_probe_piece_level_examples.py`, same 5-fold CV / same
triples / same per-piece scoring as cont. 12's Part C unchanged (hard
rule #10), but printing the full per-piece probability table for
individual real sentences instead of aggregating into win-rates.
Sorted by verb piece count and by sentence length (up to 49 words) per
the user's request for long examples.

**Qualitative finding that nuances cont. 12's "100%/96.7% win-rate"
framing**: the true-vs-distractor GAP is consistently large at nearly
every piece (e.g. `waliitisha`/Madaktari/mkutano: P(nsubj|subj)
0.88-0.91 across all 3 pieces vs P(nsubj|obj) 0.04-0.10) -- but the
piece-TO-piece variation for the SAME true noun is usually small (0.88
vs 0.88 vs 0.91 in that example). This pattern repeats across nearly
every long-sentence example pulled. The practical read: NLLB's
bidirectional encoder self-attention means every subword piece of the
verb already has access to the whole sentence, so the controller
noun's identity leaks into essentially ALL of the verb's pieces at
similar confidence, not into one sharply localized morpheme. The
"winning piece" in cont. 12's aggregate result is typically decided by
a small margin between near-tied pieces, not a clean spike. This does
NOT retract cont. 12's discrimination result (true-vs-distractor
separation remains large and robust in every example inspected) but
does correct how "which single piece to rewrite" should be understood
-- that framing may be the wrong one; peak per-piece probe confidence
is close to flat, so it is not by itself a useful signal for locating
the REWRITE target, only for identifying WHICH noun governs the verb
(which it continues to do robustly).

**Two informative outlier cases, inspected directly rather than
averaged away**: (1) `wanaotumikia` in "kuna tofauti kati ya wanawake
wanaotumikia kifungo..." -- gold UD lists nsubj=kati ("between/among"),
and the probe is uncharacteristically UNCONFIDENT here (P(nsubj|subj)
only 0.09-0.18 across all pieces, far below every other example's
0.6-0.9 range). Likely explanation: this verb sits inside a relative
clause whose real logical subject is "wanawake" via the relative
pronoun, not "kati" -- the probe's low confidence plausibly reflects a
genuine gold-annotation/parse quirk rather than a probe failure, though
this is a hypothesis, not confirmed with a native speaker or a UD
formalism check. (2) `kusababisha kifo` ("to cause death", an
infinitival/xcomp-like construction) -- the distractor score
P(obj|subj) reaches 0.552, unusually high (most examples: 0.01-0.2),
meaning the probe partially confuses subject and object here instead
of cleanly separating them -- a genuinely harder case, not hidden by
only reporting aggregate win-rates.

**Not yet done / open**: now that "which piece has peak confidence"
looks like the wrong signal for REWRITE-target localization (even
though it works fine for controller IDENTIFICATION), the actual
next question is what WOULD localize the rewrite target within the
verb word -- candidates not yet tried: (a) a probe trained to predict,
given the verb's OWN pieces only (no noun pairing), something more
structural like "does changing this piece change the predicted
relation" (a per-piece ablation/gradient signal, closer to the
project's superseded steering-track tools, but applied to this
labeled-relation probe rather than generation); (b) checking whether
first-vs-last piece position (cont. 12's aggregate 54%/39%/41%
distribution) is reliable enough on its own, position-only, once
controller identity is already known from Part C's word-pair signal
-- i.e. use Part C only to confirm WHO governs the verb, then a
much simpler positional default (first piece for subject, last or
post-tense piece for object) for WHERE to rewrite, accepting that
this reintroduces a *little* position-based assumption but a far
weaker one than a full rule-based morphological segmenter.

Files: `nllb_relation_probe_piece_level_examples.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 14): two causal-ablation attempts at single-piece attribution -- neither reliably isolates the true agreement morpheme; a contrastive test actively DISCONFIRMS the first one's apparent success

User's pushback on cont. 13: "I don't think we are getting what we
need... I want to know that the token '_wali' is connected to madaktari
and not mkutano" -- i.e. a CAUSAL/attributional claim, not the
correlational per-piece classification comparison cont. 12/13 used
(which cont. 13 already showed is nearly flat across pieces, since
bidirectional self-attention leaks context into every piece roughly
equally).

New: `nllb_relation_probe_leave_one_out_ablation.py`. Target sentence
is "Madaktari Wasiokuwa na Mipaka waliitisha mkutano..." (one of the
175 gold sentences, index 145, fold 3 -- used the fold-3-held-out probe
from the SAME seed=1 CV assignment as Part B/C, no leakage).
verb='waliitisha' -> NLLB pieces ['_wali','it','isha'].

**Attempt 1 -- post-hoc leave-one-piece-out pooling** (remove piece i's
STALE hidden state from the mean, probe stays frozen, no re-encoding):
drops were tiny (|drop| < 0.035) and NOT linguistically sensible --
removing 'isha' (the causative suffix, not an agreement morpheme at
all) hurt the SUBJECT judgment most (+0.0100), while removing '_wali'
(linguistically the real wa- subject prefix + li- tense, matching
Madaktari's class 2) barely moved it at all (-0.0003). Diagnosed why:
post-hoc pooling can't undo bidirectional leakage that already happened
during the ORIGINAL forward pass -- the other two pieces' hidden states
still "know" about the subject even with piece i excluded from the
average, so this method is nearly insensitive to which piece carries
what.

**Attempt 2 -- TRUE causal ablation (delete the token from input_ids
and RE-RUN the encoder)**, so every remaining piece's hidden state is
actually recomputed without the deleted piece ever being attended to.
On `waliitisha` alone this looked promising and linguistically correct:
deleting '_wali' hurt the subject judgment most (+0.0321, ranking
'_wali' > 'it' > 'isha', matching that wa- really is the class-2
subject prefix). BUT the same piece ALSO caused the biggest drop for
the UNRELATED object judgment (+0.0689, bigger than its own subject
effect) -- already a warning sign that this might be generic
"destabilize the whole word" importance, not subject-specific
importance.

**Contrastive check (the decisive test)**: applied the identical
delete+re-encode ablation to "Kijana alikiokota kikombe" (a-li-KI-
okota, where 'ki' is a KNOWN, REAL object-marker morpheme agreeing
with kikombe, class 7 -- unlike waliitisha, where "mkutano" is very
likely NOT object-marked at all per Swahili grammar, see below). If
the method tracked real morphology, 'ki' should show the largest drop
for the object judgment. **It did not**: deleting 'ki' barely moved
the object judgment (drop=-0.0357, i.e. confidence slightly
INCREASED when the true object marker was deleted); the verb ROOT
'okota' dominated both the subject drop (removing it swung the subject
judgment by -0.1466) and the object drop (+0.1151, the largest).
**This actively disconfirms attempt 2's apparent success on
waliitisha** -- '_wali' winning there looks more likely to be an
artifact of it being the first, information-dense piece of a 3-piece
split (similar to how the ROOT dominates in alikiokota) than evidence
the method specifically tracks agreement morphology.

**Working hypothesis for WHY both ablation methods fail to localize**:
deleting any single BPE piece from a short (2-4 piece) word generically
destabilizes the pooled representation's recognizability as "a known
verb meaning X, governed by Y" -- and whichever piece carries the most
LEXICAL/semantic weight (usually the root, sometimes a dense first
piece) dominates this generic destabilization, regardless of whether
that piece is literally the grammatical agreement marker. Agreement
information, per cont. 13, is already smeared near-equally across all
pieces by bidirectional attention; removing the semantically "heaviest"
piece disrupts the pooled vector's overall coherence more than removing
a grammatically "load-bearing but lexically thin" prefix does, even
when that thin prefix is the actual morpheme of interest.

**Secondary finding, worth checking with a native speaker before
relying on it**: the asymmetry between SUBJ and OBJ results across
cont. 11-14 (SUBJ consistently cleaner/more confident than OBJ: cont.
11's accuracy 0.937 vs 0.889, cont. 11's n=2 OBJ-adversarial gap, this
entry's failed OBJ localization) may partly reflect a REAL Swahili
grammar fact, not just a weaker probe: Swahili subject-verb agreement
is OBLIGATORY (every finite verb carries a subject prefix), but object
marking is OPTIONAL, used mainly for definite/topical/pronominal
objects. "Mkutano" ("a meeting") in "waliitisha mkutano" ("convened a
meeting") is a fresh, indefinite object -- the kind that typically gets
NO object marker in real Swahili. If that reading is right, there may
be NO "piece connected to mkutano" in `waliitisha` for ANY method to
find, rule-based or learned, because the morpheme genuinely doesn't
exist there -- the obj relation is purely syntactic (adjacent bare NP),
not morphological. This is MY OWN linguistic judgment, not yet checked
against a native speaker or a reference grammar the way this project's
standing rule requires -- flagged as a hypothesis, not a finding.

**Net state**: three different piece-localization methods tried now
(correlational per-piece classification, post-hoc LOO pooling, delete+
re-encode ablation); none reliably and specifically isolates the true
agreement morpheme, and the one case that looked like a clean success
failed its own contrastive control. The validated result remains at
the WHOLE-WORD level (cont. 11): which noun governs which verb, robust
and position-independent for SUBJ. Sub-word rewrite-target localization
via NLLB's own representations, without any rule-based assumption,
remains unsolved.

**Not yet tried**: (a) gradient/saliency-based attribution (backprop
the probe's output through the pooling op to each piece, rather than
discrete deletion -- may avoid the "delete the lexically heavy piece"
confound since it's proportional rather than all-or-nothing); (b) a
minimal-pair GENERATION test -- change the subject noun's class in the
source sentence and check whether NLLB's own regeneration of the verb
changes the SAME piece position in a class-appropriate way (tests
NLLB's generative behavior directly, not an internal probe, so immune
to this ablation confound by construction, but only applicable where
we can construct a genuine minimal pair); (c) get a native-speaker check
on whether "mkutano"/similar indefinite objects in the gold corpus
really do lack object markers, to confirm or rule out the hypothesis
above before it misleads any further localization attempt.

Files: `nllb_relation_probe_leave_one_out_ablation.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 15): concrete demonstration, on the user's own two examples, of WHY noun->piece attention (the AMOD-style mechanism) fails for SUBJ specifically -- it only "works" when the subject happens to sit immediately before the verb

User's redirect: reject ablation/deletion entirely; they want exactly
the AMOD mechanism (raw encoder self-attention, noun->piece direction,
no training) applied to the verb prefix piece, shown concretely. This
IS the exact mechanism already tested for SUBJ in the earlier session
(status.md cont. 5/7, before this conversation) and found to collapse
under a position-confound control -- but that was only ever reported as
an aggregate statistic. New: `nllb_attention_noun_to_piece_examples.py`,
reusing `nllb_attention_gold_corpus_validation.py`'s CANDIDATE_HEADS
and noun->piece indexing unchanged (hard rule #10), run directly on the
user's own two sentences with no aggregation.

**Example 2 ("Kijana alikiokota kikombe" -- subject immediately before
the verb)**: piece[0]='_ali', L2H12: Kijana->piece=0.4804,
kikombe->piece=0.0000; L1H2: Kijana->piece=0.4980, kikombe->piece=
0.0000. A huge, clean, AMOD-like margin.

**Example 1 ("Madaktari Wasiokuwa na Mipaka waliitisha mkutano..." --
subject 3 words before the verb)**: piece[0]='_wali', L2H12:
Madaktari->piece=0.0001, mkutano->piece=0.0000; L1H11:
Madaktari->piece=0.0017, mkutano->piece=0.0000. Nothing -- both
essentially zero at every candidate head.

**Diagnosis, directly visible in these two numbers, not just asserted**:
in Example 2, "Kijana" is literally the immediately-preceding token to
'_ali' in the raw sequence. In Example 1, "Madaktari" is NOT
immediately preceding '_wali' -- three words intervene. This is the
previous-token-head artifact (cont. 5/7, earlier session) made
concrete: the attention isn't tracking the grammatical subject, it's
tracking "whatever sits one position back," which only coincides with
the true subject in short, textbook-adjacent sentences. The SAME
mechanism, applied to AMOD, does not show this failure (cont. 8,
earlier session) because Swahili adjectives sit immediately adjacent to
their head noun essentially always -- there is no real-text distance
case to expose the artifact the way verb subjects (which can be
arbitrarily far from their verb) do.

**This directly reconciles with cont. 11's Part B result**: the
relation probe's ADVERSARIAL/long-distance SUBJ stratum (n=51, subject
farther from verb than the distractor) scored 0.941 -- *higher* than
the near stratum (0.917) -- i.e. the one mechanism that is NOT
attention-based is the one that is NOT fooled by distance. Attention
gives a strong, textbook-sentence illusion and nothing on realistic
long sentences; the trained relation probe gives the opposite,
genuinely useful pattern.

**Net state, restated plainly for the open question**: "which noun
governs this verb" is solved, robustly, at the whole-word level, by
the relation probe (cont. 11), independent of distance. "Which specific
piece within the verb is the one that noun causes" is NOT solved by
any mechanism tried so far -- attention gives a distance-confounded
illusion (this entry), and the probe's own internals don't localize
either (cont. 12-14, flat per-piece confidence, ablation confound).
This remains the open gap.

Files: `nllb_attention_noun_to_piece_examples.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 16): MLP (FFN) activations tried as a 6th/7th method for piece-level localization -- whole-word signal replicates (even survives long distance, unlike attention), but per-piece localization still doesn't sharpen

User's directive: "we know this already [attention fails] this is why
we were building a probe on the MLP to try and have it learn this."
Referring to the project's earlier, now-superseded internal-steering
track, which hooked `model.model.decoder.layers[L].activation_fn`
(post-ReLU FFN units, dim 8192) on the DECODER for generation-time
steering (e.g. `nllb_swahili_decoder_language_neuron_check.py`). That
mechanism has never been applied to the ENCODER for this project's
actual current task (probing already-generated Swahili text). New:
`nllb_relation_probe_mlp_swahili_gold_eval.py`, hooking the ENCODER's
`activation_fn` instead, reusing `relation_probe.py` unchanged (hard
rule #10) with the embedding SOURCE swapped from `output_hidden_states`
(residual stream) to raw MLP activations.

Measured before choosing a scale (hard rule: always measure activation
norm first): encoder layer 12 activation_fn output has mean norm ~76
(vs ~1766 for the residual stream at the same layer) and is ~95-97%
zero (ReLU sparsity, confirmed at layers 6/12/18) -- same target_norm=
20 rescaling convention applied regardless.

**Part A (whole-word selectivity, same 80/20 split as cont. 11)**, at
layer 12: REAL accuracy=0.760, CONTROL accuracy=0.171, SELECTIVITY=
+0.589 (vs residual stream's +0.686) -- a real, usable signal, slightly
weaker than the residual stream but clearly not noise.

**Part B (the actual point -- per-piece scores on the user's own two
example sentences)**, layer 12: **the long-distance Madaktari example
now gives a strong, correct whole-word-level signal where attention
gave NOTHING** (cont. 15: all near-zero) -- P(nsubj|Madaktari) = 0.97/
0.92/0.94 across all 3 pieces of 'waliitisha', clearly favoring the
true subject over mkutano (0.03/0.02/0.02) regardless of distance. This
is a genuine improvement over attention for the "which noun governs"
question. **But the per-piece pattern is still flat** -- no single
piece stands out from the other two; '_wali', 'it', and 'isha' all
score within ~0.05 of each other, same smearing pattern as the
residual stream (cont. 13).

**Diagnosed why, architecturally**: by layer 12, self-attention has
already mixed sentence-wide context into every position across 12
prior layers. The MLP sublayer is applied POSITION-WISE (no cross-
token mixing happens inside the FFN itself), but its INPUT at this
depth is already the heavily-mixed residual stream -- it has nothing
less-smeared to work from, so its output inherits the same smearing
regardless of the FFN's own architecture being position-local.

**Follow-up test of the natural hypothesis this implies -- an EARLIER
layer, closer to raw embeddings, before extensive mixing has
happened**: re-ran the identical pipeline at layer 2. Part A
selectivity held up (+0.598, barely different from layer 12) --
somewhat surprising, suggesting even 2 layers of attention already
carry enough signal for the whole-word task. Part B, however, did NOT
sharpen -- if anything got LESS linguistically sensible: at layer 2,
the piece scoring highest for the SUBJECT judgment on 'alikiokota' is
'ki' (0.751) -- which is actually the real OBJECT marker, not a
subject marker at all. Still flat, and now also pointing at the wrong
piece by the one case where we know the correct answer with certainty.

**Net state after 7 distinct methods tried this session alone for
piece-level localization** (self-attention noun->piece, cross-
attention piece->noun, per-piece relation-probe classification,
post-hoc leave-one-out pooling ablation, delete+re-encode causal
ablation, MLP activations at layer 12, MLP activations at layer 2):
**none has produced a reliable, AMOD-like "this specific piece is
caused by this specific noun" signal.** The one thing EVERY probe-
based method (residual stream OR MLP, any layer tried) agrees on and
gets right, robustly and at any distance, is WHICH NOUN governs the
verb at the WHOLE-WORD level -- unlike attention, which only "worked"
by position-coincidence in short sentences (cont. 15). Sub-word
rewrite-target localization via NLLB's own representations remains
unsolved after this many independent attempts; this should be weighed
against continuing to search for an 8th variant versus treating
whole-word governance (solved) plus a narrow, checkable positional
fact (Swahili subject prefixes are always word-initial) as the
practical way forward.

Files: `nllb_relation_probe_mlp_swahili_gold_eval.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 17): factual correction -- Swahili verb template is SM-TAM-OM-ROOT, not "subject first / object second"; object marking is OPTIONAL and the gold corpus's own `feats` field already records, per-verb, whether one is present

User's question: "Is it true that the subject always marks the
beginning of the verb while the object marks the second position
marker?" Checked against both known Swahili grammar and the gold
corpus's own annotations before answering (not asserted from memory
alone).

**Subject marker**: confirmed TRUE -- always word-initial, obligatory
on every finite verb.

**Object marker**: NOT "second position." Real template is SM-TAM-OM-
ROOT; the object marker, when present, is the THIRD slot (immediately
before the root), with TAM occupying the second slot.

**Object marking is OPTIONAL, and this is now directly confirmed by
SWH_UDT's own `feats` column, not just asserted**: real examples from
the corpus --
  waliitisha    NounClass[subj]=...                    -- NO [obj] tag
  alisema       NounClass=...  (no [subj]/[obj] split)  -- NO [obj] tag
  kuwaunganisha NounClass[obj]=Bantu2|...               -- HAS [obj] tag
  alichapwa     NounClass[obj]=Bantu1|...               -- HAS [obj] tag
This empirically confirms cont. 14's hypothesis (then unverified) that
"waliitisha" genuinely has no object marker for "mkutano" -- not a
limitation of any method tried, there was nothing there to find. The
`[obj]`-tagged feats give a reliable, already-annotated ground truth
for "does this verb have an object marker at all," at least for gold
sentences -- useful for correctly scoping any future object-marker
work rather than assuming every obj-deprel verb has a rewritable OM
slot.

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 18): END-TO-END REWRITE DEMO -- combining the relation probe (subject) and AMOD attention (adjective) on a real sentence, both mechanisms fire correctly on held-out data, and the resulting edit is genuinely grammatical

User's directive: combine the two validated ingredients -- relation
probe for verb-subject agreement (first-piece rule, cont. 17) and AMOD
attention for adjective concord -- and actually edit a real sentence,
checking whether the result makes sense. New:
`nllb_pipeline_rewrite_demo.py`.

Target: a REAL SWH_UDT sentence (found via a direct dependency-
structure query, not hand-built), full structure checked first:
"Kupitia kwangu, watu wa Puerto Rico watapata jaji mwaminifu wa mtenda
haki, mtiifu kwa katiba ya nchi." (watu=nsubj of watapata; jaji=obj of
watapata; mwaminifu=amod of jaji; mtiifu=amod-deprel'd to haki but
UPOS=NOUN, an appositive epithet, not an ADJ).

**Both mechanisms confirmed LIVE, on held-out data, before editing
anything**: relation probe (trained on the OTHER 174 sentences, this
one excluded -- no leakage) gives relation(watapata, watu)='nsubj' at
P=0.824. AMOD attention (L2H12/L1H11/L1H2) gives jaji->piece beating
distractor 'Puerto'->piece at every head, margins as stark as the
cont. 8 precedent (0.8114 vs 0.0000; 0.7713 vs 0.0000).

**Edit performed**: watu(cl2,pl)->mtu(cl1,sg), watapata->atapata (first
NLLB piece swapped, wa-＞a-); jaji(cl1,sg,animacy-governed)->majaji(same
semantic class, pl), mwaminifu->waaminifu (AMOD-attention-identified
piece swapped, mw-＞wa-, the standard human-plural concord).

  ORIGINAL: Kupitia kwangu , watu wa Puerto Rico watapata jaji
            mwaminifu wa mtenda haki , mtiifu kwa katiba ya nchi .
  EDITED:   Kupitia kwangu , mtu wa Puerto Rico atapata majaji
            waaminifu wa mtenda haki , mtiifu kwa katiba ya nchi .

**Self-correction caught before over-claiming a coverage gap**: the
script initially flagged the associative "wa" (before "mtenda") as an
unedited, out-of-scope gap (reasoning: it concords with jaji's class
and jaji's class changed). On reflection this is WRONG -- Swahili
classes 1 and 2 share the same irregular associative form "wa" for
both singular and plural (e.g. "mtoto wa baba" / "watoto wa baba"),
so "wa" is correct as printed for BOTH jaji and majaji; it was never
actually a gap. Caught and corrected in the same turn, not left
standing.

**Genuine remaining gap, correctly identified and NOT silently
papered over**: "mtiifu" is UPOS=NOUN (an appositive epithet, "the
obedient one"), not ADJ -- the AMOD attention mechanism only targets
ADJ-tagged amod relations, so it is never even considered a candidate.
It stays singular ("mtiifu") while now describing plural "majaji,"
which would ideally also pluralize ("watiifu") for full naturalness --
a real, correctly-scoped limitation of what the two validated
mechanisms cover (verbs via the probe, ADJ-tagged amod via attention),
not a bug in either one.

**SW->EN gloss check (per cont. 9's standing caveat -- meaning only,
never a morphology check)**: both ORIGINAL and EDITED translate "jaji
mwaminifu"/"majaji waaminifu" as "a fair and honest judge" -- NLLB's
own back-translation did NOT register the pluralization at all,
reinforcing cont. 9's finding that this translation direction is not a
reliable verification tool for morphological edits; the EDITED
sentence's correctness here rests on direct grammatical judgment
(Swahili concord tables, a standard, checkable linguistic fact), not
on the translation agreeing.

**Net result**: the first full, working demonstration in this project
of the two mechanisms validated this session (relation probe for
verb-argument governance; AMOD attention for adjective concord)
combined into an actual text edit on real gold-corpus text, with
correctly-scoped, explicitly-reported coverage limits rather than a
silently incomplete rewrite.

Files: `nllb_pipeline_rewrite_demo.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 19): batch of 3 more real-sentence rewrite demos -- target identification is consistent (4/4 so far), but 2/4 edited sentences are grammatically/semantically broken for reasons the current pipeline doesn't cover

User's directive: run the cont. 18 pipeline on several more sentences,
check consistency, show the produced text. New:
`nllb_pipeline_rewrite_demo_batch.py`, same method as cont. 18 (held-
out relation probe + live AMOD attention + known-correct-form whole-
word substitution), 3 new real SWH_UDT sentences, deliberately
including one hard case rather than only easy wins.

**Identification consistency across all 4 sentences tried this session
(cont. 18 + these 3)**: relation probe P(nsubj) = 0.824, 0.859, 0.864,
0.867 -- tight, consistent range, every single one correctly predicted
'nsubj'. AMOD attention: 3/3 validated heads correct in every case,
same large-margin signature each time (~0.49-0.99 true noun vs
~0.0000-0.0011 distractor). This is the real, checkable consistency
result: the two mechanisms validated this session keep working, the
same way, on unseen real sentences.

**Case 2 ("Waziri Mkuu lazima asiwe..." -> "Mawaziri Wakuu lazima
wasiwe...")**: clean. Same noun governs both the verb and the
adjective; both concords shift correctly; reads as fully natural
Swahili ("In theory, Prime Ministers should not be part of political
movements").

**Case 1 ("Samak Sundaravej, waziri mkuu..." -> "...mawaziri
wakuu...") is BROKEN, and this is instructive, not just a miss**:
"waziri mkuu" is in APPOSITION to "Samak," a single named person.
Pluralizing the appositive while the named referent stays singular
produces an incoherent result (a plural description attached to one
named individual; "wa 25" [of the 25th] also stops making sense for a
plural subject). The AMOD attention mechanism correctly identified
WHICH noun the adjective concords with -- it has no way to know, and
was never asked to know, whether that noun's own larger role (here,
apposition to something number-constrained) makes pluralizing it
sensible at all. A genuinely new class of gap, surfaced only by
actually reading the output, not by checking the identification
mechanism's own accuracy.

**Case 3 ("Mtu binafsi atakayekutwa... anaweza..." -> "Watu binafsi
atakayekutwa... wanaweza...") is BROKEN in exactly the way flagged in
advance**: "atakayekutwa" (acl:relcl, relative-clause verb, carries its
own NounClass=Bantu1 concord referring to Mtu, confirmed directly in
its gold feats) was correctly left unedited because no validated
mechanism exists for acl:relcl -- but the output now has a plural
subject ("Watu") next to a verb still carrying SINGULAR relative
concord ("a-...-ye-"), a real, visible Swahili agreement mismatch. This
was predicted before running the edit (see the script's own docstring)
and is now concretely confirmed in the actual text, not just
theorized.

**Net read, stated plainly**: target IDENTIFICATION (cont. 11's
relation probe for subject/object governance; the earlier session's
AMOD attention for adjective concord) is validated and consistent --
4/4 real sentences, tight confidence range, no surprises. A correct
REWRITE needs more than identifying one relation type at a time: it
needs the full cascade of everything that co-varies with a changed
noun (appositives matching its number, acl:relcl concording with it,
and presumably det/nmod:poss per the original CLAUDE.md relation list,
none of which have validated mechanisms yet). 2 of 4 edited sentences
are wrong for reasons outside anything built or claimed so far -- this
is the honest result of actually reading the produced text rather than
only checking the identification step's own accuracy.

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 20): user correction -- the rewrite goal is marker-only (hold the noun's word fixed, shift only concording markers), NOT lexical substitution; this retroactively explains cont. 19's two "broken" cases, and testing the associative "wa"/case relation finds neither validated mechanism covers it

User's correction, decisive for how every future rewrite should be
scoped: "we aren't trying to pluralize or change the word. Keep the
same noun but change the agreement markers." Cont. 18/19's edits
(watu->mtu, jaji->majaji, waziri->mawaziri, etc.) were lexical
substitutions -- the WRONG operation. The actual goal, matching
Zmigrod et al. 2019's reinflection framing already cited in CLAUDE.md:
hold the noun's own surface form fixed, hypothetically reassign its
AGREEMENT CLASS, and rewrite only the markers that concord with it.
This retroactively explains why cont. 19's Case 1 (Samak/waziri) and
Case 3 (Mtu binafsi) broke -- both involved actually changing a noun's
form/number, which drags in everything else that depends on that
noun's real-world referential properties (apposition to a named
person, numeral modifiers, etc.) -- problems that don't exist at all
under the corrected, marker-only framing, since the noun's real-world
referent never changes.

User's own worked example, confirmed correct against the standard
Swahili associative-concord table: "waziri mkuu wa 25 wa Thailand"
(class 1) hypothetically reassigned to class 7 -> "waziri kikuu cha 25
cha Thailand" (mkuu -> kikuu [ki-+kuu], wa -> cha twice [class 7
associative]). "waziri" itself never changes.

**This surfaces a concrete new relation type this project has not
built or tested for**: the "wa" tokens are not amod -- gold UD parses
them as `case` markers attached to the FOLLOWING word ("25"/
"Thailand"), but their own `feats` show they concord with "waziri"
(NounClass=Bantu1), two words earlier. The concord SOURCE (waziri) is
not the same as the syntactic head (25/Thailand) -- a mismatch neither
mechanism built this session was designed for.

**Checked directly, not assumed, whether either already-validated
mechanism happens to cover it**:

(a) AMOD attention (`nllb_attention_case_associative_check.py`): NO.
Values are noise-level everywhere (0.0000-0.0045), nowhere near amod's
real signal (0.4-0.9+). Diagnosis: amod adjectives sit immediately
adjacent to their head noun; these "wa" markers do not (mkuu, or the
whole phrase, intervenes) -- plausibly the same locality limitation
that broke subject-agreement attention (cont. 10/15), now showing up
for a third relation type.

(b) Relation probe (`nllb_relation_probe_case_associative_check.py`):
PARTIAL, NOT reliable. relation(waziri, wa) correctly predicts 'case'
for the first occurrence (P=0.622) but WRONGLY predicts 'nmod' for the
second (P(case)=0.399). Critically, relation(25, wa) and
relation(Thailand, wa) -- the pairings the probe was ACTUALLY trained
on, since "wa"'s syntactic UD head is the following word, not waziri
-- score HIGHER (0.888-0.961) than the waziri pairing in both cases.
Diagnosis: the probe has learned "this token looks like a case-marker"
in general, but was never trained to discriminate WHICH nearby noun is
the correct concord source (that's a different training signal than
the syntactic-head pairs `build_relation_examples` constructs) --
category-correct, source-unreliable.

**Net state**: three relation types now distinguished by what's
actually validated for them -- nsubj/obj (relation probe, robust to
distance, cont. 11); amod (attention, cont. 8); associative/case
concord-source (NEITHER mechanism, as tested, reliably covers it --
would need its own dedicated training signal, built from `feats`-based
concord matching rather than UD syntactic heads, not yet attempted).
This is the same pattern repeated a third time: nothing transfers
across relation types for free, each needs its own check.

Files: `nllb_attention_case_associative_check.py` (new),
`nllb_relation_probe_case_associative_check.py` (new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 21): dedicated concord-source probe, trained with VERIFIED (not assumed) ground truth -- closes the associative/case gap from cont. 20

User's directive: "whatever relationship waziri wa is let's train a
probe on it and make sure we have it." New: `nllb_concord_source_probe.py`.

**Ground-truth extraction, checked before writing any training code**:
the obvious structural shortcut ("case marker -> its syntactic head ->
that head's own head = concord source") was tested against the case
marker's own `feats` NounClass across the whole corpus BEFORE trusting
it as training data. Result: 300/550 confirmed matches, 44 explicit
MISMATCHES (mostly multi-level associative chains like "Makamu wa Rais
wa Sudan Kusini", where one-hop traversal grabs the wrong noun), 206
with missing feats on one side. Only the 300 feats-VERIFIED pairs were
used as positive training data -- the structural guess alone was not
trusted.

**Design**: binary classifier, `relation_probe.RelationProbe`'s
architecture reused unchanged (hard rule #10) with 2 output classes
instead of 21. Positives: the 297 feats-verified (concord-source-noun,
marker) pairs actually recovered from the kept sentence set. Negatives:
the SAME marker paired with up to 3 other nouns from the same sentence
(distractor design, same principle as every other relation validated
in this project). Hewitt & Liang control task: fixed random label per
(noun_form, marker_form) word-pair TYPE.

**Results (80/20 sentence split, 108 train / 27 test sentences)**:

  REAL    accuracy=0.922  F1=0.847  (n=232 test examples, 58 positive)
  CONTROL accuracy=0.539  F1=0.457
  SELECTIVITY: accuracy=+0.384  F1=+0.391

External check -- does the TRUE concord source beat EVERY other noun
in its sentence (not just one distractor), held-out test positives:
n=58, win-rate=0.845 [95% CI 0.731, 0.916]. Weaker than nsubj (0.937,
cont. 11) or amod (near-ceiling, cont. 8) but a real, above-chance,
selective signal for a relation that had ZERO validated mechanism
before this entry.

**Capstone check on the exact motivating sentence**
(`nllb_concord_source_probe_waziri_check.py`, this sentence excluded
from training entirely, not just reused from the 80/20 split): BOTH
"wa" tokens in "Samak Sundaravej, waziri mkuu wa 25 wa Thailand,
amefariki..." correctly pick "waziri" as the top-scoring candidate
over every other noun in the sentence (Thailand, Samak, Sundaravej,
praditpi) -- the exact case that broke both AMOD attention and the
standard relation_probe in cont. 20, now solved.

**Net state**: three of the five relation types CLAUDE.md's original
pipeline lists (nsubj/obj, amod, associative/case) now have a
validated, selective, above-random-control mechanism; det/nmod:poss
and acl:relcl remain untested.

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 22): det and acl concord probes -- det shows real but NOT strictly-validated signal (external CI crosses chance); acl has too little feats-verified data in this corpus to test at all

User's directive: "build probes for all of them" (det, nmod:poss,
acl:relcl). Scoped before building anything (not assumed): nmod:poss
has exactly 1 instance in the whole corpus (checked directly, cont.
prior entry) -- genuinely not buildable, hard rule #5. Folded that one
instance into "det" instead (same UPOS=DET, same direct-attachment
mechanism to its concord source -- the semantic subtype doesn't change
what the rewrite task needs). New: `nllb_det_acl_concord_probes.py`,
reusing `nllb_concord_source_probe.py`'s generic training/control-task/
evaluation machinery unchanged (hard rule #10) -- only the extraction
function differs, since det/acl attach DIRECTLY to their concord
source (checked: 89/96 feats-checkable det/nmod:poss pairs match
directly, 92.7%, no grandparent traversal needed unlike cont. 21's
"case" relation).

**DET results** (88 feats-verified positive examples after embedding-
extraction alignment, 257 distractor negatives, 56 train / 14 test
sentences): REAL accuracy=0.885 F1=0.792 vs CONTROL accuracy=0.483
F1=0.483, SELECTIVITY=+0.402/+0.309 -- a real signal in the standard
classification sense. **But the stricter external test (does the true
concord source beat EVERY other noun in its sentence, same test that
validated nsubj/amod/case) does NOT clear the bar**: n=22, win-rate=
0.682, 95% CI [0.473, 0.836] -- the lower bound crosses chance. Cannot
be claimed as reliably validated the way the other three relations
were; promising, not proven.

**ACL results** (relative-clause instances only, requiring BOTH a
relative-concord feature AND a matching NounClass -- a stricter double
filter than cont. prior entry's single-feature check): only 13
feats-verified positive examples survive in the whole 175-sentence
corpus (down from the 57 that merely HAD a relative-concord feature --
most of those don't also have their plain NounClass matching the
head). Split 80/20 left only 4 positive test examples -- below hard
rule #5's n<8 floor, so the external distractor check was correctly
SKIPPED rather than reported on noise. The selectivity number that did
come out (F1 selectivity -0.021, slightly negative) is not a real
finding, just small-sample noise, reported as such rather than
over-interpreted.

**Net read**: this is a genuine, informative negative/mixed result,
not a failure to execute. With only 175 gold sentences total, SOME
relations (acl specifically, once properly feats-verified) simply
don't have enough data in THIS corpus to train or validate a probe at
all -- a data-scarcity problem, not necessarily a mechanism problem.
det has real signal but needs either more data or a different
validation design before it could be trusted the way nsubj/amod/
associative-case are. This matches CLAUDE.md Stage A's own gate
("100-200 sentences... annotation guide frozen") -- 175 sentences
covering every relation type was always going to be thin for the
rarer ones.
