## 2026-10-05 (cont. 23): found 98 more usable gold sentences sitting unused locally; re-running with the expanded 273-sentence corpus pushes DET over the validation bar; ACL still can't be tested; AfriSUD (1,491 sentences) located online but gated behind HF login

User's directive: "check for more data online. if it doesn't exist try build it by translating." Before going external, checked the already-downloaded `Conlu/swahili_udt/` directory directly -- it has THREE files, and every script this entire project has only ever loaded two (`*.filtered.conllu`, 175 sentences total). The third, `GlobalVoices.ken.sw.sample.conllu`, has never been used: 98 more sentences, confirmed to parse cleanly with the existing `conllu_utils.py` unchanged, only 2 duplicate sentence IDs vs. the other files (not deduplicated -- negligible, <1% of the combined set). One quality caveat found and noted, not hidden: this file has a handful of tokens with `deprel="_"`/`head="_"` (incomplete annotation) that the ".filtered" files evidently had cleaned out -- a real, lower-but-still-usable quality tier, not silently treated as equivalent.

**Re-ran `nllb_det_acl_concord_probes.py` with all 273 sentences (145+30+98)**:

DET: 123 feats-verified positives (up from 88). External check (true concord source beats every other noun): n=31, win-rate=0.710, **95% CI [0.534, 0.839]** -- the lower bound is now ABOVE chance (was [0.473, 0.836] on 175 sentences, excluded nothing). **DET now clears the same validation bar as nsubj/obj, amod, and associative/case** -- a direct, measurable win from the free local data alone.

ACL: only 16 feats-verified positives (up from 13) -- genuinely rare in this genre regardless of corpus size; still only 4 held-out test positives, still skipped under hard rule #5. The 98 extra sentences did NOT move this one -- confirms acl:relcl specifically needs much more data, not just a modest local boost.

**Checked online for more data, as directed**: the upstream Steimel & Kübler SWH_UDT repo (git.steimel.info/ksteimel/SWH_UDT) could not be inventoried via WebFetch (no file listing with sentence counts surfaced; repo reported as 2.6 GiB total but that includes code/environment files, not just data). Found a genuinely larger, more recent resource: **AfriSUD** (Masakhane-affiliated, RAIL/ACL-adjacent 2026 paper, arxiv 2606.12708) -- 1,491 Swahili sentences, 37,417 tokens, native-speaker verified, sourced from MasakhaPOS. Traced the actual data location (via grew-nlp/corpusbank's AfriSUD.json) to
`https://huggingface.co/datasets/Lugha-Models/AfriSUD` (CoNLL-U format, swa subset). **Confirmed GATED**: requires a HuggingFace account, agreeing to the dataset's access terms, and a token -- not something to route around; this is a deliberate access control set by the dataset's (Masakhane-affiliated) creators, not merely bypassed. Also noted: AfriSUD uses the **SUD** framework (Surface-Syntactic UD), not standard UD -- the corpusbank entry references a possible `UD_Swahili-AfriSUD@conv` converted companion, existence/bundling unconfirmed -- so even once access is sorted, a SUD-to-UD conversion/compatibility check would likely be needed before merging with the existing SWH_UDT-based pipeline, not a drop-in merge.

**Net state**: DET is now validated using a resource that cost nothing to find (it was already sitting on disk, just never loaded). ACL remains blocked purely on data volume -- AfriSUD could plausibly fix this (its average sentence length, 25.1 tokens, suggests richer embedded-clause structure than this corpus's current average ~10-20 tokens), but accessing it requires the user's HuggingFace credentials/consent to the dataset terms, and format compatibility with the existing UD-based pipeline is not yet confirmed.

Files: `nllb_det_acl_concord_probes.py` (extended to load all three local
SWH_UDT files).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 24): HF access obtained, AfriSUD downloaded -- real blocker found (zero morphological feats, not just a SUD-vs-UD label difference), then resolved by realizing feats were never load-bearing for direct-head relations; acl:relcl and nmod:poss both go from untestable to validated

User obtained a HuggingFace token and authenticated (`hf auth login`,
stored in the standard HF cache, never written into the project repo
or any committed file). Downloaded AfriSUD's Swahili CoNLL-U splits
(`Lugha-Models/AfriSUD`, swa/{train,dev,test}.conllu) via
`huggingface_hub`.

**A real blocker, checked directly rather than assumed**: beyond the
expected SUD-vs-UD label mismatch (`subj` not `nsubj`, `comp:obj` not
`obj`, `mod`/`mod@relcl`/`mod:poss` collapsing UD's amod/det/acl/poss
distinctions, `udep` in place of `case`), the `feats` column is
EMPTY -- checked across all 37,188 tokens in all three splits, zero
non-"_" entries. No NounClass, no morphological annotation at all.
This is more severe than the framework difference: every concord
probe built this session (cont. 21, 22) depended on `feats`-verified
NounClass matching as ground truth.

**User's question, which reframed the whole approach**: "do we need
noun classes to build the probes?" Worked through directly rather than
assumed: NounClass was used for two different things, not equally
essential. (1) Identifying WHICH noun a concord-marker's form is
governed by -- for det/amod/acl, where the concord source IS the
direct UD/SUD head, this is already given by the tree structure
itself; NounClass was only ever a BONUS quality filter (it's what
caught cont. 22's 7/96 det mismatches), never the core signal. (2) The
associative/`case` relation specifically needs class verification
because its concord source is NOT the direct head (needs grandparent
traversal, cont. 21) -- there, and only there, losing NounClass is a
real loss with no current substitute.

Checked AfriSUD's actual structure before trusting this reframing:
`mod@relcl` attaches directly to a NOUN/PROPN head 460/497 times
(92.6%) -- same reliability SWH_UDT's own `det` had (92.7%, cont. 22)
BEFORE any feats filtering. `mod:poss` attaches directly 109/115 (train)
and 15/15 (dev) times (94.8%/100%). Both trustworthy as direct ground
truth with NO class feature needed, same rigor this project already
applied when it had feats available and chose to trust the simple
head-dependent case.

**Results, reusing `nllb_concord_source_probe.py`'s machinery
unchanged (hard rule #10), trained on AfriSUD's own `train` split and
evaluated on its own separate `dev` split (a cleaner, externally-
defined held-out boundary than this project's usual self-made 80/20
shuffle)**:

  ACL (mod@relcl): REAL acc=0.944 F1=0.891 vs CONTROL acc=0.533
  F1=0.561, SELECTIVITY=+0.411/+0.330. External check (true concord
  source beats every other noun in its sentence): n=55,
  win-rate=0.836, 95% CI [0.717, 0.911].

  NMOD:POSS (mod:poss): REAL acc=0.983 F1=0.966 vs CONTROL acc=0.533
  F1=0.222, SELECTIVITY=+0.450/+0.743. External check: n=15,
  win-rate=1.000, 95% CI [0.796, 1.000] (n modest but CI clearly
  excludes chance).

**Both relations go from "cannot be tested at all" (acl: n=13-16 in
the Swahili UD corpus; nmod:poss: n=1) to validated**, at a standard
comparable to nsubj/obj, amod, and associative/case. This closes out
the full original CLAUDE.md Stage 4 relation list except the
associative/case relation's class-dependency gap, which AfriSUD's
missing feats do not help with (still needs SWH_UDT-style
feats-verification, or a surface-prefix noun-class inference method,
neither resolved by this entry).

**Not yet done**: det/amod at AfriSUD's much larger scale (`mod` with
ADJ dependents, ~1,997 instances across splits) -- not attempted this
entry since det/amod were already validated on the smaller SWH_UDT-
based corpus (cont. 22, cont. 11/earlier-session); would mainly
firm up confidence intervals, not open a previously-blocked relation,
so lower priority than acl/nmod:poss were.

Files: `nllb_afrisud_acl_probe.py` (new, parametrized by `--deprel` to
cover both mod@relcl and mod:poss without duplicating code -- hard
rule #10), `Conlu/afrisud_swahili/swa/{train,dev,test}.conllu`
(downloaded data, new).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 25): det/amod re-validated at AfriSUD scale -- much tighter CI and a much higher point estimate, not just more of the same

User's directive: "expand det/amod on AfriSUD too for tighter CIs."
Extended `nllb_afrisud_acl_probe.py` with a `--dep-upos` filter (hard
rule #10 -- same script, same generic machinery, one new optional
filter) to isolate AfriSUD's amod-like modifiers: `mod` relations where
the DEPENDENT's own UPOS is ADJ and the head is NOUN/PROPN (AfriSUD's
generic `mod` deprel otherwise lumps adjective concord together with
adverbial/compound/other modifier types attached the same way -- not
filtering would have mixed concord-bearing and non-concord-bearing
instances together). 1,376 positive training examples, 195 positive
held-out (AfriSUD's own dev split).

**Result, same protocol as every other entry (REAL vs CONTROL
selectivity, then external distractor-beats-every-other-noun check on
the genuinely held-out dev split)**:

  REAL acc=0.965 F1=0.934 vs CONTROL acc=0.541 F1=0.487,
  SELECTIVITY=+0.425/+0.447.
  External check: n=195, win-rate=0.923, 95% CI [0.877, 0.953].

Direct comparison to the previous (SWH_UDT-based, cont. 22/23) det
result: n=31, win-rate=0.710, 95% CI [0.534, 0.839] -- wide, barely
cleared chance. The AfriSUD-scale result is not just a tighter version
of the same finding -- the POINT ESTIMATE itself jumped from 0.710 to
0.923, now in the same range as nsubj/amod's original attention-based
numbers, not merely "cleared chance with more confidence." At n=31 the
true rate could plausibly have been anywhere in a wide band; at n=195
it's pinned down as genuinely strong, not marginal.

**Net state**: det/amod join acl:relcl and nmod:poss as relations whose
validation quality measurably improved once AfriSUD's larger volume
became available, despite AfriSUD providing no morphological feats at
all -- confirming cont. 24's reframing (direct-head relations don't
need class features; the dependency structure itself is the ground
truth) generalizes cleanly across every relation type tried so far
except the associative/case relation, which remains the one gap this
particular data source cannot close.

Files: `nllb_afrisud_acl_probe.py` (extended with `--dep-upos`).

## 2026-10-05 (cont. 26): the full concord-rewrite pipeline, all five validated relations combined -- a real bug caught before trusting the output, then a result that exactly reproduces the user's own hand-verified example

User's directive: "build the full concord-rewrite pipeline using all
five validated relations." New: `nllb_concord_rewrite_pipeline.py`,
combining nsubj (relation_probe, SWH_UDT), amod/det (AfriSUD `mod`+ADJ
probe), associative/case (feats-verified concord-source probe,
SWH_UDT), nmod:poss (AfriSUD `mod:poss` probe), acl:relcl (AfriSUD
`mod@relcl` probe, IDENTIFICATION only). obj deliberately excluded --
never had an identification mechanism built (optional marking, cont.
17), not silently assumed solved.

**Design, kept honest on purpose**: IDENTIFICATION (which word
concords with a chosen target noun) is fully NLLB-representation-based,
the part validated all session -- for each candidate word of each
relation type, the relevant trained probe is asked whether the target
noun wins as concord source against every OTHER noun in the sentence
(same win-condition as every external check this session used).
REWRITE uses static, standard Swahili concord tables (SM, adjective/
possessive concord with vowel-initial alternations, associative "-a"
forms) and simple KNOWN-prefix-string substitution -- not NLLB-token
segmentation, since that thread (cont. 12-16) never reached a
trustworthy general answer. For acl:relcl specifically, the relative
marker sits inside the verb after the subject+tense prefixes, not at a
word boundary this project knows how to find in general -- its
REWRITE is deliberately NOT attempted; only identification is, and the
gap is flagged in the output rather than guessed at.

**A real bug, caught before trusting any result**: the first run
applied each rewrite via a blind `sentence_text.replace(old_form,
new_form)` over the full string. On the Samak/waziri sentence (cont.
20's own worked example), this corrupted "waziri" itself into
"chaziri" -- because the associative edit was "wa"->"cha", and
Python's `str.replace` rewrites EVERY occurrence of that substring,
including the "wa" sitting inside "wa-ziri". This directly violated
the cont. 20 rule (never touch the noun's own word). Fixed by
reworking edits to be keyed by TOKEN INDEX and rebuilding the sentence
from its own token list, replacing only the exact identified position
-- never a substring search over the full text. Re-ran after the fix
before reporting anything.

**Result after the fix, on three real sentences**:

1. "Kupitia kwangu, watu wa Puerto Rico watapata jaji..." (target:
   watu, class 2 -> hypothetically class 1): correctly identified
   watapata as nsubj-governed (-> atapata) AND, newly (not something
   worked out by hand before), that the "wa" in "wa Puerto Rico"
   concords with watu (case/assoc) -- correctly a no-op edit since
   classes 1/2 share "wa". "watu" itself correctly left untouched.

2. "praditpi: Samak Sundaravej, waziri mkuu wa 25 wa Thailand,
   amefariki leo." (target: waziri, class 1 -> hypothetically class
   7): produced "waziri kikuu cha 25 cha Thailand" -- an EXACT match
   to the user's own hand-worked example from earlier this session,
   now produced automatically by the five probes + concord tables, no
   hand-typing. Additionally, and NOT something the user's original
   by-hand example covered, correctly identified and rewrote the
   subject-verb agreement too (amefariki -> kimefariki).

3. "Jarida la Magazine Revista Fórum liliwahoji wamiliki wa anuani
   kadhaa kati ya zile 66 zilizotajwa..." (target: zile, class 10):
   correctly identified zilizotajwa as acl:relcl-governed by zile, and
   correctly refused to rewrite it, printing the explicit "IDENTIFIED
   but rewrite not attempted" flag rather than guessing at the
   relative marker's position.

**Net state**: the first working, combined, bug-checked demonstration
of all five validated relations operating together in one pipeline on
real sentences, with the one remaining known gap (acl:relcl rewrite)
surfaced explicitly rather than silently skipped or guessed.

Files: `nllb_concord_rewrite_pipeline.py` (new).

## 2026-10-06: generalization check on 3 NEW sentences (not the cont. 26
hand-picked set) -- one real identification false positive caught only
by luck, and a real rewrite-table gap (adjective concord != demonstrative
concord != possessive-pronoun concord)

User's directive: test the combined pipeline (`nllb_concord_rewrite_pipeline.py`)
on sentences it has never seen, not just re-confirm cont. 26's 3 hand-picked
cases. Extended `main()` (hard rule #10) with 3 new SWH_UDT sentences chosen
to exercise nsubj, the DET pathway specifically (cont. 26 only ever
exercised amod via an ADJ, "mkuu" -- DET was wired in but never run), and
nmod:poss (never run at all before this). Old class taken from gold
`feats` NounClass as usual; new class picked arbitrarily for contrast.
cont. 26's original 3 sentences were re-run unchanged in the same pass as
a regression check -- all three reproduced identically.

**Test A -- "Wanaharakati pia wanaziomba nchi nyingine kushinikiza
viongozi wa serikali ya Honduras , ambao hivi karibuni walizindua Tume
ya Honduras ya Kudai Amani ." (target: Wanaharakati, class 2 ->
hypothetically 7, nsubj only).** Correctly rewrote `wanaziomba ->
kinaziomba` and `walizindua -> kilizindua` (both genuinely
Wanaharakati's nsubj, three clauses apart in the sentence). But the
nsubj probe ALSO predicted `Kudai` (an unrelated infinitive, "Kudai
Amani" = "to claim peace", governing a completely different NP) as
nsubj-governed by Wanaharakati -- a real false positive, not a
corner case built to fail. It did not surface as a wrong rewrite only
because `rewrite_sm` separately checked that `Kudai` starts with the
expected SM string `wa-`, which it doesn't, and returned `None`. That
is a string-matching accident catching the error, not the
identification mechanism recognizing its own mistake -- the pipeline's
printed output still lists `Kudai` under "identified" (just flagged
"not applied"), which would read as a correct catch unless you check
why it was flagged. **This is new evidence that the nsubj probe can
misfire at longer clause-distance than anything in cont. 11's original
validation or cont. 26's hand-picked examples tested**, and the
pipeline does not currently distinguish "identification was wrong" from
"identification was right but the string-level rewrite safety check
failed" -- both print identically as "FLAGGED, not applied".

**Test B -- "Brita alitembelea kituo hiki na kugundua wajibu wake wa
kutunza uhai wa Tembo :" (target: kituo, class 7 -> hypothetically 9,
det).** `hiki` correctly identified as kituo's concord dependent --
first time the DET branch of the amod/det check has actually fired
(cont. 26's own amod/det example used an ADJ, "mkuu", never a DET).
Rewrite returned `None`: `rewrite_adj_like`/`ADJ_BASE` encodes
ADJECTIVE concord (prefix + root, e.g. ki-/vi-/m-), but Swahili
demonstratives (hiki/hiyo/hilo/...) are their own paradigm, not that
template -- `hiki` doesn't start with `ki` or its vowel-alternant `ch`,
so the known-prefix-strip check correctly refuses rather than guessing.

**Test C -- "Usisahau mbwa wako , ni lazima waondoke kwa dharura
pamoja nawe ." (target: mbwa, class 10 -> hypothetically 6,
nmod:poss).** `wako` correctly identified as mbwa's concord dependent
-- first real nmod:poss run (cont. 24's validation n=15 was all the
nmod:poss data this project ever had; this is the first time it's been
exercised inside the combined pipeline). Rewrite again returned `None`:
same root cause as Test B -- Swahili possessive-pronoun concord for
classes 9/10 uses `y-`/`z-`, not the `ADJ_BASE` table's `n-`/`ny-`.
`rewrite_adj_like` is being reused for adjective concord, demonstrative
concord, AND possessive-pronoun concord as if they were one series;
they aren't, and the two new examples are the first direct evidence of
that, not just a theoretical gap.

**Net state**: identification generalized correctly on every new
example except the one Kudai false positive. Every rewrite failure in
this entry was correctly self-flagged rather than silently applied
(no corruption of real text), consistent with the project's standing
rule -- but for a different, previously-undocumented reason in two of
the three cases: not "known unsolved problem" (acl:relcl) but
"`ADJ_BASE` is the wrong table for this concord series." **Open
follow-up, not attempted here**: (1) decide whether the Kudai-style
false positive needs the nsubj probe itself improved, or whether
"identification wrong" vs "rewrite safety-checked and refused" should
be two visibly different output states rather than one shared "FLAGGED"
label; (2) demonstrative and possessive-pronoun concord need their own
tables (distinct from `ADJ_BASE`) before DET/nmod:poss rewrite can work
in general, not just for the lucky cases where a class's adjective and
possessive prefixes happen to coincide (e.g. classes 1/2 forms
overlapped in cont. 26's original examples, which is why this gap
didn't show up until new sentences were tried).

Files: `nllb_concord_rewrite_pipeline.py` (extended `main()` with 3 new
test sentences, hard rule #10).

## 2026-10-06 (cont. 2): built the demonstrative and possessive-pronoun
concord tables the previous entry's gap required -- confirmed fixed
end-to-end, and confirmed the remaining `wako` flag is a different,
already-known issue, not a leftover table bug

User's directive: build the two missing tables. Both are standard
reference-grammar facts, not derived/guessed, consistent with how
SM_TABLE/ADJ_BASE/ASSOC_TABLE were already built:

- **POSS_TABLE** (possessive-pronoun concord, prefix before -angu/-ako/
  -ake/-etu/-enu/-ao): the SAME consonantal concord series as
  ASSOC_TABLE minus its trailing vowel (wa->w, ya->y, la->l, cha->ch,
  vya->vy, za->z) -- e.g. `mti wangu` (cl.3), `nchi yangu` (cl.9),
  `kitabu changu` (cl.7). Every possessive stem is vowel-initial, so
  (unlike ADJ_BASE) no vowel-alternation branch is needed -- confirmed
  by exhaustive identity check (word, cls, cls) for all 10 classes
  against their standard forms before trusting it.
- **DEM_PROXIMAL_TABLE / DEM_DISTAL_TABLE** (demonstrative "this"/
  "that" series, classes 1-10): a small CLOSED set of whole-word
  forms (huyu/hawa/huu/hii/hili/haya/hiki/hivi/hii/hizi;
  yule/wale/ule/ile/lile/yale/kile/vile/ile/zile) that do NOT
  decompose into prefix+root productively -- direct table lookup +
  substitution, never a strip-and-reconstruct (the mistake that
  produced yesterday's bug).

New functions: `rewrite_poss` (strip known POSS_TABLE prefix, keep
stem, reprefix), `rewrite_demonstrative` (exact-match word against
whichever series it belongs to for old_cls, substitute same series'
new_cls form), `rewrite_det_or_adj` (dispatcher: try demonstrative
first, fall back to the existing `rewrite_adj_like` for other
determiner types like "nyingine"/"kila" that this project has not
separately verified -- left unchanged, not silently assumed fixed).
Wired `rewrite_det_or_adj` into the amod/det branch (replacing the
wrong `rewrite_adj_like` call) and `rewrite_poss` into the nmod:poss
branch. Also corrected `rewrite_adj_like`'s docstring, which had
wrongly claimed to cover det/possessive concord too -- that
over-claim is exactly what caused yesterday's bug to go unnoticed
in cont. 26's original validation.

**Checked before trusting**: unit-tested both new functions standalone
(no NLLB) -- identity round-trip for all 10 classes' standard
possessive forms, cross-class rewrites (wangu 1->10 = zangu, changu
7->1 = wangu), demonstrative round-trips (hiki 7->9 = hii, hiki 7->1
= huyu, zile 10->7 = kile, zile 10->1 = yule), and confirmed
`rewrite_demonstrative`/`rewrite_poss` correctly return `None` on
non-matching inputs (nyingine, wako) rather than guessing.

**Re-ran the full pipeline (all 6 sentences from the two most recent
entries) end-to-end to confirm the fix in situ, not just at the unit
level**: the kituo/hiki sentence now correctly rewrites `hiki -> hii`
(previously flagged, not applied). Every other sentence's output is
byte-for-byte unchanged from the previous run -- no regression. The
`mbwa`/`wako` nmod:poss case is STILL flagged (`None`), but now
confirmed to be for the right, already-known reason: `POSS_TABLE[10]`
is `"z"`, and `wako` genuinely starts with `w`, not `z` -- this is the
animacy-override case (§5: animate 9/10 nouns like mbwa take class 1/2
concord), not a table defect. The table is doing exactly what it
should; the gold `feats` class (10, shape class) is not the class that
actually governs this noun's agreement (an open problem, CLAUDE.md
§8, not attempted here).

**Net state**: the DET-rewrite gap from the previous entry is closed.
The nmod:poss-rewrite gap is now understood precisely: it is NOT a
missing/wrong table (POSS_TABLE is correct and tested), it is the
pre-existing, separately-documented animacy-override problem showing
up at the rewrite stage for the first time. Still open, unchanged by
this entry: (1) the Kudai nsubj false positive from the previous
entry, (2) the "nyingine"/"kila"-type determiner rewrite path, which
still uses the unverified `rewrite_adj_like` fallback, (3) animacy
override itself.

Files: `nllb_concord_rewrite_pipeline.py` (added POSS_TABLE,
DEM_PROXIMAL_TABLE, DEM_DISTAL_TABLE, `rewrite_poss`,
`rewrite_demonstrative`, `rewrite_det_or_adj`; corrected
`rewrite_adj_like` docstring; rewired amod/det and nmod:poss branches).

## 2026-10-06 (cont. 3): fixed the nsubj win-condition -- it caught a
SECOND, previously-undetected false positive (not the one it was built
for), and confirmed with exact numbers why the original Kudai case
still isn't fixed

User's directive: fix the nsubj win-condition gap from cont. 1 (nsubj
was the only relation branch with no cross-candidate comparison --
every other branch used `wins_as_concord_source`).

Added `wins_as_nsubj(nsubj_probe, nsubj_id, hidden, spans, verb_idx,
target_idx, all_nouns)`: requires (1) target's own argmax-predicted
label is still nsubj (kept from the original check) AND (2) target's
nsubj-class logit beats every OTHER noun's nsubj-class logit for that
same verb -- the same relative comparison every other branch already
uses. Wired into the nsubj loop in place of the bare argmax check.

**Re-ran the full pipeline. Diffed against the pre-fix run line by
line, not just skimmed.** Two real changes, both verified with exact
per-candidate numbers via a standalone diagnostic (trains only the
nsubj probe, ~5min, not the full 5-probe ~20-30min run):

1. **The Kudai false positive (cont. 1) is UNCHANGED -- still fires.**
   Diagnostic: `Wanaharakati` scores nsubj_logit=5.343 for the verb
   `Kudai`, the HIGHEST of every noun in the sentence (next: viongozi
   2.878, nchi/serikali/Honduras 2.0-2.9, Amani -0.194) -- `wins_as_
   nsubj`'s condition (2) is satisfied, because Wanaharakati genuinely
   beats every competitor. **This confirms the win-condition cannot
   fix this case by construction**: the real problem isn't "the wrong
   candidate wins", it's "no candidate should win at all" (Kudai is an
   infinitive with no nsubj edge in the gold tree, see cont. 1).
   Wanaharakati -- being the real subject of the matrix verb three
   clauses up -- is simply the most subject-like noun in the whole
   sentence by the probe's own standard, so it dominates even this
   unrelated embedded verb. A relative comparison structurally cannot
   detect "none of these are right"; that needs a separate presence/
   edge-existence check (does this verb have a real nsubj at all),
   which is a DIFFERENT fix than the one asked for here, not attempted.

2. **A SECOND, previously undetected false positive was caught --
   not a regression.** The `waziri`/`amefariki` rewrite
   (`amefariki -> kimefariki`) that fired in every prior run STOPPED
   firing. First read as a regression; checked the sentence's actual
   gold parse before concluding anything (methodology preference:
   verify, don't assume): `waziri`'s real deprel is `appos` (to
   `Samak`), NOT `nsubj` -- `praditpi : Samak Sundaravej , waziri mkuu
   wa 25 wa Thailand , amefariki leo .` has `Samak` as the TRUE gold
   nsubj of `amefariki`; `waziri mkuu wa 25 wa Thailand` ("Prime
   Minister of Thailand") is an appositive TITLE describing Samak, not
   itself the agreement controller. Diagnostic: `Samak` scores
   nsubj_logit=5.774 vs `waziri`'s 4.354 for this verb -- the probe's
   own representations correctly rank the true subject above the
   appositive, and the new win-condition correctly suppresses
   `waziri`'s claim. This specific rewrite was flagged back in
   cont. 26 itself as "NOT something the user's by-hand example
   covered" -- it had been sitting in every "validated" run since as
   an unverified bonus that was never actually correct. Per the
   project's additional rule ("score agreement only on words
   controlled by the target noun"), this was ALWAYS a false positive;
   the win-condition just surfaced it.

   amod/det (`mkuu -> kikuu`) and case/assoc (`wa -> cha` x2) on this
   same sentence are unaffected -- both are genuinely controlled by
   `waziri` per the gold tree (amod head=waziri, case grandparent=
   waziri) and still fire correctly.

**Net state**: the win-condition fix is a net improvement -- it fixed
a real bug beyond the one it was requested for, at the cost of zero
regressions (everything that changed was independently confirmed
wrong-before/right-after via the gold tree, not just "different").
The original motivating case (Kudai) needs a structurally different
fix (presence-of-nsubj-edge check), not attempted. Diagnostic script
used (not checked into Code_Experiments, scratch): prints per-
candidate nsubj_logit + argmax for a given (verb, sentence) pair,
reusing `nllb_concord_rewrite_pipeline`'s own `pool_span`/`get_hidden_
and_spans` unchanged (hard rule #10).

Files: `nllb_concord_rewrite_pipeline.py` (added `wins_as_nsubj`,
rewired the nsubj branch).

## 2026-10-06 (cont. 4): FR/IT sideline -- tested the concord-transplant
methodology against a REAL benchmark with ground truth (something
Kitaita doesn't have yet), on NTREX-128 n=60. Null result at the
corpus-BLEU/chrF level, but a real, verified effect at the sentence
level -- and three real bugs found and fixed along the way.

User's directive: "see how this methodology and framework scores on
annotated data" -- build a complete IT->FR dictionary, use the
methodology to translate using Italian as donor (playing Swahili's
role) to produce French (playing Kitaita's role), score against a
translation benchmark. Donor/target roles deliberately mirror Kitaita's
structure even though French is itself resource-rich -- this validates
the INTERVENE+REINFLECT mechanism against ground truth, same spirit as
this project's EN/German steering checks ("machinery only").

**Benchmark**: FLORES-200 and every mirror tried (Muennighoff/flores200,
openlanguagedata/flores_plus, bri25yu/flores200_val_test) are gated or
use unsupported legacy loading scripts -- same situation as AfriSUD.
Found NTREX-128 (Microsoft, github.com/MicrosoftTranslator/NTREX,
openly licensed, no auth needed) as the open equivalent: 1997 sentences,
human-translated from the same English originals into every language.
Used eng/ita/fra, first 60 sentences (scaled down from a planned 150
after measuring this CPU-only environment's actual per-sentence NLLB
cost on a 15-sentence pilot -- stated plainly, not silently picked,
hard rule #5).

**Identification**: spaCy's pretrained `it_core_news_sm` dependency
parser, NOT retrained NLLB probes -- a deliberate, flagged deviation.
The NLLB-probe identification step is already validated for Swahili
(cont. 1-3 this session); this sideline's actual question is whether
INTERVENE+REINFLECT (dictionary substitution + concord-table
reinflection) beats naive substitution, orthogonal to re-proving
identification on a language with an excellent off-the-shelf parser.

**Scope, stated plainly**: singular common nouns only; `det` (articles)
+ `amod` (adjectives) + `nsubj`-controlled past-participle gender
agreement (ESSERE-governed only) + possessive determiners. New files:
`fr_adjective_gender_rules.py` (masc<->fem reinflection: lookup from
the existing 234-pair hand-verified lexicon first, unambiguous suffix
rules second -- self-check showed 0 wrong / 180 correct / 54 correctly-
flagged on held-out generalization), `fr_it_concord_tables.py` (FR/IT
article + possessive tables, singular only), `fr_it_concord_transplant_
benchmark.py` (dictionary construction + 3-condition generation +
sacreBLEU scoring).

**Dictionary**: built FROM the benchmark's own vocabulary (not a
static pre-built list), via a carrier-sentence trick -- wrap each
Italian lemma in a minimal grammatical carrier using its OWN known
Italian gender, translate via NLLB (ita_Latn->fra_Latn, greedy,
batched -- beam search measured ~4x slower for no benefit on these
short carriers), read the French word + its real gender off spaCy's
parse of the output. Literally reuses NLLB as a word-translation
oracle, i.e. what "naive dictionary substitution" means in this
project's own vocabulary. 212 entries from 228 needed (noun=150
adj=23 part=39) on the n=60 set.

**Three real bugs found and fixed, in order**:
1. "Voilà"/discourse-marker leak: when NLLB's output abandoned the
   expected carrier structure, spaCy sometimes mistagged a sentence-
   initial discourse marker as NOUN/PROPN, silently corrupting a
   dictionary entry (`proposta` -> `Voilà`) instead of being caught as
   NO CANDIDATE. Fixed with a name-based exclusion list + a position
   check (content word can never be the carrier's first token).
2. Plural nouns silently inherited a SINGULAR dictionary entry via
   lemma-only lookup (`membri` picked up the entry built from a
   different sentence's singular `membro`) -- out of this entry's
   stated scope; fixed by checking `Number==Sing` at use time, not
   just at dictionary-build time.
3. Gender-reading preferred a noun's own (sometimes wrong) morph tag
   over the governing article it was translated WITH in the same NLLB
   output -- confirmed concretely: NLLB generated `"C'est le casse-
   tête."` (unambiguously Masc via "le"), but spaCy's own Gender tag
   on "casse-tête" read Fem. Fixed by preferring the article's gender
   (the actual concord-marker signal this whole project's methodology
   is built on reading agreement off) over the noun's own tag.

**Result after all three fixes, n=60**:

  naive        BLEU=3.18 [1.34,4.90]   chrF=31.35 [29.50,33.27]
  methodology  BLEU=3.19 [1.34,4.92]   chrF=31.34 [29.48,33.30]
  nllb_direct  BLEU=19.03 [15.75,22.11]  chrF=48.79 [45.80,51.65]

Corpus-level BLEU/chrF show NO detectable difference between naive and
methodology -- CIs fully overlapping, point estimates within noise.
nllb_direct (real MT, calibration only, not something either rule-
based condition is expected to beat) scores far higher, as expected
for a resource-rich target language.

**But this is not a null result at the mechanism level -- checked
directly rather than concluding "it doesn't work" from the aggregate
number alone (methodology preference: verify before trusting a
corpus-level summary).** Diffing naive vs methodology output
sentence-by-sentence: 15/60 sentences differ, EVERY diff a single-
token determiner/adjective swap. Spot-checked several against real
French gender facts: `figura`(f)->`personnage`(m): naive wrongly kept
"la", methodology correctly gives "le". `decisione`(f)->`jugement`(m):
same pattern, correctly fixed. `decennio`(m)->`décennie`(f): naive
wrongly kept "un", methodology correctly gives "une". These are
genuine, textbook IT/FR gender mismatches, each correctly resolved.
One more diff (sentence 53, "capitano") is a different, known failure
mode: "capitano" is lexically ambiguous in Italian (noun "captain" vs.
3pl verb "they happen"), spaCt mistagged it, and the resulting
dictionary entry is garbled (`capiteine`/`capitein`) -- not a new bug,
an example of the residual tagging-ambiguity class of error.

**Why the aggregate metric can't see a real, verified effect**: each
sentence has ~15-30 words; a single corrected determiner is a small
fraction of n-gram overlap, and most of each sentence is identical
across conditions by design (hard rule: only concord-bearing
dependents differ between naive/methodology, matching the "marker-
only rewrite" rule). Corpus BLEU/chrF are known in the MT literature
to be poor instruments for localized grammaticality fixes -- this is
not a new finding, but this project had not previously measured it
directly on its own methodology. **The methodology is doing exactly
what it's supposed to on the cases that matter (verified gender
mismatches); the chosen scoring instrument is simply not sensitive
enough to show it in aggregate.**

**Residual known gaps, not attempted here**: participle flag rate
79/79->75/79 flagged (~95%) -- mostly because predicate-adjective-via-
copula constructions ("sono preoccupati" = "are worried", ADJ as ROOT
with a cop, not amod) fall outside this pass's amod/nsubj:pass scope;
a real, distinct category from what's handled, not a bug. adj flag
rate 29/48 (~60%) -- vocabulary coverage limits of the carrier-
sentence dictionary method. Plural agreement, coordination, relative
clauses: out of scope by the stated design, same as Kitaita's own
acl:relcl gap.

**Recommended next step if continued**: a sentence/word-level gender-
agreement-accuracy metric (precision/recall specifically on known
mismatch cases), not corpus BLEU/chrF, would be the sensitive
instrument this comparison actually needs -- corpus BLEU was the
metric requested and is reported in full above, but it is demonstrably
the wrong tool for detecting this specific, real effect.

Files: `fr_adjective_gender_rules.py`, `fr_it_concord_tables.py`,
`fr_it_concord_transplant_benchmark.py` (all new), `ntrex128/` (NTREX-
128 eng/ita/fra text files, downloaded), `fr_it_dictionary_cache.json`
(built dictionary, cached).

## 2026-10-06 (cont. 5): estimated the CEILING of cont. 4's null
result -- separated "bigger dictionary" from "better rules" and put a
number on each, rather than leaving "would optimizing help?" as a
guess

User's question: if the dictionary/rules were optimized further,
how high would the methodology's BLEU/chrF go? Worth separating two
different things "optimization" could mean, since they have very
different ceilings:

1. **Dictionary coverage** (more vocabulary translated at all): this
   is what actually moves naive/methodology's ~3 BLEU toward nllb_
   direct's ~19 BLEU -- it determines how much of the sentence is in
   French at all. Large effect, but orthogonal to whether the
   GRAMMAR mechanism itself helps.
2. **Rule coverage** (handling plurals, more relation types, closing
   the specific naive-vs-methodology gap): this is what the project's
   actual causal claim is about. Estimated its ceiling directly rather
   than guessing.

**Method**: took the `nllb_direct` outputs (full-coverage, high-
quality translation, saved from cont. 4's run) as a stand-in for
"what naive/methodology would produce at complete coverage." Parsed
each with spaCy FR, found every singular le/la/un/une determiner
(120 across 60 sentences), and deliberately flipped a fraction of
them to the wrong gender -- simulating a full-coverage "naive" that
still gets the SAME fraction of genders wrong as our real, measured
mismatch rate (14/103 ~= 14%, from cont. 4's hand-verified sentence
diffs). Scored the corrupted vs. clean text against the real FRA
reference with sacreBLEU (point estimates only, no bootstrap -- this
is an exploratory sensitivity sweep, not a result needing a CI).

**Result**:

  rate=0%   (clean, = "perfect methodology"):  BLEU=19.03  chrF=48.79
  rate=14%  (our real measured mismatch rate): BLEU=18.54  chrF=48.57
  rate=100% (every determiner wrong -- a worst-case bound): BLEU=15.57  chrF=47.45

**At our real mismatch rate, the ceiling gap attributable to the
grammar-correctness mechanism ALONE, even at perfect rule coverage,
is ~0.5 BLEU / ~0.2 chrF.** Even the unrealistic worst case (every
single determiner wrong, far worse than any real system) only costs
~3.5 BLEU / ~1.3 chrF. This is not a measurement artifact or a sample-
size problem -- it's a structural ceiling: a single wrong word in a
15-30 word sentence cannot move whole-sentence n-gram overlap by much,
no matter how good the underlying rules get. Confirms and quantifies
cont. 4's qualitative claim ("BLEU/chrF are the wrong instrument for
this effect") with an actual number: optimizing dictionary coverage
is the lever that matters for the ABSOLUTE score; optimizing rule
coverage for its own sake will not move corpus BLEU/chrF much even
at the limit.

Files: none checked in (exploratory analysis script, scratch only,
reused cont. 4's saved `fr_it_benchmark_outputs.json`).

## 2026-10-06 (cont. 6): back to the real target -- collected Genesis+
Exodus+Psalms in Swahili and Kitaita, built a BantuGrammar data
structure, and got a first candidate verb paradigm (subject markers +
tense markers) for Kitaita, purely from text, for native-speaker
review. This is the actual deliverable the whole project has been
working toward.

**Data collection**: `bible collection/bible_collect.py` (already in
the repo, not previously run) scrapes bible.com and aligns two
versions by USFM verse ID. Confirmed version IDs: Kitaita (Taita)
version 2138/TAITA (Bible Society of Kenya, "Biblia Ilagho Jiboie Kwa
Wandu Wose"); Swahili version 164/SUV (Swahili Union Version,
"Maandiko Matakatifu ya Mungu Yaitwayo Biblia") -- chosen as a
register-comparable standard translation. Collected Genesis+Exodus+
Psalms (GEN.1-50, EXO.1-40, PSA.1-150) in both; aligned cleanly, 5207/
5207 verse pairs, 0 mismatches. Saved under `bible collection/data/
{taita,swahili,parallel}/`.

**BantuGrammar data structure** (`Code_Experiments/bantu_grammar.py`):
noun classes, concord forms, verb-form decompositions, TAM marker
inventory, and (Kitaita-only) alignment hypotheses -- every entry
carries a `confidence` tier (`known`/`lexicon`/`prefix-pattern`/
`aligned`/`aligned+distributional`), since Swahili and Kitaita have
completely different evidence bases.

**Swahili** (`extract_swahili_grammar.py`): reuses this project's
existing `swahili_noun_lexicon_agreement_v2.py` (319 nouns) and
`nllb_concord_rewrite_pipeline.py`'s `SM_TABLE` (hard rule #10,
extended with classes 11/15); added a new standard-reference TAM-
marker table (none existed in this project before). On the full
5207-verse corpus: 1741 noun entries, 3255 decomposed verb forms.

**Kitaita** (`extract_kitaita_grammar.py` + `kitaita_verb_paradigm.py`
-- NO prior lexicon or parser exists, so this is built entirely from
the collected text):

1. Noun classes: Dice-coefficient word alignment (verse co-occurrence
   with the Swahili side) propagates a known Swahili noun's class
   onto its best-aligned Kitaita word. **Changed per user feedback
   this session**: class assignment is now PURELY alignment-based --
   the earlier version also pulled in every word sharing a productive
   prefix with an aligned word (distributional cluster-voting), which
   silently mixed verbs into noun buckets (user caught this directly:
   "I'm seeing some verbs mixed with nouns"). Fixed by dropping
   cluster-voting entirely for the noun_classes output. On 5207
   verses: 977 aligned noun entries, clean.

2. Verb paradigm induction (`kitaita_verb_paradigm.py`, new): the
   per-word Dice alignment is unavoidably noisy for TENSE specifically,
   because Swahili fuses subject+tense+root+final-vowel into one
   surface form, smearing a tense marker's co-occurrence across every
   distinct verb that happens to share it (user's own diagnosis,
   confirmed correct). Fix, per the user's own proposed method:
   group Swahili verb forms by ROOT (reusing `decompose_verb`'s
   subject/TAM/root split), find each form's best-aligned Kitaita
   word, then contrast Kitaita forms PAIRWISE within a root group --
   same TAM, different subject -> subject-marker candidate; same
   subject, different TAM -> tense-marker candidate.
   Two real bugs found and fixed while building this: (a) first
   version required ALL members of a root group to agree before
   extracting anything, so one bad alignment in a group of 4 erased a
   real 2-member agreement -- fixed by making every comparison
   PAIRWISE instead of whole-group. (b) first version used common-
   SUFFIX only, but the shared root can sit as an INFIX in one word
   and near an edge in the other (confirmed directly: "oreghambieghe"
   vs "ukighamba" share "ghamba"/"ighamba" in the MIDDLE of the first
   word) -- fixed with a proper longest-common-SUBSTRING (DP) match,
   splitting each word into (before-root, root, after-root).

**Result after scaling to the full 5207-verse corpus** (5 root groups
usable on Genesis alone -> 20 on Genesis+Exodus+Psalms; the extra
books were specifically collected to fix this data-starvation
problem, and it worked):

  Candidate Kitaita SUBJECT MARKERS (Swahili SM -> Kitaita candidate,
  support = number of independent root-group pairs agreeing):
    a  (cl.1)  -> u-   (support 4)   e.g. aliposikia/alisema -> uendasikira/u-
    wa (cl.2)  -> wi-  (support 4)   e.g. waliposikia -> wiendasikira
    zi (cl.10) -> r-/ri- (support 2)
    ki (cl.7)  -> ch-/chi- (support 2)
    u  (cl.3/11) -> ku-/k- (support 3)
    li (cl.5)  -> w-/wi- (support 3)
    ku (cl.15, infinitive) -> ghu- (support 3)
    vi (cl.8)  -> ve- (support 1)

  Candidate TAM markers:
    past              -> circumfix ore-...-ieghe (support 2, e.g.
                         alisema -> oreghambieghe)
    conditional/while -> uki- (matches Swahili's OWN -ki- exactly --
                         plausible shared retention)
    perfect           -> wada- (new, internally consistent across
                         2 forms)

**One real, unresolved discrepancy, flagged rather than silently
resolved**: 3 of 5 class-1-vs-class-2 contrastive root groups
("sem"/say, "posiki"/hear, "tok"/leave) cleanly show u-(cl.1)/wi-
(cl.2); 2 others ("ju"/know, "kuj"/come) show "wa-" for the class-1
(singular) slot instead of "u-". Could be genuine vowel-conditioned
allomorphy (common in Bantu) or alignment noise on those 2 specific
pairs -- an explicit, direct yes/no question for the native speaker,
not resolved here.

**Net state**: this is now a real, first-pass CANDIDATE Kitaita verb
paradigm (partial subject-marker table + 3 tense markers) derived
from zero prior resources, entirely from parallel text + a Swahili
reference grammar + statistical alignment. Per the user's own framing
of this whole thread ("I will take a look at the result and show it
to a native speaker... before we use it for the next step"), nothing
here is to be used downstream until confirmed.

Files: `bantu_grammar.py`, `extract_swahili_grammar.py`,
`extract_kitaita_grammar.py`, `kitaita_verb_paradigm.py` (all new);
`bible collection/data/{taita,swahili,parallel}/` (collected text);
`bantu_grammar_swahili.json`, `bantu_grammar_kitaita.json`,
`kitaita_verb_paradigms.json` (results, regenerated on the full
5207-verse corpus).

## 2026-10-07: multi-version (3 Swahili translations) re-run of the
BantuGrammar pipeline + reorganized into a reviewable 3-page HTML
artifact for the native speaker, per direct user request ("the JSON
produced yesterday was a bit difficult for humans to read... download
other swahili versions... use the result of all 3 versions to
increase confidence").

**Versions added**: fetched the live bible.com version list directly
(`https://www.bible.com/api/bible/versions?language_tag=swh&type=all`)
rather than guessing IDs. Chose two registers deliberately different
from the existing SUV (164, formal-equivalence Union Version): NEN
(1627, Kiswahili Contemporary Version "Neno", dynamic/contemporary)
and BHN (74, Swahili Common Language Bible, simplified register).
Scraped Genesis+Exodus+Psalms for both (same scope as SUV) and aligned
each against the existing Kitaita TAITA text: NEN and BHN each yield
3994 aligned verse-unit pairs (vs SUV's 5207 -- `only_a: 1213` on both
aligns, i.e. NEN/BHN combine some verses differently; not a data loss,
just a coarser unit grain on those two versions, confirmed via the
`align` subcommand's own stats, not assumed).

**Found and fixed a real data-quality issue while doing this**:
bible.com verse HTML leaks footnote/cross-reference text into the
scraped verse text, in two different shapes by version -- SUV-style
puts a chained reference list ("Yn 1:1, 3; Ebr 1:10...") BEFORE the
real sentence; BHN-style appends an explanatory footnote AFTER it.
Confirmed directly on both (not assumed from one). This was already
silently present in the existing single-version corpus (bantu_grammar_
swahili.json's token counts include some leaked reference-abbreviation
noise) but didn't matter before since it never got quoted to a human.
Fixed with a verse-text cleaner (`verse_text.py`) used throughout the
new pipeline; NOT retroactively applied to the existing single-version
files (scope: this session's new outputs only).

**New code** (`Code_Experiments/`, all new, extending rather than
forking the existing tables/functions per hard rule #10):
- `concord_families.py`: groups adjective/associative/possessive/
  demonstrative surface forms into FAMILIES by underlying concord
  relation (e.g. mzuri/wazuri/nzuri = one "-zuri" adjective family;
  wa/ya/la/cha/vya/za = one associative "-a" family) -- this is what
  the user asked for directly ("group articles and adjectives of
  different families together... so we can generalize properly").
  Adjective stems are a hand-curated, CONSONANT-INITIAL-only list
  (zuri, kubwa, dogo, refu, fupi, chafu, geni, zito, baya -- Ashton
  1944; Mohammed 2001) rather than blind corpus-pattern induction: an
  earlier version of this script blindly stripped ADJ_BASE prefixes
  from every corpus word and produced 2039 spurious "families" (noun
  singular/plural pairs misread as adjective concord, since noun and
  adjective class prefixes are the same strings in Swahili; classes
  9/10 trivially "agreeing" because they share the identical "n-"
  prefix string). Caught by inspecting the raw output before trusting
  the aggregate count (methodology preference: spot-check before
  reporting). Fixed by switching to curated-stem-plus-corpus-
  attestation; 7-8 genuine families found, matching the user's own
  worked example exactly.
- `verse_evidence.py`: for each Swahili noun, searches the pooled
  3-version corpus for a real verse where an actual agreement marker
  (adjective/associative/possessive/demonstrative) attached to it is
  consistent with its claimed class -- corpus-grounded confirmation,
  not just "the lexicon says so" (this IS the "give the verse where
  agreement was used to determine the class" the user asked for).
  Selectivity CONTROL included (hard rule #3): also checks whether a
  WRONG-class marker is present in the same verse (homophonous classes
  like 9/10's shared "n-" excluded from counting as a false positive).
  Result on the full pooled corpus: agreement evidence found for
  1476/3018 lexicon+prefix-pattern nouns (48.9%); of those, 915 verses
  also contained a competing wrong-class marker (long Bible sentences
  commonly hold several nouns) -- selectivity rate 0.38, reported
  plainly rather than cherry-picking clean examples only. Evidence
  SELECTION does prefer unambiguous, shorter verses when available
  (sorted candidates by ambiguity then length) so the quoted examples
  skew toward spot-checkable ones.
- `multi_version_pipeline.py` / `multi_version_verb_paradigm.py`:
  generalise extract_kitaita_grammar.py's Dice alignment and kitaita_
  verb_paradigm.py's pairwise root-contrast method to run once per
  Swahili version, then merge. Merge rule (the user's own requested
  preference order): highest Dice score first, then fewest competing
  partners (closer to 1:1), with agreement across >=2 INDEPENDENTLY-
  WORDED versions on the same propagated noun class flagged as "high"
  confidence (stronger than repetition within one version's register,
  since two differently-worded translations landing on the same class
  isn't explainable by shared vocabulary alone). Result: 2483 Kitaita
  words aligned across the 3 versions combined (vs 2292 on SUV alone);
  481 reach "high" (>=2-version) confidence.
- `build_pages.py` / `render_html.py`: assembles the reorganized
  3-page structure the user asked for (Page 1 = all nouns + verbs,
  verbs collapsed from individually-decomposed inflected surface forms
  down to one entry per ROOT with its observed subject/tense slots,
  same generalization principle as the adjective families; Page 2 =
  noun classes with grouping rationale + verse evidence + best
  Kitaita candidate(s); Page 3 = Swahili TAM/subject-marker reference

## 2026-10-07 (cont. 2): user correctly flagged that the "Kitaita noun
class" shown on Page 2 was COPIED from the aligned Swahili noun's
class, not determined by any agreement signal from Kitaita text
itself ("I think the classes are copied from the swahili classes
instead of being determined based off of agreement"). Accurate -- that
was always true of the alignment-propagation method (extract_kitaita_
grammar.py's own docstring already called this a "hypothesis, not a
fact"), it just wasn't visible/cross-checked in the review page.

**Added a second, independent signal that genuinely comes from
agreement WITHIN Kitaita text** (`kitaita_agreement_evidence.py`):
this project's own candidate Kitaita subject-marker-by-class table
(induced in multi_version_verb_paradigm.py from cross-version verb-
paradigm contrast, not reference grammar) is used to check whether a
Kitaita noun hypothesized to be class C co-occurs, in the SAME verse,
with another word starting with that class's candidate subject-marker
prefix -- i.e. a real subject-verb agreement check on the Kitaita
side, structurally identical to what verse_evidence.py already does
for Swahili (just with an unverified, induced prefix table instead of
reference grammar, and explicitly labelled as a prefix-match
consistency check, not a verb detector, since no Kitaita POS tagger
exists). Candidate prefixes available for 14/15 classes: {1:u, 2:wi,
3/11:ku, 4/9:i, 5:w, 6/10:r, 7:ch, 8:ve, 15:ghu}. Result: 754/1040
Kitaita noun candidates (72.5%) have at least one verse with a
matching class-prefix co-occurrence.

**Spot-checked, not just trusted the aggregate**: mungu(class 1/2)->
mlungu finds "Mlungu ukawona..." / "Mlungu ukaghamba..." -- clean,
plausible class-1 subject agreement (u-) on two different verbs,
unambiguous (no competing class prefix nearby). mtu(ANIMATE-SG)->
mundu finds "...Mlungu ukammbanga uo mundu..." -- same pattern,
plausible. But mti(class 3)->mudi's match ("Kubonye madhabahu ya mudi
ghwa mgholeka" = "build an altar of wood") is very likely a FALSE
POSITIVE: "kubonye" there is an imperative/infinitive verb form (the
Swahili infinitive/class-15 ku- prefix), not class-3 subject agreement
with "mudi" at all -- the two concord functions happen to share a
surface prefix. Reported honestly as an example of exactly the
coincidental-prefix-match risk this check's own labelling warns about;
not filtered out, since the native speaker reviewing the page can see
the actual verse text and judge it directly (same "flag, don't guess,
let a human see the real example" principle as the rest of this
pipeline).

**Fixed one more real bug while building this**: the first version of
`check_agreement` looked up `prefix_by_class.get(str(hypothesized_
class))` directly, but many noun-class labels are COMBINED ("1/2",
"3/4", "9/10") while `prefix_by_class` is keyed by single class
numbers -- every combined-label noun silently got "no candidate
prefix" even when one of its two component classes had one. Fixed by
reusing `verse_evidence.resolve_classes` (hard rule #10: extend, don't
fork) to resolve a combined label into its component classes before
lookup, checking every resolved class with a candidate prefix and
reporting which specific one the found evidence supports. This alone
raised the agreement-check hit rate from 246/1036 to 754/1040 --
confirms it was a real coverage bug, not just "most nouns have no
agreement signal".

**Page changes**: Page 2's summary now states plainly that the
Kitaita class is a hypothesis copied from alignment, cross-checked
where possible against this within-Kitaita signal. Each noun row's
summary line shows "alignment-only" vs "&#10003; agreement" at a
glance; the expanded detail shows the actual verse(s) and matched
word for the within-Kitaita check, separately from the Swahili-side
agreement evidence, so the two are never visually conflated. Page 3
now also lists the candidate Kitaita subject-marker-by-class table
directly (`kitaita_subject_marker_by_class`).

## 2026-10-07 (cont. 5): native-speaker correction to the Kitaita TAM
table (conditional ki/ka, perfect da, past re/de, present we/zero,
future cha -- replaces the earlier induced uki-/wada-/ore-ieghe
guess), used to (1) improve verb translation matching by aligning at
the ROOT level instead of whole surface forms, and (2) investigate the
conditioning rule for the two allomorphic pairs (ki/ka, re/de),
including which specific nouns/subject-markers correlate with each
variant, per direct user request.

**New module** `kitaita_tam_allomorphy.py`:
- `KITAITA_TAM_VARIANTS`: the corrected table, keyed by label with the
  attested variant(s) (empty string = zero-marked).
- `decompose_kitaita_verb`: SM + TAM-variant + root + FV decomposer for
  Kitaita, parallel to extract_swahili_grammar.py's Swahili one, using
  the existing candidate SM-by-class table. Prefers the longest SM+TAM
  match so an explicit TAM always wins over the always-available
  zero-marked "present" reading when one fits.
- Applied to the full pooled Kitaita vocabulary (min_freq=2): 4811 word
  types decomposed; by label (word-TYPE counts, not occurrence-
  weighted): present/zero 3432, conditional 989, future 357, past 30,
  perfect 3. (Occurrence-weighted conditional alone: ka=7512, ki=1032
  -- types vs occurrences differ because frequent words dominate
  occurrence counts; both are reported, not conflated.)

**(1) Root-level verb-translation alignment** (`extract_root_sets` +
`align_roots`): strips subject+TAM from BOTH Swahili and Kitaita verb
tokens first, then re-runs the same Dice-coefficient verse-co-
occurrence method on ROOT sets instead of whole surface words --
pools every inflection of a root into one count. Result: 2359 Kitaita
roots aligned (588 with kitaita_count>=8). Concrete before/after,
checked directly: Swahili root 'kuw' (be) was a weak, FRAGMENTED
signal at the surface-form level (Dice 0.26-0.61 spread across a
dozen distinct inflected forms, kitaita_verb_paradigms.json's old
"orekoghe"/"uchakaia" guesses). At the root level, Kitaita 'kai'
is the single dominant partner for 'kuw' -- 228 shared verses, next-
best competitor ('ish') only 75 -- even though the raw Dice ratio
(0.182) undershoots the word-level threshold (0.25) simply because
'kai' and 'kuw' are both extremely frequent (kc=1477, sc=1028
verse-presence counts), which mechanically caps Dice regardless of
real signal strength. Lowered the root-level min_dice to 0.15
specifically because this was checked directly before loosening the
threshold, not assumed. Folded into Page 1's verb table as
'root_level_kitaita_candidates' (now primary), with the old per-
surface-form aggregate kept alongside for comparison.

**(2) Allomorphy investigation** (`investigate_allomorphy`): tabulates,
for each variant, which Kitaita subject-marker prefix co-occurs with
it, and which specific Kitaita noun candidate appears earlier in the
same verse (fixed a real bug while building this: used list.index(t)
inside a for-t-in-list loop, which always returns the FIRST occurrence
of a repeated token instead of the current position -- fixed with
enumerate()).
- **Conditional ki/ka: NOT simple allomorphy of one category.** 'ka'
  outnumbers 'ki' ~7-8:1 in occurrences, and BOTH variants occur after
  EVERY subject-marker class (not cleanly class-split) -- the opposite
  of what phonologically-conditioned allomorphy should look like.
  Spot-checked real examples instead of trusting the aggregate: 'ka'
  examples are narrative chains ("Mlungu ukaghamba..." "Mlungu
  ukawona..." = "and then God said/saw..."); 'ki' examples are
  simultaneous/manner clauses ("...ukimzera" = "saying to him", i.e.
  "while saying"). This is the SAME distinction Swahili itself makes
  with its own -ka- (narrative/consecutive) vs -ki- (conditional/
  temporal/converbal) -- already flagged as a plausible shared
  retention in this project's 2026-10-05 findings. Put to the user as
  a hypothesis to confirm: ki/ka may be two DIFFERENT grammatical
  categories, not two allomorphs of one "conditional" slot.
- **Past re/de: DOES look subject-marker-conditioned.** Class 8
  ('ve-'): re in 60/61 (98%). Class 3/11 ('ku-'): de in 55/61 (90%).
  Class 2 ('wi-'): de in 15/15 (100%). Class 15 ('ghu-'): re in 6/6
  (100%). Classes 1 ('u-', n=7) and 4/9 ('i-', n=9) too thin to
  characterize (project rule: no claims on n<8) -- reported as counts
  only. Caveat found and flagged, not hidden: some 'de' matches likely
  collide with roots that themselves start with the syllable 'de-'
  (e.g. 'kudedanya' = "to converse" -- the root is 'dedany-', not a
  real past-tense 'de'), the same kind of segmentation ambiguity
  already documented for Swahili's class-5 'li-' vs the past-tense
  '-li-' marker.

Page 3 now shows the corrected TAM table, both allomorphy
investigations (subject-marker breakdown, governing-noun lists,
example sentences with the matched word highlighted) for direct
native-speaker confirmation. Page 1's verb table now leads with the
root-level candidate.

`render_html.py` (extended); `kitaita_concord_review.html`
(republished, same Artifact URL, now version 7).

## 2026-10-07 (cont. 6): rebuilt Kitaita noun classification FROM
SCRATCH, per direct user instruction -- "don't rely on any of the
swahili groupings let's build them from scratch" -- after the user
gave a concrete falsifying example: Swahili 'siku' (day) is class
9/10 (one shared form for singular and plural, concord ya/za), but
its two Kitaita translations are 'ituku' (singular) and 'matuku'
(plural) -- an i-/ma- shape alternation that is the classic Bantu 5/6
pattern, not 9/10 -- and the user predicted they take DIFFERENT
agreement ("ituku uses ja and matuku a different one").

**Confirmed directly, first, before building anything**: the word
immediately following 'ituku' across 262 pooled occurrences is 'ja'/
'jija'/'jeni'/'jimu'/'jimweri' (71% share, one "j-" series, 9 distinct
follower types); the word after 'matuku' across 401 occurrences is
'ghose'/'gha'/'ghapo'/'ghake'/'ghawo' (66% share, one "gh-" series,
12 types). Two different concord series -- the user was right.

**New module** `kitaita_noun_class_induction.py`, two independent,
purely Kitaita-internal signals, no Swahili class used to decide
anything:
1. **Follower-marker discovery**: for each candidate Kitaita noun,
   the word immediately following each occurrence (the standard Bantu
   associative/possessive/demonstrative/quantifier diagnostic slot);
   looks for a dominant SHARED INITIAL-CONSONANT CLUSTER across its
   most frequent followers, requiring >=2 distinct follower word
   TYPES (not one repeated word) to call it a real series rather than
   a collocation. First version was polluted by generic connectives
   ('na' "and" follows 36.2% of ALL 914 candidate nouns regardless of
   class, 'kwa' 23.1% -- vs every real class-marker candidate found so
   far sitting at 4.6-7.5%) -- fixed empirically (not via any Swahili
   category): a word that follows >=10% of all candidate nouns is
   excluded as a generic connective before looking for a dominant
   marker.
2. **Subject-marker discovery** (reuses kitaita_tam_allomorphy.py's
   decomposer, per the user's own suggestion to "use subject markers
   to investigate farther"): for each noun, which subject-marker
   prefix the verb in the next 1-2 tokens most often carries.
3. Clusters nouns PRIMARILY by the follower-marker signature (the
   better-powered signal); subject-marker and the OLD Swahili-copied
   class are attached per cluster as comparison/corroborating
   evidence only, never used to split a cluster the follower marker
   already formed.

**Validated beyond the siku case**: mundu (person) -> follower 'u-'
(38%, n=642); mlungu (God) -> follower 'w-' (33%, n=2043) -- these
overlap/alternate (w~u, a plausible phonological conditioning, not
pinned down) but both differ cleanly from mudi (tree) -> 'gh(w)-'
(81%, n=73) and from ituku/isanga's 'j-' series -- i.e. the method
recovers sensible, differentiated groupings on known cases, not just
noise. isanga (land, Swahili class 9/10 like siku) ALSO groups with
ituku's 'j-' series (77%, n=674) -- i.e. isanga may be the SAME
Kitaita class as ituku, independent of what either is in Swahili.
mkake (wife) correctly comes back "no dominant marker" (its most
frequent followers are proper names -- Sara, Rebeka -- not a concord
particle, an honest real limitation of this text genre, not hidden).

**Scope limit disclosed, not hidden**: the candidate-noun LIST itself
is still sourced from the existing Swahili-alignment data (deciding
WHICH Kitaita words are worth checking at all, from zero, is a
separate and much bigger problem, not attempted) -- only the CLASS
ASSIGNMENT is now 100% from within-Kitaita evidence. 918 candidate
nouns checked; 66 clusters found; ~327 nouns have no clear marker
either way (insufficient occurrences or no dominant series),
honestly reported rather than forced into a class.

**Page restructure**: Page 2 now opens with "Kitaita classes (from
scratch)" as the PRIMARY tab (case-study callout, searchable per-noun
table showing follower marker + subject marker + the old class for
comparison only, plus the cluster overview). The original Swahili-
centric view moved to a new "2b" tab, explicitly relabelled as the
old, superseded method, kept only as a comparison baseline.

`render_html.py` (extended); `kitaita_concord_review.html`
(republished, same Artifact URL, now version 8).

**Two-check filter added** (`classify_word_quality`,

1. Does the word decompose with an EXPLICIT, non-zero Kitaita TAM

   prefix and ending in a vowel (true of most Bantu words, nouns very
   much included) -- it even matched 'ituku' and 'isanga', the two
   nouns from the case study that motivated the whole page. A first
   version used ANY verb-shaped match (including zero) and wrongly

2. The existing alignment-confidence tier (high/medium/low, from

   be caught by either check).

Result: 408 words kept as reliable noun candidates (feed the

-- shown, not dropped, each tagged with WHY (likely-verb + its

## 2026-10-07 (cont. 9): built a sentence GENERATOR using every rule
this project has produced so far -- noun translation, root-level verb
alignment, the native-speaker-corrected TAM table, the from-scratch
noun classes' subject markers -- to turn hand-decomposed Swahili
sentences into Kitaita, per direct user request. New module
`kitaita_sentence_generator.py`; new `page4_sentence_generation.json`
/ Page 4 ("Generate a sentence") on the review artifact.

Not a general Swahili parser -- each Swahili verb is hand-decomposed
(SM+TAM+root+FV) since no Swahili morphological analyser exists in
this project beyond the existing greedy decomposer. Every substitution
step is traced with its own evidence (Dice, shared-verse count,
support count) so a wrong step is visible, not hidden.

**3 worked examples, deliberately chosen to show a clean success, a
real failure mode, and the current limit of the evidence base:**

1. "Mungu akasema." (And God said.) -> generated "**Mlungu
   ukaghamba.**" -- this INDEPENDENTLY RECONSTRUCTS a sentence
   already directly attested in the real corpus (Genesis 1:6),
   purely by composing noun translation + root-level verb alignment +
   the corrected TAM table + subject marker. Strongest validation
   available that these substitutions do something real. One real
   phonological rule found and applied along the way: Kitaita class-
   "w" subject marker surfaces as 'u-' before a consonant-initial TAM
   (never "wkaghamba" -- confirmed against the real attested form,
   not guessed) and stays 'w-' before a vowel-initial one -- standard
   Bantu glide alternation.
2. "Mtu akaona mti." (And the man saw a tree.) -> generated "Mundu
   wichawona mudi." -- demonstrates a REAL FAILURE MODE, not hidden:
   root-level alignment found NO Kitaita candidate for Swahili root
   'on' (see), because the unrelated root 'kuw' (be) is so frequent
   it statistically outranks the correct answer in the verse-co-
   occurrence comparison (checked directly: Kitaita root 'won'
   co-occurs with 'kuw' in 32 verses vs only 18 with 'on' -- the same
   frequency-dilution problem already seen with 'na'/'kwa' as
   generic connectives, now affecting a VERB root instead of a
   function word). Falls back to the weaker per-surface-form method,
   which returns a full inflected word ('wichawona') with the WRONG
   person/number/tense (future, 3rd plural) for this sentence --
   used as-is and flagged, not silently corrected to look clean.
3. "Mti ulikuwa mzuri." (The tree was good.) -> generated "Mudi
   idekaia." -- both the subject-marker choice (n=30, 33% coverage)
   and the past-tense choice (n=6, below this project's own n=8
   confidence rule) are thin and flagged in the trace. The adjective
   step ('mzuri') could not be completed at all -- no confirmed
   Kitaita adjective-concord table exists yet for any class -- and is
   reported as an explicit gap rather than guessed.

Files: `kitaita_sentence_generator.py` (new); `build_pages.py`,
`render_html.py` (extended -- new Page 4 tab); `kitaita_concord_
review.html` (republished, same Artifact URL, now version 11).

**Found and fixed a real scraper bug while doing this**: `bible_
collect.py`'s "next chapter" detection broke at EVERY book boundary.
bible.com's own "Next Chapter" link at a book's last chapter points
to the NEXT BOOK'S INTRO page (e.g. "EXO.INTRO1"), not its chapter 1
-- the existing regex required a plain chapter number and didn't
match "INTRO1", so `next` silently resolved to None and the scrape
stopped. This had NEVER been exercised before: the original GEN+EXO+
PSA pass pulled each book via its own separate --start command, so
automatic chaining across a book boundary was never actually tested
until this run (confirmed directly: re-parsing the same cached GEN.50
page reproduced `next=None` before the fix, `next='EXO.1'` after).
Fixed by recognizing the INTRO-page pattern and mapping it to that
book's chapter 1 (the intro page itself is editorial, not canonical
text, so it is skipped, not fetched).

Verified version completeness via bible.com's own version-metadata
API before scraping (not assumed): all 4 versions (2138/164/1627/74)
report the full 66-book, 1189-chapter canon.

coverage), and repointed multi_version_pipeline.py's VERSIONS list at
the new full-corpus parallel directories.

## 2026-10-07 (cont. 11): built the focused correction workflow the
user asked for, replacing "comb through giant tables" with "judge one
generated sentence at a time, correct it if wrong, feed the
correction back into specific rule diagnoses."

**`kitaita_sentence_batch.py`** (new): generates a deliberately
DIVERSE batch of 22 Swahili->Kitaita sentence pairs (via kitaita_
sentence_generator.py) -- spanning multiple noun classes (mungu,
mtu, mti, siku, nchi, mwana, samaki, nyumba), multiple tenses
(narrative -ka-, past, present, future), a couple of already-known-
weak verbs (on/see) included on purpose, and 4 adjective trials
specifically because no Kitaita adjective-concord table exists yet --
any correction there is new data, not a mismatch.

**Found and fixed 2 real bugs in kitaita_sentence_generator.py while
building this**:
1. A sentinel dict key ("(no subject-marker data)", used internally
   by kitaita_noun_class_induction.py to bucket nouns with no SM
   evidence) was leaking into generated sentences as literal text
   ("Nyumba (no subject-marker data)kaghamba.") -- the lookup-table
   builder now explicitly skips that bucket.
2. The full-Bible subject-marker re-induction (cont. 10) often
   returns a BARE CONSONANT ('k', 'gh') rather than a consonant+vowel
   form, which cannot concatenate onto a consonant-initial TAM
   without an illegal cluster ("k"+"ka"="kka"). This is a genuine,
   UNSOLVED morphophonology gap -- not invented away: a default
   linking vowel ('u') is now inserted and the result is explicitly
   flagged in the trace as a GUESS needing confirmation, rather than
   either crashing or silently presenting "kkaghamba" as clean output.

**Published as a SEPARATE, dedicated artifact** (deliberately not
mixed into the big review page, per the user's own stated reason --
"too much data to comb through"): **Kitaita Sentence Judge**,
https://claude.ai/artifact/2gKgkwb1N4azwfjiso1KNv -- one sentence
card at a time, Correct/Wrong buttons, a correction textarea + note
field that only appears on "Wrong", a progress bar, dot navigation,
and a collapsed-by-default "Show reasoning" trace for anyone curious.
Judgments save to this artifact's own db (`judgments` collection).

**`kitaita_correction_analysis.py`** (new): given a batch of
judgments pulled from that db, reinterprets each "wrong" + correction
into a SPECIFIC rule diagnosis by decomposing the corrected Kitaita
verb with the same decomposer the generator uses, then diffing
component-by-component against what was actually generated (recorded
structurally in a new `components` field on every generator output,
not just prose) -- noun translation, subject marker (by class),
TAM marker, verb-root translation, or (when the generator had no
root-level candidate at all, as for 'ona'/see) a brand-new candidate
root translation. Aggregates matching diagnoses across multiple
judgments into proposals, explicitly NOT auto-applying anything to
any table -- a single correction is a lead, not an update (same
spirit as the project's existing n<8 rule, calibrated down to n>=3
agreeing corrections here since each one is a much higher-quality
signal than a corpus co-occurrence count). Self-tested with 2
synthetic (clearly-labelled, not real) corrections to confirm the
diagnosis logic fires correctly before any real judgment exists:
correctly identified a subject-marker mismatch (generated 'ku',
corrected 'ji', for siku/class 9) and correctly recognized a
corrected verb as new root-translation data (root 'on'/see had no
existing candidate at all).

**Not yet done**: no real judgments exist yet -- this all needs the
native speaker to actually use the Judge page. Once judgments come
in, re-run kitaita_correction_analysis.py against them (via
ArtifactData against the Judge artifact's db) to get real proposals.

Files: `kitaita_sentence_batch.py`, `kitaita_correction_analysis.py`
(new); `kitaita_sentence_generator.py` (2 bug fixes + new
`components` field); `sentence_judging_batch.json` (new);
`kitaita_sentence_judge.html` (new, published as a separate Artifact).

sentences (s12/13/33/38) when caught by the regression check. Fixed

mechanism already used for ituku/isanga/nyumba/samaki) -- 5 separate
correct judgments (s12/13/22/33/38/52) directly confirm 'u-', vastly
outweighing one noisy corpus vote. No backup of the pre-rerun JSON
exists (project has no version control) -- the override IS the fix.
Lesson: don't leave `build_pages.py` running unsupervised for an
unrelated question again -- it is the canonical full pipeline, not a
narrow utility, and reruns it non-deterministically.

**Present tense: reverse the cont.14 corpus-frequency default.**
Batch 3 confirmed the zero-marked present (corpus-dominant, cont. 14)
is grammatical but NOT what the speaker wants generated by default --
5 corrections (s42/44/45/46/52) all added the '-we-' TAM syllable back
in, and s42's own note says the zero form is "still correct" but
asks to "match Swahili on this rule" (Swahili's own -na- is explicit).
`PRESENT_TAM_DEFAULT` flipped from zero to "we" -- a style choice, not
a correctness fix; zero stays documented as the corpus-dominant,
also-valid alternative. The underlying subject-marker-vowel rule
itself (consonant fixed, vowel -> 'a' before present) was independently
RECONFIRMED by every noun in this batch, including 'gha-' (not
'ghwa-') for mti -- the cont. 14 corpus-grounded glide fix was right.

**'kuwa' (be) past tense: no governing rule -- alternate.** Direct
user instruction: "we got wrong the kuwa verb it is -ka and then the
past tense is deka. Also I see koghe also maps to kuwa. I do not see
a general rule for when to use which and we can just alternate for
now." Confirmed from the data: BOTH 'kogh'+TAM'-re-'+fv'e' and
'dek'+zero-TAM+fv'a' are real, attested past-tense realizations of
'kuwa', and nothing found so far (adjective presence, class, tense)
cleanly predicts which a given noun takes -- nyumba's own BARE
existential (no adjective at all) uses 'dek' ("Nyumba redeka", s17),
which is exactly the case the project's old "adjective=dek,
none=kogh" rule said should be 'kogh'. Replaced that rule with
`KUWA_PAST_ALTERNATES` (both full root+TAM+fv patterns, since TAM and
final vowel are COUPLED to which root is picked, not independent) --
the generator still defaults to 'kogh' for continuity on new combos,
but the trace now explicitly says this is an unconfirmed, arbitrary
pick, not a confirmed rule, per direct instruction.

**'kuwa' future tense: a third, different root.** s53 ("Nyumba
itakuwa" -> "Nyumba ichaka") confirms the future form is SM + TAM
'-cha-' + a bare root 'k' + fv 'a' -- NOT 'kogh'+'cha'+'e' as the
generator previously assumed (extending the one existing future
example, nchi's "jichakoghe" from s11, which predates this finding
and was never re-asked -- flagged, not silently changed). Generator
now branches future 'kuwa' separately from past/bare 'kuwa'.

**Samaki has a singular/plural subject-marker split the project had
been treating as noise.** Direct user correction: "for samaki in
singular form uses e/i and in plural form uses ra/re/ri." Swahili
'samaki' (fish) doesn't mark number, so every test sentence was
silently ambiguous, and the speaker answered either way across
judgments: PLURAL ('ri'/'ra'/'re') in 7 of 8 judged samaki sentences
(the existing default), SINGULAR ('e'/'i') in exactly 1 (s48,
"Samaki edeka izamie"). This also broke the new `BAYA_STEM`
generalized adjective rule, which had predicted the plural 'rizamie'
for s48 -- the real answer used the singular prefix. `BAYA_STEM` now
explicitly EXCLUDES samaki (flags the ambiguity and defaults to
singular, since that's the one confirmed data point for this specific
adjective) rather than silently applying the general rule to a noun
it's already been shown to get wrong.

**'kubwa' (big) needed a noun-keyed table, not a class-keyed one.**
s51 ("Nyumba ilikuwa -kubwa" -> "Nyumba edeka mbaa") confirms nyumba
takes 'mbaa' (the same form as mungu/mti), NOT nchi's 'ibaa' --
despite nyumba and nchi sharing the Swahili "9/10" class label in
every spec. `VERIFIED_ADJECTIVES` was keyed by (stem, Swahili class),
which would have silently collided the two answers; rekeyed to
(stem, Swahili SUBJECT NOUN) instead -- the same "same label,
different real Kitaita class" pattern this project keeps finding
(siku/matuku, mtu/samaki), now also true of 'kubwa' concord.

**One more exact-form fix, one unresolved inconsistency flagged, not
reconciled.** s50 ("Siku ilikuwa -baya" -> "Ituku jideka jizamie")
fixes a real bug: the generated "jidedeka" has a spurious extra TAM
syllable that doesn't belong; the real zero-TAM "[vowel]+dek+a"
pattern matches mtu/mwana/nyumba/samaki-singular exactly. BUT nchi's
own s26 ("Isanga jidedeka jizamie") uses the SAME "jidedeka" pattern
this correction just said is wrong, and was never flagged as wrong
for nchi (only the missing adjective word was corrected there) --
nchi and siku share subject marker 'ji' and the same root, so this is
a direct, unreconciled contradiction between two judgments, not a
different class. Kept as two separate exact overrides; flagged for a
future re-ask, not silently merged either way.

Regression-checked against all 52 checkable judgments after every
fix: 0 mismatches (the mwana regression above was the only real
breakage, caught and fixed before publishing anything).
