## 2026-10-07 (cont. 18): direct question -- "are these rules
generalizing to class level or specific to the noun?" -- answered by
auditing each rule against where it's coded and how many distinct
nouns/markers actually confirm it, then prepared batch 5 to test the
weakest links directly with brand-new nouns.

**Audit result** (see chat for the full per-rule table): the rules
ARE coded at the subject-marker level (keyed by marker string, not by
noun) for present-tense vowel shift, 'baya' (BAYA_STEM), and 'kubwa'
(KUBWA_IBAA_SM) -- any noun sharing a marker automatically gets the
same answer. The future-'kuwa' bare-root-'k' and past-existential
'kogh'-default rules are tied to the ROOT 'kuw', not really to class
at all, and are confirmed across EVERY marker tried (u/gh/ji/ri) --
the most general findings so far. BUT breadth of confirmation varies
a lot per marker: 'u' has 3 nouns confirming most rules, 'ji' has 2,
while 'gh' and 'ri' each have only the ONE original noun (mti,
samaki) -- meaning for those two markers, "class-level" was really
only a hypothesis extrapolated from n=1 until now. Also flagged: the
copula 'dek' SM-vowel is NOT cleanly class-level -- mtu/mwana (same
marker 'u') agree with each other, but mungu (ALSO marker 'u')
disagrees with itself across 2 judgments, so that specific
inconsistency is noun-specific (mungu), not explained by class.

**Batch 5 built specifically to test this** (`ROUND_5_SPECS`, 10 new
sentences, s63-s72): three BRAND NEW nouns, never used in any prior
batch, each independently confirmed (via page2_noun_classes.json's
raw induction, not assumed) to share a marker with an already-tested
noun -- 'malaika' (angel, marker 'u', same as mlungu/mundu/mwana),
'mfupa'/'indi' (bone, marker 'j', same as isanga/ituku), 'msalaba'
(cross, marker 'gh', same as mudi). All three have independently
high-confidence Kitaita translations (dice 0.80-0.95). Tests present
tense + future 'kuwa' + 'baya' + 'kubwa' on malaika (u-class, pushing
it to 4 confirming nouns if right), future 'kuwa' + past existential +
'kubwa' on mfupa (j-class, pushing 'kogh'-default and KUBWA_IBAA_SM to
a 3rd confirming noun), and future 'kuwa' + past existential + present
tense on msalaba (gh-class, the FIRST test of anything beyond mti for
that marker).

**Found and fixed one more real bug while building this**: 'indi'
(the brand-new j-class noun) inherits its subject marker directly
from the RAW induction as a bare consonant 'j' (never speaker-
confirmed to a vowel, unlike isanga/ituku's hand-corrected 'ji') --
the bare-consonant linking-vowel check only looked at whether `kit_tam`
was consonant-initial, missing the ZERO-TAM case entirely (every
copula 'dek' answer is zero-TAM), so a bare 'j' directly followed the
consonant-initial root 'dek', producing the illegal cluster "jdeka".
Fixed by checking the NEXT SOUND generically (TAM if present,
otherwise the root) rather than just TAM. Regression-checked against
all 61 known judgments after the fix: 0 mismatches.

## 2026-10-08: first/second-person sentences -- a genuinely new
capability, not just another noun/class combination. Direct user
request: "let's check first and second person sentences to see how
they work." Every prior round (s0-s72) only ever generated 3RD-person
sentences -- `translate()` always required a Swahili subject NOUN,
and no one had looked at "I"/"you"/"we"/"you-pl" at all.

**Corpus investigation first** (per CLAUDE.md's "never claim a
model/corpus covers a phenomenon without checking directly" and this
project's own "analyse before intervene" method), new file
`kitaita_person_marker_investigation.py`: scanned the full 5207-verse
parallel corpus for Swahili 1st/2nd-person-marked verbs on roots this
project already trusts a Kitaita correspondence for (sema/ona/jua/
simama/sikia/fanya), read the subject-marker prefix off the aligned
Kitaita verb. Two real methodology bugs caught and fixed WHILE
building this (documented in the script, not just fixed silently):
(1) a lazy prefix-capture regex with no left word-boundary anchor
found the STEM's own start instead of the WORD's start, silently
losing the prefix (e.g. "namanya" -> captured "" instead of "na");
(2) verses with 2+ person-marked forms of the SAME Swahili root (e.g.
GEN.26.9 has both "ulisema" and "nalisema") make it impossible to
tell which Kitaita hit belongs to which -- now dropped rather than
silently misattributed (4 matches dropped this way).

**Clean result: future tense only**, consistent across every root
tried, zero counterexamples (after excluding the 'fanya'/'bony' root's
own irregular bare-'ku-' future as a per-lexeme TAM quirk, same
pattern as 'kuwa' already having its own irregular future -- not
counted against the person-marker finding):
  1sg ni- + -cha- + ROOT + a   (nichamanya/nichadeda/nichasikira, n=7+)
  2sg ku- + -cha- + ROOT + a   (kuchawona/kuchamghoria[+obj infix], n>=3)
  1pl di- + -cha- + ROOT + a   (dichaghamba/dichasikira, n=2)
  2pl m-  + -cha- + ROOT + a   (mchamanya x2, n=2)
This is NOT a new TAM rule -- it's the SAME already-confirmed
future "-ta- -> -cha-" mapping; only the person-marker CONSONANT is
new. Present tense has exactly ONE usable data point across all 4
persons (1sg "ninajua"->"namanya", consistent with the ALREADY-
confirmed "vowel->'a' before present" rule, just never tested on a
person marker -- n=1, flagged not confident). Past tense is thin and
entangled with an already-unresolved general TAM-realization puzzle
(extra '-ieghe'/'-eghe' suffix on some past forms, never resolved for
3rd person either) -- deliberately NOT given a rule.

**IMPORTANT distinction from every table so far**: these person-marker
entries are corpus-induced only, NOT native-speaker-verified -- kept
in a separate table (`PERSON_SUBJECT_MARKERS_FUTURE_HYPOTHESIS`,
`PERSON_PRESENT_SM_HYPOTHESIS` in `kitaita_verified_corrections.py`)
specifically so they are never confused with `VERIFIED_SUBJECT_
MARKERS`'s "trusted even at n=1" tier, which is direct human
correction.

**Extended `kitaita_sentence_generator.translate()`** with a new
`person=` parameter ("1sg"/"2sg"/"1pl"/"2pl") used instead of
`swahili_subject_noun` -- reuses every existing TAM/root branch
unchanged, only the subject-marker lookup source differs. Two things
had to be handled specially, not just left to fall through: (1)
Kitaita is pro-drop in every clean corpus example (no separate
pronoun word ever appears next to the verb prefix) -- output is the
inflected verb alone, not a fabricated independent-pronoun word with
zero evidence; (2) the generic bare-consonant linking-vowel GUESS
(built for the noun-class induction's unconfirmed bare consonants)
would have wrongly inserted an unattested vowel into 2pl's bare 'm-'
before a consonant-initial TAM ("m-cha-" -> guessed "mu-cha-") --
excluded for the person path specifically, since 'm-cha-' already has
its own direct corpus attestation, not a guess needing a linking
vowel at all. Present tense for person subjects also does NOT inherit
the noun-class generator's "-we-" stylistic default (a preference
confirmed only for noun-class subjects, batch 3) -- the one real
person-marker data point is zero-marked, so zero is used instead of
silently carrying over an unrelated style choice.

**Batch 6** (`ROUND_6_SPECS`, 12 new sentences, s73-s84): future tense
across all 4 persons x sem/on/ju roots plus the 'kuwa' existential
future on 1sg/2sg (testing whether the hypothesis generalizes beyond
the exact items the corpus evidence showed); present tense 1sg (the
n=1 hypothesis) and 2sg (deliberately ZERO evidence -- generator
outputs the explicitly-flagged "?manya"); past existential 1sg
(deliberately ZERO evidence -- outputs "?rekoghe"). The last 3 are
included on purpose, same philosophy as every prior batch: a weak
spot where ANY native-speaker answer is new information, not just
confirmation.

All 12 generated without error; spot-checked predictions: Nitajua.->
Nichamanya., Utaona.->Kuchawona., Tutasema.->Dichaghamba., Mtajua.->
Mchamanya., Nitakuwa.->Nichaka., Utakuwa.->Kuchaka., Ninajua.->
Namanya., Unajua.->?manya., Nilikuwa.->?rekoghe.

`PERSON_SUBJECT_MARKERS_BY_TAM`, keyed by `(person, tam_category)` --
the same kind of relationship `PRESENT_SM_VOWEL_CONFIRMED` and

- 2sg PRESENT: 1 data point ("unajua"->"kumanyagha") -- consonant

  "nereghambieghe"/"nereobueghe" -- vowel i->e before Kitaita's '-re-'
  TAM, the FRONT-VOWEL mirror of kogh_re_o_shift's back-vowel u->o,
  but explicitly NOT the same mechanism -- noun-class 'ji'/'ri'
  markers are confirmed to stay unchanged before '-re-', so person

  conflict: 'dere' (n=1, matches the i->e pattern) vs 'da' (n=2,
  looks zero/narrative) -- 'dere' kept as the default (cross-person
  consistency), 'da' kept as a flagged alternate, same style as
  `KUWA_PAST_ALTERNATES`.
- 2sg NARRATIVE (-ka-, not -li-/-re-): 1 data point ("ulisikia"->
  "ukasikira" -- Kitaita rendered a Swahili past as its own narrative
  tense, another instance of the already-documented "Kitaita text
  doesn't always mirror the Swahili TAM" finding) -- consonant DROPS
  from the future form's 'ku' to bare 'u' before '-ka-' specifically
  (plausibly haplology, ku+ka avoiding two k-initial syllables, but
  reported as a surface fact only, no mechanism asserted).

Rewired `kitaita_sentence_generator.translate()`'s person path to do
ONE lookup against the unified table (keyed by the Kitaita TAM
category, with "ka" checked directly since `TAM_SWAHILI_TO_LABEL` has
no entry for Swahili's narrative -ka-) instead of two separate hand-
written branches -- the present-tense branch no longer re-derives
`kit_sm`, it just applies the zero-vs-'-we-' TAM choice to whatever
the unified lookup already set. Regression-verified by hand: 1sg/1pl
past existential now compose through the EXISTING `is_kuwa_pastlike`
branch unchanged and correctly produce "Nerekoghe."/"Derekoghe." (SM

SHAPE, just with a person marker instead of a class marker); 2sg

pattern). Future-tense predictions (s73-s81) are unchanged -- this
was a restructuring of HOW the lookup works, not a change to that
cell's values.

## 2026-10-08 (cont. 3): direct user catch -- "example 86 is very
confusing[,] Ndege inaogopa chui[.] Ndege i -> refers to aeroplane
but ogopa chui guides one to a bird so I think it might be testing
the wrong thing." Right, and checking it directly surfaced something
more specific than just a confusing gloss.

**Checked the full-Bible corpus directly** (parallel_full_suv, 31102
verses -- the smaller Genesis/Exodus/Psalms file this project's other
scripts use doesn't even contain 'chui' at all, which is why that one
wasn't used for this check): 'ndege' NEVER takes the shape-class 9/10
marker ('i-'/'zi-') as a subject in this corpus. Every real
occurrence uses the ANIMATE marker ('a-'/'wa-': "ndege waruke",
"ndege arukaye", "ndege wakavila", "ndege watakula", GEN.1.20 through
PSA.104.17). This is a SECOND real Swahili animacy-override noun
this project hadn't catalogued (CLAUDE.md section 5 lists kipepeo/
paka/nyoka/chama) -- 'ndege' (bird) overrides to animate concord over
its shape class, exactly like those. 'chui' (leopard) was already
tagged ANIMATE-SG in the lexicon and is now independently corpus-
confirmed too ("chui atalala"/"chui ataivizia", ISA.11.6/JER.5.6, 'a-'
not 'i-').

**The bug was in the hand-written SWAHILI GLOSS `sm` field**, not in
the Kitaita output -- confirmed directly that `kitaita_sentence_
generator.translate()` never reads `swahili_verb["sm"]` anywhere (grep
came back empty); the Kitaita subject marker is always derived from
the KITAITA noun's own class data. So the generated Kitaita ("Nyonyi
iweobua inge.") was correct the whole time; only the DISPLAYED
Swahili sentence used the wrong (shape-class 'i-') marker instead of
the real animate one, which is exactly what made it read ambiguously
-- 'i-' could plausibly describe an inanimate thing (a plane), while
the grammatically-correct 'a-' could not, so fixing the grammar error
also resolves the "which ndege did you mean" complaint as a direct
side effect: "Ndege anaogopa chui" can only mean the bird.

**Also checked whether KITAITA mirrors either override -- it does
NOT, for either noun.** 'nyonyi' (ndege's Kitaita word) consistently
keeps its OWN 'ri-'/'ra-' class marker in real Kitaita text
("nyonyi nderiburuke", "nyonyi ra mbari rose", GEN.1.20-2.20), never
switching to an animate-style marker; 'inge' (chui's Kitaita word) is
messier (ri-/i-/ya- across different books) but shows no animate
pattern either. Consistent with this project's central null
hypothesis -- Swahili's animacy overrides do not transfer to Kitaita.

**Found 2 more careless `sm` mistakes while re-checking every item
in the same batch for the same class of error** (same corpus-check
method, not assumed): 'sanduku' (box) used 'i-' but is corpus-
confirmed class 5 'li-' ("sanduku la agano la BWANA likatangulia",
NUM.10.33; "sanduku liliposafiri", NUM.10.35); 'kikombe' (cup) used
'i-' but is corpus-confirmed class 7 'ki-' ("kikombe cha Farao",
GEN.40.11; "kikombe kikaonekana", GEN.44.12). Both fixed the same
way -- gloss-only, zero effect on the Kitaita output.

Fixed all 4 (s87 ndege, s89 chui-as-subject, s90 sanduku, s91
kikombe) in `ROUND_7_SPECS`. Regenerated and diffed: every one of
the 4 Kitaita predictions is byte-for-byte unchanged, confirming the
fix really was gloss-only. Regression-checked the other 94
sentences (s0-s86, s88, s92-s97): 0 mismatches. Judge Artifact
republished in place (version 9, still 98 sentences, only the 4
Swahili gloss strings changed). File: `kitaita_sentence_batch.py`
(comment + 4 `sm` values). **Next step**: s73-s97 still need

## 2026-10-08 (cont. 5): restructured the Kitaita Concord Review
artifact (the OTHER artifact, https://claude.ai/artifact/
ArieG4VR7VBmETaDUy3inm -- not the Judge Artifact) into 3 pages per
direct request: Page 1 stays the dictionary as-is; Page 2 is now
Taita noun classes, each with its own subpage (class id, subject-
marker-by-TAM table, adjective prefix); Page 3 is the verb TAM-marker
table. Dropped the old "2b Swahili classes" and "4 Generate a
sentence" tabs to match the 3-page request.

**Page 2 is a genuine upgrade, not just a re-skin**: the OLD page 2
showed the 2026-10-07 from-scratch induction's raw follower-marker
clusters, frozen at that date. The new one groups nouns by their
CURRENT best-known subject marker (kitaita_verified_corrections.py's
VERIFIED_SUBJECT_MARKERS, falling back to the induced dominant marker
only where no override exists) -- which means it reflects every
correction made this session (mwalimu/sanduku/kikombe/mori/shimba all
moved classes). New file `export_grammar_pages.py` builds this as
`page2_classes.json` (7 classes: u/ghu/ji/ri/i/ch/y, 18 member nouns),
with a sanity-check assertion that every member's class matches
VERIFIED_SUBJECT_MARKERS directly (fails loudly on drift rather than
silently). Each class shows: narrative/future/present/past-existential
subject-marker forms with a confidence badge (verified / unresolved-
split / untested) and a short note where relevant (e.g. the ji-class's
genuine ji/je past-tense split, the u-class's mwana exception), plus
the 'baya'/'kubwa' adjective-prefix forms.

Page 3 keeps the native-speaker-corrected TAM table (now with hand-
written meanings per label) and the two allomorphy investigation
sections (ki/ka split, re/de conditioning) -- dropped the raw Swahili-
reference tables and induced-candidate tables, which were either
redundant with Page 2 or superseded noise.

**Method**: surgical edit of the saved full HTML (10MB) via Python
string splicing on unique markers, NOT a full rebuild -- Page 1's
HTML/JS and the shared flag/correction infrastructure (used by Page 1)
are untouched byte-for-byte. Verified before publishing: no leftover
JS references to removed element IDs (would throw and silently halt
later script execution), `node --check` on the extracted inline
`<script>` for syntax validity, and that `page2_classes.json` parses
and matches the live Python data. Page 2's new content is NOT wired
into the existing flag/correction widget (a deliberate scope
simplification -- it's a settled reference now, sourced from already-
judged data, not a fresh hypothesis needing review the way the old
page's raw induction output did).

Files: `export_grammar_pages.py` (new), `page2_classes.json` (new,
generated). Artifact republished in place, version 13.

## 2026-10-08 (cont. 8): RETRACTION. Direct correction: "it is
supposed to be sanduku jerekoghe instead of sanduku jirekoghe" (s110,
"Example 111 in judge"). The db already showed this -- the user had

match, not re-litigate it.

**This overturns cont. 7's reading of the ji/je split, not just one
sentence.** s110 had genuinely been judged "correct" as generated
("Sanduku jirekoghe") at the time cont. 7 processed it, so counting
it as a 3rd "ji" vote (a 2-2 tie) was the right call on the
information available then -- the speaker has now revised that own
earlier judgment, not something this project got wrong by reasoning
badly. With the real answer in hand, the tally is 3 ('je': siku,
mfupa, sanduku) vs 1 ('ji': nchi only) -- 'je' is the real default,
nchi is a flagged exception, not a coin flip.

**Generalized rather than left as another one-off override**: 'ji'
shifting to 'je' before existential 'kogh'+'-re-' is the SAME kind of
front-vowel vowel shift as the already-generalized back-vowel 'u'->
'o' shift (confirmed on mungu/mtu and mti/msalaba) -- just never
connected to it before. Extended `kogh_re_o_shift()` (kitaita_
verified_corrections.py) to handle both, and updated its call site in

only, silently never invoking the function for 'ji' at all -- fixed
to also check `kit_sm == "ji"`). nchi's own exact `VERIFIED_SENTENCES`
override is unaffected (confirmed directly: still generates "Isanga
jirekoghe") since exact overrides take priority before this shift
logic ever runs.

w-glide insertion (ku->kwa) that CROSS-CONFIRMS, independently, this
project's own earlier person-marker finding for 2sg ('ku'->'kwa',

## 2026-10-09: "Let's take a step back to put everything together and
test the end to end pipeline. 1) NLLB and the probes for different
language aspects. 2) Grammar book as is with the various
translations. Connect the pipeline and give a google translate kind
of page... so that we can see how far we have come and how far we
have left to go." This superseded yesterday's "verbs and adjectives"
plan for the session.

**Environment check (direct, not assumed):** `nvidia-smi` fails ("couldn't
communicate with the NVIDIA driver") -- no GPU, CPU-only. `torch`/
`transformers`/`sentencepiece` installed; NLLB-200 600M/1.3B/3.3B all
already cached locally (`~/.cache/huggingface/hub/`). Confirmed real
generation works: `facebook/nllb-200-distilled-1.3B`, CPU, ~2-7s/sentence
(tested directly, not assumed) -- e.g. "The big dog saw the student."
-> "Mbwa mkubwa alimwona mwanafunzi." Artifacts are client-side-only JS
sandboxes (confirmed from the capabilities skill, not assumed) -- cannot
run Python/NLLB, so the real model can only run via a local script.

**Architecture decision, made and acted on (not just proposed):** the
parent project's NLLB-encoder probe track (`nllb_concord_rewrite_
pipeline.py` and siblings) was deliberately NOT wired into this
pipeline. It solves identifying agreement targets inside an EXISTING
Swahili sentence for internal rewriting, not Swahili->Kitaita
generation, and its own prior findings (carried in memory) found the
analogous subject/object attention signal unreliable for exactly the
subject/TAM concord this pipeline needs -- the project's own
deterministic decomposer already covers that need more completely.
Kept as a separate, un-integrated research track; not a regression,
a scoping choice, stated here so it isn't silently forgotten.

**Built, in order:**
1. `kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py` -- a free-text Swahili sentence decomposer
   (subject noun / verb {sm,tam,root,fv} / object noun / adjective),
   reusing `extract_swahili_grammar.py`'s `decompose_verb()`/SM_TABLE/
   TAM_MARKERS, the 319-word lexicon, `page1_vocabulary.json`'s
   high/medium-confidence statistical noun candidates, and `nllb_
   concord_rewrite_pipeline.py`'s ADJ_BASE table (hard rule #10:
   extended existing machinery, didn't fork it) -- feeding the
   existing, UNCHANGED `kitaita_sentence_generator.translate()`. SCOPE
   is explicit and enforced, not implied: exactly one subject, one
   verb, at most one object, at most one of the 2 adjectives
   (`kubwa`/`baya`) this project has concord data for -- anything else
   (coordination, relative clauses, negation, a 2nd modifier, pronoun
   subjects) is FLAGGED in the output, never silently guessed or
   dropped. Plus a lazy-loaded, optional real-NLLB English->Swahili
   leg (`english_to_swahili()`), CPU-only, confirmed working.
2. **Fixed a real, pre-existing gap while testing**: `extract_swahili_
   grammar.py`'s `TAM_MARKERS` had NO entry for Swahili narrative/
   consecutive `-ka-` at all (every `-ka-` sentence failed to
   decompose, e.g. "Mungu akaona"), even though `kitaita_sentence_
   generator.translate()` has had its own dedicated `-ka-` branch for
   a long time. Added `"ka": "narrative/consecutive"` to the shared
   table (not a one-off patch for this script -- a real omission in
   reference-grammar data every caller of `decompose_verb()` shares).
3. **Flagged, did not fix, a real limitation**: `decompose_verb()`
   does not strip infixed object markers (e.g. `-mw-` in "a-li-mw-on-
   a"), so a verb like "alimwona" decomposes to a corrupted root
   ("mwon" instead of "on") that can still accidentally match a WEAK
   statistical root-level candidate (checked directly: Dice 0.22 for
   'mwon'/'kimbi', 0.25 for 'ogop') and silently produce a confident-
   looking but unreliable sentence. Added an explicit flag (`kitaita_
   e2e_pipeline.py`'s `OBJECT_MARKER_RISK_ROOT_DICE_THRESHOLD = 0.4`)
   that fires whenever a non-verified root's best match is this weak,
   naming the specific risk rather than a generic "low confidence"
   note. Object-marker stripping itself remains unsolved (consistent
   with the parent project's own documented gap for `obj`
   identification) -- out of scope to fix today, but now visibly
   flagged instead of silently wrong.
4. Ran the Python pipeline on 6 hand-picked + 2 real-NLLB-sourced
   sentences (not previously tested as free text, only ever as
   `translate()` call-sites in `ROUND_N_SPECS`) -- all behaved exactly
   as the flags above predict: clean sentences translate correctly,
   `-ka-` sentences now work, the one genuinely-missing root ('won',
   Swahili "kuona"'s root with no reliable Kitaita candidate AT ALL in
   this project's own data -- not a decomposer bug, a real gap)
   surfaces as an honest error, not a guess.
5. `export_e2e_js_tables.py` -- dumps every table `translate()`/the
   decomposer actually consult into one 275KB JSON (lexicon, SM/TAM
   tables, ADJ_BASE, trimmed statistical noun/root candidates at
   Dice>=0.15, all VERIFIED_* tables, noun_class_of, past-tense
   allomorphy). Disclosed directly on the resulting page: the full
   statistical tables are 28MB+ raw, not embeddable under the 16MB
   Artifact limit, so the browser demo has somewhat LOWER noun/verb
   coverage than the real Python pipeline -- stated as a known gap,
   not hidden.
6. `kitaita_translate.js` -- a 1:1 JS port of `decompose_sentence()` +
   `translate()`'s full branching logic (kuwa future/past/copula,
   baya/kubwa adjective rules, present-tense vowel shifts, narrative
   ka, the weak-root contamination flag), since Artifacts are
   client-side JS sandboxes that cannot run Python.
7. **Verified the port, not just written it**: `compare_js_python_
   translate.py` runs the same 14-sentence batch through the real
   Python pipeline and through the JS port (via `node`), diffing the
   output sentence for each. First pass: 11/14 matched, 3 mismatched
   (`kimbi`/`mwon`/`ogop` -- all below the JSON export's root-Dice
   cutoff, i.e. a data-trimming artifact, not a logic bug, confirmed
   by checking their real scores directly: 0.22/0.22/0.25). Lowered
   the cutoff from 0.3 to 0.15 and re-ran: **14/14 exact match.** This
   is the actual regression check for a deliberately-duplicated
   implementation (hard rule #10's spirit extended to a cross-
   language port): not "I translated the code," but "I checked it
   against the thing it's supposed to match."
8. Published the **Kitaita Workbench** Artifact (https://claude.ai/
   artifact/21wvpDBL5sRNusGHPoyibP) -- live Swahili-in/Kitaita-out
   page running the verified JS port directly (not a mockup), with: a
   live stats strip computed from the embedded tables (not hardcoded,
   can't go stale); full per-word evidence trail (reusing `translate(
   )`'s own trace mechanism, the same transparency device the Python
   pipeline has always used); flagged/weak output chips; a scope note
   stating exactly what is and isn't covered and why (the coverage
   gap from step 5, the object-marker limitation from step 3, and
   that the probe track is deliberately not wired in); and an
   OPTIONAL English-input path that asks Claude directly for a
   Swahili gloss via the `sample` capability -- explicitly labeled
   "not NLLB" everywhere it appears (project rule: never let a
   convenience feature be mistaken for a validated result), since the
   real NLLB leg can only run locally (`kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py
   --with-nllb`), not inside a browser Artifact.

**Net effect on "how far we've come / how far is left":** the
grammar-book half of the pipeline (Swahili decomposition -> Kitaita
concord rewrite) is now connected end-to-end and live-testable by
anyone with the link, with its real coverage and real gaps visible
on the page itself rather than asserted. The NLLB half is real and
working but CPU-local-only. The probe/relation-identification track
remains a separate, un-integrated research line -- explicitly, not
by oversight.

## 2026-10-09 (cont. 2): "Shouldn't the probes still work with longer
context?" / "Before we started work on Kitaita we did test this no?
...let's try longer sentences as well" -- recalled a real, directly
relevant precedent, then tried longer sentences on today's decomposer
and found two genuine, newly-introduced correctness bugs (not coverage
gaps) from the SAME failure category as that precedent.

**The precedent, confirmed by re-reading, not from memory alone**: the
parent project's probe-based concord-rewrite work (nllb_concord_
rewrite_pipeline.py and predecessors) DID test exactly this question on
"Samak Sundaravej, waziri mkuu wa 25 wa Thailand, amefariki leo."
(2026-10-05 cont. 19-21, 2026-10-06 cont. 3). Net finding, worth
restating precisely: the probes did not visibly fail on this longer,
appositive-bearing sentence -- they produced CONFIDENT, plausible-
looking identifications that were quietly WRONG. "waziri" fired as
nsubj of "amefariki" (-> wrongly rewriting to "kimefariki") in every
run for several rounds, read as a validated bonus result, until
someone checked the real gold parse and found the TRUE subject is
"Samak" (a name), with "waziri mkuu wa 25 wa Thailand" merely an
appositive title. A second long sentence tested the same day
("Wanaharakati...kushinikiza viongozi...ambao...walizindua Tume ya
Honduras ya Kudai Amani") produced a second, independent false
positive at clause-distance for the identical reason: relative-
comparison scoring has no way to express "none of these candidates is
actually right," so the real subject three clauses up simply dominated
an unrelated embedded infinitive by being the most subject-like noun
in the whole sentence. **Length/complexity didn't make the mechanism
visibly break; it made it confidently wrong in a way only caught by
checking against ground truth.**

**Applied the same test to TODAY's Kitaita decomposer** (`kitaita_e2e_
pipeline.py`/`kitaita_translate.js` -- not probes, the rule-based
decomposer built this session) on 6 longer/complex sentences never
tried before: an appositive analogue of the Samak case, a coordination
case, a relative clause, a negation, a 2-clause sentence with 2 nouns
each carrying an adjective, and a double-adjective case. Relative
clause and negation failed CLEANLY (correctly refused, matching the
parent project's own long-standing, separately-documented acl:relcl
and negation gaps). But two cases reproduced the EXACT same failure
category as the Samak precedent -- confident, plausible, SILENTLY
wrong output, not a clean refusal:

1. **"Mbwa na chui walikimbia."** (the dog and the leopard ran --
   coordinated subject, no object at all) produced "Koshi idekimbia
   inge." ("the dog ran [at/to] the leopard") -- the coordinated
   second noun was silently slotted into the OBJECT position
   (decompose_sentence's noun-hit-2-is-always-object rule had no
   concept of word order relative to the verb). The only flag printed
   was "unparsed: na", which does not warn about this at all.

2. **"Mwalimu mzuri alisoma kitabu kikubwa kisha akalala."** produced
   "Mwalimu udeshoma chuo mbaa." -- "kikubwa" (which concords with
   "kitabu", the OBJECT) was silently misattributed to "mwalimu" (the
   SUBJECT), because the adjective scan matched any leftover kubwa/
   baya-shaped token anywhere in the sentence with no adjacency check
   at all.

**Fixed both, verified, and republished (this is a correctness fix,
not a new feature -- same discipline as every other retraction in this
file)**:
- Object assignment now requires the second noun to appear AFTER the
  verb (true postverbal position). A second noun appearing before the
  verb is flagged explicitly as a likely coordinated subject and left
  unused, never silently treated as an object.
- Adjective attachment now requires direct adjacency to the noun it's
  being attached to. An adjective-shaped token directly following the
  SUBJECT attaches as before; one directly following the OBJECT is now
  flagged ("concords with the object, but this generator has no
  object-adjective mechanism") and left unused, never guessed onto the
  subject.
- Ported identically to kitaita_translate.js (same comments, same
  logic). Re-ran `compare_js_python_translate.py` on the original
  14-sentence batch PLUS these 2 new cases: **16/16 exact match** --
  no regressions, both fixes confirmed identical in both
  implementations before republishing.
- Republished the Kitaita Workbench Artifact (version 2, same URL)
  with the fix and added "Mbwa na chui walikimbia." / the mwalimu/
  kitabu sentence to the page's quick-try examples, so the fix (and
  the honest flag it now produces) is visible on the page itself.

**Why this matters beyond these two bugs**: this is now a second,
independent confirmation (parent-project probes, then this session's
own rule-based decomposer) that the exact same category of risk --
silent, confident misassignment on longer/more complex sentences,
invisible unless someone actually reads the output rather than
trusting that "no error means correct" -- shows up in BOTH a learned/
statistical mechanism and a deterministic rule-based one. The fix here
was straightforward because the rules are hand-written and inspectable
(word-order/adjacency checks); the parent project's probes needed a
human to check the gold parse by hand to catch the analogous bug,
which is a slower, less scalable detection path. Neither kind of
mechanism gets longer-sentence correctness "for free" from being
theoretically length-agnostic -- both needed a deliberate check on
real longer/complex examples before trusting them, exactly the
caution this project's hard rules already insist on.

## 2026-10-09 (cont. 3): user caught 2 more bugs by hand ("chui mkubwa
aliona mbwa" / "samaki mbaya alikuwa") -- one real fix (object+adjective
decomposer gap), one retracted fix (adjective word order -- checked the
LIVE judgment database before trusting my own hypothesis and it was
WRONG), one non-bug (my own test sentence's wording, not the generator)

User reported two outputs that looked wrong: (1) "chui mkubwa aliona
mbwa" -> "Inge idemmbona koshi mbaa." reads back as "chui alimwona mbwa
mkubwa" (leopard saw BIG DOG, adjective seemingly on the object); (2)
"samaki mbaya alikuwa" -> "Samaki edeka izamie." reads back as "samaki
alikuwa mbaya" (fish was bad).

**Case 2 is NOT a generator bug -- it's a mismatch in MY OWN test
sentence's word order, caught by checking `build_swahili_sentence()`
directly.** That function has ALWAYS built every Swahili prompt in this
project as noun+verb+[object]+"-adjective" (adjective LAST, trailing,
never attributive-before-the-verb) -- confirmed by running it directly:
the spec behind the verified answer "Samaki edeka izamie." (s48) has the
canonical prompt "Samaki alikuwa -baya.", not "Samaki mbaya alikuwa."
(my own invented wording, attributive-before-verb order). "Samaki edeka
izamie." IS the correct, native-speaker-verified Kitaita for the
predicate-adjective reading ("the fish was bad") -- my test sentence's
word order just doesn't match what the project's own data was built on,
the same category of mistake flagged in memory before ("the hand-written
test spec had guessed... instead of checking").

**Case 1 produced a real fix, then a real retraction, in sequence --
worth recording both steps, not just the end state.** First checked
directly: of this project's 24 adjective-bearing specs, 23 use root
'kuw' (the verified predicate-adjective/copula construction) and
exactly ONE ("mwalimu"/"fik"/"kubwa", no object) is non-copula --
and NONE has ever combined an object with a subject adjective. So the
combination the user hit is genuinely untested. First attempted fix:
moved the adjective to immediately after the subject for non-copula
cases (standard Bantu attributive adjacency), reasoning the trailing
position was just an artifact of the code's string-building order.
**Retracted after checking the LIVE Judge Artifact database for that
one non-copula spec (s86), not just the static tables**: s86's real
native-speaker correction is "mwalimu ukavika mbaa" -- Subject Verb
Adjective, the SAME trailing order as the copula case, NOT Subject
Adjective Verb. The "fix" would have been a regression against real
judged data. Reverted `kitaita_sentence_generator.py` to its original
behavior (adjective always trails at the end) -- confirmed correct,
not just restored for safety.

**What's actually new and real**: s86's trailing order is unambiguous
there because there's no object to compete with. Once BOTH an object
and a subject adjective are present (the user's actual sentence), the
trailing position sits right after the OBJECT, and whether a reader
(without inside knowledge of the generation process) would read it as
the subject's or the object's adjective is a genuine, UNVERIFIED
question -- no native speaker has ever judged this combination either
way. Added an explicit flag for exactly this case in `kitaita_e2e_
pipeline.py`/`kitaita_translate.js` (fires whenever `d.object` and
`d.adjective` are both set) rather than asserting either reading.

**Also fixed a real decomposer completeness gap, found while checking
this**: the decomposer could not even recognize s86's own verified
shape ("Mwalimu akafika kubwa." -- adjective trailing right after the
verb, no object) -- it only ever checked for an adjective immediately
after the SUBJECT or immediately after the OBJECT, never immediately
after the VERB when there's no object at all, so a bare trailing
adjective was silently dropped as "unparsed". Added that third
position (tried only after the subject-adjacent check fails, so
attributive "chui mkubwa aliona" is still recognized too). Verified:
`'Mwalimu akafika kubwa.'` now produces `'Mwalimu ukavika mbaa.'`,
an EXACT match to s86's real native-speaker correction.

**Verification before publishing, same discipline as every other
round**: ported both changes to `kitaita_translate.js` identically,
re-ran `compare_js_python_translate.py` on the full batch (19 sentences
now, the original 14 + the 2 coordination/adjective-adjacency fixes
from cont. 2 + 3 new ones from this entry) -- **19/19 exact match**.
Republished the Kitaita Workbench (version 3, same URL) with "Mwalimu
akafika kubwa." and "Chui mkubwa aliona mbwa." added to the quick-try
examples, so the honest flag on the latter is visible on the page.

**Net takeaway**: direct verification against the LIVE judgment
database -- not just "this looks like better linguistics" -- caught a
plausible-looking fix before it shipped as a regression. This is the
second time this exact caution has mattered today (see cont. 2's
discussion of the Samak/waziri nsubj false positive sitting unnoticed
for several rounds) -- a hypothesis that sounds right is not a
substitute for checking the actual recorded judgment.

## 2026-10-09 (cont. 4): direct, sharp user correction -- "I think we
are trying to do too much on top of what we had initially planned...
substitution should be algorithmic... no step required a word order
change." This correctly identified that cont. 3's entire framing
("where does Kitaita put adjectives") was itself a methodological
drift from the project's own founding principle (CLAUDE.md, memory:
marker-only substitution, NEVER rearrangement) -- traced to root
cause and fixed architecturally, not patched again.

**Root cause, found by re-examining cont. 3 with this framing in
mind**: `kitaita_sentence_batch.py`'s `build_swahili_sentence()` has
ALWAYS displayed its hand-built test prompts as noun+verb+[object]+
"-adjective" (adjective trailing LAST), purely as a DISPLAY/AUTHORING
convention so a test-writer could isolate one spec variable at a
time -- confirmed by running it directly. s86's real judged
correction ("mwalimu ukavika mbaa") is simply a faithful, structure-
preserving translation of THAT artificially-ordered prompt ("Mwalimu
akafika -kubwa."), not evidence that Kitaita grammar requires
trailing adjectives in general. Cont. 3 mistook a test-authoring
convention for a linguistic fact, then spent an entire round trying
to verify/reconcile something that was never a real question -- the
exact "doing too much on top" the user flagged.

**The actual, much simpler fix**: `kitaita_sentence_generator.
translate()` is UNCHANGED (still correct for its real use case: hand-
built specs with no real input order to preserve, and VERIFIED_
SENTENCES passthrough, which stays authoritative and untouched).
Added `kitaita_verb_word` to its returned `components` dict (one
field, no logic change) so a caller that DOES have a real input
sentence can use the computed PIECES directly instead of translate()'s
own fixed-order assembled string. New function `assemble_in_order()`
in `kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py` (ported identically to `kitaita_
translate.js` as `assembleInOrder()`): takes the decomposer's own
recorded token positions (subject_idx/verb_idx/object_idx/
adjective_idx) and places each substituted Kitaita word AT THAT SAME
POSITION in the output -- sorted by original index, nothing else.
Skips reordering entirely when an EXACT VERIFIED_SENTENCES match
fired (that string is a real, whole, already-correct answer with no
"pieces" to reposition).

**Net effect, stated plainly**: "Chui mkubwa aliona mbwa." now
produces "Inge mbaa idewona koshi." (adjective immediately after the
subject, exactly where "mkubwa" sat after "chui" in the input) --
pure positional substitution, no linguistic claim made or needed.
"Mwalimu akafika kubwa." still produces "Mwalimu ukavika mbaa."
(matches s86 exactly, because in THAT input the adjective trails, and
preserving order reproduces it) -- same algorithm, no special-casing
by verb root, no "which construction is this" branching. Both
examples now fall out of ONE uniform rule instead of two competing,
partially-contradictory hypotheses. Removed the now-obsolete "object+
adjective combination is ambiguous/unverified" flag from cont. 3 --
once assembly preserves input order, there is no ambiguity to flag;
an adjective directly after the OBJECT still correctly flags as
"concords with the object, no object-adjective mechanism exists" (a
real, separate, missing-mechanism gap, unrelated to word order).

**Verified before publishing, same discipline as every round**:
`compare_js_python_translate.py` extended to 21 sentences (the 19 from
cont. 2-3 plus 2 new natural-order cases) -- **21/21 exact match**.
Republished the Kitaita Workbench (version 4, same URL).

**Methodology note, worth keeping visible**: this is now logged
explicitly in both `kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py`'s module docstring and
`kitaita_sentence_generator.py`'s own comment at the relevant site, so
a future session doesn't re-derive "maybe Kitaita needs trailing
adjectives" from the same test-authoring-convention artifact again.

## 2026-10-09 (cont. 5): "why aren't we able to translate sentences
with multiple nouns" -> direct, sharp follow-up correction -- "we
should be able to coordinate sentences... I really don't understand
this limitation we are imposing on ourselves... in case you miss a
word use the swahili word... would show us the true limits of the
capability." Worked through the user's own hand-derived example
("kitabu -> chuo, cha -> cha, mwalimu -> mwalimu, kilikuwa -> chedeka,
kikubwa -> kibaa") and confirmed every piece really does resolve from
existing tables (checked directly: "Chuo chedeka kibaa." is already a
real VERIFIED_SENTENCES entry for kitabu/kuw/li/kubwa) -- the refusal
was an unnecessarily strict PIPELINE POLICY ("cap at one subject + one
object, drop everything else with a flag"), not a real data gap.

**Rearchitected `kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py`'s decompose_sentence()/
assemble_in_order() (ported identically to `kitaita_translate.js`) to
never drop a token and never refuse a whole sentence for one missing
piece:**
- Only the PRIMARY subject (first noun before the verb) and PRIMARY
  object (first noun after the verb) still feed `translate()`'s
  agreement computation -- that genuinely needs exactly one noun per
  role. Every OTHER noun (a possessor, a coordinated subject/object)
  is now substituted INDEPENDENTLY via a plain lookup (`lookup_noun_
  kitaita`, new function) and kept at its OWN original position --
  Kitaita word if known, else the original Swahili word, NEVER
  dropped. A noun directly following a known associative particle
  (cha/wa/ya/la/za/vya) is recognized as a possessive construction;
  one sitting before the verb is flagged as a likely coordinated
  subject (closest-conjunct agreement used for the verb -- stated
  plainly as ONE of three candidate answers this project's own
  research already found and never resolved with a speaker, per
  CLAUDE.md -- not a new guess invented here).
- Every token that previously triggered "unparsed, dropped" (unknown
  particles, a second verb-shaped token/clause, an adjective adjacent
  to the object with no concord mechanism) now becomes an explicit
  PASSTHROUGH: the original Swahili word, kept at its own position,
  individually flagged.
- `translate_sentence()`/`assemble_in_order()` now ALWAYS attempt a
  best-effort output, even when no verb or no subject was found at
  all, or when `translate()` itself errors (e.g. no Kitaita candidate
  for the verb root) -- every noun still gets substituted
  independently and everything else stays Swahili, rather than
  returning nothing.
- `assemble_in_order()`'s EXACT-VERIFIED-SENTENCE case now SPLITS the
  verified string into [subject-word, rest-of-string] instead of
  returning it as one untouchable block, so OTHER material (the
  possessive phrase "cha mwalimu") can still be correctly interleaved
  around a real, verified subject+verb+adjective answer without
  touching its own internal order at all.

**Found and fixed a real, separate JS-port data gap while verifying**:
`export_e2e_js_tables.py` never exported `root_kitaita_fallback` (the
weaker per-surface-form root-matching path `translate()` uses when
root-level alignment finds nothing) -- "Mwalimu alimpa mwanafunzi
kitabu." (root 'mp', no root-level candidate) succeeded in Python via
this fallback but ERRORED in the JS port, which had no fallback table
at all to try. Exported it (`rootsFallbackMin`, Dice>=0.3, 1108
entries) and wired it into `kitaita_translate.js`'s existing
(previously dead -- `rootIsFullForm` was declared but never set to
`true` anywhere) fallback branch.

**Verified before publishing**: ran the user's own worked example
directly -- `translate_sentence('Kitabu cha mwalimu kilikuwa
kikubwa.', ...)` -> **`'Chuo cha mwalimu chedeka kibaa.'`**, an EXACT
match to the user's own hand-derived prediction. Confirmed zero
regressions on every prior sentence (sentences with no extra material
are byte-identical; sentences that previously silently dropped an
unknown word, e.g. "Mwalimu mzuri alisoma kitabu.", now correctly keep
"mzuri" visible as Swahili instead of vanishing -- an intentional
behavior change, not a bug). `compare_js_python_translate.py` extended
to 24 sentences (8 new: the possessive example, 2 coordination
variants, an indirect-object example) -- **24/24 exact match** after
the fallback-table fix. Republished the Kitaita Workbench (version 5,
same URL) with updated scope copy and 2 new quick-try examples.

**Net effect**: the pipeline now produces a best-effort, word-by-word
substitution for ANY input sentence, with the output itself showing
exactly what is and isn't covered (Kitaita where known, Swahili where
not) rather than an opaque refusal. The only remaining things that
stay out of scope (a second clause/verb, negation, non-subject-noun
adjective concord) are still handled the same way -- kept as Swahili,
flagged, never guessed -- consistent with the project's standing
"flag, don't guess" rule, just no longer conflated with "refuse the
whole sentence."

## 2026-10-09 (cont. 6): "This approach does not make use of the one
key tool we have. NLLB... We already have probes to do that for us"
-> wired the trained NLLB relation probes into the free-text pipeline
as the identification layer, replacing the adjacency heuristic for
subject/object/adjective-target identification. Also: "remove the
medium-high confidence [filter]... let's see the full limit and
identify the actual bugs" -- found 2 real bugs by doing exactly that.

**Confidence-filter removal (direct, bounded fix) found two real
bugs, not just noise**:
1. `_noun_lookup`'s 'high'/'medium'-only restriction on statistical
   noun candidates was removed. Immediately surfaced: "kubwa" (an
   ADJECTIVE) matched a low-confidence statistical NOUN candidate
   mapping it to "ibaa" -- which is literally kubwa's own Kitaita
   ADJECTIVE concord form, mistaken for a noun translation because
   the statistical table is built from raw co-occurrence with no
   concept of part-of-speech. Fixed with a narrow, correct guard
   (exclude the small, closed ADJ_ROOTS set from noun candidacy --
   not a reintroduced confidence threshold, since it's based on
   certain knowledge of the word's real part of speech, not a
   precision/recall tradeoff).
2. "Askari alimwona mwizi." (soldier saw thief): "askari" isn't
   recognized at ANY confidence, but "mwizi" (thief, the real OBJECT)
   is -- the old code took noun_hits[0] (whichever noun was found
   FIRST, regardless of position) as the subject regardless, inverting
   the sentence's real meaning. Fixed: the primary subject must come
   from a noun hit BEFORE the verb specifically; with none, every noun
   found is substituted independently rather than forced into the
   subject role. Ported to kitaita_translate.js, re-verified (24/24).

**NLLB probe integration (the larger piece)**: checked directly before
building anything (hard rule: verify, don't assume) -- NOTHING is
cached anywhere in this codebase; every prior run of `nllb_concord_
rewrite_pipeline.py`'s `train_all_probes()` re-encodes the full
SWH_UDT + AfriSUD corpora through NLLB from scratch. Also checked
directly: relation_probe.py's CORE_RELATIONS already includes "obj"
as one of the 21 labels the SAME multiclass model trains for nsubj --
this project's own earlier "obj was never built" note referred to the
KITAITA-SIDE object-marker rewrite mechanism (irrelevant here, since
Kitaita object substitution is marker-free), not to the probe's
ability to classify an obj relation at all.

New `train_and_save_identification_probes.py`: runs `train_all_probes()`
ONCE and saves every probe's state_dict (+ the nsubj/obj label vocab)
to `saved_identification_probes/` via `torch.save` -- took 375s (~6
min), far under the ~20-30 min estimate. New `nllb_probe_identification.
py`: loads the saved probes and NLLB, and reuses `get_hidden_and_spans`/
`wins_as_nsubj`'s own cross-candidate win-condition DIRECTLY (confirmed
it already generalizes to free text -- it only ever needs a lightweight
Sentence/Token wrapper with `.idx`/`.form`, not a gold-parsed one) to
score every candidate noun as nsubj and obj for the sentence's verb,
and every candidate adjective against every candidate noun for amod.

New `decompose_sentence_with_probes()`/`translate_sentence_with_probes()`
in kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py: SAME candidate detection (lexicon/decompose_
verb()/ADJ_ROOTS -- no separate POS probe was built, a deliberate
scoping choice stated in the module docstring, not an oversight) and
SAME substitution/reassembly (translate(), assemble_in_order()) as the
heuristic path -- only identification differs. New `compute_adjective_
concord()`/`resolve_class_marker()`: generalize translate()'s 'baya'/
'kubwa' concord rules (previously hardcoded to the SUBJECT's own
marker) to work for ANY target noun, needed because the amod probe can
now correctly say an adjective modifies the OBJECT, not just the
subject -- something the adjacency heuristic could never represent.

**Verified, not just built**: ran the probe pipeline against all 16
sentences tested anywhere this session -- **16/16 identical output**
to the heuristic path, confirming no regression. AND a genuinely NEW,
correct capability the heuristic structurally could not produce:
"Mwalimu alisoma kitabu kikubwa." -> "Mwalimu udeshoma chuo mbaa." --
the amod probe correctly identifies "kikubwa" as modifying "kitabu"
(the OBJECT), and `compute_adjective_concord` correctly computes its
chi-class form ("mbaa"), where the old heuristic could only flag this
case as unresolved and pass "kikubwa" through as Swahili.

**What's still out of scope, stated plainly**: the associative/case
probe (for "cha"/"wa" possessive constructions) and the acl:relcl probe
were both trained and saved but NOT yet wired into identification --
"cha mwalimu"-style possessives still go through the existing
particle-adjacency handling, unchanged. The browser Artifact (Kitaita
Workbench) still uses the JS heuristic exclusively and always will for
this reason -- Artifacts cannot run Python/NLLB/trained-probe inference
at all; this is a hard platform constraint, not a remaining task.

Files: `train_and_save_identification_probes.py` (new), `nllb_probe_
identification.py` (new), `saved_identification_probes/*.pt` (new,
trained weights), `kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py` (extended, hard rule #10).

## 2026-10-09 (cont. 7): "but mdogo is mtini I don't see the issue
there?" -> real retraction, then "Do #2, build the POS probe properly"
-> a genuine, validated, trained POS probe (not a lookup list) now
gates noun/adjective candidate detection.

**First, a retraction, not a fix.** Testing "Mbwa mkubwa aliona Kijana
mdogo akitembea." (dog saw young-person small walking) surfaced
"mdogo" -> "mtini" via the statistical table and I called it a bug by
pattern-matching to the earlier "kubwa"/"ibaa" case, WITHOUT checking
the actual evidence the way that earlier case required. User correctly
pushed back. Checked directly: the real corpus attestations (GEN.19.38,
GEN.29.26) show "mtini" used as a SUBSTANTIVE adjective ("the younger
one"), taking real class-1 noun agreement, in contexts that genuinely
match "mdogo"'s meaning -- a real, independently-attested correspondence
(standard Bantu adjective-used-as-noun), not a co-occurrence artifact.
Unlike "kubwa"/"ibaa" (where "ibaa" collided with an ALREADY-ESTABLISHED,
independently-sourced adjective-concord form elsewhere in this
project's own verified tables), nothing else claims "mtini" for
anything else. Retracted the "bug" framing for this specific word-level
claim -- mdogo->mtini stands as correct.

**The REAL issue, precisely located by the user's own follow-up
question** ("or do you mean the probe identified mdogo as a noun
instead of an adjective?"): in THIS sentence, "mdogo" functions
attributively (modifying "Kijana", same role as "mkubwa" modifying
"Mbwa"), but it was never even OFFERED to the amod probe as an
adjective candidate -- candidate detection ran noun-lookup FIRST and
matched "mdogo" there (via its real but here wrong-ROLE substantive
usage) before adjective detection, which was itself hardcoded to the
closed ADJ_ROOTS={"kubwa","baya"} set, ever got a chance to consider
it. Not a probe failure -- a pre-probe candidate-detection gap.

**Built the fix (#2, the real one, not the cheap list-broadening
patch)**: new `pos_probe.py` -- a genuine per-token NLLB-representation
part-of-speech classifier (NOUN/PROPN/VERB/ADJ/PRON/OTHER), same
architecture spirit as relation_probe.py's RelationProbe (pure linear,
no learned nonlinearity) but over a SINGLE pooled vector, not a head/
dependent pair, since POS tagging is per-token not relational. Trained
on the SAME SWH_UDT+AfriSUD corpora (real UD UPOS annotations, checked
directly) via new `train_and_save_pos_probe.py`, with a full Hewitt &
Liang control task + 80/20 held-out split, per this project's standing
rule that every probe needs one. Took 378s (~6.3 min).

**Results, real evidence not just a claim**: REAL accuracy 0.906,
CONTROL accuracy 0.695, SELECTIVITY +0.211 (n=6645 test tokens) -- a
real, above-control signal. Per-class, with 95% CI (n>=8 for every
one reported, per hard rule #5): NOUN 1602/1732=0.925 [0.912,0.936],
VERB 818/895=0.914 [0.894,0.931], ADJ 410/518=0.792 [0.754,0.824] --
weaker than NOUN/VERB but genuinely, substantially above both chance
and the control baseline.

**Wired into `kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py`'s `decompose_sentence_with_
probes()`**: new `nllb_probe_identification.tag_pos()` tags every
token BEFORE noun/adjective candidacy is decided. A token tagged ADJ
is excluded from noun candidacy outright, even if it has a (different-
usage) noun-table entry, and becomes an adjective candidate regardless
of whether it's in ADJ_ROOTS -- known-root stripping (so "mkubwa"
still correctly resolves to stem "kubwa") happens BEFORE the POS-tag
fallback, so this does not regress any existing kubwa/baya sentence
(a real bug caught and fixed in my own first draft of this change,
before testing). Falls back to lookup-only detection with an explicit
flag if the POS probe isn't trained yet or NLLB alignment fails for a
given sentence -- never silently guesses.

**Verified**: "Mbwa mkubwa aliona Kijana mdogo akitembea." now produces
"Koshi mbaa idewona mdawana mdogo akitembea." -- "mdogo" correctly
excluded from noun candidacy, identified as an adjective, and honestly
flagged ("no concord mechanism for that target") instead of being
confidently mistranslated as "mtini". Re-ran the full 16-sentence
regression battery from cont. 6: **16/16 still identical** -- zero
regressions from adding the POS probe.

Files: `pos_probe.py` (new), `train_and_save_pos_probe.py` (new),

## 2026-10-09 (cont. 8): "also remove the one verb restriction. we
don't need it. we can handle multiple verbs" -> removed it, for the
probe-based pipeline specifically (the heuristic path keeps the
restriction -- see below for why that's a real, not arbitrary,
distinction).

**Architecture**: `nllb_probe_identification.identify_relations()`
now takes a LIST of verb positions instead of one chosen "primary"
verb, encoding the sentence ONCE and running the nsubj/obj probe for
EVERY verb against the SAME candidate-noun pool -- a noun can
legitimately win as the shared, pro-dropped subject of more than one
verb (e.g. "Mwalimu alisoma kitabu kisha akalala", mwalimu is subject
of both "alisoma" and "akalala"), which is correct, not a conflict.
`Decomposition` gained a `clauses: list[dict]` field, one per verb
found, each independently carrying its own subject/object/adjective
(subject/verb/object/adjective singular fields kept as the FIRST
clause's values, for backward compatibility with the heuristic path's
single-clause expectations). `translate_sentence_with_probes()` now
calls `translate()` ONCE PER CLAUSE -- translate() itself needed no
change at all, it was always a per-clause function, just never called
more than once per sentence before. New `assemble_multi_clause()`
generalizes the position-preserving assembly: every clause's pieces
go in at their own original token position, deduplicated so a shared
subject token is placed exactly once even though multiple clauses
"claim" it.

**Deliberately NOT extended to decompose_sentence()/translate_
sentence() (the adjacency heuristic, used when NLLB isn't available --
the browser Artifact, which structurally cannot run NLLB at all)**:
identifying a SECOND verb's own subject by adjacency alone would be
exactly the unreliable guessing this whole probe-based track exists
to replace -- there is no "next noun over" heuristic that generalizes
safely across clause boundaries the way the probe's cross-candidate
comparison does. Stated as a real, principled scope boundary in the
module docstring, not an oversight.

**Verified, two real multi-clause sentences, not synthetic toys**:
"Mbwa mkubwa aliona Kijana mdogo akitembea." -- "akitembea" (while
walking, a participial clause) is now fully analyzed: mbwa correctly
re-identified as ITS subject too (shared, pro-dropped), root 'tembe'
found (weak statistical match, honestly flagged UNRELIABLE). This
also surfaced a genuine, PRE-EXISTING gap, newly visible only because
a second verb finally reached translate() at all: Swahili's `-ki-`
(conditional/participial) TAM has NO Kitaita mapping rule in this
project's tables -- translate()'s own existing "?" placeholder
mechanism (kit_tam defaults to literal "?" when unresolved) fired
correctly, producing "i?sela" -- an honest gap surfacing, not a new
bug introduced by this change.
"Mwalimu alisoma kitabu kisha akalala." -- both verbs translated
("udeshoma"/"ukalala"), "mwalimu" correctly placed ONCE despite being
identified as nsubj for both clauses, "kisha" (then) correctly kept
as Swahili (no table for it). Re-ran the full 17-sentence regression
battery -- **17/17 still exact match**, zero regressions from this
change.

**Still open, stated plainly**: Swahili's `-ki-` TAM mapping is a real,
newly-surfaced gap, not addressed here. The probe's per-verb object
identification is somewhat noisy when a verb has no real object at all
(e.g. "akalala"/slept got "kitabu" identified as its object too, which
is probably spurious) -- currently harmless only because the position-
dedup guard in assemble_multi_clause() prevents any double-substitution,
but worth a dedicated check later with more multi-clause examples.

Files: `nllb_probe_identification.py` (extended: `identify_relations`
multi-verb), `kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py` (extended: `Decomposition.
clauses`, multi-clause `decompose_sentence_with_probes`/`translate_
sentence_with_probes`/`assemble_multi_clause`, hard rule #10).

## 2026-10-09 (cont. 9): two failed attempts to fix the "-ki-" subject
gap (more negatives on the multiclass probe; a dedicated binary edge-
presence probe), then a user-proposed diagnostic (NLLB's own round-
trip self-correction) that worked, got systematically validated, failed
to distill into a fast probe, and was wired in LIVE instead.

**Attempt 1 (more training examples on the existing nsubj/obj probe)**:
added negative sampling (relation_probe.build_relation_examples_with_
negatives) to the multiclass probe. Direct re-test: motivating case
STILL wrong (mbwa still beat kijana, same margin), AND it broke 2
previously-correct simple sentences ("Samaki mbaya alikuwa.", "Kiti
kitakuwa.") that have zero competing candidates at all -- reverted,
confirmed 17/17 restored.

**Attempt 2 (dedicated binary edge-presence probe)**: new edge_presence_
probe.py, trained on SWH_UDT+AfriSUD with real negative sampling (max 8
per positive, the SAME discipline the amod/poss/acl probes already
use). Held-out selectivity +0.430 and a targeted multi-verb
discrimination check at 624/733=0.851 [CI 0.824,0.875] -- genuinely
validated improvements in general. Direct re-test: STILL wrong on the
motivating case (mbwa=2.04 > kijana=0.73). Saved but never wired in.

**Root cause, found by direct corpus check, not assumed**: of 226
"-ki-"-marked VERB tokens across SWH_UDT+AfriSUD, only 5 (2.2%) have
their own nsubj/csubj dependent in the gold tree at all -- the other
221 attach as comp/mod/conj/parataxis/advcl, standard control-
structure behavior (the participle's subject is shared/controlled by
the matrix clause, never given its own dependency edge in UD/SUD).
With 5 real positive examples in the ENTIRE combined corpus, no amount
of retraining on THIS kind of label could ever work -- confirmed, not
guessed.

**User-proposed diagnostic: does NLLB's own SW->SW regeneration
"correct" a deliberately wrong subject marker on a "-ki-" verb?**
Tested directly: "Mbwa mkubwa aliona kijana mdogo ikitembea/
wakitembea." (2 wrong variants) both regenerated to the IDENTICAL,
correct "...akitembea." -- and a cleaner test (mvulana/kalamu,
different Swahili classes, no shared-marker confound) showed NLLB
spontaneously changing "ALIYOVUNJIKA" (wrong) to "ILIYOVUNJIKA"
(correct) on SW->SW regeneration. 14/14 confirmed across a 2-sentence
hand check plus a 12-sentence systematic battery (validate_roundtrip_
and_attention.py) using a cleaner, continuous, automatable signal:
NLLB's teacher-forced SELF-TRANSLATION LOSS (lower loss = more self-
consistent) rather than free-generation + string matching, which
turned out to be unreliable for scripting at scale (NLLB paraphrases
too freely for naive substring checks -- manual re-reading showed the
REAL rate was 11/12 + 1 ambiguous, not the 5/12 a naive automated
check first reported).

**Also checked, and explicitly NOT trusted**: a per-head cross-
attention scan (not blind-averaged, matching how the amod heads were
validated historically) found 10 heads at a suspicious 12/12=1.000.
Flagged directly as likely a position confound (every test sentence
had the object closer to the generation point than the subject) --
never validated with a reordered control set, never used.

**Attempt 3: distill the self-loss signal into a fast trained probe.**
Mined 185 "-ki-"-verb candidates from the 31,102-verse Swahili Bible
corpus (NOT limited to the tiny treebanks, since silver labels come
from NLLB's own self-loss, not gold annotation) via mine_ki_
candidates.py, silver-labeled 138 of them (margin>=0.05) via self-loss,
trained a probe on them. Held-out selectivity only +0.054 (far below
every gold-trained probe this session), and BOTH direct re-tests
failed -- including a regression on the mvulana/kalamu case the raw
signal got right. Diagnosis: self-loss is a full decoder/generation
computation, likely not linearly present in a single pooled mid-layer
encoder embedding at all -- no amount of architecture tweaking at this
scale fixes that. Saved but never wired in; this distillation attempt
is a dead end as attempted, not a tuning problem.

**Wired in LIVE instead** (nllb_probe_identification.
resolve_ki_subject_via_self_loss(), called from kitaita_e2e_pipeline.
decompose_sentence_with_probes() specifically when a clause's verb has
tam_marker=="ki"): for each candidate noun with a DISTINCT Swahili
class marker, builds a variant with that marker on the verb, scores
self-loss directly at inference time (no training), picks the lowest-
loss candidate as subject, overriding the (confirmed-unreliable-here)
trained probe's own guess. Explicitly flagged in the trace as a
DIFFERENT evidence tier (NLLB's own generative self-consistency
preference, not independently verified grammar) every time it fires.

**Verified on the two real test sentences, with an honest, important
asymmetric result**:
- "Mvulana aliona kalamu ikivunjika." -- correctly overrides "kalamu"
  as ikivunjika's subject (was wrongly "mvulana" per the trained
  probe). A real fix.
- "Mbwa mkubwa aliona Kijana mdogo akitembea." -- still "mbwa", NOT a
  failure of the new mechanism: checked directly and found "kijana"'s
  Swahili class is WRONGLY computed as "7/8" (ki-/vi-, by surface
  shape) in the statistical table, when "kijana" is actually one of
  Swahili's known animate ki-shaped EXCEPTIONS and takes class 1/2
  ("a-") agreement -- a real, separate, still-open bug. But even fixing
  that would not change this specific sentence's outcome: mbwa (already
  correctly ANIMATE-SG, "a-") and kijana (correctly reclassified, also
  "a-") would then share the EXACT SAME marker, and marker-swapping
  (the only mechanism self-loss or any trained probe here can exploit)
  has literally nothing to compare when two candidates share one
  marker. This is exactly the "leakage" the user flagged when first
  proposing the cleaner mvulana/kalamu test -- confirmed now as a
  structural, not incidental, limit of this whole approach family.

**Real bug found and fixed while wiring this in**: overriding a
clause's subject discarded the OLD subject index from used_noun_idxs
unconditionally, even when an EARLIER, already-finalized clause still
depended on that same shared noun -- caught directly on "Mvulana
aliona kalamu ikivunjika." (clause 0's own subject, "mvulana", got
wrongly bumped into secondary_nouns when clause 1's subject was
overridden away from it). Fixed: only discard if no already-built
clause still references that index.

Re-ran the full 17-sentence regression battery after both the wiring
and the bugfix: **17/17**, zero regressions.

**Net state, stated plainly**: a real, live, working fix for "-ki-"
subject identification exists now, for cases where the candidates have
genuinely different Swahili classes. For cases where they share a
marker (mbwa/kijana-style), NO mechanism tried this session -- trained,
distilled, or live self-loss -- can resolve it, because there is no
morphological signal to exploit in the first place; that specific case
remains open and may need a non-morphological signal (semantic
plausibility / selectional restrictions) entirely, not a better probe.
Also still open: kijana's (and presumably other ki-shaped animate
nouns') Swahili class misclassification in the statistical table.

## 2026-10-09 (cont. 10): confirmed webapp was serving stale code (restarted);
found + fixed a real sentence-boundary bug in the probe pipeline; user
then called a halt on incremental patching and redirected to the real
bottleneck -- an efficient general relation probe

**Webapp**: user asked directly "so on the locally hosted page what are
we running?" -- checked the running process (PID 129205, started before
today's self-loss fix existed) via `ps`/`curl` and confirmed it was
serving STALE code (Python doesn't hot-reload). Restarted (new PID
153794); confirmed via curl that the mvulana/kalamu override flag now
fires correctly through the webapp, not just in direct script tests.

**New bug found+fixed**: user reported "Mbwa anakunywa maji. mtoto
analia. We do not identify the correct subject for lia either." Tested
each sentence ALONE first (hard rule: check before guessing) -- both
were already correct in isolation ('mtoto' correctly won subject of
'analia'). Tested the two sentences together, exactly as the user typed
them, and reproduced the failure: 'mbwa'/'maji' (sentence 1's subject/
object) were ALSO assigned as subject/object of 'analia' (sentence 2's
verb), while 'mtoto' -- the only real candidate in its own sentence --
was never even offered to that verb and was dropped untranslated.

Root cause: `decompose_sentence_with_probes` has no sentence-boundary
concept at all. `tokenize()` (extract_swahili_grammar.py) strips '.'/
'!'/'?' outright, so a multi-sentence input becomes one flat token
list and `identify_relations` pools every noun/verb across ALL
sentences into one candidate set. This is NOT a subject-identification
weakness (the trained probe and the "-ki-" self-loss override were
both working correctly) -- it's a missing preprocessing step, and
exactly the risk the project's own open-decisions note already flagged
("probe distances exist only within a sentence... cross-sentence is a
coreference problem, out of scope").

Fix (extends the existing pipeline, hard rule #10 -- no new parallel
path): added `split_sentences()` to `kitaita_e2e_pipeline.py`, splits
on `.`/`!`/`?` before any decomposition. `translate_sentence_with_probes`
now splits multi-sentence input first, runs the existing per-sentence
logic on each sentence completely independently, then joins the
Kitaita outputs in order. Added a top-level `report["flags"]` key (a
reference to `d.flags`, so later appends still show up) so the
multi-sentence case -- where `report["decomposition"]` is now a LIST,
one per sentence, not one object -- still has a single place to read
flags from; updated the one other caller (`kitaita_local_webapp.py`)
to read `flags` from there instead of reaching into
`.decomposition.flags` directly, with a fallback to the old path for
the heuristic (non-probe) mode which doesn't set `report["flags"]`.

Verified directly, no regressions: single-sentence cases (the mvulana/
kalamu "-ki-" case, the mbwa/kijana leakage-limit case, a plain two-
noun sentence) all produce identical output to before; the two-sentence
case now correctly produces 'Mtoto analia.' as its own clause with
'mtoto' as subject, separate from sentence 1's 'mbwa'/'maji'.

**Pivot**: user: "I think we have lost the thread. I identify the
following as the most critical step. We need an efficient probe for
determining relations between words." Reading of "lost the thread":
this session has been reactively patching individual reported sentences
(mdogo, kijana, mbwa/maji/mtoto, the "-ki-" case) one at a time, while
the actual recurring blocker underneath all of them is the SAME
component -- relation identification (nsubj/obj, and by extension
amod/case/poss/acl) -- which has a real, validated signal for the
ordinary case (cont. 11 baseline: selectivity +0.69 accuracy/+0.64
macro-F1 on SWH_UDT, n=175 sentences, per-class F1 nsubj 0.790/obj
0.754/amod 0.606/det 0.809) but a known, three-times-unfixed gap for

persisted regression battery (none existed before -- every prior "16/16"/

Read CLAUDE.md (both copies), this file from 2026-10-05 cont. 11 through
cont. 26 and all of 2026-10-09, and the carried-over memory before writing
any code, per the handoff prompt's own instructions.

**(1) Efficiency fix for the LIVE self-loss mechanism (the one thing that
actually works for "-ki-" subjects) -- verified safe, not just faster.**
`nllb_probe_identification.resolve_ki_subject_via_self_loss` used to run
one full tokenizer+model forward pass PER CANDIDATE, sequentially. New
`_batched_self_loss()` batches every candidate variant for a given verb
into ONE padded forward pass instead, computing each row's own loss by
hand from the logits (excluding padded positions via -100) rather than
relying on the model's own aggregate `.loss` (which would pool all rows
into one mean and hide which candidate is better). Checked directly
BEFORE replacing the sequential loop: losses from the batched and
sequential paths match to <1e-4 on real variant sentences (mvulana/kalamu-
style), confirming this is a pure engineering change, not a new empirical
claim. Measured speedup: 1.75x at n=2 candidates (the typical case), 1.94x
at n=4, 2.44x at n=6 -- benefits grow with candidate count since fixed
per-call overhead is amortized across the batch. This is the concrete
"efficient" answer for the ONE mechanism that currently resolves this
gap correctly; see (3) below for why it still hasn't been replaced by a
fast static probe.

**(2) New: `probe_pipeline_regression.py` -- a persisted regression
battery for the probe-based pipeline.** Checked first: no such script

The handoff prompt's own open-question list named this as untried:
